At 4 years the child "skips and hops proficiently on one foot and catches a ball reliably." At 5 years the child "skips on alternate feet, jumps rope, and begins to skate and swim." Motor development in this period "consists of increases in strength and refinement of previously learned skills."
q_0211.trap: (B) moves the 5-year skill back a year, and it pulls because the word "skips" appears in both descriptions. The discriminator is one foot at 4 years versus alternate feet at 5.

q_0212.topic: preschooler growth and gross motor refinement
q_0212.stem: Parents of a 5-year-old ask about enrolling the child in a formalized, competitive training program for a sport. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Muscle development and bone growth are still far from mature and overexertion can injure delicate tissues; the most important aspect of organized play at this age is that the activity be developmentally appropriate and occur in a nonthreatening, fun, and safe environment, with readiness determined individually
Formalized training should begin as early as possible to maximize athletic potential
Organized sports should be avoided entirely until school age, since preschoolers cannot follow rules
Physical activity should be limited to quiet indoor play, because preschoolers are prone to falls
q_0212.rationale: "Muscle development and bone growth are still far from mature. Excessive activity and overexertion can injure delicate tissues." Whether young children should begin formalized training "is controversial," and "readiness must be determined individually." "The most important aspect of organized play for preschoolers is that the activity is developmentally appropriate and occurs in a nonthreatening, fun, and safe environment." Children at this age "benefit from free play and exposure to a variety of physical activities."
q_0212.trap: (D) inverts the injury picture for this age: "Because of improved gross and fine motor skills, coordination, and balance, preschoolers are less prone to falls than toddlers," and motor activity levels "continue to be high" and are therefore encouraged.

q_0213.topic: preschooler growth and gross motor refinement
q_0213.stem: A 5-year-old's examination reveals that a permanent tooth is erupting, the child writes consistently with the right hand, and the child cannot yet manage the small print in a workbook. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: All are expected at 5 years; eruption of permanent dentition may begin, handedness is established with about 90% right-handed, and the child is not ready for concentrated close work because of slight farsightedness and still-unrefined eye-hand coordination
Permanent dentition should not begin until 7 years, so dental referral is needed
Difficulty with small print indicates a visual defect requiring correction
Established handedness at 5 years is premature and should not be reinforced
q_0213.rationale: Table 13.1 gives for age 5 years: "eruption of permanent dentition may begin"; "handedness is established (about 90% are right-handed)"; and the child is "not ready for concentrated close work or small print because of slight farsightedness and still unrefined eye-hand coordination."
q_0213.trap: (C) reads a normal developmental limitation as pathology, and it is the reading that sends children for unnecessary vision workups. The farsightedness named here is the expected state at this age, not a defect.

q_0214.topic: preschooler drawing and fine motor progression
q_0214.stem: A 3-year-old is handed a crayon and shown a model. Which performance is expected?
options: Copies a circle and imitates a cross and vertical and horizontal lines, but cannot draw a complete stick figure
Copies a square and traces a cross and diamond
Copies a diamond and triangle and adds seven to nine parts to a stick figure
Can only scribble, and cannot name what has been drawn
q_0214.rationale: At 3 years the child "copies a circle and imitates a cross and vertical and horizontal lines," holds the writing instrument "with the fingers rather than the fist," scribbles but "can name what has been drawn," and cannot draw a complete stick figure. At 4 to 5 years the child "can trace a cross and copy a square"; the triangle and diamond are "usually the last geometric figures to be mastered," at 5 to 6 years.
q_0214.trap: (B) is the 4-year-old's performance and (C) the 5-year-old's. The distractors swap the verb rather than the shape, and the verb is the whole discriminator: copying works from a finished model, imitating follows a demonstration, and tracing follows an outline — with the same shape moving through all three across two years.

q_0215.topic: preschooler drawing and fine motor progression
q_0215.stem: A 4-year-old draws a stick figure with a head, a body, and legs — three parts in all. How should the nurse document this?
options: Expected; adding three parts to a stick figure is the 4-year milestone, and seven to nine parts belongs to 5 years
Delayed; seven to nine parts is expected at 4 years
Advanced; a 4-year-old cannot draw a stick figure at all
Concerning; the absence of facial features indicates a perceptual problem
q_0215.rationale: Table 13.1 gives "adds three parts to stick figure" at 4 years and "adds seven to nine parts to stick figure" at 5 years. At 3 years the child "cannot draw stick figure but may make circle with facial features."
q_0215.trap: (B) applies the 5-year count to a 4-year-old. These are the only two stick-figure numbers in the chapter, which is exactly why they get swapped more often than any other pair in it.

q_0216.topic: preschooler drawing and fine motor progression
q_0216.stem: A nurse uses a child's drawings during assessment. Which statements reflect the chapter's guidance on children's art?
options: Children progress through placement, shape, design, and pictorial stages; two united diagrams make a combine and three or more an aggregate; and because drawings before age 6 are strikingly similar universally while later drawings are shaped by culture and environment, nurses need to consider children's backgrounds when interpreting drawings
Drawings are a precise and validated measure of intelligence and personality
The pictorial stage, in which designs are recognizable as familiar objects, appears at 3 years
A combine is three or more united diagrams and an aggregate is two
q_0216.rationale: Children "advance through four distinguishable stages": placement at 15 months, shape at 3 years, design immediately after, and pictorial at 4 to 5 years, "in which their designs are recognizable as familiar objects." "When two diagrams are united, the resulting design is called a combine"; "Three or more united diagrams produce an aggregate." Drawings before age 6 years "are strikingly similar universally," after which "cultural and environmental influences... shape much of what children draw," so nurses "need to consider children's backgrounds when interpreting drawings."
q_0216.trap: (B) overstates evidence the chapter deliberately qualifies: drawing is used to assess intelligence, personality development, and psychosocial adjustment, but "the precise value of using drawing to measure such concepts is still a nebulous science." (D) reverses combine and aggregate.

q_0217.topic: initiative versus guilt in the preschooler
q_0217.stem: A 4-year-old energetically tries to pour milk for the whole family, spills it across the table, and then becomes tearful and says "I'm bad." Which psychosocial conflict does this illustrate?
options: Autonomy versus shame and doubt
Initiative versus guilt
Industry versus inferiority
Trust versus mistrust
q_0217.rationale: "The chief psychosocial task of this period is acquiring a sense of initiative." Children this age "play, work, and live to the fullest and feel a real sense of accomplishment and satisfaction in their activities," and the conflict "arises when children overstep the limits of their ability and inquiry and experience guilt for not having behaved appropriately."
q_0217.trap: (A) is the toddler's conflict, and it pulls because shame and guilt feel like one emotion. The discriminator sits in the stem: a child who attempted something beyond their ability and then feels bad about it is showing guilt, which is the preschooler's half of the pair.

q_0218.topic: initiative versus guilt in the preschooler
q_0218.stem: A 5-year-old whose father died suddenly tells the nurse, "I got mad at Daddy last week and wished he would go away. Then he died." What is the essential nursing response?
options: Clarify for the child that wishes cannot make events occur
Reassure the child that everyone has angry thoughts, without addressing the wish itself
Tell the child the thought was wrong and should not be repeated
Redirect the conversation, since discussing the death will increase the child's distress
q_0218.rationale: "A particularly stressful thought is wishing one's parent dead." The contest normally resolves when the child "strongly identifies with the same-sex parent and peers during the school years," but if that parent dies before identification is complete, "the preschooler can be overwhelmed with guilt for having wished and therefore 'caused' the death." The chapter states the intervention directly: "Clarifying for children that wishes cannot make events occur is essential in helping them overcome their guilt and anxiety."
q_0218.trap: (B) offers general reassurance and leaves the child's actual belief — that the wish caused the death — completely untouched, which is what magical thinking requires the nurse to name explicitly. (C) confirms the guilt rather than relieving it.

q_0219.topic: initiative versus guilt in the preschooler
q_0219.stem: A parent asks why verbal warnings now work with their 4-year-old when they did nothing for their 2-year-old. Which explanation does the chapter give?
options: Verbal enforcement of limits is much more effective in this age group than with toddlers; the preschooler still needs close supervision but is much more aware of danger and can listen and obey in most instances
Preschoolers understand why a behavior is unacceptable, so explanation alone is now sufficient
Preschoolers have completed superego development and no longer need parental limits
The change reflects the end of negativism rather than any change in comprehension
q_0219.rationale: "Verbal enforcement of limits is much more effective in this age-group than with toddlers." The preschooler "still needs close supervision but is much more aware of danger and can listen and obey in most instances." Development of the superego, or conscience, "starts toward the end of the toddler years and is a major task for preschoolers."
q_0219.trap: (B) overstates comprehension. Children this age "are generally unable to understand why something is acceptable or unacceptable" and are "aware of appropriate behavior primarily through punishment or reward," relying "almost completely on parental principles for developing their own moral judgment."

q_0220.topic: initiative versus guilt in the preschooler
q_0220.stem: A 4-year-old boy announces that he is going to marry his mother and has been unusually hostile toward his father. His parents are alarmed. Which response is accurate?
options: This reflects the oedipal stage, and the conflict normally resolves through identification with the same-sex parent; Table 13.1 records that the 4-year-old identifies strongly with the opposite-sex parent while the 5-year-old identifies strongly with the same-sex parent
This indicates a disturbance in gender identification and warrants referral
This is expected at 2 years and is delayed at 4
Girls show the same pattern but fear castration rather than experiencing penis envy
q_0220.rationale: Freud "described this goal in psychosexual terms and labeled the period the oedipal, or phallic, stage," in which the boy "wishes that his father were dead so he could marry his mother (Oedipus complex)." The resolution is "identification with the same-sex parent." Table 13.1 records that the 4-year-old "identifies strongly with parent of opposite sex" while the 5-year-old "strongly identifies with parent of same sex, especially boys with their fathers."
q_0220.trap: (D) reverses the girls' side of the pair. Girls "do not fear castration; rather they experience penis envy"; it is the boy whose guilt about his feelings toward his father "makes him fear the same punishment of mutilation, resulting in the castration complex."

q_0221.stem: A 3-year-old and a 4-year-old are both described as preoperational. Which statement places each more precisely?
options: The 3-year-old is in the preconceptual phase, ages 2 to 4 years, and the 4-year-old is in the phase of intuitive thought, ages 4 to 7 years
The 3-year-old is in the phase of intuitive thought and the 4-year-old in the preconceptual phase
The 3-year-old is sensorimotor and the 4-year-old preoperational
The 4-year-old has entered concrete operational thought
q_0221.rationale: The preoperational phase "covers the age span from 2 to 7 years and is divided into two stages: the preconceptual phase, ages 2 to 4 years, and the phase of intuitive thought, ages 4 to 7 years." Table 13.1 tags the 3-year-old as "in preconceptual phase" and the 4-year-old as "in phase of intuitive thought." The main transition across the two is "the shift from totally egocentric thought to social awareness and the ability to consider other viewpoints."
q_0221.trap: (D) jumps a whole period; concrete operational thought belongs to the school-age child. Note that calling a 3-year-old preoperational would not be wrong — the sub-stage is the finer discriminator, and it is what the table supplies.

q_0222.stem: A 4-year-old whose newborn brother died of sudden infant death syndrome tells the nurse he had wished the baby would "go back." Which characteristic of preoperational thought does this illustrate?
options: Magical thinking — because of egocentrism and transductive reasoning, preschoolers believe that thoughts are all powerful
Animism — ascribing lifelike qualities to inanimate objects
Inability to conserve — judging everything according to one dimension
Egocentric speech — assuming everyone thinks as they do
q_0222.rationale: "Because of their egocentrism and transductive reasoning, they believe that thoughts are all powerful," which leaves preschoolers "feeling guilty and responsible for bad thoughts that may coincide with the occurrence of a wished event." The chapter's own example is a child who wishes a new sibling dead: if the sibling dies, "young children think their wish caused the death."
q_0222.trap: (B) is the adjacent characteristic and the one this pair is most often swapped with. Both arise from egocentrism, and the object of the stem tells you which: a thought or a wish points to magical thinking, a thing points to animism.

q_0223.stem: A 4-year-old refuses to use the toilet after watching a television commercial in which the toilet bowl turns into a monster. Which characteristic does this illustrate?
options: Magical thinking — the belief that thoughts are all powerful
Animism — ascribing lifelike qualities to inanimate objects
Transductive reasoning — reasoning from one particular to another
Literal belief in the power of words
q_0223.rationale: Animism, "ascribing lifelike qualities to inanimate objects," is what "helps explain why children fear objects." The chapter gives this exact example: a child "may refuse to use the toilet after watching a television commercial in which the toilet bowl is portrayed as turning into a monster."
q_0223.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. Nothing here turns on the child's own thoughts causing an event; the fear is of the object itself, which is what makes it animism.

q_0224.stem: A hospitalized 4-year-old repeatedly asks when her mother is coming. Which response is most appropriate?
options: "Your mother will visit you after you finish your lunch."
"Your mother will be here at two o'clock."
"Your mother will be here tomorrow afternoon."
"Your mother will come back in about three hours."
q_0224.rationale: Preschoolers interpret time "according to their own frame of reference" — "A long time means until Christmas." The chapter directs explaining time by event and gives this sentence verbatim as its example, advising against "yesterday," "tomorrow," "next week," or "Tuesday." Associating time "with usual expected daily occurrences" helps children learn temporal relationships "while increasing their trust in others' predictions."
q_0224.trap: (B) and (D) both use clock time, which a preschooler cannot convert into waiting. (C) uses a calendar word the chapter names specifically as one to avoid; it sounds concrete to an adult and carries no meaning for the child.

q_0225.stem: A 5-year-old overhears a nurse describe another child as "a bad patient." Later the 5-year-old says she must be a bad girl too. Which principle applies, and what is the correct practice?
options: Preschoolers believe in the power of words and accept their meaning literally, so the act should be labeled rather than the child, as in "That was a bad thing to do"
Preschoolers understand figurative language by 5 years, so the comment carries no risk
The child should be told she misunderstood, and the matter dropped
Preschoolers cannot generalize a comment made about another child to themselves
q_0225.rationale: "Preschoolers believe in the power of words and accept their meaning literally" — calling a child "bad" means, in the child's mind, that they are bad. The chapter's nursing translation is to label the act rather than the child: "That was a bad thing to do."
q_0225.trap: (D) underestimates precisely what this age does most. A child in the preconceptual stage is "able to imagine an event without actually experiencing it," which is why "Seeing someone hurt is sufficient for realizing what the hurt must be like," and why a preschooler watching another child get an injection "may become upset, almost as if he or she received the injection."

q_0226.topic: preschooler body image, fears, and the fear of annihilation
q_0226.stem: A 4-year-old who has just received an intramuscular injection becomes distressed and insists on a bandage, though there is no further bleeding. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Apply the bandage, because preschoolers have poorly defined body boundaries and fear that all their blood and insides can leak out if the skin is broken
Explain that the bleeding has stopped, so a bandage is unnecessary
Apply the bandage, but explain that it is only for decoration
Distract the child, since the request reflects attention seeking
q_0226.rationale: Preschoolers "have poorly defined body boundaries and little knowledge of their internal anatomy. Intrusive experiences are frightening, especially those that disrupt the integrity of the skin (e.g., injections and surgery). They fear that all their blood and 'insides' can leak out if the skin is 'broken.' Therefore preschoolers may believe it is critical to use bandages after an injury."
q_0226.trap: (B) is the factually correct and developmentally useless answer, and it is the one an adult reaches for. The child's concern is not bleeding but body integrity, and no explanation of hemostasis touches it.

q_0227.topic: preschooler body image, fears, and the fear of annihilation
q_0227.stem: A 4-year-old screams and clings to the side of the bathtub when the drain is opened. Which explanation is correct, and what is a useful intervention?
options: Fear of annihilation, arising from poorly defined body boundaries and the inability to understand concepts of size, so the child cannot grasp that the body is too large to disappear down the drain; letting the child bathe a doll allows the child to observe that large objects cannot go down the drain
Ordinary stranger fear, which resolves without intervention
A sensory processing difficulty requiring referral
Deliberate bath-time resistance that should be ignored
q_0227.rationale: Fear of annihilation is "peculiar to this age." Because of "poorly defined body boundaries and improved cognitive abilities," children develop "concerns related to loss of body parts, such as their body going down the drain," and because they "cannot understand concepts of size, they cannot understand that their body is too large to disappear down the drain." The chapter's own remedy is "letting the child bathe a doll so that the child can observe that large objects cannot go down the drain," which reconstructs the experience "without involving the child directly as the victim."
q_0227.trap: (B) names a fear the preschooler has largely outgrown — preschoolers "have overcome much of their anxiety associated with strangers and the fear of separation of earlier years." This age brings the greatest number and variety of fears, but they are different fears.

q_0228.topic: preschooler body image, fears, and the fear of annihilation
q_0228.stem: A 5-year-old is terrified of dogs. Which approaches does the chapter support? Select all that apply.
options: Gradually introducing the child to the experience by watching other children play with a dog
Actively involving the child in finding practical methods to deal with the frightening experience
Having others demonstrate fearlessness, allowing the child to progress at their own rate
Placing the child's hand on a calm dog, so the child learns there is nothing to fear
Keeping a dim night-light in the bedroom, for the child's separate fear of the dark
q_0228.rationale: "The best way to help children overcome their fears is by actively involving them in finding practical methods to deal with frightening experiences." Desensitization means "Exposing children to the feared object in a safe situation"; children afraid of dogs "should never be forced to approach or touch one, but they may be gradually introduced to the experience by watching other children play with the animal." Modeling — "having others demonstrate fearlessness" — "can be effective if children are allowed to progress at their own rate." A dim night-light is the chapter's own example for fear of the dark.
q_0228.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it is forced exposure rather than desensitization. It pulls because the contact looks like the logical endpoint of a graded approach; the chapter says such children "should never be forced to approach or touch one."

q_0229.topic: preschooler body image, fears, and the fear of annihilation
q_0229.stem: Parents of a 4-year-old are exasperated by the child's many fears and ask whether something is wrong. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: The greatest number and variety of real and imagined fears are present during the preschool years and usually by 5 or 6 years children relinquish many of them; parents should also know that when they demonstrate their own fears, those concerns are communicated to the child and tend to be long-lasting and difficult to dispel
Fears at this age indicate an anxiety disorder and warrant referral now
Fears peak in the school-age years, so this is early and unusual
Parents' own fears have no bearing on a preschooler's fears
q_0229.rationale: "The greatest number and variety of real and imagined fears are present during the preschool years," typically of "the dark, being left alone (especially at bedtime), animals (particularly large dogs and snakes), ghosts, sexual matters (castration), and objects or persons associated with pain." "Usually by 5 or 6 years of age, children relinquish many of their fears." And: "When parents demonstrate their fears, these concerns are communicated to the children. Such fears tend to be long-lasting and difficult to dispel."
q_0229.trap: (B) medicalizes a normative peak. Professional help is indicated only "when children experience severe fears that disrupt family life," which this stem does not describe.

q_0230.topic: preschooler language, play, and imaginary companions
q_0230.stem: A 4-year-old speaks in four- and five-word sentences, asks constant questions, and has a vocabulary a parent estimates at about 1500 words. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Expected; vocabulary is 1500 words or more at 4 years, sentences run four or five words, and questioning is at its peak
Delayed; a 4-year-old should have about 2100 words
Advanced; 1500 words is the 5-year figure
Concerning; constant questioning at this age indicates anxiety
q_0230.rationale: Table 13.1 gives vocabulary as about 900 words at 3 years, "1500 words or more" at 4 years, and about 2100 words at 5 years; the narrative gives the span as "from 300 words at age 2 years to more than 2100 words at the end of age 5 years." Sentences run three or four words at 3 years, four or five at 4 years, and six to eight at 5 years. At 4 years "questioning is at peak," and children "usually repeat the question until they receive an answer."
q_0230.trap: (B) applies the 5-year count to a 4-year-old, which is the commonest swap in a chapter whose vocabulary figures are its most swappable numbers. (D) pathologizes the single most characteristic behavior of the age.

q_0231.topic: preschooler language, play, and imaginary companions
q_0231.stem: Four preschoolers in a playroom are all building with blocks in the same area, talking to one another and borrowing pieces, but with no assigned roles, rules, or shared goal. Which type of play is this?
options: Parallel play
Associative play — group play in similar or identical activities but without rigid organization or rules
Cooperative play, with assigned roles and a shared goal
Solitary play
q_0231.rationale: The preschooler's play is associative, defined as "group play in similar or identical activities but without rigid organization or rules." Table 13.1 still describes the 3-year-old's play as "parallel and associative"; by 4 and 5 years it is simply associative. Play "should provide for physical, social, and mental development."
q_0231.trap: (C) is the next stage, and it pulls because the children are plainly interacting. The absence of rules, organization, and assigned roles is the cue; a stem describing organized, goal-directed team play has moved to the school-age child.

q_0232.topic: preschooler language, play, and imaginary companions
q_0232.stem: A preschool teacher plans a holiday art session for a class of 3-year-olds. Which planning rule does the chapter give?
options: One simple project per year of age — a 3-year-old usually has the patience to decorate three eggs but will become bored and restless with more
As many projects as the session allows, since preschoolers have high activity levels
One project per session, regardless of age
Projects should be avoided at 3 years, since fine motor skills are insufficient
q_0232.rationale: "A helpful rule in planning creative activities is one simple project per year of age. For example, a 3-year-old child usually has the patience to decorate three eggs but will become bored and restless with more."
q_0232.trap: (B) confuses activity level with attention span. Preschool motor activity is high, but this rule is about how many discrete projects a child can see through, which scales with age rather than with energy.

q_0233.topic: preschooler language, play, and imaginary companions
q_0233.stem: Parents of a 4-year-old with an imaginary companion ask for guidance. Which responses reflect the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: The child's fantasy is a sign of health that helps differentiate between make-believe and reality
Imaginary companions usually appear between ages 2½ and 3 years and last until the child enters school
Parents may acknowledge the companion by name and agree to simple requests, such as setting an extra place at the table
Parents should discourage the companion, since it delays the child's grasp of reality
If the child blames the companion for a mess, parents should state clearly that the child is the only person they see and is therefore responsible for cleaning up
q_0233.rationale: Parents "should be reassured that the child's fantasy is a sign of health that helps differentiate between make-believe and reality." Imaginary companions "usually appear between ages 2½ and 3 years and, for the most part, last until the child enters school." Parents may acknowledge the companion by name and "even agree to simple requests such as setting an extra place at the table," but "should not allow the child to use the playmate to avoid punishment or responsibility"; if the child blames the companion, "the parents need to clearly state that the child is the only person they see, and therefore the child is responsible for cleaning up."
q_0233.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort. The correct guidance has two halves — acknowledge the companion, and refuse to let it carry the blame — and the common wrong answers supply only one: either bare reassurance with no limit, or the instruction here to discourage the companion altogether.

q_0234.topic: school readiness and preparing the preschooler for school
q_0234.stem: Parents ask the nurse whether their 5-year-old is ready for kindergarten. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: There are no absolute indicators for school readiness; it is influenced by social, emotional, and physical development, health status, ability and desire to learn, life experiences, family environment, and parental support — and the child's social maturation, especially attention span, is as important as academic readiness
A specific readiness test score is the definitive indicator
Chronologic age alone determines readiness
Academic skills such as letter recognition are the priority indicator
q_0234.rationale: Readiness is influenced by "a child's social, emotional, and physical development; health status; ability and desire to learn; life experiences; family environment; and parental support. There are no absolute indicators for school readiness." The chapter's own priority statement is that "The child's social maturation, especially attention span, is as important as academic readiness."
q_0234.trap: (D) is the metric parents usually apply, and the chapter deliberately balances it against social maturation. (B) contradicts "there are no absolute indicators" outright, and it pulls because a test result feels like the objective answer a nurse ought to be able to give.

q_0235.topic: school readiness and preparing the preschooler for school
q_0235.stem: A school offers both readiness testing and developmental screening. How should the nurse explain the difference?
options: Readiness testing focuses on evaluation of skill acquisition, while developmental screening focuses on the potential to learn and identifies children who may benefit from further diagnostic testing
Readiness testing focuses on the potential to learn, while developmental screening evaluates skill acquisition
The two terms describe the same process
Developmental screening is diagnostic, and readiness testing is a screening tool
q_0235.rationale: Readiness testing "focuses on evaluation of skill acquisition"; developmental screening "focuses on the potential to learn," addresses "cognitive (especially language), social, and physical milestones," and identifies "children who may benefit from further diagnostic testing." Use "varies by state and local district," and "there is controversy over the most beneficial form of evaluation."
q_0235.trap: (B) is the straight inversion of the pair, and it is the only thing separating them. The cue words carry the whole distinction: skill belongs to readiness testing, potential belongs to developmental screening.

q_0236.topic: school readiness and preparing the preschooler for school
q_0236.stem: A parent asks how to handle their 4-year-old's first day of preschool. Which guidance reflects the chapter?
options: Present the idea as exciting and pleasurable beforehand; behave confidently on the day; introduce the child to the teacher and facility; and if remaining for part of the first day, be available to the child but inconspicuous
Leave without saying goodbye, to avoid triggering tears
Stay with the child throughout the entire first week, remaining actively involved in the activities
Begin with a full-day schedule, so the child adjusts to the routine immediately
q_0236.rationale: Before school, parents "should present the idea as exciting and pleasurable," talking about painting, blocks, swings, and outdoor equipment so children can "fantasize about the forthcoming event in a positive manner." On the first day "parents should behave confidently. Such behavior requires parents to have resolved their own feelings regarding the experience." Parents should introduce the child to the teacher and facility, and "If parents stay, they should be available to the child but inconspicuous."
q_0236.trap: (D) contradicts the chapter's own concession that a full-day routine "is often too overwhelming for a child and could be shortened to a morning or afternoon session if possible." (C) keeps the parent present but drops the word carrying the instruction — inconspicuous — and staying actively involved works against the separation the day exists to accomplish.

q_0237.topic: school readiness and preparing the preschooler for school
q_0237.stem: A slow-to-warm-up 4-year-old and a high-activity-level 4-year-old are both starting preschool. What does the chapter recommend for each?
options: The slow-to-warm-up child needs gradual introduction to new situations and may benefit from the parent's presence until settled; the high-activity-level child adjusts better to environments allowing freedom of movement rather than a structured or regimented classroom
Both children should be placed in the most highly structured classroom available
Temperament changes markedly during the preschool years, so early observations should not guide placement
The high-activity-level child needs gradual introduction, and the slow-to-warm-up child needs freedom of movement
q_0237.rationale: Temperamental characteristics "tend to remain stable," and the preschool-specific concern is "the effect of temperament on adjustment in group situations, especially school." "Slow-to-warm-up children need gradual introduction to new situations and may benefit from the parent's presence until they have settled in." "High-activity-level children tend to adjust better to environments that allow freedom of movement, rather than a structured or regimented classroom." The Behavioral Style Questionnaire "helps identify temperamental characteristics in children from 3 to 7 years old."
q_0237.trap: (D) swaps the two recommendations, which is easy to do because both amount to accommodating the child; the accommodations are opposite in kind. (C) contradicts the stability the chapter asserts, and that stability is why these observations are worth making at all.

q_0238.topic: preschooler sex education and sexual curiosity
q_0238.stem: A 4-year-old asks her mother, "Where did I come from?" What should the nurse advise the mother to do first?
options: Find out what the child already knows and thinks, before answering
Give a complete, anatomically correct explanation of conception and birth
Tell the child she is too young to know about that
Offer a simplified stork story, to avoid frightening the child
q_0238.rationale: The first rule is to find out what children know and think, so the answer corrects the child's own theory and avoids an "unasked for" answer. The chapter's illustration is 4-year-old Lauren, who after a full sex-education explanation said, "I don't know about all that! All I know is Mary came from New York, and I want to know where I came from." A child "who asks one question is looking for one answer."
q_0238.trap: (B) is the well-prepared parent's answer, and it is second in priority rather than first; given too much information, "the child will simply become bored or end the conversation with an irrelevant question." (C) and (D) are the two responses the chapter says teach children "to keep such questions to themselves," after which magical thinking supplies "any fantastic and often terrifying explanation."

q_0239.topic: preschooler sex education and sexual curiosity
q_0239.stem: A parent worries that honest answers about reproduction will harm a 4-year-old. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: In general, knowledge is not harmful when delivered in a developmentally appropriate manner; children process information at their own pace, correct anatomic words become important for explaining other concepts later, and what matters is that parents are approachable
Detailed information at this age causes lasting anxiety and should be deferred to school age
Children should be given as much information as possible at once, so the subject need not be revisited
Nurses should avoid genital terminology during physical examinations, to prevent embarrassment
q_0239.rationale: "In general, knowledge is not harmful when delivered in a developmentally appropriate manner." Children "will process information at their own pace. What matters is that parents are approachable and do not dismiss their child's inquiries." Correct anatomic words "become important for explaining other concepts later on," and the child "will forget or misunderstand much of the correct information, but the correct information can be restated until the child absorbs and comprehends the facts."
q_0239.trap: (D) closes an opening the chapter specifically assigns to nurses, who "have the opportunity to contribute to early sex education by conveying accurate information regarding genital terms during physical examinations." (C) ignores scope control — a child asking one question is looking for one answer.

q_0240.topic: preschooler sex education and sexual curiosity
q_0240.stem: Parents discover their 4-year-old and a playmate undressed and examining each other during "doctor play." Which parental response does the chapter recommend?
options: Neither condone nor condemn the behavior; tell the children that if they have questions they should ask the parents, then encourage them to engage in some other activity
Punish both children, so the behavior is not repeated
Allow the exploration to continue without restriction, since curiosity is normal
Explain the reproductive function of the genitalia in detail
q_0240.rationale: Parents should "neither condone nor condemn the behavior, but... tell the children that, if they have questions, they should ask the parents; the parents should then encourage the children to engage in some other activity." This "in no way condemns the act but stresses alternative methods by which to seek solutions and answers." The chapter also notes that these children are often "still unaware of the reproductive function of the genitalia" and are "curious about the eliminative function of the anatomy."
q_0240.trap: (C) is the permissive extreme, and the chapter rejects it with a reason: "Allowing children unrestricted permissiveness only intensifies their anxiety and concern because exploring and searching usually yield little evidence to satisfy their curiosity." (B) is the opposite extreme; the recommended response sits between them and carries a redirection.

q_0241.topic: preschooler sex education and sexual curiosity
q_0241.stem: A parent reports that their 4-year-old touches his genitals while watching television. Which nursing response is appropriate?
options: This occurs at any age for a variety of reasons and, if not excessive, is normal and healthy; management is parent education and reassurance, redirection to other activities, and teaching that it is a private act
This always indicates sexual abuse and requires immediate reporting
The child should be told the behavior is dirty, so that it is extinguished
The behavior requires no discussion of any kind with the child
q_0241.rationale: Masturbation, "self-stimulation of the genitalia," "occurs at any age for a variety of reasons and, if not excessive, is normal and healthy." For preschoolers "it is part of sexual curiosity and exploration." Management is "parent education and reassurance, redirection of the child to other activities, and discussion with the child regarding appropriate boundaries," and parents "should emphasize that masturbation is a private act, thus teaching children socially acceptable behavior."
q_0241.trap: (B) applies the exception to the rule: it is *excessive* masturbation that "may be associated with emotional or behavioral problems and physical or sexual abuse," and this stem carries no such qualifier. Where parents are concerned, the chapter directs assessing the circumstances, since the behavior "can be an expression of anxiety, boredom, or stress."

q_0242.stem: A 5-year-old is described by his parents as well behaved at home, but he is a persistent discipline problem at school and a bully among playmates. Which mechanism does the chapter identify?
options: Frustration — the continual thwarting of self-satisfaction by parental disapproval, humiliation, punishment, and insults, which children displace on peers and other authority figures, especially if they fear their parents
Modeling — imitating the behavior of significant others
Reinforcement — a reward that shapes the behavior
Normal preschool assertiveness, requiring no intervention
q_0242.rationale: Frustration is "the continual thwarting of self-satisfaction by parental disapproval, humiliation, punishment, and insults." Children "displace their anger on others, particularly peers and other authority figures, especially if they fear their parents" — and the chapter names this child specifically as the one "who is well behaved at home but a discipline problem at school or a bully among playmates."
q_0242.trap: (B) and (C) are the two neighbouring mechanisms and both are plausible on their face. The discriminator here is the split between settings: compliance at home with aggression everywhere else is displacement, which is frustration's signature.

q_0243.stem: Parents of an aggressive 4-year-old say they spank him after every incident and otherwise pay him little attention. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: If a child is spanked for an aggressive act, aggression is being used to teach a lesson against aggression; negative attention can itself be reinforcing, and time-out and solitary play are the effective disciplinary measures in the preschool years
Spanking is the most effective disciplinary measure for aggression at this age
Ignoring the aggression entirely is the recommended approach
Aggression at 4 years always requires professional treatment
q_0243.rationale: "If a child is spanked for an aggressive act, aggression is being used to 'teach' a lesson against aggression." A reward may be negative and still reinforcing "because it brings attention" — children ignored until they hit a sibling "learn that this act attracts attention." "The use of time-out and solitary play are effective disciplinary measures in the preschool years," and "minimizing anger and frustration can lead to fewer opportunities for acting out."
q_0243.trap: (C) is the other reinforcement error the chapter names: parents who permit aggression "by not interfering communicate silent, implicit approval." Neither punishing nor ignoring is the answer; naming an alternative measure is. The chapter warns separately that "inconsistency in disciplinary practices may also foster behavior problems in children."

q_0244.stem: A nurse evaluates whether a preschooler's aggressive behavior is problematic. According to the chapter, the difference between normal and problematic behavior lies in which features? Select all that apply.
options: Quantity, meaning the number of occurrences
Severity, meaning interference with social or cognitive functioning
Duration, with a threshold of at least 4 weeks
The specific behavior itself, independent of how often or how long it occurs
Onset, meaning when the behavior started
q_0244.rationale: "Generally, the difference between normal and problematic behavior is not the behavior itself but its" quantity, "number of occurrences"; severity, "interference with social or cognitive functioning"; distribution, "different manifestations"; onset, "when the behavior started"; and duration, "at least 4 weeks." "Extreme aggression requires professional treatment and is often difficult to change."
q_0244.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it states exactly what the chapter denies in the same sentence that introduces the list. It pulls because an act such as hitting sounds inherently pathologic, and the chapter's whole point is that the same act is normal or problematic depending on these five dimensions.

q_0245.stem: A 3-year-old has been repeating the initial sounds of words for the past few weeks. Which findings would warrant referral for speech evaluation? Select all that apply.
options: The stuttering persists for 3 to 6 months
There is a family history of stuttering
There is evidence of struggling or distress related to the stuttering
The child is 3 years old, which falls outside the normal range for developmental stuttering
The parents report that the child stutters more when excited
q_0245.rationale: Refer for speech evaluation if stuttering "persists for 3 to 6 months," if "there is a family history of stuttering," or if "there is evidence of struggling or distress related to stuttering." Developmental stuttering "is common during language development in children ages 2 to 5 years" and "usually resolves during childhood," affecting boys more frequently than girls. The most critical period for speech development is 2 to 4 years, when "children are using their rapidly growing vocabulary faster than they can produce the words."
q_0245.trap: (D) and (E) are the two options from the normal side of the sort. (D) misstates the age range — 3 years sits squarely inside the 2-to-5-year window — and (E) describes ordinary variation rather than a referral criterion. The parent instruction meanwhile is to "speak slowly and relaxed" and "take time to listen attentively," never to interrupt, complete the child's sentences, or place "undue emphasis on a child's stuttering," which "may exacerbate the problem."

q_0246.topic: preschooler nutrition, dental health, and injury prevention
q_0246.stem: A nurse teaches the 5-2-1-0 framework to the parents of a preschooler. Which statements correctly state the framework? Select all that apply.
options: 5 servings of fruits and vegetables per day
2 hours or less of screen time per day
1 hour of physical activity per day
0 or limited servings of sugar-sweetened beverages
5 hours of physical activity per week and 2 servings of fruits and vegetables per day
q_0246.rationale: The Nursing Alert gives the framework as "5 servings of fruits and vegetables per day, 2 hours or less of screen time per day, 1 hour of physical activity per day, and 0 (or limited) servings of sugar-sweetened beverages." Fruit juice for ages 1 to 6 years is separately limited to 4 to 6 oz/day, because excessive juice and other sugar-sweetened beverages are associated with "dental caries" and "adverse cardiometabolic effects."
q_0246.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it keeps both digits while swapping their units — which is exactly how this mnemonic fails in practice. Each digit attaches to a different quantity, and the order is fixed.

q_0247.topic: preschooler nutrition, dental health, and injury prevention
q_0247.stem: A parent is distressed that their 4-year-old "eats nothing." The child's growth is tracking normally. Which counseling reflects the chapter?
options: Quality is much more important than quantity, children self-regulate their caloric intake across meals, a preschooler eats approximately half of an adult's portion, and keeping a weekly record of everything the child eats with measured amounts gives a more accurate estimate
The child should be required to finish a full portion at each meal
The child should be offered only preferred foods until the appetite improves
A caloric supplement should be started, since 4-year-olds cannot self-regulate intake
q_0247.rationale: "In general, the quality is much more important than the quantity, which nurses should stress during nutritional counseling." "There is some evidence that children self-regulate their caloric intake. If they eat less at one meal, they compensate at another meal or snack." Preschoolers "eat only slightly more than toddlers, or approximately half of an adult's portion." The intervention is to advise "parents to keep a weekly record of everything the child eats," measuring the amount to "provide a more accurate estimate of food intake at each meal" — after which parents "are usually amazed at how much the child consumed."
q_0247.trap: (B) is the pressure that turns a normal phase into a contest. At 4 years children "seem to enter another period of finicky eating," and by 5 years they "are more agreeable to trying new foods, especially if encouraged by an adult who allows the child to help with food preparation."

q_0248.topic: preschooler nutrition, dental health, and injury prevention
q_0248.stem: A parent of a 4-year-old asks who should handle the child's oral care now that fine motor skills have improved. Which response is correct?
options: The child still requires assistance and supervision with brushing, and parents should perform flossing
The child can brush and floss independently at this age
Flossing is unnecessary until the permanent dentition erupts
Eruption of the deciduous teeth is still in progress and will not be complete until age 6
q_0248.rationale: "Although preschoolers' fine motor control is improved, they still require assistance and supervision with brushing, and parents should perform flossing." "By the beginning of the preschool period, the eruption of the deciduous (primary) teeth is complete," and permanent dentition may begin erupting at 5 years. Professional care and routine prophylaxis, especially fluoride supplements, should continue, with frequency individualized by risk assessment.
q_0248.trap: (D) inverts the dentition timeline: deciduous eruption is complete at the start of this period rather than at its end. Note also that if oral trauma occurs, "prompt evaluation by a dentist is necessary," because preserving the space of an avulsed tooth matters for eruption of the secondary tooth.

q_0249.topic: preschooler nutrition, dental health, and injury prevention
q_0249.stem: A nurse plans injury-prevention teaching for the parents of a 4-year-old. Which statement reflects the chapter?
options: Preschoolers are less prone to falls than toddlers and prevention can now include education about safety and hazards, but pedestrian motor vehicle injuries increase and poisoning is still a danger
Poisoning risk has passed, because putting objects in the mouth has ceased
Falls increase during the preschool years as children become more daring
Education is ineffective at this age, so every environmental safeguard must remain in place
q_0249.rationale: "Because of improved gross and fine motor skills, coordination, and balance, preschoolers are less prone to falls than toddlers." "Putting objects in the mouth as part of exploration has all but ceased, but poisoning is still a danger." "Pedestrian motor vehicle injuries increase because of activities such as playing in the street, riding tricycles, running after balls, or forgetting safety regulations when crossing streets." Prevention "can now include education regarding safety and potential hazards," and outlet caps "may be discontinued, with verbal explanations given of why danger exists and how to avoid it."
q_0249.trap: (B) draws the intuitive inference from the end of mouthing behavior, and the chapter blocks it in the same sentence. Note too that "Because preschoolers are great imitators, it is essential that parents set a good example by 'practicing what they preach,'" since children "quickly observe discrepancies between what they are told to do and what they observe."

q_0250.stem: A 5-year-old scores 132 on an intelligence test, and the parents ask whether that score settles the question of whether she is gifted. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Giftedness is commonly recognized as a minimum intelligence quotient of 130, but giftedness may be present in both academic and nonacademic areas, so not all gifted children are identified when intelligence or achievement tests alone are used
An intelligence quotient of 130 or above is the sole and sufficient criterion for giftedness
Giftedness is recognized at a minimum intelligence quotient of 100, which this score exceeds
Intelligence testing has no role in identifying giftedness
q_0250.rationale: "Although the definition of gifted varies, giftedness is commonly recognized as a minimum intelligence quotient (IQ) of 130." But "giftedness may be present in both academic and nonacademic areas. Therefore not all gifted children are identified when IQ tests or achievement tests alone are used," and identification "based solely on test scores may result in the tragic loss of the opportunity to develop a child's full potential." The broader gifted-talented view includes "specific academic aptitudes, advanced memory skills, creative thinking, ability in the visual or performing arts, and psychomotor ability, either individually or in combination."
q_0250.trap: (B) states the true half of the pair and then draws the conclusion the chapter warns against. Both halves are examinable and both are true at once: 130 is the recognized threshold, and a threshold used alone under-identifies. An item can test either half, so holding only one of them is how this gets missed.

q_0251.stem: A teacher says a 5-year-old with a diagnosed learning disability is "obviously not gifted, given the diagnosis." Which response is correct?
options: Giftedness can exist in children who have learning disabilities, a pattern termed twice-exceptional
A learning disability rules out giftedness by definition
The child should be retested once the learning disability has been remediated
Giftedness is identified only through academic aptitude, so the teacher is correct
q_0251.rationale: The chapter names this directly: "giftedness can exist in children who have learning disabilities," and such students are described as twice-exceptional.
q_0251.trap: (B) treats the two as mutually exclusive, which is the assumption that makes twice-exceptional children invisible, because each condition masks the other. (D) narrows identification to the one channel the chapter says is insufficient on its own; giftedness "may be present in both academic and nonacademic areas."

q_0252.stem: Parents of a gifted 5-year-old say they hesitate to set limits because the child is "smarter than we are," and they are frustrated that she reads fluently but cannot tie her shoes. Which counseling reflects the chapter?
options: Gifted children are children first and have the same needs for love, security, and consistent boundaries as other youngsters; advanced skill in one area may cause adults to exaggerate abilities in all areas, and slower achievement in a particular skill may be mislabeled as lack of trying when it represents the natural progression of abilities
Limits should be relaxed for gifted children, since their reasoning exceeds their parents'
Uneven skill development indicates that the giftedness assessment was in error
A gifted child should be expected to perform at an advanced level across all domains
q_0252.rationale: Parents "may be intimidated by having a child smarter than themselves," but "gifted children are children first and have the same needs for love, security, and consistent boundaries as other youngsters." Advanced skills in one area "may also cause adults to exaggerate their abilities in all areas and thus expect excessively mature behavior," and parents "may mislabel slower achievement in a particular skill as lack of trying, when really it represents children's natural progression of abilities."
q_0252.trap: (D) is the over-generalization the chapter names as its own distinct parenting challenge, and it is what produces the frustration described in this stem. (B) waives the boundaries at exactly the wrong moment: high energy level and persistence "can lead to discipline problems similar to those seen in children with difficult temperaments."

q_0253.stem: A nursing student asks the instructor for the textbook's definition of family. What is the accurate response?
options: A family is a married couple and their dependent children
There is no universal definition of family; a family is what an individual considers it to be
A family is any group sharing a household and pooling income
The Census Bureau's four categories are the accepted definition
q_0253.rationale: The chapter opens by refusing a single definition: "The term family has been defined in many different ways according to the individual's own frame of reference, values, or discipline. There is no universal definition of family; a family is what an individual considers it to be" (p. 15).
q_0253.trap: (D) is the reflex pick for a learner who has just memorized the four Census definitions. Those four are a classification the Census Bureau uses, not the chapter's definition of the term, and the chapter names numerous other family types outside them.

q_0254.stem: A child lives with his mother, his mother's unmarried partner, and a sibling who is the partner's biologic child. No other relatives live in the home. Which Census Bureau category does this household fit?
options: Traditional nuclear family
Nuclear family
Extended family
Blended family only, since the parents are unmarried
q_0254.rationale: The nuclear family is "composed of two parents and their children. The parent-child relationship may be biologic, step, adoptive, or foster. Sibling ties may be biologic, step, half, or adoptive. The parents are not necessarily married. No other relatives or nonrelatives are present in the household" (p. 18).
q_0254.trap: (A) is the pick that misses two requirements at once. The traditional nuclear family requires the couple to be married and all children to be biologic; the plain nuclear family requires neither. A distractor that makes marriage the only difference gets half the discrimination.

q_0255.stem: Two children in a household share the same mother but have different fathers. How are they related?
options: Stepsiblings, because one father is not the biologic parent of both
Half-siblings, because they share one biologic parent
Stepsiblings, because the household is blended
Full siblings, because they share a residence and a mother
q_0255.rationale: "Stepsiblings do not share a common biologic parent; the biologic parent of one child is the stepparent of the other. Half-siblings share only one biologic parent" (p. 18).
q_0255.trap: (A) and (C) are the mirror error of the pair. Stepsiblings share no biologic parent; half-siblings share one. That single count is the whole distinction, and either presence of a stepparent in the home tempts the wrong label.

q_0256.stem: A nurse admits a child whose grandmother brings him in, states that she has reared him since infancy, and answers all history questions while the child's young mother stands quietly beside her. What should the nurse recognize about this extended family?
options: The mother is the legal decision-maker and must be addressed directly for all teaching
The older relative may hold the authority and make decisions in consultation with the young parents, so identifying the actual decision-maker is part of the assessment
The grandmother's involvement suggests the mother is neglectful and warrants a referral
Extended family arrangements delay care and should be discouraged
q_0256.rationale: "Within the extended family, grandparents often find themselves rearing their grandchildren. Young parents are often considered too young or too inexperienced to make decisions independently. Often, the older relative holds the authority and makes decisions in consultation with the young parents" (p. 18). Sharing a residence also "assists with the management of scarce resources and provides child care for working families."
q_0256.trap: (C) reads a culturally patterned arrangement as a red flag. The chapter presents extended-family authority descriptively and connects it to its later instruction to ask families what the nurse should know about them rather than to apply assumptions.

q_0257.stem: A nurse notes that a father's job loss has changed the mother's work hours, the children's school arrangements, and the family's mealtimes. Which family systems theory assumption does this illustrate?
options: Circular causality — a change in any one part of a family system affects all other parts
Direct causality — each change produces a single predictable effect
Morphostasis — the family resists all change
Boundary maintenance — the family closes itself to the environment
q_0257.rationale: Table 2.1 states the assumption as "A change in any one part of a family system affects all other parts of the family system (circular causality)" (p. 15). General systems theory "expanded scientific thought from a simplistic view of direct cause and effect."
q_0257.trap: (B) is the chapter's own NCLEX question 2 distractor, and it is a one-word inversion of the printed line — direct for circular. That question's other distractors work the same way: react for initiate, primarily for as-well-as.

q_0258.stem: A family in crisis begins praising a child's small successes to encourage a change in his behavior, while a grandparent insists the household routine stay exactly as it always has been. Which two processes are at work?
options: Positive feedback in the praise, since praise is by definition positive feedback, and negative feedback in the criticism
Positive feedback in the effort to initiate change, and negative feedback in the effort to resist it
Morphogenesis in the grandparent's stance and morphostasis in the parents'
Neither; feedback applies only to communication, not to behavior change
q_0258.rationale: "Positive feedback initiates change; negative feedback resists change" (p. 16). Feedback processes "help identify strengths and needs and determine how well goals are accomplished."
q_0258.trap: (A) is the reflex pick and the chapter's flagged inversion: positive and negative here mean change-initiating and change-resisting, not praise and criticism. (C) reverses the other pair — morphogenesis is change, morphostasis is no change, and "a balance between morphogenesis (change) and morphostasis (no change) is necessary."

q_0259.stem: A couple describes the birth of their first child as joyful and also exhausting and destabilizing. Which family stress theory assumption applies?
options: Only negative events function as stressors for a family system
Stress is an inevitable part of family life, and any event, even if positive, can be stressful for the family
Stressors affect individual members but not the family as a unit
Normative transitions are excluded from stress theory, which addresses situational stressors only
q_0259.rationale: Table 2.1's first family stress theory assumption is that "Stress is an inevitable part of family life, and any event, even if positive, can be stressful for family," and the family "encounters both normative expected stressors and unexpected situational stressors over the life cycle." Transition to parenthood is listed first among the theory's applications (p. 15).
q_0259.trap: (A) restricts stressors to negative events, which is the intuitive reading and the one the assumption is written to exclude. (D) drops half the framework — both normative and situational stressors are named.

q_0260.stem: A remarried couple has a 14-year-old from one partner's first marriage and a 2-year-old together. A student tries to place them in Duvall's stages and cannot. What explains the difficulty?
options: Duvall's stages apply only to families with more than two children
The stage marker is the age of the oldest child, which makes the model hard to apply to stepfamilies and single-parent families
The stage marker is the age of the youngest child, and the model has no stage for toddlers
Duvall's model was replaced by family systems theory and no longer applies
q_0260.rationale: "This theory is based on the predictable changes in the family's structure, function, and roles, with the age of the oldest child as the marker for stage transition" (p. 17), and Table 2.1 lists as a limitation that "Use of age of oldest child and marital duration as marker of stage transition sometimes problematic (e.g., in stepfamilies, single-parent families)."
q_0260.trap: (C) inverts the marker, which is the most likely single item from this section — the chapter states "oldest" twice, once in the narrative and once in the table's limitations.

q_0261.stem: Which statements accurately describe Duvall's Developmental Stages of the Family? (Select all that apply.)
options: They are stages families progress through in adulthood
They designate how parenting progresses as a child develops
They describe the journey a couple will take as their children mature
They are stages an individual progresses through in moral and spiritual development
They designate appropriate discipline related to developmental stages
q_0261.rationale: These are the keyed options in the chapter's own NCLEX question 1 (p. 38). Stages I through VIII run from marriage to aging families, entirely in adulthood; stages II through VI are named by the children's stage; and the couple thread runs throughout — stage I is "Reestablish couple identity" and stage VII is "Reinvest in couple identity" (p. 17).
q_0261.trap: (D) and (E) are the two to reject, and both fail the same way — they treat the stages as a schedule for the *child*. Duvall described "eight developmental tasks of the family," the cycle begins before children arrive and continues after they leave, and no stage in Box 2.1 concerns discipline.

q_0262.stem: A father states that his household rules are to be followed without discussion, and that when his daughter asks why, he tells her "because I say so." Which parenting style does this describe?
options: Authoritative
Authoritarian
Permissive
Neglectful
q_0262.rationale: Authoritarian parents "try to control their children's behavior and attitudes through unquestioned mandates" and establish standards of conduct "that they expect to be followed rigidly and unquestioningly." The chapter gives the message as "Do it because I say so" (pp. 20–21).
q_0262.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the two words differ by four letters and both involve firm rules. The authoritative parent's control is firm but explained; the authoritarian parent's is firm and not open to question.

q_0263.stem: A mother says she explains her reasoning for household rules and asks her son's opinion before deciding, but she rarely enforces the rules and does not want to upset the household routine. Which style does this describe, and what distinguishes it?
options: Authoritative, because she explains her reasoning and consults the child
Permissive, because explaining reasons does not distinguish the styles — control does, and she exerts little or none
Authoritarian, because she sets the rules unilaterally
It cannot be classified without knowing whether she uses corporal punishment
q_0263.rationale: Permissive parents "exert little or no control over their children's actions," employ "lax, inconsistent discipline; do not set sensible limits," and "rarely punish the children" — and yet, if rules exist, "the parents explain the underlying reason, elicit the children's opinions, and consult them in decision-making processes" (p. 21).
q_0263.trap: (A) is the trap the fact bank flags explicitly: permissive parents do explain reasons, and so do authoritative parents. Explaining is not the discriminator. The authoritative parent explains and then enforces "firm and consistent" control; the permissive parent explains and does not enforce.

q_0264.stem: A nurse describes a child who is self-reliant, assertive, inquisitive, content, and highly interactive with peers, and who behaves well because of an internal sense of right and wrong rather than fear of being caught. Which parenting style does the chapter associate with this outcome?
options: Permissive
Authoritarian
Authoritative
No style is associated with a predictable outcome
q_0264.rationale: Authoritative parenting produces "children with high self-esteem who are self-reliant, assertive, inquisitive, content, and highly interactive with other children," and fosters "inner-directedness, a conscience that regulates behavior based on feelings of guilt or shame for wrongdoing, not on fear of being caught or punished" (p. 21).
q_0264.trap: (B) can produce children who are "courteous, loyal, honest, and dependable, but docile" — and only conditionally, when "close supervision and affection accompany parental authority." Without that affection the same style "may be associated with both defiant and antisocial behaviors," so a distractor stating the authoritarian outcome unconditionally is wrong.

q_0265.stem: A nurse recognizes that a family's parenting style differs from her own upbringing and from what she considers ideal. What does the chapter direct her to do?
options: Teach the parents that authoritative parenting produces the best outcomes
Give differing styles equal respect, since childrearing is a culturally bound phenomenon
Document the style as a risk factor and refer to social work
Withhold parenting guidance until the family adopts an authoritative approach
q_0265.rationale: "There are differing philosophies in regard to parenting. Childrearing is a culturally bound phenomenon, and children are socialized to behave in ways that are important to their family," and "When working with individual families, nurses should give these differing styles equal respect" (p. 21).
q_0265.trap: (A) is the reflex pick because the chapter really does describe the authoritative outcomes most favorably, and a learner converts that into a teaching mandate. The chapter does not rank the styles for the nurse. The teachable content is specific practices — limits, consistency, timing — not the label on a parent's style.

q_0266.topic: limit setting and types of discipline
q_0266.stem: A parent asks the nurse to explain the difference between limit setting and discipline. Which response is accurate?
options: They are two words for the same childrearing activity
Limit setting establishes the rules or guidelines for behavior; discipline, in its narrow sense, is the action taken to enforce the rules after noncompliance
Limit setting is used with young children and discipline with older children
Discipline establishes the rules and limit setting enforces them
q_0266.rationale: Discipline "means to teach or refers to a set of rules governing conduct. In a narrower sense, it refers to the action taken to enforce the rules after noncompliance." Limit setting "refers to establishing the rules or guidelines for behavior" (p. 21). The relationship between them: "The clearer the limits that are set and the more consistently they are enforced, the less need there is for disciplinary action."
q_0266.trap: (D) is the mirror error — a straight swap of the two definitions. (A) is the more common one in practice, and the chapter separates the terms precisely because they are used interchangeably.

q_0267.topic: limit setting and types of discipline
q_0267.stem: A mother says her 3-year-old constantly tests the household rules and asks how to stop this. What should the nurse teach?
options: Limit testing is misbehavior and should be extinguished by ignoring it
Children want and need limits, and testing them is how children learn the extent to which they can manipulate their environment and gain reassurance that others will protect them
Limit testing indicates the limits are too strict and should be relaxed
Limit testing at this age suggests a developmental concern warranting referral
q_0267.rationale: "Children want and need limits. Unrestricted freedom is a threat to their security and safety. By testing the limits imposed on them, children learn the extent to which they can manipulate their environment and gain reassurance from knowing that others are there to protect them from potential harm." The chapter lists "Test their limits of control" as the first function limits and discipline serve (p. 21).
q_0267.trap: (A) treats limit-testing as a behavior problem when the chapter names it as a function limits are there to serve. This is the inversion the fact bank flags.

q_0268.topic: limit setting and types of discipline
q_0268.stem: Which principles are among the nine guidelines for implementing discipline? (Select all that apply.)
options: Consistency — implement disciplinary action exactly as agreed on and for each infraction
Timing — initiate discipline as soon as the child misbehaves
Behavior orientation — always disapprove of the behavior, not the child
Termination — after the discipline is administered, consider the child as having a clean slate and avoid bringing up the incident or lecturing
Escalation — increase the severity of the consequence with each repetition of the behavior
q_0268.rationale: The Family-Centered Care box on implementing discipline lists nine principles: consistency, timing, commitment, unity, flexibility, planning, behavior orientation, privacy, and termination (p. 21).
q_0268.trap: (E) is the one to reject, and it is the mechanism the chapter names as the third flaw of *corporal punishment* — children "become accustomed to spanking, requiring more severe corporal punishment over time" (p. 23). Escalation is a failure mode in this chapter, never a principle.

q_0269.topic: limit setting and types of discipline
q_0269.stem: A mother tells her misbehaving son in the grocery store, "Wait until your father gets home." How should the nurse evaluate this?
options: Appropriate, because it avoids embarrassing the child in public
Problematic on two counts: delaying punishment weakens its intent, and the phrase conveys negative messages about the other parent
Appropriate, because it gives the mother time to calm down before disciplining
Problematic only because it delays the consequence
q_0269.rationale: "Delaying punishment weakens its intent, and practices such as telling the child, Wait until your father comes home are not only ineffectual but also convey negative messages about the other parent" (p. 21). It also violates the Unity principle, which exists "to prevent confusion and alliances between child and one parent."
q_0269.trap: (A) is close to a real exception and misapplies it. When delay is unavoidable — to avoid embarrassment, for instance — the Timing principle requires the parent to "verbally disapprove of the behavior and state that disciplinary action will be implemented." Announced deferral is permitted; silent deferral to the other parent is not. (D) catches only half the fault.

q_0270.topic: limit setting and types of discipline
q_0270.stem: A parent reports that since she began ignoring her son's tantrums, the tantrums have become louder and more frequent, and she is ready to abandon the plan. What should the nurse tell her?
options: The plan has failed and a different strategy should be selected
This is a response burst — the undesired behavior increases after ignoring is initiated because the child is testing whether the parents are serious — and the plan should continue
The tantrums indicate an underlying disorder and warrant evaluation
She should ignore the tantrums only when they are mild
q_0270.rationale: Response burst is "a phenomenon that occurs when the undesired behavior increases after ignoring is initiated because the child is testing the parents to see if they are serious about the plan" (p. 22). Being aware of it is one of the four requirements for ignoring to work. The chapter warns that when parents "give in and resort to previous patterns of discipline... the behavior is actually reinforced because the child learns that persistence gains parental attention."
q_0270.trap: (A) is the intuitive and the harmful reading, and it is the specific error the chapter is written to prevent. Abandoning the plan mid-burst teaches the child that persistence works — the outcome worse than never having started.

q_0271.topic: limit setting and types of discipline
q_0271.stem: A parent lists the types of consequences as natural, logical, unrelated, and transforming. Which statement requires correction?
options: Natural consequences are those that occur without any intervention
Logical consequences are those directly related to the rule
Transforming consequences allow the child to come to the conclusion on his or her own
Unrelated consequences are those imposed deliberately
q_0271.rationale: "The strategy of consequences involves allowing children to experience the results of their misbehavior. It includes three types" — natural, logical, and unrelated (p. 22). There is no transforming type. This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 3, keyed to the invented fourth category.
q_0271.trap: (A), (B), and (D) are all verbatim-correct definitions, so a learner searching for a factual error finds none and guesses. Knowing the set is closed at three is sufficient to answer. Note also that time-out is an unrelated consequence, stated twice, and that natural consequences are preferred but "effective if they are meaningful to children" — the chapter's own messy-room example shows a natural consequence failing where a logical one works.

q_0272.stem: A parent asks how long her 4-year-old should sit in time-out. What should the nurse advise?
options: Four minutes, following the rule of 1 minute per year of age
Ten minutes, a standard duration for preschoolers
The duration should be scaled to how serious the misbehavior was
Until the child apologizes
q_0272.rationale: "A rule for the length of time-out is 1 minute per year of age; use a kitchen timer with an audible bell to record the time rather than a watch" (p. 23).
q_0272.trap: (C) is the reflex pick because scaling punishment to severity feels like fairness, and the chapter's Flexibility principle does mention severity — but that principle governs which *strategy* is chosen, not the length of a time-out. The duration rule is fixed to age.

q_0273.stem: The same parent reports that her son screams for the first several minutes of every time-out, and asks whether that time counts. What is the correct guidance?
options: The time counts from the moment the child is sent, regardless of behavior
The time-out period begins after the child quiets down
The time-out should be ended early if the child becomes upset
An additional minute should be added for each outburst
q_0273.rationale: The published procedure states: "If they cry, refuse, or display any disruptive behavior, the time-out period will begin after they quiet down," and "When they are quiet for the duration of the time, they can then leave the room" (p. 23).
q_0273.trap: (A) is the mechanic most often gotten wrong, and it is what makes time-out fail for exactly this child — a 4-year-old who screams for five minutes serves no quiet time at all. Note also that the audible kitchen timer is specified rather than a watch, so the endpoint is signalled objectively rather than by the parent.

q_0274.stem: A parent asks where time-out should take place and how many warnings to give. Which response reflects the chapter's procedure?
