Chronic salicylate exposure is always less serious than a single large ingestion
Bleeding is not a feature of salicylate toxicity at any dose
The early findings of acute salicylate poisoning are bradycardia and hypoventilation
q_0494.rationale: Chronic salicylate toxicity is ">100 mg/kg/day for ≥2 days" and "can be more serious than acute ingestion," with the "same as listed above but subtle onset and nonspecific symptoms (often mistaken for viral illness)" plus bleeding tendencies. Acute early findings are nausea, hyperventilation, vomiting, and tinnitus.
q_0494.trap: (D) inverts the two most characteristic early acute findings — the child hyperventilates rather than hypoventilates, and tinnitus is the other early cue. (B) is the intuition this fact overturns, and it is why a history of several days of dosing matters more than the size of any single dose.

q_0495.stem: A child with severe salicylate toxicity requires enhanced elimination. Which interventions does the chapter name?
options: Activated charcoal as soon as possible, sodium bicarbonate to correct metabolic acidosis with urinary alkalinization to enhance elimination, external cooling for hyperpyrexia, and hemodialysis rather than peritoneal dialysis in severe cases
Gastric lavage, which reliably removes aspirin concretions
Peritoneal dialysis, which is preferred over hemodialysis in children
Aspirin reversal with vitamin K alone, which corrects both the acidosis and the bleeding
q_0495.rationale: "Activated charcoal is given as soon as possible (unless contraindicated by altered mental status)." "Sodium bicarbonate transfusions are used to correct metabolic acidosis, and urinary alkalinization may be effective in enhancing elimination; hypokalemia may interfere with achieving urinary alkalinization." Use "external cooling for hyperpyrexia," vitamin K for bleeding, and "In severe cases, hemodialysis (not peritoneal dialysis) is used."
q_0495.trap: (B) is explicitly refuted: "Lavage will not remove concretions of ASA." (C) reverses the dialysis preference, which the chapter states in a parenthesis precisely because it is the swappable half.

q_0496.stem: A parent insists their toddler cannot have lead poisoning because he has never been seen eating paint chips. Which response is correct?
options: A child does not need to eat loose paint chips to be exposed; normal hand-to-mouth behavior, coupled with lead dust in the environment that has settled over decades, is the usual method of poisoning
Eating paint chips is the only meaningful route of childhood lead exposure
Lead exposure occurs only through inhalation during renovation
Lead poisoning cannot occur in a home built after 1950
q_0496.rationale: "A child does not need to eat loose paint chips to be exposed to the toxin; normal hand-to-mouth behavior, coupled with the presence of lead dust in the environment that has settled over decades, is the usual method of poisoning." In most cases of acute childhood lead poisoning "the source is nonintact lead-based paint in an older home or lead-contaminated bare soil in the yard." Ingestion "happens during normal day-to-day play and mouthing activities," while inhalation "usually occurs during renovation and remodeling."
q_0496.trap: (D) attaches the wrong date to the wrong rule: lead in paint was *decreased* in 1950 and *banned* in 1978, so a home built in 1960 can still carry lead paint. Those two dates are also the ones the personal risk questions use, which is where the swap does the most damage.

q_0497.stem: A nurse is teaching about how lead behaves in a child's body. Which statement is accurate?
options: Lead ultimately settles in the bones and teeth, where it remains inert and in storage, making up approximately 75% to 90% of the body burden, and at the cellular level it competes with calcium
Lead is stored primarily in the liver and is cleared within weeks
Lead affects only the hematologic system
A child's developing nervous system is less vulnerable to lead than an adult's
q_0497.rationale: Lead "moves via an equilibration process between the blood, the soft tissues and organs, and the bones and teeth. Lead ultimately settles in the bones and teeth, where it remains inert and in storage. This makes up the largest portion of the body burden, approximately 75% to 90%." At the cellular level "it competes with molecules of calcium, interfering with the regulating action of calcium." Lead "can affect any part of the body, including the renal, hematologic, and neurologic systems."
q_0497.trap: (D) inverts the chapter's central concern: of most concern "is the developing brain and nervous system, which are more vulnerable than those of older children and adults." That vulnerability is the entire reason for screening children rather than adults.

q_0498.stem: A 3-year-old with an elevated blood lead level is also found to be iron deficient. Why does this combination matter, and what does it mean for teaching?
options: Children who are iron deficient absorb lead more readily, and lead can interfere with iron binding onto the heme molecule, sometimes creating a picture of anemia even when the child is not iron deficient; teaching therefore includes adequate calcium and iron and regular meals
Iron deficiency protects against lead absorption, so supplementation should be withheld
The anemia proves the child is iron deficient, so lead can be excluded as a cause
Nutrition has no bearing on lead absorption
q_0498.rationale: "Children who are iron deficient absorb lead more readily than those with sufficient iron stores. Lead can interfere with the binding of iron onto the heme molecule. This sometimes creates a picture of anemia even though the child is not iron deficient." Education for a child with a blood lead level of 5 mcg/dl or above includes the "Importance of good nutrition in reducing the absorption and effects of lead," with "adequate intake of calcium and iron and importance of regular meals."
q_0498.trap: (C) reads the anemia backward. Lead can produce the appearance of iron-deficiency anemia in a child whose iron stores are adequate, so the blood count cannot be used to rule lead in or out — only a venous blood lead level can.

q_0499.stem: A child's blood lead level has been elevated for months. The parents ask whether the damage can be undone once the lead is removed. Which response is accurate?
options: Although most of the pathophysiologic effects of lead are reversible, the most serious consequences are on the central nervous system, and low-dose exposure may also cause permanent neurologic deficits
All effects of lead reverse completely once the blood lead level normalizes
Only high-dose exposure carries any risk of permanent injury
Lead poisoning at this age produces no cognitive effects
q_0499.rationale: "Although most of the pathophysiologic effects of lead are reversible, the most serious consequences of both high and low lead exposure are the effects on the central nervous system." In lead encephalopathy "permanent brain damage can result in cognitive impairment, behavior changes, possible paralysis, and seizures." "However, low-dose exposure may also cause permanent neurologic deficits." Even mild and moderate poisoning can cause "aggression, hyperactivity, impulsivity, delinquency, disinterest, and withdrawal."
q_0499.trap: (C) is the reassuring half-truth most families hold, and the chapter refuses it in a single sentence. Long-term signs include "developmental delays, lowered intelligence quotient (IQ), reading skill deficits, visual-spatial problems, visual-motor problems, learning disabilities, and lower academic success."

q_0500.topic: lead screening and the blood lead level action ladder
q_0500.stem: A healthy 18-month-old is at a well-child visit and has no symptoms. The parents ask why lead testing is being suggested. Which response is correct?
options: Children with lead poisoning rarely have symptoms even at levels requiring chelation therapy, and universal screening should be done at 1 and 2 years of age
Screening is indicated only for children with behavioral symptoms or pica
Screening begins at 5 years of age, when school entry is required
A fingerstick sample is diagnostic and no further testing is needed
q_0500.rationale: "Children with lead poisoning rarely have symptoms even at levels requiring chelation therapy." Universal screening "should be done at 1 and 2 years old. Any child between 3 and 6 years old who has not been previously screened should also be tested. All children with risk factors should be screened more often."
q_0500.trap: (B) waits for symptoms that usually never come, which is precisely the reasoning screening exists to override. (D) misstates the diagnostic standard: "A diagnosis of lead poisoning is based only on the lead testing of a venous blood specimen from a venipuncture," collected carefully "to avoid contamination by lead on the skin."

q_0501.topic: lead screening and the blood lead level action ladder
q_0501.stem: A family cannot be screened under a universal program, so targeted screening is used. Which questions does the chapter give as the personal risk questions?
options: Does the child live in or regularly visit a house built before 1950; a house built before 1978 with recent or ongoing renovations within the past 6 months; or have a sibling or playmate who has or had lead poisoning
Does the child live in a house built before 1978; a house with well water; or attend day care
Does the child have pica; a family history of anemia; or a sibling in school
Does the child live in a house built before 1920; a house painted within the past year; or have a pet
q_0501.rationale: Children should be screened if their family cannot answer "no" to three questions: "Does your child live in or regularly visit a house that was built before 1950?"; "Does your child live in or regularly visit a house built before 1978 with recent or ongoing renovations or remodeling within the past 6 months?"; and "Does your child have a sibling or playmate who has or had lead poisoning?"
q_0501.trap: (B) collapses the two dates into one and drops the renovation qualifier, which is what makes the second question different from the first. The 1950 question asks about age of housing alone; the 1978 question asks about age plus recent disturbance of the paint.

q_0502.topic: lead screening and the blood lead level action ladder
q_0502.stem: A 2-year-old's venous blood lead level returns at 52 mcg/dl. Which actions does Table 14.2 direct?
options: Provide lead education, refer to a clinical center specializing in lead poisoning, provide diagnostic testing within 24 to 48 hours, perform clinical evaluation and management within 48 hours, provide appropriate chelation therapy, and ensure aggressive environmental intervention
Provide education and rescreen in 1 year
Provide education and retest within 1 month, with no chelation at this level
Withhold chelation until the child develops symptoms
q_0502.rationale: For a blood lead level of 45 to 69 mcg/dl, Table 14.2 directs providing lead education, referral to a clinical center specializing in lead poisoning with coordination of care, "diagnostic testing within 24-48 hours," clinical evaluation and management "within 48 hours," "appropriate chelation therapy," "aggressive environmental intervention," and follow-up testing "at least once per month."
q_0502.trap: (D) is the error the chapter blocks twice over: children with lead poisoning "rarely have symptoms even at levels requiring chelation therapy," and a level of 70 or above requires immediate testing and chelation "whether symptoms are present or not." (B) is the action for a level below 5.

q_0503.topic: lead screening and the blood lead level action ladder
q_0503.stem: A 3-year-old's blood lead level is 8 mcg/dl. Which elements belong in the education and follow-up for this child? Select all that apply.
options: Explanation of the child's blood lead level and what it means, and the potential adverse health effects of an elevated level
The importance of wet cleaning to remove lead dust from floors, windowsills, and other surfaces
The hazards of improper removal of lead paint, such as dry sanding, scraping, or open-flame burning
Follow-up testing within 1 month, and then every 3 to 4 months
Erythrocyte protoporphyrin testing as the preferred screening method going forward
q_0503.rationale: Education for every child with a blood lead level of 5 mcg/dl or above covers the level and its meaning, potential adverse health effects, sources of exposure and how to reduce it "such as the importance of wet cleaning," the importance of good nutrition, the need for follow-up testing, results of any environmental investigation, and "Hazards of improper removal of lead paint (dry sanding, scraping, or open-flame burning)." For a level of 5 to 14, Table 14.2 directs follow-up testing "within 1 month, and then every 3-4 months."
q_0503.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort. Erythrocyte protoporphyrin "is no longer used as a screening test" because it "is not sensitive to BLLs of less than about 16 to 25 mcg/dl" — though a level above 35 mcg/dl still indicates toxicity and reflects duration of exposure and body burden.

q_0504.stem: Parents of a child beginning chelation therapy ask whether it will undo the effects of the lead. Which response is accurate?
options: Chelation removes lead from circulating blood and some from organs and tissues, but it does not counteract any effects of the lead, and it is unclear whether it affects lead stores in bones
Chelation reverses the neurologic effects of lead exposure
A single course of chelation removes the entire body burden of lead
Chelation eliminates the need for environmental remediation
q_0504.rationale: Chelation is "the term used for removing lead from circulating blood and, theoretically, some lead from organs and tissues. It is unclear whether chelation affects lead stores in bones." Although it resembles an antidote in purpose, "chelation does not counteract any effects of the lead." Because of the equilibration process "there is often a rebound of the BLL after chelation," and "Multiple chelation treatments may be necessary."
q_0504.trap: (C) ignores the rebound the chapter describes: the level rises again as lead redistributes from tissue stores, and rebound ceases only once the body burden has fallen enough to stabilize the blood level. (D) is contradicted by the discharge requirement for "confirmation that the child will be discharged to a home without lead hazards."

q_0505.stem: A child with a peanut allergy and a blood lead level of 58 mcg/dl, without symptoms, requires chelation. Which agent consideration is correct?
options: British antilewisite is contraindicated in children with peanut allergies or hepatic insufficiency and must not be given with iron; succimer is oral, is appropriate for levels of 45 to 69 mcg/dl in the absence of symptoms, and can be used in conjunction with iron
British antilewisite is the agent of choice here, since peanut allergy is not a contraindication
Succimer must never be given with iron
Calcium disodium edetate is contraindicated in all children with any allergy
q_0505.rationale: British antilewisite "is contraindicated in children with peanut allergies or hepatic insufficiency, nor should it be given in conjunction with iron"; it is given "only at a deep intramuscular site" and is used with calcium disodium edetate for high lead levels or lead encephalopathy. Succimer is oral, for "lead levels of 45 to 69 mcg/dl and an absence of symptoms," and "DMSA can be used in conjunction with iron."
q_0505.trap: (C) inverts the iron rule between the two agents, which is the single most swappable fact in this section — it is British antilewisite that must not be combined with iron, and succimer that may be. Both facts matter because iron supplementation is often indicated in the same child.

q_0506.stem: A child is receiving intramuscular calcium disodium edetate. Which nursing actions are required?
options: Ensure adequate urinary output and adequate oral fluid intake, rotate injection sites to prevent painful fibrotic areas, and use a topical anesthetic cream or injected procaine to reduce injection pain
Restrict fluids to reduce renal workload during chelation
Give the drug subcutaneously to reduce pain
Substitute disodium edetate if calcium disodium edetate is unavailable
q_0506.rationale: "Adequate urinary output must be ensured with administration of calcium EDTA. Children receiving the drug intramuscularly must be able to maintain adequate oral intake of fluids." Chelating agents "are administered deeply into a large muscle mass," and "Rotation of sites is essential to prevent the formation of painful areas of fibrotic tissue." For pain, "the local anesthetic procaine is injected with the drug," and topical EMLA or LMX4 may be applied before injection.
q_0506.trap: (B) inverts a requirement that exists because "the chelates are excreted via the kidneys," so hydration is essential rather than restricted. (D) names a substitution the chapter flags as lethal: "Incidences of child death from hypocalcemia have been recorded when Na₂EDTA was substituted for CaNa₂EDTA."

q_0507.topic: child maltreatment types, scope, and predisposing factors
q_0507.stem: A nurse is reviewing national child maltreatment data. Which statement is accurate?
options: Neglect is the most common form of maltreatment, accounting for 75.3% of confirmed cases, and 74.8% of reported neglect cases involve children 3 years old or younger
Physical abuse is the most common form of confirmed maltreatment
Sexual abuse accounts for the majority of confirmed cases
Reported statistics closely represent the true incidence of maltreatment
q_0507.rationale: Of 683,000 children confirmed as victims in 2015, 75.3% involved neglect, 17.2% physical abuse, 8.4% sexual abuse, and 6.9% psychologic maltreatment or emotional abuse. "Child neglect is the most common form of maltreatment, and 74.8% of reported neglect cases involve children 3 years old or younger." Of children who died, "72.9% suffered from neglect either exclusively or in combination with another type of maltreatment."
q_0507.trap: (B) is the reflex answer because physical abuse is the most visible form and the one that generates images. (D) is contradicted directly: "Reported statistics only partially represent the actual incidence of child maltreatment because many cases are believed to go unreported."

q_0508.topic: child maltreatment types, scope, and predisposing factors
q_0508.stem: A nurse is asked which children are at highest risk of physical abuse. Which statement reflects the chapter?
options: Children from birth to 1 year old are at highest risk, and the onus for child abuse is always on the abuser
Preschoolers are at highest risk, because of negativism and testing behavior
School-age children are at highest risk, because of increased independence
Risk is evenly distributed across childhood
q_0508.rationale: "Children from birth to 1 year old are at highest risk for being abused." Infants and small children "require constant attention and must have all their needs met by others," which can produce "parental or caregiver fatigue that results in striking out at the child." The chapter states plainly that "The onus for child abuse is always on the abuser."
q_0508.trap: (B) is the intuitive answer in a chapter titled Health Problems of Early Childhood, and the age band it names is the wrong one. Note that premature infants are separately at risk "because of failure of parent-child bonding during early infancy, increased physical needs, or irritability."

q_0509.topic: child maltreatment types, scope, and predisposing factors
q_0509.stem: A nurse suspects maltreatment in a family that is affluent and well educated. Which statement reflects the chapter?
options: Child maltreatment occurs across all socioeconomic, religious, cultural, racial, and ethnic groups; abuse in lower socioeconomic groups is more likely to be reported, but concealed crises may also be present in upper-class families
Maltreatment essentially does not occur in higher-income families
Reporting thresholds should be higher for educated families
A single predictive factor identifies families in which abuse will occur
q_0509.rationale: "Child maltreatment occurs across all socioeconomic, religious, cultural, racial, and ethnic groups." Although most reporting has come from lower socioeconomic populations, "child abuse is not a problem of any one societal group… abuse in these groups is more likely to be reported. However, concealed crises may also be present in upper-class families."
q_0509.trap: (D) states what the chapter denies about all three risk categories: "no single factor or group of factors is predictive of abuse. Rather, the interaction of these factors is thought to increase the risk," and predisposing characteristics "are never predictive of actual abuse."

q_0510.topic: child maltreatment types, scope, and predisposing factors
q_0510.stem: In an abusive family, one child appears to be singled out. A colleague suggests removing only that child. Which consideration does the chapter raise?
options: Removing the singled-out child often places the other siblings at risk for abuse, so no child is safe if left in the abusive environment unless the parents can learn new parenting skills
Removing the singled-out child reliably protects the remaining siblings
Siblings are never at risk once the scapegoated child is removed
Removal decisions are made by the nurse rather than the court
q_0510.rationale: "One child may be singled out in an abusive family. Removing that child from the home often places the other siblings at risk for abuse. Therefore no child is safe if left in the abusive environment unless the parents can be helped to learn new parenting skills."
q_0510.trap: (B) treats the scapegoating as fixed to one child rather than as a pattern in the household, which is the assumption this passage exists to correct. (D) misassigns authority: referrals go to Child Protective Services, and "A court proceeding may be necessary before the child can be placed outside the home."

q_0511.topic: child maltreatment types, scope, and predisposing factors
q_0511.stem: A mother repeatedly brings her toddler in with seizures that no clinician has witnessed, has some medical training, and requests extensive testing. The child improves during a hospital stay when the mother is absent. Which condition should the nurse suspect, and what confirms it?
options: Munchausen syndrome by proxy; the resolution of symptoms after separation from the perpetrator confirms the diagnosis
Abusive head trauma; retinal hemorrhage confirms the diagnosis
Physical neglect; growth failure confirms the diagnosis
A seizure disorder that is simply difficult to capture on monitoring
q_0511.rationale: Munchausen syndrome by proxy is "a rare but serious form of child abuse in which caregivers deliberately exaggerate or fabricate histories and symptoms or induce symptoms," for "the gratification of the caregiver." "In most cases, the perpetrator is the biologic mother with some degree of health care knowledge and training." Commonly presented symptoms include seizures, vomiting, diarrhea, and altered mental status, "usually witnessed only by the perpetrator," and "The resolution of symptoms after separation from the perpetrator confirms the diagnosis."
q_0511.trap: (D) is where this diagnosis usually hides, and the chapter notes that "Health care providers can become easily misled and unknowingly enable the perpetrator" — the child then "endures painful and unnecessary medical testing and procedures."

q_0512.topic: recognizing physical abuse and abusive head trauma
q_0512.stem: A 4-month-old is brought in with vomiting, irritability, poor feeding, and listlessness. There is no external injury. Imaging shows subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhage, and the ophthalmology examination shows bilateral retinal hemorrhages. Which condition does this describe?
options: Abusive head trauma, in which most often there are no signs of external injury
Gastroenteritis with dehydration
A bleeding disorder, which this presentation confirms
Accidental head injury, since no external marks are present
q_0512.rationale: Abusive head trauma is "a serious form of physical abuse caused by violent shaking of infants and young children." Characteristic injuries are "intracranial bleeding (subdural and subarachnoid hematomas) and, in approximately 80% of cases, bilateral retinal hemorrhages, which are classic results of repetitive acceleration-deceleration head trauma," sometimes with rib and long-bone fractures. "Most often, there are no signs of external injury, making diagnosis difficult," and presenting symptoms such as "vomiting, irritability, poor feeding, and listlessness, are often mistaken for common infant and childhood ailments."
q_0512.trap: (B) is the diagnosis this presentation is most often given, which is exactly why the chapter lists those four symptoms. (D) treats absence of external injury as reassurance when the chapter names it as characteristic of the mechanism.

q_0513.topic: recognizing physical abuse and abusive head trauma
q_0513.stem: A nurse is teaching new parents about preventing abusive head trauma. Which teaching best targets the mechanism the chapter names?
options: Coping mechanisms for caring for a child with inconsolable crying, since abusive head trauma most often results from the caregiver's frustration with crying
Instruction to never shake a baby, without further content
Information on choosing a safe crib
Guidance on infant sleep position
q_0513.rationale: Abusive head trauma is "most often a result of the caregiver's frustration with crying, maternal stress, or depression." The Nursing Alert directs: "Stress to parents the danger of shaking infants (shaking can cause AHT). Education must include coping mechanisms on caring for children with inconsolable crying." An estimated 1200 to 1400 children are shaken each year, "and of these victims, 25% to 30% die as a result of their injuries. The rest have lifelong complications."
q_0513.trap: (B) states the prohibition without addressing what produces the impulse, and it is the incomplete half of the teaching. Parents who already know not to shake a baby still need a plan for the hour in which the crying will not stop.

q_0514.topic: recognizing physical abuse and abusive head trauma
q_0514.stem: A nurse evaluates a child's injuries. Which findings are among Box 14.5's warning signs of abuse? Select all that apply.
options: The history is incompatible with the pattern or degree of injury
Bruising or other injury is present in a nonmobile patient
The patient has multiple fractures of differing ages
A 4-year-old has a single bruise over the shin after a fall from a bicycle, and the account is consistent
There was a delay in seeking care
q_0514.rationale: Box 14.5 lists a history "incompatible with the pattern or degree of injury"; a vague explanation or reluctance to provide information; contradictory histories among caregivers; a mechanism "not possible given age or developmental level"; "Bruising or other injury… in a nonmobile patient"; "multiple fractures of differing ages"; "a delay in seeking care"; an inappropriate affect; and disappearance of the accompanying adult.
q_0514.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort — a mobile child with a single injury over a bony prominence and a consistent history is the ordinary accidental pattern. The chapter is explicit that "No one indicator can be used to diagnose maltreatment. It is a pattern or combination of indicators."

q_0515.topic: recognizing physical abuse and abusive head trauma
q_0515.stem: A nurse is reviewing findings that can be mistaken for abuse. Which are named in the chapter as mimics that must be ruled out? Select all that apply.
options: Cupping and coin rubbing
Mongolian spots
Osteogenesis imperfecta and bleeding disorders
Spiral fracture from a twist-and-fall injury
Burns with sharply demarcated margins and no splash marks
q_0515.rationale: The chapter lists medical conditions such as "bleeding disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta, or sudden infant death syndrome"; cultural practices such as "cupping or coin rubbing"; unintentional injuries such as "burns from metal buckles on car seats, bruising from seat belts, or spiral fractures from a twist-and-fall injury"; and normal variants such as "mongolian spots and congenital anomalies of genitalia."
q_0515.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it belongs to Box 14.6's abuse findings rather than to the mimics: "sharply demarcated areas from immersion in scalding water" with "absence of 'splash' marks and presence of symmetric burns" is the immersion-burn pattern, which is the opposite of an accidental scald.

q_0516.topic: recognizing physical abuse and abusive head trauma
q_0516.stem: A hospitalized 3-year-old with unexplained injuries is unusually clingy toward the parent suspected of abuse, does not cry during a painful dressing change, and is indiscriminately friendly with staff. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: These are recognized responses in maltreated children; a child may be overly attached to the abusive parent, may show inappropriate reaction to injury such as failure to cry from pain, and may be indiscriminately friendly
The child's attachment to the parent makes abuse unlikely
The absence of crying indicates the injuries are not painful
Indiscriminate friendliness indicates the child is well adjusted
q_0516.rationale: Among children's responses, "no one pattern is typical," but "extremes of behavior may be observed." Children "may be overly attached to the abusive parent, possibly in the hope of preventing any upset that may precipitate anger and another attack." Box 14.6 lists "inappropriate reaction to injury, such as failure to cry from pain," "lack of reaction to frightening events," and "indiscriminate friendliness and displays of affection" among suggestive behaviors.
q_0516.trap: (B) is the reassuring inference an observer naturally draws from a child who seeks the parent out, and the chapter inverts it. The same pattern appeared in Chapter 12 as a concern rather than a comfort, and in Chapter 11 as disinhibited social engagement disorder.

q_0517.topic: sexual abuse recognition and the nursing response
q_0517.stem: A 6-year-old begins to disclose sexual abuse and asks the nurse to promise not to tell anyone. What is the correct response?
options: Do not promise not to tell; tell the child that you are required by law to report the abuse
Promise confidentiality, so the child feels safe enough to continue
Promise not to tell the family, but explain that other staff will be informed
Stop the conversation until a parent can be present
q_0517.rationale: The Nursing Care Guidelines direct: "Do not promise not to tell; tell them that you are required by law to report the abuse." The guidance also directs providing a private time and place, not expressing shock or criticizing the family, using the child's own vocabulary for body parts, avoiding leading statements, reassuring the child that telling was the right thing and that the abuse is not their fault, determining immediate need for safety, and explaining what will happen when the nurse reports.
q_0517.trap: (B) is the humane instinct and it makes a promise that cannot be kept, which risks the child experiencing the mandated report as a betrayal. (D) may place the child with the person who is the source of the danger.

q_0518.topic: sexual abuse recognition and the nursing response
q_0518.stem: A 7-year-old is examined after a disclosure of sexual abuse, and the genital examination is entirely normal. What does this finding mean?
options: In most cases the genital examination findings are normal, which does not mean that sexual abuse did not occur
A normal examination rules out sexual abuse
A normal examination indicates the abuse occurred more than a year ago
A normal examination means forensic evidence collection is unnecessary
q_0518.rationale: "In most cases, the genital examination findings are normal, which does not mean that sexual abuse did not occur." "Fondling or genital-to-genital contact without penetration may leave no physical findings," and "Genital tissue heals very quickly and most often without scars." The chapter also names two myths directly: "the size of the hymeneal opening is not predictive of the likelihood of sexual abuse," and because the mucosa is elastic, penetration without tissue disruption is possible, which "defies another myth that there is always evidence of female virginity."
q_0518.trap: (B) is the inference the examination invites and the reason the chapter states the negative so plainly. Forensic timing matters separately: evidence from the body "diminishes greatly after 24 hours," with "the best chance for evidence collection coming from bed linens or the child's underwear," and contact within 72 to 96 hours should prompt consideration of forensic testing.

q_0519.topic: sexual abuse recognition and the nursing response
q_0519.stem: Which statements about sexual abuse definitions and offenders reflect the chapter?
options: Incest requires no blood relationship and includes stepparents and unrelated siblings, while pedophilia denotes a preference of an adult for prepubertal children rather than a type of sexual activity; a typical abuser is a man whom the victim knows
Incest requires a blood relationship between the parties
Pedophilia is defined as a specific sexual act performed against a child
Most offenders are strangers to the victim with prior criminal records
q_0519.rationale: Incest is "Any physical sexual activity between family members; blood relationship is not required (abusers can include stepparents, unrelated siblings, grandparents, uncles, and aunts)." Pedophilia "does not denote a type of sexual activity but rather the preference of an adult for prepubertal children as the means of achieving sexual excitement." "Anyone, including siblings and mothers, can be sexual abusers, but a typical abuser is a man whom the victim knows."
q_0519.trap: (D) is the stranger-danger picture, and the chapter contradicts each part: many offenders "hold full-time jobs, are active in community affairs, and may not have prior criminal records," and often work or volunteer "in positions such as teaching or coaching."

q_0520.topic: sexual abuse recognition and the nursing response
q_0520.stem: A nurse is documenting findings in a case of suspected maltreatment. Which approach is correct?
options: Describe behaviors rather than interpret them, record conversations verbatim as much as possible, use a body diagram, and photograph injuries with a measurement tool
Record the nurse's conclusion that the child appears abused, so the record is unambiguous
Summarize the child's statements in the nurse's own words for clarity
Omit parent-child interaction, since it is subjective
q_0520.rationale: "Accurate and factual documentation is essential. Behaviors are described, not interpreted, and are recorded daily to establish a progress record." "Conversations among the nurse, child, and parent are recorded verbatim as much as possible." Recording includes bruise location, size, shape, and color "on drawing of body outline," distinguishing characteristics, symmetry or asymmetry, evidence of past injuries, and "description of parent-child interactions (verbal interactions, eye contact, touching, parental concern)."
q_0520.trap: (B) records a conclusion in place of the evidence supporting it, which weakens the record in precisely the setting — a court proceeding, where "Nurses may be subpoenaed" — that the documentation exists to serve. (C) discards the verbatim quality the chapter requires, and the child's own words are the evidence.

q_0521.stem: A 9-year-old boy has grown noticeably stronger over the past year and wants to begin an intensive weight-training program. Which consideration should the nurse raise?
options: By the end of this period both boys and girls double their strength and physical capabilities, but this increased strength is often misleading, because muscles are still functionally immature compared with those of the adolescent and are more readily injured by overuse
Strength gains at this age indicate muscular maturity equivalent to an adolescent's
Strength does not increase appreciably during the school-age years
Overuse injury is not a concern until after puberty
q_0521.rationale: "By the end of this age period, both boys and girls double their strength and physical capabilities." But "this increased strength is often misleading. Although strength increases, muscles are still functionally immature compared with those of the adolescent, and they are more readily injured by overuse." Bones also continue to ossify, and "mineralization is not completed until maturity."
q_0521.trap: (B) draws the natural inference from visible strength and is exactly the reasoning that produces overuse injuries in this age group. The fact that makes this item worth writing is that capability and tissue maturity diverge here, and only one of them is visible.

q_0522.stem: A 7-year-old is the size of a typical 10-year-old, and his parents have begun expecting him to behave accordingly. Which principle should the nurse teach?
options: Physical maturity is not necessarily correlated with emotional and social maturity; a 7-year-old who looks 10 will think and act like a 7-year-old, and expecting otherwise can be detrimental to competence and self-esteem
Physical size is a reliable indicator of emotional readiness at this age
Children who are large for their age mature emotionally faster to match
Treating a 10-year-old as though they were 7 carries no developmental cost
q_0522.rationale: "Physical maturity is not necessarily correlated with emotional and social maturity. Seven-year-old children who look like 10-year-old children will think and act like 7-year-olds." Expecting 10-year-old behavior "is unrealistic and can be detrimental to their development of competence and self-esteem."
q_0522.trap: (D) is the other half of the same principle, and the chapter closes it off deliberately: "Conversely, treating 10-year-old children as though they were 7 years old is an equal disservice." The mismatch cuts both ways, and an item can test either direction.

q_0523.stem: A parent asks when to expect pubertal changes in their 9-year-old daughter and 9-year-old son. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Generally puberty begins at 10 years in girls and 12 years in boys, with onset in either sex after age 8 years considered normal; the average age is 12 years in girls and 14 years in boys, with approximately a 2-year difference between the sexes
Puberty begins at 12 years in girls and 10 years in boys
Onset before age 10 is abnormal in both sexes and requires evaluation
Boys and girls begin pubertal changes at the same average age
q_0523.rationale: "Generally, puberty begins at 10 years in girls and 12 years in boys, but its onset in either sex after age 8 years is considered normal. The average age of puberty is 12 years in girls and 14 years in boys." On average "there is a difference of approximately 2 years between girls and boys in the age of onset of pubescence," and first signs appear "at about 9 years (particularly in girls)."
q_0523.trap: (B) swaps the two sexes, which is the commonest inversion here because the numbers themselves are easy to hold and their owners are not. (C) would make normal development pathologic — the chapter sets the lower boundary of normal at 8 years, not 10.

q_0524.stem: A 10-year-old girl has developed breasts well ahead of her classmates, and a 12-year-old boy in the same clinic has shown no pubertal changes. What does the chapter say about the psychosocial implications?
options: Early appearance of secondary sex characteristics in girls is often associated with dissatisfaction with physical appearance, greater general unhappiness, and lower self-esteem, while late-developing boys often have a negative self-concept; both have been linked to participation in risk-taking behaviors
Off-schedule development carries psychosocial risk only for girls
Early development in girls is consistently associated with higher self-esteem
Neither pattern has any documented psychosocial association
q_0524.rationale: "Early appearance of secondary sex characteristics in girls is often associated with dissatisfaction with physical appearance, greater general unhappiness, and lower self-esteem. Late-developing boys often have a negative self-concept." Both "have been linked to participation in risk-taking behaviors (e.g., early sexual activity, substance use, and reckless vehicle use)."
q_0524.trap: (C) assumes that developing early confers status, which is the intuition the data overturn for girls. Note the underlying driver the chapter names: preadolescent children "do not want to be different," and the variability at this age is striking in both directions.

q_0525.topic: industry versus inferiority in the school-age child
q_0525.stem: An 8-year-old proudly shows the nurse a birdhouse he built and asks whether it is good enough to enter in a competition. Which psychosocial task does this reflect?
options: Initiative versus guilt
Industry versus inferiority, achieving a sense of personal and interpersonal competence through the acquisition of technologic and social skills
Identity versus role confusion
Autonomy versus shame and doubt
q_0525.rationale: "A sense of industry, or a stage of accomplishment, occurs somewhere between age 6 years and adolescence." The goal is "to achieve a sense of personal and interpersonal competence through the acquisition of technologic and social skills." School-age children "are eager to build skills and participate in meaningful and socially useful work," and they "want to engage in tasks that they can complete."
q_0525.trap: (A) belongs to the preschooler and (C) to the adolescent. The discriminator is what the child is seeking: the preschooler is testing whether it is permissible to try, while the school-age child is asking whether the finished product is good — accomplishment rather than permission.

q_0526.topic: industry versus inferiority in the school-age child
q_0526.stem: A 9-year-old who struggles in athletics tells the nurse she is "bad at everything." Which understanding should guide the nurse's response?
options: No child is able to do well in everything, and all children feel some degree of inferiority regarding a specific skill they cannot master; repeated failures can make a child reluctant to attempt any new task
A child who reports feeling inferior in one area has a pathologic self-concept requiring referral
Children who fail at one skill readily compensate through any other skill they possess
Feelings of inferiority arise only from the social environment, never from the child
q_0526.rationale: "No child is able to do well in everything… All children, even children who usually have positive attitudes toward work and their own capabilities, feel some degree of inferiority in regard to a specific skill that they cannot master." "Repeated failures can generate such strong feelings that eventually the child is reluctant to attempt any new task… Consequently, the child may no longer try."
q_0526.trap: (C) understates a real obstacle the chapter names: "society places a higher value on success in team sports than on success in repairing a bicycle," so compensating through a less valued skill "is difficult for children." (D) drops half the source — feelings of inferiority come "from children themselves or from the social environment."

q_0527.topic: industry versus inferiority in the school-age child
q_0527.stem: A 10-year-old consistently sets goals far beyond what he can achieve and is repeatedly disappointed. Which principle applies?
options: Children who aspire to more than they are capable of usually experience failure, whereas children who set their aspirations lower than their level of achievement are likely to experience success
Setting the highest possible goals always builds industry
Aspiration level has no relationship to experienced success at this age
The child should be told to stop setting goals until he is older
q_0527.rationale: "Children who aspire to more than they are capable of usually experience failure. In contrast, children who set their aspirations lower than their level of achievement are likely to experience success." The chapter also notes that at this age "Most accomplishments during the school years are very public. Family, teachers, and peers are all aware of success or failure in school."
q_0527.trap: (B) is the encouraging advice adults reach for, and in this stage it manufactures the repeated failure that leads to a child refusing to attempt anything new. What builds industry is completing tasks, which requires aspirations the child can actually reach.

q_0528.topic: industry versus inferiority in the school-age child
q_0528.stem: A slow-to-warm-up 8-year-old becomes tearful and complains of stomachaches before each new after-school activity. What should the nurse advise the parents?
options: Encourage the child to try new experiences but allow adaptation at the child's own speed; pressure to move quickly into new situations only strengthens the tendency to withdraw
Insist the child attend every session without exception, so avoidance is not reinforced
Withdraw the child from all new activities until adolescence
Treat the somatic complaints as a medical problem requiring workup before proceeding
q_0528.rationale: Slow-to-warm-up children "exhibit discomfort when introduced to new situations and need time to become accustomed to a new environment, authority figures, and expectations," and may respond "with tears, somatic complaints, or other maneuvers to avoid the event." The guidance is to "Encourage them to try new experiences but allow them to adapt to their surroundings at their own speed," because "Pressure to move quickly into new situations only strengthens the tendency to withdraw." Attending with a friend, or contracting for permission to withdraw after a specified number of tries, may help.
q_0528.trap: (B) is the firm-hand answer and it produces the opposite of the intended effect in this temperament. (C) abandons the encouragement half of the instruction — the child is meant to try new things, just not on someone else's schedule.

q_0529.topic: concrete operations and conservation in the school-age child
q_0529.stem: A 9-year-old is shown two identical balls of clay, and one is flattened into a pancake. She says, "It's still the same amount — you could roll it back into a ball." Which concept is she using?
options: Identity
Reversibility
Reciprocity
Seriation
q_0529.rationale: Children justify conservation with one of three concepts. Reversibility is that "The clay can be reshaped into its original form (a ball)." Identity is that "Because nothing has been added and nothing has been taken away, the pancake is still the same clay. Nothing has changed but the shape." Reciprocity is that "Although the pancake appears larger in circumference, the ball is much thicker."
q_0529.trap: (A) is the neighbouring justification and the most commonly substituted one, because both amount to "it's still the same clay." The discriminator is the child's reasoning: identity appeals to nothing having been added or removed, while reversibility appeals to the transformation being undoable.

q_0530.topic: concrete operations and conservation in the school-age child
q_0530.stem: A second child, shown the same flattened clay, says, "It's wider, but it's a lot thinner too." Which concept is this, and what ability does it demonstrate?
options: Identity, demonstrating that nothing was added or removed
Reciprocity, demonstrating the ability to deal with two dimensions at the same time and to comprehend that a change in one dimension compensates for a change in another
Reversibility, demonstrating that the action can be undone
Classification, demonstrating grouping by shared attributes
q_0530.rationale: Reciprocity is the justification that "Although the pancake appears larger in circumference, the ball is much thicker." The child "demonstrates the ability to deal with two dimensions at the same time and to comprehend that a change in one dimension compensates for a change in another." Once children can use all three concepts, "they can conserve along any physical dimension."
q_0530.trap: (C) is the mirror error of the previous item. Nothing in this child's reasoning refers to undoing the change; the reasoning tracks two dimensions simultaneously, which is the cognitive step reciprocity names.

q_0531.topic: concrete operations and conservation in the school-age child
q_0531.stem: A 7-year-old can conserve number and liquid but insists that a ball of clay weighs more after being flattened. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Expected; there is a developmental sequence to conservation — number at 5 to 6 years, liquids, mass, and length at about 6 to 7 years, weight at 9 to 10 years, and volume last at 9 to 12 years
Delayed; conservation of weight is expected by 6 years
Concerning; conservation is acquired all at once or not at all
Advanced; conservation of liquid is not expected until 10 years
q_0531.rationale: "There appears to be a developmental sequence in children's capacity to conserve matter": numbers at 5 to 6 years, "liquids, mass, and length" at about 6 to 7 years, weight at 9 to 10 years, and "volume or displacement" at 9 to 12 years.
q_0531.trap: (C) is the assumption that conservation is a single switch, and the staggered sequence is precisely what makes this child's answer normal. A 7-year-old who conserves liquid but not weight is exactly on schedule.

q_0532.topic: concrete operations and conservation in the school-age child
q_0532.stem: An 8-year-old has begun amassing large collections of cards, rocks, and stuffed animals, and ranks her friends as "first best friend" and "second best friend." Which cognitive ability underlies both behaviors?
options: Classification — the ability to group objects according to attributes they have in common, holding a concept in mind while making decisions based on it
Conservation of volume
Egocentrism
Metalinguistic awareness
q_0532.rationale: Classification is "the ability to group objects according to the attributes that they have in common." School-age children "can place things in a sensible and logical order, group and sort, and hold a concept in their minds while they make decisions based on that concept." This is why they "become occupied with numerous and varied collections," and why "They even begin to order friends and relationships (e.g., first best friend, second best friend)."
q_0532.trap: (C) belongs to the preschooler and is what concrete operations is replacing: "Their rigid, egocentric outlook is replaced by thought processes that allow them to see things from another's point of view."

q_0533.topic: concrete operations and conservation in the school-age child
q_0533.stem: A nurse is explaining what changes cognitively when a child enters concrete operations, between ages 7 and 11. Which statement is accurate?
options: Children progress from making judgments based on what they see, which is perceptual thinking, to judgments based on what they reason, which is conceptual thinking, and they can delay an action until they have evaluated alternative responses
Children in concrete operations can reason abstractly about hypothetical situations
Children in concrete operations must still carry out an action before they can anticipate its result
Egocentrism increases during this stage
q_0533.rationale: "The concrete operational stage occurs between ages 7 and 11 years." Children "progress from making judgments based on what they see (perceptual thinking) to making judgments based on what they reason (conceptual thinking)," and "are able to delay an action until they have evaluated alternative responses to situations." Their "steady reduction in egocentricity helps form the basis for logical thought and the development and maturation of morality."
q_0533.trap: (C) describes the preschooler and is what reversibility replaces: school-age children "have the ability to think through an action sequence, anticipate the consequences, and, if needed, return to the beginning and rethink the action in a different direction. They no longer need to experience an action before they can anticipate the results." (B) belongs to adolescence — abstract, principled reasoning is "not until adolescence or beyond."

q_0534.topic: school-age moral, spiritual, and language development
q_0534.stem: A 6-year-old says that a child who accidentally broke five cups is naughtier than one who deliberately broke a single cup. A 10-year-old in the same family disagrees. What explains the difference?
options: Younger school-age children usually judge an act by its consequences, while older school-age children are able to judge an act by the intentions that prompted it rather than just by the consequences
The 6-year-old is showing delayed moral development
Younger children judge by intentions and older children by consequences
Moral reasoning does not change across the school-age years
q_0534.rationale: Younger school-age children, 6 to 7 years, "know the rules and behaviors expected of them, but they do not understand the reasons behind them" and "usually judge an act by its consequences. Rewards and punishment guide their judgment." Older school-age children are "able to judge an act by the intentions that prompted it rather than just by the consequences," and rules become "less absolute and authoritarian."
q_0534.trap: (C) is the straight inversion of the pair. (B) mistakes a normal stage for a delay — this is exactly what a 6-year-old's moral reasoning is expected to look like, and it is the reason the two children in this stem disagree.

q_0535.topic: school-age moral, spiritual, and language development
q_0535.stem: A hospitalized 8-year-old asks the nurse whether she got sick because she was mean to her brother last week. Which understanding should guide the response?
options: School-age children often view illness or injury as a punishment for a real or imagined misdeed, are developing a conscience, and want and expect to be punished for misbehavior
This reflects magical thinking that should have resolved by age 5 and warrants referral
Children this age do not connect behavior with illness
The child is attempting to avoid a procedure
q_0535.rationale: School-age children "are fascinated by heaven and hell and, with a developing conscience and concern about rules, they fear going to hell for misbehavior. School-age children want and expect to be punished for misbehavior and, if given the option, tend to choose a punishment that 'fits the crime.' Often they view illness or injury as a punishment for a real or imagined misdeed."
q_0535.trap: (B) mislabels a normal feature of this stage as a residue of preschool magical thinking. The mechanism differs: the preschooler believes thoughts cause events, while the school-age child believes misdeeds earn punishment — a moral framework rather than a magical one.

q_0536.topic: school-age moral, spiritual, and language development
q_0536.stem: A 10-year-old is delighted by puns and riddles and can explain what "A stitch in time saves nine" means. Which language development does this demonstrate?
options: Metalinguistic awareness — an ability to think about language and comment on its properties, which enables appreciation of jokes, riddles, and puns and understanding of metaphors and figurative statements
Telegraphic speech
The minimum-distance principle
Egocentric speech
q_0536.rationale: Metalinguistic awareness is "an ability to think about language and to comment on its properties." This "enables them to appreciate jokes, riddles, and puns that involve play on words, sounds, or double meanings," and to begin understanding "metaphors and figurative statements, such as 'A stitch in time saves nine.'" Children become "less likely to engage in literal interpretation of messages."
q_0536.trap: (C) names a real school-age language rule, but a different one — the minimum-distance principle is "the rule that the subject of a verb in an active sentence is the noun or pronoun that immediately precedes it," which is why a 6-year-old understands "Ask Mary her last name" but is confused by "Ask Mary what to bring to the party" until age 9 or 10.

q_0537.topic: school-age moral, spiritual, and language development
q_0537.stem: A nurse plans religious and spiritual support for a hospitalized 8-year-old. Which approach fits the chapter?
options: Present religious concepts in concrete terms, since children this age have difficulty understanding symbols, and recognize that the beliefs of family and religious personages are more influential than those of peers in matters of faith
Use abstract theological explanations, since concrete operations allow abstract reasoning
Rely on peer influence, which predominates over family in matters of faith at this age
Avoid religious ritual, which increases anxiety in hospitalized children
q_0537.rationale: "Religious concepts must be presented to them in concrete terms" because children this age "have difficulty understanding symbols." "The beliefs and ideals of family and religious personages are more influential than those of their peers in matters of faith," and religious rituals "can help children cope with threatening situations."
q_0537.trap: (C) generalizes the chapter's emphasis on peer influence into a domain where the chapter says the opposite. Peers dominate standards for dress, behavior, and acceptance; family and religious figures dominate faith.

q_0538.topic: school-age peer groups, clubs, and team play
q_0538.stem: A 10-year-old belongs to a club with a secret code, a required style of dress, and elaborate rules for membership. The parents ask whether this rigidity is healthy. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: A prominent feature of middle childhood groups is the code of rigid rules imposed on members, and conforming to the rules provides children with feelings of security and relieves them of the responsibility of making decisions
Rigid group rules at this age indicate an unhealthy need for control
Conformity to peer rules replaces family values permanently
Formalized clubs are unusual in middle childhood and warrant assessment
q_0538.rationale: "One of the outstanding characteristics of middle childhood is the formation of formalized groups or clubs," and "A prominent feature of middle childhood groups is the code of rigid rules imposed on the members." "Conformity is the core of the group structure." Membership is marked by "secret codes, shared interests, special styles of dress, and special words," and "Conforming to the rules provides children with feelings of security and relieves them of the responsibility of making decisions."
q_0538.trap: (C) overstates what conformity displaces, and the chapter is explicit that children "substitute conformity to a peer-group pattern for conformity to a family pattern while they are still too insecure to function independently" — a substitution that is temporary and partial.

q_0539.topic: school-age peer groups, clubs, and team play
q_0539.stem: A parent worries that their 11-year-old is adopting peer values that conflict with the family's. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Although the peer group is highly influential and necessary to normal development, parents are the primary influence in shaping personality, setting standards, and establishing values, and family values usually predominate when parental and peer value systems come into conflict
Peer values reliably displace family values by this age
Children who test peer values have rejected family values permanently
Peer influence is not significant until adolescence
q_0539.rationale: "Although the peer group is highly influential and necessary to normal child development, parents are the primary influence in shaping children's personalities, setting standards for behavior, and establishing value systems. Family values usually predominate when parental and peer value systems come into conflict." Children "may appear to reject parental values while testing the new values of the peer group," but "ultimately they retain and incorporate many parental values into their own value systems."
q_0539.trap: (B) is the fear that brings parents to this conversation, and the chapter answers it directly. Note the related finding: children "need and want restrictions placed on their behavior" and "are uneasy if they succeed" in breaking down parental limits.

q_0540.topic: school-age peer groups, clubs, and team play
q_0540.stem: A 10-year-old on a losing soccer team is distraught about having let the team down. What does the chapter say team play teaches, and what caution applies?
options: Team play teaches subordinating personal goals to group goals and the concept of interdependence, with each member's behavior open to public evaluation; however, winning is not universally given high value, and some cultures emphasize the game and consideration for one's companions rather than the outcome
Team play teaches that winning is the universal measure of success
Children this age are unaffected by team loss
Team play has no cognitive benefit at this age
q_0540.rationale: Each child on a team "is accountable to the other team members," each member's behavior "is open to public evaluation," and children "risk ostracism, ridicule, or scapegoating if they contribute to a team loss," learning "the concept of interdependence." Because "losing is often interpreted as failure," children go to great lengths to avoid public embarrassment — "However, winning is not universally given high value. Some cultures and subcultures emphasize the game and consideration for one's companions rather than the outcome."
q_0540.trap: (D) misses a named benefit: team play requires children "to learn many complex rules, make judgments about those rules, plan strategies, and assess the strengths and weaknesses" of both teams, which is cognitive growth as well as social.

q_0541.topic: school-age peer groups, clubs, and team play
q_0541.stem: A nurse is explaining what children gain from peer interaction that they cannot gain from family. Which statement reflects the chapter?
options: Because age-mates are not authorities, other children have a significant influence on decreasing the egocentric outlook, and children learn to argue, persuade, bargain, cooperate, and compromise to maintain friendships
Peer interaction primarily reinforces what the family has already taught
Peer relationships at this age are interchangeable and carry no lasting significance
Best friendships are discouraged at this age in favor of larger group membership
q_0541.rationale: Through peers, children "discover that there are many occupations for fathers and mothers, more than one version of the same song, different rules for the same game." Because age-mates are not authorities, "other children have a significant influence on decreasing the egocentric outlook," and children "learn to argue, persuade, bargain, cooperate, and compromise to maintain friendships."
q_0541.trap: (C) dismisses what the chapter treats as formative: school age "is the time when children have 'best friends' with whom they share secrets, private jokes, and adventures," and these dyadic relationships "seem to be important as a foundation for relationships in adulthood." Because "neither child has authority over the other," the children must work through differences themselves.

q_0542.stem: A school nurse is asked to define bullying for a staff in-service. Which definition reflects the chapter?
options: Any recurring activity that intends to cause harm, distress, or control toward another individual where there is a perceived imbalance of power between the aggressor and the victim
Any single act of physical aggression between two children of equal status
Any conflict between children in which one child becomes upset
Physical aggression only, since verbal acts are classified separately
q_0542.rationale: Bullying is "any recurring activity that intends to cause harm, distress, or control toward another individual where there is a perceived imbalance of power between the aggressor(s) and the victim." It "can occur in varying degrees of severity in a physical, social, or emotional context."
q_0542.trap: (B) drops both defining elements — the recurrence and the power imbalance — which is what separates bullying from an ordinary conflict between peers. (C) drops them too and would classify every playground dispute as bullying, which makes the term useless for the interventions that follow from it.

q_0543.stem: A school nurse is advising on where to concentrate supervision to reduce bullying. Which statement reflects the chapter?
options: Although bullying can occur in any setting, it usually takes place in school hallways or on the playground where supervision is minimal but peers are present to witness the attack
Bullying occurs most often in the classroom, under direct teacher observation
Bullying occurs mainly when no other children are present
Location has no bearing on where bullying occurs
q_0543.rationale: "Although bullying can occur in any setting, it usually takes place in school hallways or on the playground where supervision is minimal but peers are present to witness the attack."
q_0543.trap: (C) misses the audience element, which is part of why location matters: the attack requires witnesses to accomplish what it is for. That combination — minimal supervision plus present peers — is what makes hallways and playgrounds the characteristic setting, and it is why high levels of playground supervision is a named effective intervention.

q_0544.stem: A nurse compares traditional bullying with cyberbullying for a parent group. Which statement is accurate?
options: Cyberbullying can be more harmful than traditional bullying because the attack can instantly reach a wider audience while allowing the bully to remain anonymous; traditional bullying risk is greater in elementary and middle school, while cyberbullying is more frequent in high school
Cyberbullying is less harmful than traditional bullying because there is no physical contact
Both forms peak in elementary school
Cyberbullying always identifies the perpetrator, making intervention easier
q_0544.rationale: Cyberbullying "involves an electronic medium to harm or bother another individual and can be more harmful than traditional bullying because the attack can instantly reach a wider audience, while allowing the bully to remain anonymous." Risk of traditional bullying is greater in elementary and middle school than high school, while cyberbullying is more frequent in high school. Up to 30% of school-age children engage in bullying, and 11% to 42% in cyberbullying as bully or victim.
q_0544.trap: (B) is the intuition that physical harm is the measure of severity, and the chapter names the two features that make the electronic form worse instead: reach and anonymity.

q_0545.stem: A school nurse notes that boys and girls in the school bully differently. Which statement reflects the chapter?
options: Boys tend to use physical force, referred to as direct bullying, while girls usually use methods such as exclusion, gossip, or rumors, referred to as indirect bullying
Boys use indirect bullying and girls use direct bullying
Exclusion and gossip are not classified as bullying
Only physical force meets the definition of bullying
q_0545.rationale: Boys who bully "tend to use physical force, referred to as direct bullying," while girls usually use "bullying methods, such as exclusion, gossip, or rumors, which is referred to as indirect bullying."
q_0545.trap: (C) and (D) both exclude the indirect form from the definition, which would make most girls' bullying invisible to a school's response. Bullying occurs "in a physical, social, or emotional context," and social exclusion qualifies on the definition's own terms.

q_0546.stem: A school is planning an antibullying program. Which approaches does the chapter identify as effective? Select all that apply.
options: High levels of playground supervision
Schoolwide rules related to bullying
Teacher training
Grouping students who bully together
Parent training activities and meetings
q_0546.rationale: Effective approaches are "high levels of playground supervision," "schoolwide rules related to bullying," "teacher training," and "parent training activities and meetings." Bullying "can be reduced or prevented through supportive relationships with family, intervention of school personnel, and involvement with positive peer groups."
q_0546.trap: (D) is one of two approaches the chapter names as ineffective, the other being "brief (e.g., 1-day) awareness campaigns." It pulls because grouping looks like targeted intervention; in practice it concentrates children who "have aggressive attitudes" and "a positive view of violence" into one room.

q_0547.topic: school-age self-concept, sexuality, and sex education
q_0547.stem: A nurse is assessing an 11-year-old's self-concept. Which statement reflects the chapter's definitions?
options: Self-concept is a conscious awareness of a variety of self-perceptions including physical characteristics, abilities, values, and self-ideals and one's idea of self in relation to others, and it includes body image, sexuality, and self-esteem
Self-concept and self-esteem are interchangeable terms
Body image is determined solely by the opinions of significant others
Self-esteem consists only of positive qualities
q_0547.rationale: Self-concept is "a conscious awareness of a variety of self-perceptions, such as one's physical characteristics, abilities, values, and self-ideals, and one's idea of self in relation to others. It also includes one's body image, sexuality, and self-esteem." Children's self-concepts are "composed of their own critical self-assessments plus their interpretations of the opinions of others."
q_0547.trap: (C) drops the qualifier the chapter puts in the definition: body image is "what children think about their bodies and is influenced, but not solely determined, by significant others." (D) drops the other half of self-esteem, which "consists of both positive and negative qualities."

q_0548.topic: school-age self-concept, sexuality, and sex education
q_0548.stem: Parents discover their 9-year-old engaging in sex play with a same-age friend and ask the nurse whether this indicates a problem. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Many children experience some form of sex play during or before preadolescence as a response to normal curiosity, not as a result of love or sexual urge; it is incidental and transitory, and adverse emotional consequences depend largely on how the parents manage the behavior
Sex play at this age indicates prior sexual abuse in all cases
Expressions of anger or disgust are the most effective parental response
Sex play at this age reflects a precocious sexual urge requiring evaluation
q_0548.rationale: "Many children experience some form of sex play during or before preadolescence as a response to normal curiosity, not as a result of love or sexual urge. Children are experimentalists by nature, and this play is incidental and transitory." "Any adverse emotional consequences or guilt feelings depend on how the parents manage the behavior and whether children view their actions as wrong in the eyes of significant persons, particularly their parents."
q_0548.trap: (C) names a response the chapter specifically identifies as harmful: parents who discourage exploration through "expressions of anger or disgust" communicate that children "should not engage in such activities, discourage questions about sex, and limit the sources of information."

q_0549.topic: school-age self-concept, sexuality, and sex education
q_0549.stem: A parent believes their 10-year-old has learned everything needed about sex from home. Which finding should the nurse share?
options: Sexual information received in childhood is often acquired almost entirely from peers, is transmitted in secret conversation, and contains misinformation; in one study most parents believed they were open about sex education, but only a few communicated direct information about safe sex practices
Children reliably obtain accurate sexual information from peers
Formal sex education is inappropriate during middle childhood
Parents are the sole source of sexual information for most school-age children
q_0549.rationale: "Sexual information received in childhood is often acquired almost entirely from peers." One study found that although most parents "believed they were open with sex education discussions… only a few parents communicated direct information about safe sex practices." Peer-sourced information "is often transmitted and exchanged in secret conversation and contains misinformation."
q_0549.trap: (C) contradicts the chapter's own judgment that middle childhood "is an ideal time for formal sex education," particularly when presented "from a life span perspective" and treated "as a normal part of growth and development," which makes the information "less likely to contain overtones of uncertainty, guilt, or embarrassment."

q_0550.topic: school-age self-concept, sexuality, and sex education
q_0550.stem: A nurse is planning sex education sessions for a fifth-grade class. Which approach reflects the chapter?
options: School-age children may be more comfortable when boys and girls are segregated for discussions, but each group needs information about both sexes
Boys and girls should always be taught together, since separating them creates shame
Each group needs information only about its own sex
Preadolescents should be given general principles rather than concrete answers to specific questions
q_0550.rationale: "School-age children may be more comfortable when boys and girls are segregated for discussions; however, each group needs information about both sexes." The nurse should treat sex "as a normal part of growth and development" and answer questions "honestly, matter-of-factly, and at the child's level of understanding."
q_0550.trap: (C) takes the first half of the guidance and drops the second, which is the half that matters — segregating the audience is a comfort measure, not a restriction on content. (D) inverts what preadolescents need: they ask concrete questions such as "What if I start my period in the middle of class?" and should be told "what they want to know and what they can expect to happen as they mature sexually."

q_0551.topic: school experience, discipline, and dishonest behavior
q_0551.stem: Parents ask the nurse how to support their child's success at school. Which guidelines does the chapter give? Select all that apply.
options: Demonstrate an interest in content and growth more than in grades
Provide a quiet, well-lit area for study without television or music
Make it clear to the child that schoolwork is between the child and the teacher
Complete difficult homework problems for the child to prevent frustration
Send the child to school every day, since other plans convey that school is unimportant
q_0551.rationale: The specific guidelines include "send the child to school every day" because other plans "convey the impression that school is unimportant"; "demonstrate an interest in content and growth more than in grades"; "make it clear to the child that schoolwork is between the child and the teacher" so the child feels "responsible for school successes and failures"; and "provide a quiet, well-lit area for study… do not allow television or music."
q_0551.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and the chapter draws the line precisely: "help with homework should focus on explaining the question, not giving the answer." Doing the work removes the responsibility the third guideline exists to establish.

q_0552.topic: school experience, discipline, and dishonest behavior
q_0552.stem: Parents of a 9-year-old ask whether spanking is an effective disciplinary measure. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Parents should not use punitive actions or corporal punishment, because these methods are of limited value and are associated with poor internalizing behaviors such as depression and anxiety, poor externalizing behaviors such as aggression, slower cognitive development, and increased risk for physical abuse
Spanking is effective when used consistently and immediately
Corporal punishment is appropriate for school-age children but not for preschoolers
Discipline at this age should be limited to withholding affection
q_0552.rationale: "Parents should not use punitive actions or corporal punishment because these methods are of limited value and are associated with multiple negative consequences." Spanking is linked to "poor internalizing behaviors such as depression, anxiety, and hopelessness; poor externalizing behaviors such as aggression and violence; slower cognitive development; and increased risk for physical abuse." Reasoning "is an effective disciplinary technique for school-age children," with time-out to stop a behavior acutely, and withholding privileges, requiring recompense, imposing penalties, and contracting as cognitive skills advance.
q_0552.trap: (D) names a technique with its own documented harm and is not among the alternatives the chapter offers. The chapter's stated best approach is different again: "Problem solving is the best approach to limit setting, and children themselves can be included in the process of determining appropriate disciplinary measures."

q_0553.topic: school experience, discipline, and dishonest behavior
q_0553.stem: A 6-year-old repeatedly cheats at board games to win. What should the nurse tell the parents?
options: Cheating is most common in young children ages 5 to 6 years, who find it difficult to lose and have not yet acquired the full realization of the wrongfulness of the behavior; it usually disappears as they mature
Cheating at this age predicts dishonesty in adulthood and requires intervention
Cheating indicates the child does not understand the rules of the game
The child should be excluded from games until the behavior stops
q_0553.rationale: "Cheating is most common in young children, ages 5 to 6 years." They "find it difficult to lose at a game or contest, and they cheat to win. They have not yet acquired the full realization of the wrongfulness of this behavior and do it almost automatically. It usually disappears as they mature."
q_0553.trap: (B) treats a developmental behavior as a character trait. The chapter does name a real risk, but it lies with the adults: "when children observe parental behaviors such as boasting about cheating on income taxes, they assume this to be appropriate behavior."

q_0554.topic: school experience, discipline, and dishonest behavior
q_0554.stem: A 7-year-old has taken money from a parent's wallet. Which approach does the chapter recommend?
options: In most situations it is best not to attempt to find a hidden or deep meaning to the stealing; a reprimand together with an appropriate and reasonable punishment, such as having the older child pay back the money or return the stolen items, will ordinarily suffice
