Ask the child directly whether they took the money, to establish honesty
Search the child's room and belongings without explanation
Assume the behavior signals serious emotional disturbance requiring referral
q_0554.rationale: "In most situations it is best not to attempt to find a hidden or deep meaning to the stealing. A reprimand, together with an appropriate and reasonable punishment, such as having the older child pay back the money or return the stolen items, will ordinarily take care of most cases." Between ages 5 and 8 years "children's sense of property rights is limited."
q_0554.trap: (B) is the parent's natural first move and the chapter advises against it: "It is seldom helpful to trap children into admission by asking directly if they did the offensive thing," since children "do not take on such responsibility until nearer the end of middle childhood." (C) undermines the very thing being taught — "If children's personal rights are respected, they are more likely to respect the rights of others."

q_0555.topic: school experience, discipline, and dishonest behavior
q_0555.stem: A 10-year-old has begun telling elaborate untrue stories about family vacations. Which understanding should guide the nurse's counseling?
options: School-age children can distinguish what is real from what is make-believe and often exaggerate a story as a means to impress family or friends; older children may also lie because of low self-esteem or to meet expectations they have been unable to meet
A school-age child who lies cannot yet distinguish fantasy from reality
Lying at this age always indicates an underlying conduct disorder
Severe punishment is the most effective deterrent to lying
q_0555.rationale: School-age children "still tell stories but can distinguish between what is real and what is make-believe." They often "exaggerate a story… as a means to impress their family or friends." Older children "may lie to meet expectations set by others to which they have been unable to measure up," "because of low self-esteem," or "as a means of getting ahead."
q_0555.trap: (B) describes the preschooler, who does "not have the cognitive capacity to deliberately mislead." (D) is contradicted directly: "Lying is more common in families in which punishment is severe," and "If parents lie, the children will emulate their behavior."

q_0556.topic: school-age stress, fears, and latchkey children
q_0556.stem: A school nurse is teaching parents which changes in a school-age child warrant further exploration for stress. Which findings does the Nursing Alert name? Select all that apply.
options: Stomach pains or headache
Bedwetting, or regression to earlier behaviors such as thumb sucking
Trouble concentrating or changes in academic performance
Wanting to spend increasing time with same-sex friends
Aggressive or stubborn behavior, or withdrawal and reluctance to participate
q_0556.rationale: The Nursing Alert directs exploring further on observing "Stomach pains or headache; Sleep problems; Bedwetting; Changes in eating habits; Aggressive or stubborn behavior; Withdrawal or reluctance to participate; Regression to earlier behaviors (e.g., thumb sucking); Trouble concentrating or changes in academic performance."
q_0556.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort and describes normal school-age social development rather than distress. "Identification with peers is a strong influence in children's gaining independence from parents," and same-sex peer groups are characteristic of this stage.

q_0557.topic: school-age stress, fears, and latchkey children
q_0557.stem: An 11-year-old tells the nurse privately that he is afraid of failing sixth grade but would never admit it to friends. Which understanding applies?
options: Most new fears troubling school-age children relate to school and family, and children are inclined to hide their fears to avoid being ridiculed or labeled; hiding fears does not end them, and children afraid to communicate them may develop displaced fears or phobias
School-age children readily disclose fears to peers
Fears at this age are the same as those of the preschool years
A child who hides a fear has resolved it
q_0557.rationale: "Most new fears that trouble school-age children are related to school and family" — "fear of failing, fear of teachers and bullies, or fear of something bad happening to their parents." School-age children "are inclined to hide their fears to avoid being ridiculed or labeled as a 'baby' or 'chicken'. Hiding fears does not end them, and children who are afraid to communicate their fears may develop displaced fears or phobias."
q_0557.trap: (C) misses a real shift: school-age children are "less fearful of body safety" and have "less fear of noises, darkness, storms, and dogs" than preschoolers, but they "fear death and are fascinated by all aspects of death and dying." The content of the fears changes even as the number does not.

q_0558.topic: school-age stress, fears, and latchkey children
q_0558.stem: A nurse is teaching a 10-year-old to manage stress. Which approach reflects the chapter?
options: Teach the child to recognize signs of stress in themselves, such as a pounding heart, rapid breathing, or butterflies in the stomach, and teach deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, positive imagery, and physical activity
Shield the child from all sources of stress, since any stress is harmful at this age
Teach the child to suppress physical signs of stress so peers do not notice
Have the child list only the solutions that will definitely work, to avoid wasting effort
q_0558.rationale: Children "need to learn how to recognize signs of stress in themselves, such as a pounding heart, rapid breathing, or 'butterflies' in the stomach." Techniques include "deep-breathing exercises, progressive relaxation of muscle groups, and positive imagery," and "blow[ing] off steam' through physical activity."
q_0558.trap: (D) truncates the problem-solving sequence the chapter gives, which deliberately starts wide: list all possibilities "including those they know will not work," examine the consequences of each, then select the best option. Adaptive coping is described as problem solving, emotional regulation, and cognitive reappraisal; maladaptive coping shows as withdrawal and helplessness or as aggression and blaming others.

q_0559.topic: school-age stress, fears, and latchkey children
q_0559.stem: A nurse counsels the parents of a 10-year-old who stays alone after school. Which instructions does the chapter give? Select all that apply.
options: Teach the child not to enter the house after school if the door is ajar, a window is open, or anything appears unusual
Teach the child to tell callers that parents are busy and cannot come to the phone right now
Teach the child to tell callers honestly that the parents are not at home
Teach the child not to display keys and to always lock doors
Be punctual in arriving home, since a child's anxiety accelerates when parents are not home when expected
q_0559.rationale: The Family-Centered Care guidance directs teaching the child "not to display keys and to always lock doors," and to not enter the house "if the door is ajar, a window is open, or anything appears unusual." For the telephone: "Teach the child to tell callers that parents are 'busy' and cannot come to the phone right now; instruct the child not to tell a caller that parents are not at home." On loneliness: "be punctual in arriving home. A child's anxiety level accelerates when parents are not home when expected."
q_0559.trap: (C) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it is the instruction the chapter explicitly reverses. Honesty is the child's default and the reason the script has to be taught deliberately; the number of school-age children spending time alone has decreased to about 15%, but the ones who do are at greater risk for injury and delinquent behavior.

q_0560.topic: school-age injury prevention and bicycle safety
q_0560.stem: A nurse compares injury patterns in school-age children with those of younger children. Which statements reflect the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: The incidence of unintentional injury is diminished in middle childhood compared with early childhood, because of more refined muscular coordination and control
The incidence of injury is significantly higher in school-age boys than girls, and boys' death rate is twice that of girls
The incidence of transportation-related injuries is higher in school-age children than in younger children
Injuries from burns and poisonings are at their peak during the school-age years
Most injuries occur in or near the home or school
q_0560.rationale: Because school-age children "have developed more refined muscular coordination and control," the incidence of unintentional injury "is diminished in middle childhood compared with early childhood," though they encounter more environments with less supervision. "The incidence of injury during middle childhood is significantly higher in school-age boys than in school-age girls, and their death rate is twice that of girls." "Most injuries occur in or near the home or school," and transportation-related injury incidence is higher than in younger children.
q_0560.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort and inverts the chapter's statement: "Injuries from burns and poisonings are lowest in school-age children." What is high instead is "childhood fractures, strains, and sprains," along with cuts and abrasions.

q_0561.topic: school-age injury prevention and bicycle safety
q_0561.stem: A 7-year-old weighing 52 pounds and measuring 48 inches is being restrained with the vehicle's adult lap-shoulder belt alone. Which response is correct?
options: A booster seat should be used until the child is 57 inches tall, and the rear vehicle seat is the safest place for children younger than 13 years old
An adult belt is appropriate once a child reaches 7 years of age
The front seat is acceptable for children over 6 years old
Booster seats are discontinued at 40 pounds
q_0561.rationale: "Booster seats should be used until the child is 57 inches tall," and "The rear vehicle seat is the safest place for children younger than 13 years old." In 2014, 602 children ages 0 to 12 years died in motor vehicle accidents and 121,350 were injured, and "34% of those who died were not using a seat belt."
q_0561.trap: (B) uses age where the chapter uses height, which is the substitution that leaves children in adult belts too early. The chapter explains why belts fail children ages 5 to 9 specifically: the child's "center of gravity is located above the level of the lap belt," so body mass above the belt causes "jackknifing over the belt," and the child's "smaller and less developed iliac crests" cannot anchor an adult restraint.

q_0562.topic: school-age injury prevention and bicycle safety
q_0562.stem: A parent asks why a bicycle helmet matters so much when their child only rides on quiet streets. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Head injury is the major cause of bicycle-related fatalities, so the single most important aspect of bicycle safety is wearing a protective helmet; helmet use reduces head injury by 51%, serious head injury by 69%, and fatal head injury by 65%
Helmets primarily prevent facial injury rather than head injury
Helmets are needed only for riding in traffic
Helmet effectiveness has not been quantified
q_0562.rationale: "Because head injury is the major cause of bicycle-related fatalities, the single most important aspect of bicycle safety is to encourage the rider to wear a protective helmet." Helmet use reduces head injury by 51%, serious head injury by 69%, facial injury by 33%, and fatal head injury by 65%. Hard-shelled helmets lined with expanded polystyrene "provide the best head protection," should fit securely without limiting vision or hearing, should carry a Consumer Product Safety Commission seal, and "should be replaced after any damage or crash."
q_0562.trap: (B) names the smallest of the four reductions and misses the one that drives the recommendation. Note the fitting rule too: the helmet "should sit on top of the head in a level position and should not rock back and forth or from side to side," with the strap "fastened securely under the chin."

q_0563.topic: school-age injury prevention and bicycle safety
q_0563.stem: Parents say their 9-year-old refuses to wear a bicycle helmet, and neither parent wears one. Which information is most useful?
options: Ninety percent of children reported they were likely to wear a helmet if their parent used a helmet, compared with only 38% of children reporting a likelihood to wear one if their parent did not
Helmet laws are more influential than parental behavior
Children's helmet use is unrelated to parental modeling
Children this age cannot be expected to wear helmets consistently
q_0563.rationale: "Ninety percent of children reported they were likely to wear a helmet if their parent used a helmet, compared with only 38% of children reporting a likelihood to wear a helmet if their parent did not use a helmet." Legislation has a smaller effect: "51% of children always wearing a helmet in states that have helmet laws and only 40% of children always wearing a helmet in states that do not."
q_0563.trap: (B) reverses the relative size of the two effects. Both matter, but the gap produced by parental modeling — 90% against 38% — is far larger than the gap produced by state law, which makes the parents in this stem the intervention rather than the audience.

q_0564.stem: A 9-year-old girl's body mass index falls at the 91st percentile for her age and sex. How should the nurse classify this?
options: Overweight, which is a body mass index at the 85th to 94th percentile
Obesity, which is a body mass index at or above the 95th percentile
Normal weight, since the value is below the 95th percentile
Severe obesity, requiring immediate referral for bariatric evaluation
q_0564.rationale: Overweight is a body mass index at the "85th to 94th percentile," age- and gender-specific; obesity is a body mass index "at or above the 95th percentile for children of the same age and sex." Body mass index is "the most accurate method for screening children and adolescents for obesity," calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared.
q_0564.trap: (B) names the adjacent band, and these two percentile ranges are the single most swappable pair of numbers in the chapter. Note the wording that decides borderline cases: obesity is "at or above" the 95th percentile, so a child exactly at the 95th percentile is obese rather than overweight.

q_0565.stem: A 12-year-old competitive swimmer has a body mass index at the 96th percentile but very low measured body fat. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: A subset of adolescents such as athletes may have a high body mass index because of increased muscle mass rather than fat mass, and clinical judgment is needed
The body mass index is diagnostic and the child should be treated for obesity
Body mass index in children uses fixed cut-points, so athletic status is irrelevant
Body mass index is not a useful screening tool in any child
q_0565.rationale: "A subset of adolescents (e.g., athletes) may have a high BMI because of increased muscle mass rather than fat mass. Clinical judgment is needed." Body mass index remains "currently considered the best method to assess weight in children and adolescents," but in children it "varies to accommodate age- and gender-specific changes in growth," unlike the fixed adult definitions.
q_0565.trap: (C) imports the adult framework, where "BMI definitions are fixed measures without regard for sex and age." Pediatric body mass index is interpreted by percentile precisely because the same raw number means different things at different ages.

q_0566.stem: A parent of an obese 10-year-old asks whether a thyroid problem or a slow metabolism explains the weight. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Fewer than 5% of childhood obesity is attributable to an underlying disease, and there is little evidence to support a relationship between obesity and low metabolism; energy imbalance is the usual explanation
Endocrine disease accounts for the majority of childhood obesity
A low basal metabolic rate is the most common identified cause
No endocrine condition ever causes childhood obesity
q_0566.rationale: Fewer than 5% of childhood obesity has an underlying disease, and there is "little evidence to support a relationship between obesity and low metabolism." Hypothyroidism, Cushing-type states, and hypothalamic damage do occur but are the minority.
q_0566.trap: (C) is the explanation families most often arrive with, and the chapter addresses it directly. (D) overcorrects — organic causes exist and are worth evaluating when the history suggests them; they are simply not where the answer usually lies.

q_0567.stem: A child with hypotonia, short stature, hypogonadism, almond-shaped eyes, and relentless food seeking is being evaluated for obesity. Which syndrome does this suggest, and what does it imply for management?
options: Prader-Willi syndrome; these children lack the internal mechanism that regulates satiety and go to great lengths to obtain food, so environmental control of food access is required
Prader-Willi syndrome; appetite counseling and portion education are sufficient
Cushing syndrome; corticosteroid excess explains the food seeking
Hypothyroidism; the food seeking resolves with hormone replacement
q_0567.rationale: Prader-Willi syndrome presents with hypotonia, hyperphagia, short stature, hypogonadism, and almond-shaped eyes. The functional key is that these children "lack the internal mechanism that regulates satiety and as a result go to great lengths to obtain food."
q_0567.trap: (B) names the right syndrome and the wrong intervention, which is the more consequential half of the item. Counseling a child to recognize fullness cannot work when the satiety mechanism itself is absent; the environment has to supply the limit the physiology does not.

q_0568.stem: An asymptomatic obese 11-year-old is being evaluated. Which findings are recognized complications of childhood obesity? Select all that apply.
options: Insulin resistance syndrome, which develops before hyperinsulinemia, obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia individually appear
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, the most common liver disease in children
Obstructive sleep apnea, reported in 20% to 30% of obese children and adolescents
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis and Blount disease
A low incidence of bullying, since peer groups accommodate weight differences at this age
q_0568.rationale: "The incidence of metabolic syndrome was 30% in obese children," and insulin resistance syndrome — hyperinsulinemia, obesity, hypertension, and dyslipidemia — "develops before any of these conditions develops." Between 10% and 25% of obese youth are diagnosed with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, "the most common liver disease in children." Obstructive sleep apnea "is reported in 20% to 30%." Musculoskeletal complications include slipped capital femoral epiphysis and Blount disease.
q_0568.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort and inverts the chapter: "overweight children are more frequently the victims of bullying compared with children of normal weight," including "name calling, teasing, threats, physical harm, rejection, rumors, and sexual harassment."

q_0569.stem: An obese 13-year-old has a normal alanine aminotransferase and feels well. The parent concludes the liver is unaffected. Which response is correct?
options: Liver enzymes in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease are either normal or slightly elevated, and people with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis may feel healthy and show no outward signs of liver disease, so a normal enzyme does not exclude it
A normal alanine aminotransferase reliably excludes fatty liver disease
Fatty liver disease in children always produces jaundice
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease does not progress in children
q_0569.rationale: In nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, alanine and aspartate aminotransferase are "either normal or slightly elevated," and "People with NASH may feel healthy and show no outward signs of liver disease." Approximately 25% of pediatric cases progress to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, in which fatty infiltration "causes liver inflammation… and may cause scarring," and may progress to "cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease" requiring transplantation. Diagnosis is by ultrasound, computed tomography, or liver biopsy; treatment is weight loss.
q_0569.trap: (B) is the inference the laboratory value invites, and it is why the chapter states the negative. A normal enzyme in a child with the risk factor is not reassurance; it is a reason to image rather than to stop looking.

q_0570.stem: An obese 13-year-old reports hip pain and has begun walking with a limp. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
options: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis, in which the cartilage plate at the top of the femur slips out of place; it is the most common hip disorder among young teenagers
Blount disease, an overgrowth of the medial proximal tibial metaphysis
Obstructive sleep apnea referred pain
Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis with referred pain to the hip
q_0570.rationale: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is "the most common hip disorder among young teenagers," occurring when "the cartilage plate (epiphysis) at the top of the femur slips out of place." Blount disease is a different entity: "overgrowth of the medial aspect of the proximal tibial metaphysis that causes the lower leg to angle inward (tibia vara)," with "a dose-response relationship between BMI and Blount disease."
q_0570.trap: (B) is the paired musculoskeletal complication and is distinguished by site: the hip points to slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and inward bowing of the lower leg points to Blount disease. Both are obesity complications, so the presenting location is the whole discriminator.

q_0571.stem: A 10-year-old with obesity bows inward at the lower legs below the knees. Which complication does this suggest?
options: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Blount disease, an overgrowth of the medial aspect of the proximal tibial metaphysis causing the lower leg to angle inward, known as tibia vara
A normal variant requiring no referral
Rickets from vitamin D deficiency, which obesity does not affect
q_0571.rationale: Blount disease is "overgrowth of the medial aspect of the proximal tibial metaphysis that causes the lower leg to angle inward (tibia vara)," and the chapter notes "a dose-response relationship between BMI and Blount disease." Orthopedic referral is the named pathway for it.
q_0571.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item. Both conditions share obesity as the driver and differ only in which joint is affected, so an item on this pair always turns on the anatomic site named in the stem.

q_0572.stem: A nurse is counseling the family of an obese 10-year-old about diet. Which approach reflects the chapter?
options: Focus dietary counseling on improving the nutritional quality of the diet rather than on dietary restriction, and advise the child to avoid fad diets
Prescribe a specific calorie restriction and weigh the child weekly
Recommend a commercially available fad diet, since adherence is higher
Restrict the child's food at home while allowing free choice elsewhere
q_0572.rationale: "Dietary counseling focuses on improving the nutritional quality of the diet rather than on dietary restriction. Children should avoid fad diets." The recommended profile is "no trans fats, low saturated fat, moderate total fat (≤30%), low sodium, and at least nine servings of fruits and vegetables," with high-fiber foods promoted and refined starches and sugars avoided.
q_0572.trap: (D) splits the environment in a way the chapter argues against; the emphasis is on parents taking "charge of family meals and the home food environment" so that "healthy choices are readily available," with meals eaten together "away from distractions such as television."

q_0573.stem: A nurse wants to increase physical activity in an obese 11-year-old. Which intervention does the chapter identify as most effective?
options: Limiting sedentary screen time behaviors, which is the most effective way to encourage physical activity, targeting 60 minutes or more of activity per day and less than 2 hours of screen time
Enrolling the child in a competitive sports league regardless of interest
Beginning a supervised weight-training program
Setting a daily pedometer target and no other change
q_0573.rationale: "Limiting sedentary screen time behaviors… is the most effective way to encourage physical activity." The paired figures are 60 minutes or more of physical activity per day and less than 2 hours of screen time, with a daily target of 10,000 to 15,000 steps.
q_0573.trap: (C) is addressed separately and with an age restriction, as the next item shows. (D) names a real target but adopts it in isolation; the pedometer measures the activity that removing screen time makes room for.

q_0574.stem: Parents of a prepubertal 9-year-old ask about starting weight training to reduce body fat. Which response is correct?
options: Weight training increases basal metabolic rate and replaces fat mass with muscle mass, but it is not generally recommended for prepubertal children until they have reached physical and skeletal maturity; increased outdoor playtime is the appropriate alternative
Weight training is the first-line activity intervention at any age
Weight training is contraindicated at every age in childhood
Prepubertal children gain muscle mass more efficiently than adolescents
q_0574.rationale: Weight training "increases basal metabolic rate and replaces fat mass with muscle mass" but is "not generally recommended for prepubertal children until they have reached physical and skeletal maturity." For this age group, increased outdoor playtime is the recommended approach. Chapter 15 gives the underlying reason: school-age muscles are "still functionally immature… and they are more readily injured by overuse."
q_0574.trap: (C) overcorrects into a blanket prohibition; the restriction is developmental rather than permanent, and it lifts at physical and skeletal maturity.

q_0575.stem: A 14-year-old is brought in by a parent who insists the adolescent begin a weight-loss program. The adolescent is uninterested and says the visit was not their idea. What should the nurse do first?
options: Explore the reasons behind the desire to lose weight, recognizing that it may be wiser to defer treatment until the family is ready
Begin a structured diet and exercise plan at this visit, since delay worsens outcomes
Refer immediately for bariatric surgical evaluation
Counsel the adolescent privately that the parent's concern should be disregarded
q_0575.rationale: The Nursing Alert makes motivation the pivot: explore "the reasons behind the desire to lose weight." And on timing, "It may be wiser to defer treatment until the family is ready." Treatment of obesity "is difficult," and "the average individual only loses about 5% to 10% of his or her weight with available therapies," with lost weight "frequently regained in a year or two."
q_0575.trap: (B) starts a plan with no one committed to carrying it out, which is what the deferral guidance exists to prevent. Beginning and failing is not neutral — it adds a documented failure to a child already at risk for "a negative self-image and low body satisfaction that persists into adulthood."

q_0576.stem: A severely obese 16-year-old is being considered for bariatric surgery. Which criteria apply? Select all that apply.
options: Attainment of Tanner stage 4 or 95% of adult linear growth
A body mass index of 35 or above with severe comorbidity
A body mass index of 40 or above with less severe comorbidity
Avoidance of pregnancy for at least 18 months postoperatively
Completion of at least 5 years of documented dietary failure before consideration
q_0576.rationale: The bariatric surgery criteria are attainment of Tanner stage 4 or 95% of adult linear growth; a body mass index of 35 or above with severe comorbidity, or 40 or above with less severe comorbidity; and avoidance of pregnancy for at least 18 months postoperatively.
q_0576.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort — no such duration requirement appears in the criteria. Note the relationship among the real ones, which is counterintuitive and therefore testable: the *higher* body mass index threshold pairs with the *milder* comorbidity, because either severe disease or extreme weight alone can justify the procedure.

q_0577.topic: dental disorders in the school-age child
q_0577.stem: A parent asks which is worse for a child's teeth — a large soda with dinner or a lollipop eaten between meals. Which response reflects the chapter?
options: Sucrose has been consistently implicated as the most cariogenic, and the damage depends on form and timing, so sticky or chewy candy and lollipops ingested between meals are worse than a larger quantity of sugar taken with a meal
The total quantity of sugar is the only factor that matters
Liquid sugars are more cariogenic than sticky candies in all circumstances
Timing of sugar intake has no effect on caries risk
q_0577.rationale: "Sucrose has been consistently implicated as the most cariogenic," and the damage depends on form and timing — sticky or sour chewy candy and lollipops, "ingested between meals." Conversely, "saliva, some foods, and chewing gum after a meal" help neutralize acid.
q_0577.trap: (B) is the intuitive metric and it is the weaker answer here. Quantity matters less than how long the sugar stays in contact with the tooth and whether the meal's own saliva response is available to neutralize the acid.

q_0578.topic: dental disorders in the school-age child
q_0578.stem: A nurse is teaching about caries risk in a 7-year-old whose permanent incisors have just erupted. Which statement is accurate?
options: Newly erupted teeth are more susceptible to decay than those that have been erupted for 2 years or longer, because they have not yet acquired sufficient surface minerals
Newly erupted permanent teeth are highly resistant to decay
Susceptibility to caries is unrelated to how recently a tooth erupted
Permanent teeth are not at risk for caries until adolescence
q_0578.rationale: Newly erupted teeth are "more susceptible to decay than those that have been erupted for 2 years or longer" because they have not "acquired sufficient surface minerals." This is why middle childhood, when the permanent teeth erupt, is the peak susceptibility window, and more than half of US children have dental caries.
q_0578.trap: (B) assumes the permanent dentition arrives fully protected, which is the opposite of the case and is why this period carries the risk it does.

q_0579.topic: dental disorders in the school-age child
q_0579.stem: A child has inflamed, bleeding gums. Radiographs show loss of connective tissue and bone in the supporting structures. How should the nurse describe this?
options: Gingivitis, which is simple inflammation of the gums
Periodontitis, which is inflammation plus loss of connective tissue and bone in the supporting structures
Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, also called trench mouth, which is common in this age group
Normal eruption-related inflammation requiring no intervention
q_0579.rationale: Gingivitis is "simple inflammation of the gums." Periodontitis is inflammation plus "loss of connective tissue and bone in the supporting structures." Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, or trench mouth, is a distinct entity and is uncommon.
q_0579.trap: (A) names the milder condition on the same spectrum, and bone loss is the single finding that separates them. (C) attaches a memorable name to an uncommon condition, which is the reason it stays in memory out of proportion to how often it is the answer.

q_0580.topic: dental disorders in the school-age child
q_0580.stem: A 9-year-old has a permanent central incisor knocked out during a soccer game. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Hold the tooth by the crown rather than the root
Rinse the tooth gently under running water or saline, with the sink stoppered
Scrub the root surface thoroughly to remove debris before reinsertion
Reinsert the tooth into the socket and transport the child immediately
Understand that reimplantation within 1 hour gives the best chance of success
q_0580.rationale: Hold an avulsed permanent tooth "by the crown," rinse it gently under running water or saline with the sink stoppered, do not scrub, reinsert it into the socket, and transport immediately. Reimplantation "within 1 hour" gives the best chance of success. An unsuccessfully reimplanted tooth is retained 6 months to 12 years.
q_0580.trap: (C) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it is the step that destroys the tooth — scrubbing removes the periodontal ligament cells that reattachment depends on. Note also the exception that a distractor may exploit: avulsed *primary* teeth are usually not reimplanted.

q_0581.stem: A 6-year-old wets the bed about three nights a week and has done so continuously for the past 5 months. Which statement is correct?
options: This meets the diagnostic criteria for enuresis, which require occurrence at least twice a week for at least 3 months in a child at least 5 years of age
This does not meet criteria, because the child must be at least 7 years old
This does not meet criteria, because the events must occur nightly
Enuresis cannot be diagnosed before puberty
q_0581.rationale: Enuresis requires occurrence at least twice a week for at least 3 months, in a child at least 5 years old. Prevalence falls with age: 20% at age 5, 10% at age 8, and 3% at age 12. It is more common in boys, and the risk reaches up to 77% when both parents were enuretic.
q_0581.trap: (B) substitutes the wrong minimum age. These three parameters — twice a week, 3 months, age 5 — pair with encopresis's three, which are once a month, 3 months, and age 4, and the six numbers get cross-swapped more than any other set in the chapter.

q_0582.stem: A nurse is calculating the expected functional bladder capacity of a 6-year-old. Which figure is correct?
options: 8 ounces, using the formula of age in years plus 2 ounces
10 ounces, using age plus 4 ounces
6 ounces, equal to the child's age in ounces
12 ounces, which is the adult capacity
q_0582.rationale: Normal functional bladder capacity is age plus 2 ounces, so a 6-year-old's capacity is 8 ounces, or 237 ml. Separately, 10 to 12 ounces — 300 to 350 ml — is the volume sufficient to hold a night's urine.
q_0582.trap: (B) uses the common distractor formula of age plus 4. (D) borrows the volume needed to hold a night's urine and presents it as the child's current capacity, which is in fact the gap the treatment aims to close.

q_0583.stem: Parents of an 8-year-old with enuresis ask about the urine alarm. Which teaching is accurate?
options: The alarm requires at least 6 to 8 weeks to be effective, children may relapse once they stop using it, and relapse is treated by reinstituting the alarm
The alarm works within a few nights or not at all
The alarm is a second-line option after medication has failed
Relapse after alarm use means the treatment should not be repeated
q_0583.rationale: The urine alarm needs "at least 6 to 8 weeks," children "may relapse once they stop using it," and relapse is treated by reinstituting the alarm. It is inexpensive and free of side effects, and drug therapy is explicitly second-line, with imipramine third-line and cardiotoxic at high doses. Successful treatment is defined as 7 to 28 consecutive dry nights.
q_0583.trap: (B) sets an expectation that guarantees the family abandons an effective treatment before it has had time to work, which is the practical reason the 6-to-8-week figure matters. (C) inverts the treatment order.

q_0584.stem: A provider is considering desmopressin for a child with enuresis. Which statement reflects current recommendations?
options: The tablet form is used and can produce a response in up to 70% of children, but the nasal spray caused hyponatremia and seizures and is no longer recommended; the drug must be tapered off rather than stopped abruptly
The nasal spray is preferred because of more reliable absorption
Desmopressin may be discontinued abruptly once dryness is achieved
Desmopressin is first-line therapy ahead of the urine alarm
q_0584.rationale: Desmopressin response can reach 70%, but the nasal spray "caused hyponatremia and seizures and is no longer recommended," and the drug "must [be] tapered off," since abrupt discontinuation carries a high relapse rate.
q_0584.trap: (B) names the route that was withdrawn for causing seizures, and it pulls because a nasal spray sounds gentler than a tablet in a child. (D) promotes a second-line drug over the first-line behavioral treatment.

q_0585.stem: A frustrated parent says they have begun making their enuretic 7-year-old wash his own sheets every morning as a consequence. What should the nurse advise?
options: Punishment must not be used to correct enuresis, and parents need reassurance that bed-wetting does not represent willful misbehavior; the child may participate in changing linens as part of self-care, but not as a penalty
Requiring the child to launder the sheets is an appropriate natural consequence
The child should be excluded from all linen changing to avoid shame
Withholding evening fluids and adding a consequence is the recommended combination
q_0585.rationale: "It is imperative that punishment not be used to correct enuresis," and parents "need reassurance that the bed-wetting does not represent willful misbehavior."
q_0585.trap: (B) describes the same physical activity as the correct answer and differs only in framing, which is precisely the distinction the chapter draws. Having the child change linens as participation in self-care is appropriate; imposing it as a consequence makes it punishment for something involuntary. Note also that enuresis "may serve as a trigger for child abuse."

q_0586.stem: A 6-year-old has been soiling his underwear several times a week for 4 months. Examination reveals loose stool leakage and small amounts of hard stool in the rectum. What does this pattern suggest, and what is the first treatment?
options: Leakage around an impaction; the first treatment is disimpaction, and customary dosages are usually insufficient
Infectious diarrhea; the first treatment is an antidiarrheal agent
Irritable bowel syndrome; the first treatment is dietary fiber alone
Normal variation requiring no treatment
q_0586.rationale: Loose leakage together with "small amounts of hard stool… suggests leakage around an impaction." The first treatment is disimpaction, and "customary dosages are usually insufficient."
q_0586.trap: (B) treats the most visible finding — loose stool — as the problem, and an antidiarrheal would worsen the impaction that is producing it. The stem's combination of loose leakage *and* palpable hard stool is the signature that separates overflow from true diarrhea.

q_0587.stem: A parent reports that their 5-year-old stiffens, stands in a corner with straight legs and a red face, and "does a little dance" before soiling. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Retentive posturing, which looks like effort to defecate but is in fact withholding
Effective straining that indicates constipation is resolving
A seizure equivalent requiring neurologic evaluation
Normal toileting behavior for the age
q_0587.rationale: Retentive posturing presents as "Stiffening, standing in a corner with straight legs and a bright red face, 'doing a little dance,' crawling, or hiding." A parent who reports the child "straining" may in fact be describing withholding.
q_0587.trap: (B) is the parent's usual reading of the behavior, and it points the assessment in the opposite direction from the truth. The child is working to keep stool in, not to pass it, which is why the history taken at face value can be misleading.

q_0588.stem: A nurse suspects encopresis in a 7-year-old but the family has not raised it. What is the best approach, and what are the diagnostic criteria?
options: Ask directly about soiling, since parents and children are reluctant to volunteer the information; encopresis requires occurrence at least once a month for at least 3 months in a child at least 4 years of age
Wait for the family to raise the topic, to avoid embarrassing the child
Ask directly; the criteria are twice a week for 3 months in a child at least 5 years old
Ask the child alone, without informing the parents
q_0588.rationale: "Because the parents and child are reluctant to volunteer information, direct questioning about the soiling is more successful." Encopresis requires occurrence at least once a month for at least 3 months in a child at least 4 years of age. The toileting routine is 10 to 15 minutes after meals, for 10 minutes.
q_0588.trap: (C) has the right approach and imports enuresis's criteria — twice a week, age 5 — onto encopresis. Those two criteria sets are adjacent in the chapter and differ in both frequency and minimum age, which is exactly what makes them swappable.

q_0589.stem: A 9-year-old is being evaluated for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Which elements are required by the DSM-5 criteria? Select all that apply.
options: At least six symptoms of inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity
Symptoms present for at least 6 months
Onset of symptoms before age 12 years
Symptoms present in two or more settings
Onset of symptoms before age 7 years
q_0589.rationale: The criteria require six symptoms — five suffice at age 17 years and older — present for at least 6 months, with onset before age 12 years, in two or more settings. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder affects about 11% of school-age children, and a parent with the condition has a more than 50% chance of having a child with it.
q_0589.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it is the superseded DSM-IV threshold. It remains the classic distractor precisely because it was correct under the previous edition, so a learner who studied from older material will select it confidently.

q_0590.stem: A 5-year-old has been diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Which first-line treatment does the chapter specify for this age?
options: Behavior therapy first, with methylphenidate only if behavior interventions fail and the disturbance is moderate to severe
Stimulant medication first, with behavior therapy added if medication is insufficient
Medication and behavior therapy started simultaneously in all cases
No treatment until the child reaches school age
q_0590.rationale: The treatment algorithm is age-banded. At ages 4 to 5, behavior therapy comes first, with methylphenidate only if behavior interventions fail and the disturbance is moderate to severe. At ages 6 to 11, medication and/or behavior therapy, "preferably both." At ages 12 to 18, medication with the adolescent's assent and/or behavior therapy.
q_0590.trap: (B) applies the school-age approach to a preschooler, which is the distinction this algorithm exists to draw. Note the assent requirement that appears only in the oldest band — the adolescent's agreement is part of the criterion, not a courtesy.

q_0591.stem: A child with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder also has a motor tic disorder, and a stimulant is being considered. Which concern applies?
options: Stimulants may exaggerate tics, so they are avoided when tics or a family history of Tourette syndrome are present
Stimulants reliably suppress tics and are therefore preferred
Tics are a contraindication to all attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder treatment
Tics and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder never coexist
q_0591.rationale: Stimulants "may exaggerate tics," so they are avoided when tics or a family history of Tourette syndrome are present. This is the one hard contraindication in the attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder section, and it links directly to the tic-disorder content later in the chapter.
q_0591.trap: (C) converts a medication-specific caution into a blanket bar on treatment. Behavior therapy remains available and is first-line at several ages regardless, so the presence of tics changes the agent rather than removing the option of treatment.

q_0592.stem: A child taking a stimulant for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder has lost appetite and is having difficulty falling asleep. Which management strategies apply? Select all that apply.
options: Give the medication with or after meals to manage appetite loss
Offer evening snacks and small frequent meals
Give the medication early in the day and use the minimal effective dose for sleeplessness
Add caffeinated beverages to enhance the medication's effect
Monitor growth, since long-term dextroamphetamine use is associated with growth suppression
q_0592.rationale: For appetite loss, give the medication "with or after meals," with evening snacks and small frequent meals. For sleeplessness, give it "early in the day" at the minimal effective dose. Growth suppression is associated with long-term dextroamphetamine use, so growth is monitored. Insulin requirements may change.
q_0592.trap: (D) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort and reverses the interaction: "Caffeine decreases efficacy." It pulls because caffeine is itself a stimulant, so combining the two sounds additive.

q_0593.stem: A parent of a child with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder says the child "will learn to listen if I just tell him what to do." What should the nurse advise?
options: Verbal instructions should be accompanied by visual references
Instructions should be given verbally and repeated more forcefully
Written instructions alone are sufficient at this age
The child should be expected to recall multistep instructions without support
q_0593.rationale: "Verbal instructions should be accompanied by visual references." This appears in the chapter's own review questions, which makes the phrasing worth holding exactly.
q_0593.trap: (B) is the parent's instinct — that the problem is volume or firmness rather than the channel — and it is what the visual-reference guidance replaces. Repetition without a visual anchor addresses the wrong limitation.

q_0594.stem: A parent asks to move their child with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder out of a classroom with "too many rules." Which response is correct?
options: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder need an orderly, predictable, and consistent classroom environment with clear and consistent rules, so a highly structured classroom is the goal rather than a problem
A less structured classroom allows the child freedom to self-regulate
Classroom structure has no bearing on outcomes in this disorder
The child should be removed from the general classroom entirely
q_0594.rationale: Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder need "an orderly, predictable, and consistent classroom environment with clear and consistent rules."
q_0594.trap: (B) is the request in the stem restated as a rationale, and it reverses what helps. The structure a parent perceives as rigidity is the external scaffolding that compensates for the self-regulation the child cannot yet supply.

q_0595.stem: A 9-year-old reads far below grade level despite an above-average intelligence quotient, with normal vision and hearing. Which statement reflects the chapter's concept of learning disability?
options: Children with learning disabilities tend to have normal or above-average intelligence with a wide gap between verbal and performance scores, and the diagnosis explicitly excludes problems arising primarily from visual, hearing, or motor disabilities, cognitive impairment, emotional disturbance, or environmental disadvantage
Learning disability requires below-average intelligence
Uncorrected hearing loss is a common form of learning disability
Learning disability and cognitive impairment are the same diagnosis
q_0595.rationale: Children with learning disabilities "tend to have normal or above-average intelligence," with "a wide gap between verbal and performance scores." Explicitly excluded are problems arising primarily from visual, hearing, or motor disabilities, cognitive impairment, emotional disturbance, or environmental disadvantage.
q_0595.trap: (B) inverts the intelligence requirement, which is the defining feature: the disability is the discrepancy between ability and achievement, so normal intelligence is part of the definition rather than an exception to it.

q_0596.stem: A school proposes a plan providing a child with specialized instruction and related services. Which plan is this?
options: An individualized education program, which provides specialized instruction and related services
A 504 plan, which provides accommodations for access and academic success
Either plan, since the two are interchangeable
Neither, since specialized instruction is provided outside these frameworks
q_0596.rationale: An individualized education program provides specialized instruction and related services. A 504 plan provides accommodations for access and academic success. The cue word is the discriminator: *instruction* signals the individualized education program, and *accommodation* signals the 504 plan.
q_0596.trap: (B) names the other framework, and the two are confused constantly because both are school-based supports triggered by a disability. What separates them is whether the school is changing what is taught and how, or changing the conditions under which the standard curriculum is accessed.

q_0597.stem: A student with a documented disability needs extended test time and preferential seating but does not require changes to the curriculum itself. Which plan fits?
options: An individualized education program
A 504 plan, which provides accommodations for access and academic success
No plan is needed for accommodations of this kind
An individualized education program, because any disability triggers one
q_0597.rationale: A 504 plan provides accommodations for access and academic success, while an individualized education program provides specialized instruction and related services. Extended time and seating change the conditions of access rather than the instruction itself.
q_0597.trap: (A) is the mirror error of the previous item, and (D) states the assumption behind it — that a documented disability automatically calls for the more intensive framework. What decides between them is the nature of the support needed, not the presence of a diagnosis.

q_0598.stem: A parent reports that their 8-year-old's facial tics worsen before a school performance, lessen while he is absorbed in building a model, and are absent while he sleeps. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: This is the expected pattern: tics decrease during concentration, are markedly diminished during sleep, and become more exaggerated with stress or excitement
This pattern is atypical and suggests a seizure disorder
Tics that disappear during sleep are voluntary
Tics characteristically worsen with concentration and persist in sleep
q_0598.rationale: Tics "decrease during concentration, are markedly diminished during sleep, and become more exaggerated with stress or excitement."
q_0598.trap: (D) states what most people assume about involuntary movements, which is why this pattern is the discriminating feature. (C) draws the wrong conclusion from the sleep finding — disappearance in sleep does not make the movements voluntary, and the chapter is explicit that they are not.

q_0599.stem: A child with a tic disorder repeats his own words immediately after saying them. Which term describes this?
options: Echolalia, repeating another person's words
Palilalia, repeating one's own words
Coprolalia, using socially unacceptable or obscene words
Metalinguistic awareness
q_0599.rationale: Echolalia is repeating another person's words; palilalia is repeating one's own; coprolalia is the use of socially unacceptable or obscene words. Only coprolalia belongs to the chronic end of the tic spectrum.
q_0599.trap: (A) is the better-known term and the one that surfaces first, which is what makes this trio worth separating. The discriminator is simply whose words are being repeated — another's for echolalia, one's own for palilalia.

q_0600.stem: A 10-year-old has had motor tics but no vocal tics for the past 14 months, with no secondary cause identified. Which classification applies?
options: Tourette syndrome, since the duration exceeds 12 months
A chronic, or persistent, tic disorder, since Tourette syndrome requires both motor and vocal tics
A provisional tic disorder, since 14 months is under the threshold
No tic disorder, since vocal tics are absent
q_0600.rationale: A chronic or persistent tic disorder is defined by duration of more than 1 year. Tourette syndrome requires both motor and vocal tics, onset before 18 years, duration of more than 12 months, and no secondary cause. Tic disorders affect about 6 per 1000 children, with a 3:1 male predominance.
q_0600.trap: (A) applies the duration criterion alone and ignores the requirement that both tic types be present, which is the single feature separating Tourette syndrome from a chronic tic disorder. Duration is satisfied here; the symptom profile is not.

q_0601.stem: A teacher asks whether a student should lose privileges when his tics disrupt the class. What should the nurse advise?
options: Punishment for the behaviors is inappropriate because these actions are involuntary, and although the child can suppress tics somewhat, persistent pressure for control constitutes an additional stress
Consistent consequences will reduce the frequency of tics
The child should be required to suppress tics throughout the school day
The child should be removed from the classroom whenever tics occur
q_0601.rationale: "Punishment for the behaviors is inappropriate because these actions are involuntary." Although the child can suppress tics to a degree, "persistent pressure for control constitutes an additional stress."
q_0601.trap: (C) exploits the fact that suppression is partially possible, and turns a limited capacity into an expectation. Because stress and excitement exaggerate tics, sustained pressure to suppress them predictably makes them worse — the intervention produces the behavior it targets.

q_0602.topic: school phobia, posttraumatic stress, and childhood depression
q_0602.stem: A 10-year-old has stomachaches and headaches every school morning that resolve promptly once he is allowed to stay home, and he is symptom-free on weekends and holidays. Which understanding should guide the nurse?
options: In school phobia the child fears leaving home rather than going to school; symptoms subside promptly when the child may stay home and are absent on weekends and holidays
The child fears a specific threat at school that must be identified before he can return
The pattern indicates an undiagnosed gastrointestinal disorder
Symptoms that resolve at home indicate the complaints are fabricated
q_0602.rationale: In school phobia the child fears leaving home rather than going to school. Symptoms "subside promptly when the child may stay home" and are "absent on weekends and holidays." The condition is more common at 10 years and older.
q_0602.trap: (B) is the axis swap the chapter states outright, and it sends the assessment toward the school when the fear is about separation from home. (D) misreads the pattern as malingering — the symptoms are genuine, and their timing reflects what triggers them.

q_0603.topic: school phobia, posttraumatic stress, and childhood depression
q_0603.stem: Parents of a child with school phobia ask whether to let him stay home until he feels ready. What should the nurse advise?
options: The goal is attendance, and the longer the child is permitted to stay out of school, the more difficult it is to reenter; parents should be told gently but firmly that the child must return
The child should remain home until the anxiety resolves fully
Home schooling is the recommended first-line response
Attendance should be deferred until a psychiatric evaluation is complete
q_0603.rationale: "The longer the child is permitted to stay out of school, the more difficult it is to reenter," and parents must be told gently but firmly that the child is to return.
q_0603.trap: (B) is the compassionate response and the one that entrenches the problem, because avoidance relieves the anxiety in the short term and therefore strengthens it. Every additional day away raises the barrier to the return that is the actual treatment goal.

q_0604.topic: school phobia, posttraumatic stress, and childhood depression
q_0604.stem: A child who witnessed a traumatic event appeared numb and detached about 2 weeks afterward, and the parents say he seemed unaffected. Two months later he is tearful, irritable, and clearly struggling. How should the nurse interpret these two phases?
options: The second phase, at about 2 weeks, is numbness and denial, during which severe depression, aggression, or psychosis can develop without support; the third phase, at 2 to 3 months, is when the child appears to be getting worse when actually he or she is getting better
The child deteriorated because the trauma was inadequately treated in the first weeks
The apparent recovery at 2 weeks indicates the trauma had no lasting effect
Distress emerging at 2 months indicates a new, unrelated stressor
q_0604.rationale: Posttraumatic stress in children runs in phases of 1 to 2 hours, about 2 weeks, and 2 to 3 months. The second phase is numbness and denial, in which the child "appears to have produced no impression," and it is when "severe depression, aggression, or psychosis" can develop without support. In the third phase the child "appears to be getting worse, when actually he or she is getting better."
q_0604.trap: (C) reads the numb phase as resilience, which is the more dangerous of the two misreadings because it withdraws support precisely when it is most needed. Reading the third phase as deterioration is the mirror error, and it can prompt intervention changes at the point where recovery has begun.

q_0605.topic: school phobia, posttraumatic stress, and childhood depression
q_0605.stem: A previously cheerful 9-year-old has become withdrawn and aggressive over the past month with no obvious cause identified. What does the chapter direct?
options: Children exhibiting any sudden change in behavior need to be assessed for exposure to a traumatic event, since the precipitant may go unrecognized and bullying and psychologic abuse are most common in school-age children
Sudden behavior change at this age is developmentally normal and needs no assessment
Assessment for trauma is warranted only when a traumatic event is already known
The behavior indicates conduct disorder, which requires three criteria over 12 months
q_0605.rationale: "Children exhibiting any sudden change in behavior need to be assessed for exposure to a traumatic event." The precipitant may go unrecognized, and "bullying and psychologic abuse are most common in school-age children."
q_0605.trap: (C) inverts the logic of screening: the reason to assess is precisely that the event may not be known, since the kinds of trauma most common at this age happen out of adult view. (D) reaches for a diagnosis whose own threshold — three of fifteen criteria over 12 months, one within 6 months — this stem does not come close to meeting.

q_0606.topic: school phobia, posttraumatic stress, and childhood depression
q_0606.stem: An adolescent is started on an antidepressant for childhood depression, and the family asks when to expect improvement. Which response is accurate?
options: Antidepressants take 2 to 4 weeks to produce a therapeutic effect
Improvement should be evident within 48 hours
The medication works immediately or should be changed
Antidepressants are not used in children at any age
q_0606.rationale: Antidepressants require 2 to 4 weeks to reach a therapeutic effect. Persistent depressive disorder, or dysthymia, requires a duration of at least 2 years.
q_0606.trap: (C) sets an expectation that leads families to abandon an adequate trial before the drug has had time to act, which is the practical reason this interval is worth teaching at the time of prescribing rather than at follow-up.

q_0607.stem: A 16-year-old shows the greatest push for emancipation, a peer-dominant orientation, and what the parents describe as the low point of their relationship with him. Which phase of adolescence does this describe?
options: Early adolescence, ages 11 to 14 years
Middle adolescence, ages 15 to 17 years
Late adolescence, ages 18 to 22 years
Preadolescence, ending at the thirteenth birthday
q_0607.rationale: The three phases are early adolescence at 11 to 14 years, middle at 15 to 17 years, and late at 18 to 22 years. Early adolescence is dominated by the physical changes of puberty and the emotional reaction to them; middle adolescence brings the shift to a peer-dominant orientation, experimentation, the greatest push for emancipation, and the low point in the parent-child relationship; late adolescence brings full maturation, stable intimate relationships, and independent management of health care.
q_0607.trap: (A) is chosen by anyone who associates conflict with the onset of adolescence. The turbulence peaks in the middle phase rather than at the beginning, when the adolescent's attention is still largely on the physical changes themselves.

q_0608.stem: A nurse is teaching about self-esteem across adolescence. Which pattern does the chapter describe?
options: Self-esteem falls in early adolescence and rises in late adolescence
Self-esteem improves steadily throughout adolescence
Self-esteem is highest in early adolescence and declines thereafter
Self-esteem is stable across all three phases
q_0608.rationale: Table 17.1 states both directions explicitly: self-esteem falls in early adolescence and rises in late adolescence.
q_0608.trap: (B) is the reassuring trajectory adults expect as a teenager matures, and it misses the early dip entirely. That dip coincides with the phase in which the physical changes of puberty and the emotional reaction to them dominate, which is what makes it worth knowing.

q_0609.stem: A 12-year-old has recently become preoccupied with her changing body and emotionally reactive to comments about her appearance, but still relies mainly on her family rather than peers. Which phase does this fit?
options: Early adolescence, in which the physical changes of puberty and the emotional reaction to them predominate
Middle adolescence, in which peer orientation predominates
Late adolescence, in which intimate relationships stabilize
School age, since peer orientation has not yet emerged
q_0609.rationale: Early adolescence, at 11 to 14 years, is characterized by the physical changes of puberty and the emotional reaction to them. The shift to a peer-dominant orientation belongs to middle adolescence, and stable intimate relationships with independent management of health care belong to late adolescence.
q_0609.trap: (D) reads continued family orientation as evidence the adolescent phase has not begun. The marker of early adolescence is the pubertal change and the response to it, not the point at which peers displace parents — that displacement is the *next* phase.

q_0610.stem: A nursing student asks what actually triggers puberty. Which explanation is correct?
options: The pituitary gland and gonads are capable of mature function at any age; what changes at puberty is that the hypothalamus loses its negative sensitivity, releasing gonadotropin-releasing hormone from inhibition
The pituitary gland matures at puberty and becomes able to secrete gonadotropins for the first time
The gonads mature first and then signal the hypothalamus
Puberty begins when the adrenal glands first produce androgens in adolescence
q_0610.rationale: "The pituitary gland and gonads are capable of mature function… at any age." What changes is that "the hypothalamus loses this negative sensitivity," which releases gonadotropin-releasing hormone from inhibition and begins the cascade.
q_0610.trap: (B) describes maturation of a gland that was already competent, which is the intuitive but incorrect model. The change is the removal of an inhibition rather than the acquisition of a capability, and that distinction is what the chapter states in its own sentence.

q_0611.stem: A nurse is explaining the roles of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone in an adolescent girl. Which description is correct?
options: Follicle-stimulating hormone drives follicle growth and estrogen production, while luteinizing hormone drives ovulation, corpus luteum formation, and progesterone production
Luteinizing hormone drives follicle growth and estrogen, while follicle-stimulating hormone drives ovulation
Both hormones act only on the adrenal cortex in girls
Follicle-stimulating hormone produces progesterone directly
q_0611.rationale: In girls, follicle-stimulating hormone stimulates follicle growth and estrogen production, while luteinizing hormone triggers ovulation, corpus luteum formation, and progesterone production.
q_0611.trap: (B) swaps the two hormones, which is the commonest inversion in this material because the name "follicle-stimulating" is the only mnemonic anchoring either one. Luteinizing hormone is named for the corpus luteum it produces, which is the anchor for the other half.

q_0612.stem: A nurse is explaining the same two hormones in an adolescent boy. Which description is correct?
options: Luteinizing hormone stimulates the Leydig cells to produce testosterone, and follicle-stimulating hormone, together with luteinizing hormone, drives sperm production
Follicle-stimulating hormone stimulates the Leydig cells to produce testosterone
Luteinizing hormone has no role in the male
Testosterone is produced by the pituitary gland in response to gonadotropin-releasing hormone
q_0612.rationale: In boys, luteinizing hormone stimulates the Leydig cells to produce testosterone, and follicle-stimulating hormone acting with luteinizing hormone drives sperm production.
q_0612.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item, carried across sexes. The same two hormones act in both sexes with different targets, so an item can test either sex and the distractor is always the other hormone's job.

q_0613.stem: A nurse is asked why girls typically stop growing earlier than boys. Which explanation does the chapter give?
options: Estrogen stimulates skeletal growth at low levels and inhibits it at high levels, so rising estrogen eventually closes the growth process
Estrogen inhibits skeletal growth at every concentration
Girls produce less growth hormone than boys throughout puberty
Testosterone has no effect on skeletal growth
q_0613.rationale: Estrogen stimulates skeletal growth at low levels and inhibits it at high levels. This dose-dependent reversal explains why girls stop growing sooner, and the chapter states it in a single sentence.
q_0613.trap: (B) takes half the relationship and generalizes it, which loses the mechanism entirely — a hormone that only inhibited growth could not also have driven the growth spurt that preceded the inhibition.

q_0614.stem: A 12-year-old girl has just had her first menstrual period, and a 13-year-old boy has had a first ejaculation. Both families ask about fertility. Which response is correct?
options: An adolescent should be considered potentially fertile with a first menstrual period or a first ejaculation
Girls are not fertile for about a year after menarche, because ova are not yet mature enough to be released
Boys are not fertile until viable sperm appear months after first ejaculation
Fertility cannot be assumed until Tanner stage 5 is reached
q_0614.rationale: The chapter states the clinical rule flatly: "an adolescent should be considered potentially fertile with a first menstrual period or a first ejaculation." It also notes that at menarche "ova still do not generally mature enough to be released," and that viable sperm follow first ejaculation.
q_0614.trap: (B) and (C) both quote the chapter's own physiology correctly and draw the wrong clinical conclusion from it. The physiology is deliberately the distractor here: the counseling rule is set at the earliest possible point rather than at the average one, because an individual adolescent's timing cannot be known in advance.

q_0615.topic: adolescent sexual maturation and its variations
q_0615.stem: An 11-year-old girl's mother reports that the first change she noticed was a small firm lump under one nipple. Which statement is correct?
options: The first visible change in girls is nipple and areolar change with a breast bud, called thelarche; pubarche typically follows, although many girls have underarm or pubic hair before breast development
Pubic hair development always precedes breast development in girls
A unilateral breast bud is abnormal and requires evaluation
Menarche is the first sign of puberty in girls
q_0615.rationale: The first visible change in girls is nipple and areolar change with a breast bud, or thelarche. Pubarche "typically follows," but "many have strands of underarm and/or pubic hair before breast development."
q_0615.trap: (B) is too absolute, and the chapter deliberately qualifies the sequence rather than fixing it. The usual order is thelarche then pubarche, but reversal is common enough that the book names it, so an option asserting an invariable order is wrong.

q_0616.topic: adolescent sexual maturation and its variations
q_0616.stem: A 12-year-old boy is being assessed for the earliest signs of puberty. Which finding appears first?
options: Testicular enlargement, accompanied by thinning, reddening, and increasing looseness of the scrotum
Voice change
Facial hair
Pubic hair
q_0616.rationale: The first pubescent change in boys is testicular enlargement "accompanied by thinning, reddening, and increasing looseness of the scrotum." Voice change and facial hair are mid-to-late events.
q_0616.trap: (B) and (C) are the changes families notice and comment on, which is why they feel like the beginning. They arrive well after the process has started, so an assessment waiting for them would miss the first year or more of puberty.

q_0617.topic: adolescent sexual maturation and its variations
q_0617.stem: A 13-year-old girl and her mother are worried about a clear-to-white vaginal discharge that has been present for several months without itching, odor, or dysuria. What is the nurse's best response?
options: Reassure them that physiologic leukorrhea is normal and a sign that her body is maturing
Obtain a culture and begin empiric treatment for candidiasis
Advise douching to reduce the discharge
Refer for gynecologic evaluation of possible infection
q_0617.rationale: Girls or parents "may be concerned that this vaginal discharge is a sign of infection." The nursing response is reassurance that "the discharge is normal and a sign that their body is maturing."
q_0617.trap: (B) and (D) both treat a normal maturational finding as pathology, and the stem gives the discriminators that rule infection out — no itching, odor, or dysuria. Physiologic leukorrhea is a reassurance item, not a workup item.

q_0618.topic: adolescent sexual maturation and its variations
q_0618.stem: A 14-year-old boy is distressed by tender breast tissue that developed over the past several months. Which response is correct?
options: Gynecomastia occurs in up to 70% of boys in midpuberty and usually disappears within 2 years, although it may persist in obese individuals; reassurance is appropriate
This finding requires endocrine referral in all cases
Gynecomastia in adolescent boys is rare and always pathologic
The tissue should be expected to persist permanently
q_0618.rationale: Gynecomastia affects up to 70% of boys, "disappears within 2 years," and "may persist in obese individuals."
q_0618.trap: (B) medicalizes a finding that occurs in most boys and resolves on its own, and the referral itself communicates to an already self-conscious adolescent that something is wrong. The prevalence figure is what makes reassurance defensible rather than dismissive.

q_0619.topic: adolescent sexual maturation and its variations
q_0619.stem: A nurse reviews thresholds for abnormal pubertal timing. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Precocious puberty is the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age in either sex
Delayed puberty in girls includes no breast development by age 13
Delayed puberty in girls includes no menarche by age 15
Delayed puberty in boys includes no testicular or scrotal change by age 14
Precocious puberty is defined as onset before age 10 in girls and 12 in boys
q_0619.rationale: Precocious puberty is the appearance of secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years old in both sexes. Delayed puberty in girls is no breast development by 13 or no menarche by 15; in boys it is no testicular or scrotal change by 14.
q_0619.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort, and it substitutes the *average* ages of pubertal onset for the *abnormal* threshold. Those average figures are real — from Chapter 15, puberty generally begins at 10 in girls and 12 in boys — which is exactly what makes them a convincing wrong answer here.

q_0620.stem: A 12-year-old girl has just experienced her peak height velocity. Her mother asks how much more she will grow. Which response is accurate?
options: Peak height velocity in girls occurs at about 12 years, 6 to 12 months before menarche, and few girls grow more than 5 cm, about 2 inches, after menarche
Peak height velocity follows menarche by about a year in girls
Most girls gain another 15 cm after menarche
Growth in girls continues at the same rate until age 18
q_0620.rationale: Peak height velocity in girls occurs at about 12 years, 6 to 12 months before menarche, and "Few girls grow more than 5 cm (2 inches) after menarche." Growth in height usually ceases 2 to 2½ years after menarche.
q_0620.trap: (B) inverts the order of the two events, which matters clinically because it changes what a parent should expect. Menarche is a late marker in the growth sequence rather than an early one, so a girl who has begun menstruating has already completed most of her linear growth.

q_0621.stem: A 14-year-old boy is at his peak height velocity. Where does this fall relative to his other pubertal changes?
options: Peak height velocity in boys occurs at about 14 years, after testicular and penile growth and after axillary and mature pubic hair
Peak height velocity in boys precedes all genital development
Peak height velocity in boys and girls occurs at the same age
Boys reach peak height velocity before menarche-equivalent maturation
q_0621.rationale: Peak height velocity in boys occurs at about 14 years, after testicular and penile growth and after axillary and mature pubic hair.
q_0621.trap: (B) is the mirror error of the previous item applied to boys. In girls the growth spurt comes early in the sequence and precedes menarche; in boys it comes late, after the genital changes, which is why boys often appear to mature genitally before they visibly grow.

q_0622.stem: A nurse compares weight and height spurts in adolescent boys and girls. Which statement is correct?
options: Peak weight velocity occurs about 6 months after peak height velocity in girls, whereas weight and height spurts occur simultaneously for boys
Peak weight velocity precedes peak height velocity in girls
Weight and height spurts occur simultaneously in girls and sequentially in boys
Weight gain is not a measured component of the pubertal growth spurt
q_0622.rationale: "Peak weight velocity occurs about 6 months after PHV in girls. In contrast, weight and height spurts occur simultaneously for boys."
q_0622.trap: (C) reverses which sex shows the lag. The practical consequence is that a girl who has just finished her height spurt is still expected to gain weight, and mistaking that expected gain for excess is a common source of unnecessary dieting at exactly the wrong age.

q_0623.stem: A 13-year-old suddenly needs longer pants but the same shirt size, and his parent wonders whether this is abnormal. Which changes reflect the expected adolescent growth sequence? Select all that apply.
options: Leg length increases before trunk length, by about 6 to 9 months
Shoulder and chest growth follows leg growth by about a year
Heart rate decreases through adolescence while systolic blood pressure increases
Boys gain more in red cell mass, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and serum iron than girls
Trunk and shoulder growth precede leg growth, so shirt size changes first
q_0623.rationale: Leg length precedes trunk growth by 6 to 9 months, and shoulders and chest by about a year. Heart rate decreases while systolic blood pressure increases through adolescence, and boys gain more in red cell mass, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and serum iron because of greater muscle mass. Girls run a higher pulse and lower systolic pressure than boys.
q_0623.trap: (E) is the one option from the wrong side of the sort and reverses the sequence in the stem. The order is shoes, then pants, then shirts — a teenager outgrowing footwear and trouser length while shirts still fit is following the normal pattern, not deviating from it.

q_0624.stem: A 16-year-old can reason abstractly about hypothetical situations in class but makes an impulsive decision about drinking at a party. Which understanding does the chapter offer?
options: Formal operational thought emerges at 11 to 14 years, but under stress, time pressure, sleep deprivation, or peer pressure adolescents abandon their rational thought processes, and most risky health decisions occur under exactly those conditions
An adolescent with formal operational thought will reason reliably in any setting
Formal operational thought does not develop until age 18
Risky decisions indicate the adolescent has not reached formal operations
q_0624.rationale: Formal operational thought emerges at 11 to 14 years, but under "stress, time pressure, sleep deprivation, or peer pressure," adolescents "abandon their rational thought processes," and most risky health decisions occur precisely under those conditions.
q_0624.trap: (B) assumes capacity equals performance, which is the assumption behind a great deal of ineffective adolescent health education. The reasoning ability is genuinely present; the conditions under which risk decisions get made are the conditions that suspend it.

q_0625.stem: A 15-year-old with newly diagnosed diabetes refuses to use an insulin pump at school because "everyone will notice it." Which cognitive distortion does this illustrate?
options: The imaginary audience — the belief that everybody will notice
The personal fable — the belief that it cannot happen to me
Formal operational reasoning
Concrete operational thinking
q_0625.rationale: The imaginary audience is the belief that "everybody will notice," and the chapter's own clinical example is the teen with diabetes refusing to use an insulin pump at school. The discriminator is the theme of being watched.
