q_0768.rationale: The chapter states that "A cochlear implant bypasses the hair cells to directly stimulate surviving auditory nerve fibers," that the trend is toward implantation "usually by 12 months old," and that because pneumococcal meningitis has been reported, "all children receiving a cochlear implant must be vaccinated with the pneumococcal polyvalent vaccine" (p. 642).
q_0768.trap: (B) describes an amplifier rather than a bypass, which is the whole distinction between an aid and an implant; (C) inverts the timing trend, and (D) drops the single most actionable safety item in the hearing section.

q_0769.topic: communication with the child who has hearing impairment
q_0769.stem: A nurse is caring for a hospitalized 6-year-old with a hearing impairment. Which action is correct?
options: Make certain the child can see the nurse before any procedure, including routine ones such as changing a diaper or adjusting an infusion
Reserve the requirement to be seen first for invasive or painful procedures, to avoid disrupting the child unnecessarily
Communicate procedures through the parents, who understand the child's speech best
Awaken the child at night by turning on the overhead light before approaching the bed
q_0769.rationale: The chapter directs the nurse to "always make certain that the child can see him or her before any procedures, even routine ones such as changing a diaper or regulating an infusion," because the child "may not be aware of the nurse's presence until alerted through visual or tactile cues" (p. 644).
q_0769.trap: (C) is the failure the chapter names outright — caregivers "communicate only with the parents" and "the child's needs and feelings remain unrecognized" (p. 644); (D) misses the specific technique, which is to gently shake the child or turn on the hearing aid before arousing them.

q_0770.topic: refractive errors, amblyopia, and eye injuries
q_0770.stem: A school-age child has a corrected visual acuity of 20/100 in the better eye. How should the nurse classify this?
options: Partial sight, and the child can generally use normal-sized print because near vision usually exceeds distance vision
Legal blindness, which requires immediate registration for special educational services
Partial sight, which requires large-print materials as the first educational accommodation
Within normal limits for school-age children with corrective lenses
q_0770.rationale: Partial sight is "a visual acuity between 20/70 and 20/200," and the chapter notes that such a child "can generally use normal-sized print because near vision is almost always better than distance vision"; legal blindness begins at 20/200 or lower, or a visual field of 20 degrees or less in the better eye (p. 645).
q_0770.trap: (C) supplies large print reflexively for any visual impairment, which the chapter does not; note also that legal blindness "is not a medical diagnosis but a legal definition" used to determine tax status, school entrance, and financial aid.

q_0771.topic: refractive errors, amblyopia, and eye injuries
q_0771.stem: A 9-year-old cannot read the whiteboard from her seat but reads her book easily. Her eye examination shows the image focusing in front of the retina. What does the nurse expect?
options: Myopia, resulting from an eyeball that is too long, corrected with biconcave lenses
Hyperopia, resulting from an eyeball that is too short, corrected with convex lenses
Astigmatism, resulting from unequal curvature of the cornea, corrected with compensating lenses
Anisometropia, resulting from different refractive strength in each eye, corrected with contact lenses
q_0771.rationale: The chapter states that in refractive disorders light rays "fall in front of the retina (myopia) or beyond it (hyperopia)," that myopia "Results from eyeball that is too long," and that it is "Corrected with biconcave lenses that focus rays on retina" (p. 645).
q_0771.trap: (B) is the mirror condition with the mirror lens, and it is worth noting that hyperopia in a young child is usually normal — "Most children are normally hyperopic until about 7 years old" — and is treated only when required.

q_0772.topic: refractive errors, amblyopia, and eye injuries
q_0772.stem: A 4-year-old with untreated strabismus is at risk for amblyopia. Which statement about the mechanism and treatment is correct?
options: The brain suppresses the image from the weaker eye until the visual cortex stops responding, and treatment patches the stronger eye, preventing loss if begun before 6 years old
The weaker eye loses acuity from disuse of the eye muscles, and treatment patches the weaker eye to strengthen it
The retina of the weaker eye degenerates progressively, and treatment is surgical realignment alone
Vision loss is permanent once strabismus is detected, so treatment aims only at cosmetic alignment
q_0772.rationale: Box 20.5 describes the chain — one eye receives insufficient stimulation, each retina receives a different image, the "Brain accommodates by suppressing less intense image," and the "Visual cortex eventually does not respond" — and states amblyopia is "Preventable if treatment of primary visual defect, such as anisometropia or strabismus, begins before 6 years old"; treatment "May involve occlusion therapy (patching stronger eye)" (p. 646).
q_0772.trap: (B) patches the affected eye, which is the classic reversal and would accelerate the very suppression the therapy exists to interrupt; the loss in amblyopia is cortical rather than ocular, which is why (C) is wrong and why the developmental window in (A) matters.

q_0773.topic: refractive errors, amblyopia, and eye injuries
q_0773.stem: A 10-year-old is brought in after being struck in the eye with a baseball. The lid is swollen and bruised. What should the nurse do first?
options: Use a flashlight to check for gross hyphema before applying anything to the eye
Apply ice immediately to reduce the swelling, then assess the eye
Patch both eyes and refer the child to an ophthalmologist
Irrigate the eye with lukewarm tap water for 20 minutes
q_0773.rationale: For a hematoma the chapter directs the nurse to "Use a flashlight to check for gross hyphema," then "Apply ice for first 24 hours to reduce swelling if no hyphema is present," and "Refer to an ophthalmologist immediately if hyphema is present" (p. 646).
q_0773.trap: (B) reverses the order, and the order is what the item tests — ice is conditional on the absence of hyphema; (D) applies the chemical-burn rule to a blunt injury, and (C) applies the ultraviolet-burn rule.

q_0774.topic: refractive errors, amblyopia, and eye injuries
q_0774.stem: A child arrives with a pencil embedded in the left eye. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Leave the object in place and do not irrigate the eye
Apply a Fox shield rather than a regular eye patch
Patch the unaffected eye to prevent bilateral movement
Maintain bed rest with the child in a 30-degree Fowler position
Flush the eye copiously with lukewarm tap water for 20 minutes before transport
q_0774.rationale: The Emergency Treatment box for penetrating injuries directs the nurse never to remove a penetrating object, not to irrigate, to "Apply a Fox shield if available (not a regular eye patch) and apply patch over unaffected eye to prevent bilateral movement," and to "Maintain bed rest with child in a 30-degree Fowler position" (p. 646).
q_0774.trap: (E) is the chemical-burn action, and the two categories carry exactly opposite irrigation rules — copious tap water for 20 minutes for a chemical splash, never for a penetrating injury; (C) is the member most often dropped, since patching the uninjured eye seems pointless until you remember the eyes move together.

q_0775.topic: nursing care of the child with visual impairment
q_0775.stem: The parents of an infant with severe permanent visual impairment tell the nurse the baby "does not seem to know when we come in." What should the nurse teach them?
options: To watch for alternative cues — whether the eyelids blink, whether activity level changes, whether breathing patterns change, and whether the infant makes throaty sounds when they speak
That infants with visual impairment bond more slowly and that responsiveness typically emerges after 6 months
To increase the volume of their voices so the infant can locate them more easily
That attachment behaviors in a visually impaired infant are best assessed by a specialist rather than by parents
q_0775.rationale: The chapter names four cues the nurse teaches parents to read — eyelid blinking, acceleration or slowing of activity level, change in respiratory pattern when the parents come near, and throaty sounds when the parents speak — and adds that "In time, parents learn that the infant has unique ways of relating to them" (p. 648).
q_0775.trap: (B) offers a timeline instead of a skill, and (D) removes the observation from the people best placed to make it; the keyed intervention here is teaching an assessment, which parallels the Down syndrome instruction that lack of molding is physical rather than rejection.

q_0776.topic: nursing care of the child with visual impairment
q_0776.stem: A nurse is assigned to a 7-year-old admitted with bilateral eye patches after surgery. Which action is correct?
options: Identify herself as soon as she enters the room and before approaching the child
Provide a cane so the child can navigate to the bathroom independently
Rearrange the furniture each shift so the child learns to adapt to changes
Perform most of the child's routine care to keep the child safe
q_0776.rationale: The chapter directs that nurses "should always identify themselves as soon as they enter the room and before they approach the child," and that "Whenever possible, the same nurse should care for the child to ensure consistency in the approach" (pp. 648, 649).
q_0776.trap: (B) supplies a cane to a child who has had no training with one — the chapter states that "Unlike the child who is visually impaired, these children are not familiar with navigating with a cane"; (C) reverses the rule that furniture "is always placed in the same position to prevent collisions"; and (D) violates the stated objective to encourage independence.

q_0777.topic: nursing care of the child with visual impairment
q_0777.stem: A child with a prolonged visual impairment is to be admitted for an extended stay. Which measure best supports a safe environment?
options: Keep the furniture in the same position at all times and remind cleaning personnel to keep the room in order
Keep the room lights on continuously so shadows do not confuse the child
Keep the side rails up and the bed in low position at all times to prevent the child from getting up
Provide loose slippers and a long robe so the child can dress without assistance
q_0777.rationale: The chapter directs that "The furniture is always placed in the same position to prevent collisions" and to "Remind cleaning personnel to keep the room in order," adding that a rope may be attached from the bed to the bathroom if the child has difficulty navigating by feeling the walls (p. 649).
q_0777.trap: (C) achieves safety by removing independence, which the chapter lists as a nursing objective in its own right; (D) inverts a specific instruction, since the chapter calls for "well-fitting slippers and robes that do not drag on the floor" to prevent tripping.

q_0778.topic: nursing care of the child with visual impairment
q_0778.stem: Two days after surgery restores vision to a child who has been blind for years, the child is tearful and withdrawn. The parents are distressed that she is not happy. How should the nurse respond?
options: Explain that a period of depression can follow restored sight and must be respected and supported, and that the child should not be bombarded with visual stimuli
Explain that the mood change likely indicates a surgical complication requiring evaluation
Encourage the parents to increase visual stimulation to help the child appreciate her new abilities
Reassure the parents that the reaction will resolve once the child begins reading print instead of braille
q_0778.rationale: The chapter states that newly sighted children "may also go through a period of depression, which must be respected and supported," that "They should not be bombarded with visual stimuli," and that they often need "to talk about what they see and to compare the visual images with their mental ones" (p. 649).
q_0778.trap: (C) is the well-meaning opposite of the pacing rule; (D) pushes a transition the chapter explicitly allows the child to defer, since a newly sighted child "may prefer to use braille to read rather than learning a new visual approach because of familiarity with the touch system."

q_0779.stem: The mother of a newly diagnosed 3-year-old asks tearfully whether her return to work when he was an infant caused his autism. What is the nurse's best response?
options: Explain from a biologic standpoint what is known about the disorder, including that it is not related to socioeconomic level, race, or parenting style
Reassure her that many parents feel guilty and that her feelings will lessen with time
Explain that the cause is unknown, so no parenting factor can be entirely excluded
Refer her to a counselor, since guilt of this kind is outside the nurse's scope
q_0779.rationale: The chapter states that autism spectrum disorder "is not related to socioeconomic level, race, or parenting style," that nurses can "alleviate the guilt and shame often associated with this disorder by stressing what is known from a biologic standpoint," and that "It is imperative to help parents understand that they are not the cause of the child's condition" (pp. 650, 653).
q_0779.trap: (C) is technically hedged and does real harm, because it leaves the parenting hypothesis alive when the chapter has already excluded it; (B) normalizes the guilt without supplying the information that dissolves it, which is the specific method the chapter names.

q_0780.stem: A nurse is reviewing well-child visit schedules. At what ages does the American Academy of Pediatrics recommend screening for autism spectrum disorder, and what follows a concerning result?
options: At 18 and 24 months, with a concerning result leading to a comprehensive developmental evaluation by a specialist
At 18 and 24 months, with a concerning result establishing the diagnosis
At 12 and 18 months, with a concerning result leading to referral for speech therapy
At 24 and 36 months, with a concerning result leading to repeat screening in 6 months
q_0780.rationale: The chapter states that providers should "administer two ASD screenings at ages 18 and 24 months using a valid screening tool," names the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers and its follow-up interview, and directs that children with concerning results "should receive a comprehensive developmental evaluation from either a developmental pediatrician, child neurologist, child psychiatrist, or child psychologist" (p. 651).
q_0780.trap: (B) collapses screening into diagnosis, which is the distinction the chapter draws explicitly; (D) delays, and delay is already the named problem — diagnosis "is often not made until 2 to 3 years after symptoms are first recognized."

q_0781.stem: At a 16-month well visit, a mother reports her son babbles but has never used a single word, and adds that he had been saying "mama" at 12 months but stopped. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Immediate hearing and language evaluation, since single words are expected by 16 months and regression is a red-flag event
Referral to speech therapy alone, since the concern is expressive language
Reassessment at the 18-month visit, when autism screening is due
Reassurance that expressive language commonly fluctuates in the second year
q_0781.rationale: The chapter recommends "immediate hearing and language evaluation" for any child not displaying "babbling or gesturing by 12 months old, single words by 16 months old, and two-word phrases by 24 months old," and describes autism regression — developing normally and then regressing suddenly — as "a red-flag event that has been frequently displayed in expressive language" (p. 651).
q_0781.trap: (B) is the most common wrong pick because the presenting problem is speech, but the chapter pairs hearing with language every time, since hearing loss is the differential; (D) treats regression as normal variation, which this chapter never does.

q_0782.stem: A 6-year-old with autism spectrum disorder is admitted for a scheduled procedure. Which measures should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Provide a structured routine for the child to follow
Place the child in a private room and reduce extraneous auditory and visual distractions
Use minimal holding and eye contact to avoid behavioral outbursts
Encourage the parents to stay with the child as much as possible and to bring familiar possessions
Assign a roommate of similar age so the child has company in an unfamiliar setting
q_0782.rationale: The chapter names a structured routine as "a key in the management of ASD," directs decreasing stimulation "by using a private room, avoiding extraneous auditory and visual distractions, and encouraging the parents to bring in possessions the child is attached to," states that "minimal holding and eye contact may be necessary to avoid behavioral outbursts," and says the parents "ideally should stay with the child as much as possible" (p. 653).
q_0782.trap: (E) is the generic pediatric kindness this chapter specifically contradicts, and it is the distractor in the chapter's own review item; every wrong option in that item is an intervention that is correct in other contexts and wrong here, which is what makes this material worth drilling as a block.

q_0783.topic: stressors of hospitalization and children's vulnerability
q_0783.stem: A nurse is orienting a new graduate to the pediatric unit and explains that nearly every psychosocial intervention on the unit traces back to a short list of stressors. Which are the major stressors of hospitalization named by the chapter? Select all that apply.
options: Separation
Loss of control
Bodily injury
Pain
Loss of privacy
q_0783.rationale: The chapter names the major stressors of hospitalization as "separation, loss of control, bodily injury, and pain" (p. 658), and organizes both the developmental reactions and the nursing interventions around them.
q_0783.trap: (E) is the plausible non-member — privacy is genuinely addressed in the intensive care measures, but it is not one of the four; the chapter's stated reason children are vulnerable at all is that they "have a limited number of coping mechanisms to resolve stressors."

q_0784.topic: stressors of hospitalization and children's vulnerability
q_0784.stem: A 3-year-old is admitted after a previous hospitalization at age 2. The nurse assumes she will settle in easily because she has been through this before. How should this assumption be evaluated?
options: It is unwarranted; the chapter directs nurses to avoid assuming a child has learned to cope from prior medical experiences
It is reasonable, since previous experience is listed as a factor that shapes a child's reaction
It is reasonable for children over 2, who retain procedural memories of hospitalization
It is unwarranted only if the prior admission involved painful procedures
q_0784.rationale: The chapter states explicitly that "Nurses should avoid assuming the child has learned how to cope from prior medical experiences" (p. 661), and adds that "all children, even those who have been hospitalized before, benefit from an introduction to the environment and routine of the hospital unit" (p. 662).
q_0784.trap: (B) is true as far as it goes — previous experience with illness and hospitalization is listed among the factors shaping a reaction — and then draws exactly the wrong inference; multiple and continuing stresses such as frequent hospitalizations are a *risk* factor, not a protective one.

q_0785.topic: stressors of hospitalization and children's vulnerability
q_0785.stem: A nurse is reviewing two children admitted the same morning. One protests loudly, refuses to cooperate, and demands his parents. The other accepts every change quietly and does whatever she is asked. Which child does the chapter say may need more support?
options: The quiet, compliant child, because children who are active and strong willed tend to fare better when hospitalized
The protesting child, because his distress is unmistakable and immediate
Both equally, since outward behavior does not predict adjustment in either direction
Neither, since the response to admission does not predict the response to hospitalization
q_0785.rationale: The chapter states that "children who are active and strong willed tend to fare better when hospitalized than those who are passive," and directs that "nurses should be alert to children who passively accept all changes and requests; these children may need more support than" oppositional "children" (p. 661).
q_0785.trap: (B) is the intuitive triage, and it is the same reflex that makes staff misread despair as settling in and detachment as good adjustment; in this chapter, quiet compliance is a finding to investigate rather than a sign of coping.

q_0786.topic: stressors of hospitalization and children's vulnerability
q_0786.stem: The parents of a 7-year-old ask whether hospitalization will leave lasting harm. Which response reflects the chapter's position?
options: Children are remarkably adaptable and permanent ill effects are rare, and hospitalization can even be an opportunity to master stress and feel competent
Lasting effects are common, so the stay should be shortened as much as possible
Permanent effects depend entirely on the length of stay rather than on the family's involvement
Lasting harm is unlikely because school-age children do not experience separation anxiety
q_0786.rationale: The chapter states that "even with stressors, children are remarkably adaptable, and permanent ill effects are rare" (p. 658), and lists among the beneficial effects that hospitalization "can present an opportunity for children to master stress and feel competent in their coping abilities" (p. 661).
q_0786.trap: (C) names the wrong variable, since what lessens adverse responses is "family-centered care and frequent family visiting"; (D) is simply false, as school-age children's separation concerns are described in detail, and they may want parental support but be unwilling to ask for it.

q_0787.topic: stressors of hospitalization and children's vulnerability
q_0787.stem: A nurse is designing a unit survey and wants to ask about what children themselves say frightens them most about being in the hospital. Which fears does the chapter report children naming?
options: Being separated from family and friends, being in an unfamiliar environment, receiving treatments, and losing self-determination or choices
Needle sticks, surgery, and the possibility of dying
Missing school, falling behind classmates, and losing contact with teachers
Unfamiliar food, uncomfortable beds, and being woken at night
q_0787.rationale: The chapter reports that children name "being separated from family and friends, being in an unfamiliar environment, receiving treatments, and losing self-determination or choices," and that children 5 to 9 years old described hospitalization in stories focused on "being alone and feeling scared, angry, or sad" (p. 660).
q_0787.trap: (B) lists the fears adults expect children to name, and the chapter's own list leads with separation instead; note that three of the four map directly onto the four major stressors, which is why those four organize the whole chapter.

q_0788.topic: the three stages of separation anxiety
q_0788.stem: An 18-month-old admitted this morning screams when his mother steps out, refuses to let the nurse touch him, and tries to climb out of the crib to follow her. Which stage of separation anxiety does this describe?
options: Protest
Despair
Detachment
Regression
q_0788.rationale: In the protest stage "children react aggressively to the separation from the parent. They cry and scream for their parents, refuse the attention of anyone else, and are inconsolable in their grief" (p. 658), and Box 21.1 adds the toddler behaviors of attempting to escape to find the parent and physically forcing the parent to stay.
q_0788.trap: (D) names a real behavior from a different stage — regression to thumb sucking, bedwetting, or bottle use belongs to despair; protest behaviors "may last from hours to days" and may cease "only with physical exhaustion," which is what makes the next stage look like improvement.

q_0789.topic: the three stages of separation anxiety
q_0789.stem: On the third hospital day, the same toddler has stopped crying. He lies quietly, will not play, refuses meals, and has begun sucking his thumb again. A staff member remarks that he has finally settled in. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: These are despair behaviors, and the child's physical condition may deteriorate from refusal to eat, drink, or move
These are detachment behaviors, indicating the child has formed new attachments on the unit
The child has adjusted, and parental visits can now be reduced to avoid re-triggering protest
The quiet behavior indicates effective coping and requires no additional intervention
q_0789.rationale: In despair "the crying stops and depression is evident. The child is much less active, is uninterested in play or food, and withdraws from others," with regression to earlier behavior, and Box 21.1 notes the child's "physical condition may deteriorate from refusal to eat, drink, or move" (p. 658).
q_0789.trap: (C) and (D) act on the misreading the chapter names outright — staff "may think that the child is finally settling in to the new surroundings" (p. 658) — and (C) compounds it by reducing the very parental contact that is the intervention; this is the mirror of the previous item, where the same child's loud protest was misread as bad behavior.

q_0790.topic: the three stages of separation anxiety
q_0790.stem: A hospitalized 2-year-old now smiles at every staff member, plays readily with whoever enters, and appears happy. A nurse documents that she has adjusted well. What should a more experienced nurse point out?
options: Behaviors like these can represent detachment, which is resignation rather than contentment, though detachment is rarely seen in hospitalized children
These behaviors confirm adjustment, since forming relationships with staff is the goal of the stay
These behaviors indicate the child has moved backward into protest and needs her parents recalled
These behaviors are diagnostic of detachment and indicate permanent harm has occurred
q_0790.rationale: In detachment the child "superficially appears to adjust to the loss" and forms "new but superficial relationships," but "this behavior is the result of resignation and is not a sign of contentment"; the chapter adds that detachment "usually occurs after prolonged separation from parent" and "is rarely seen in hospitalized children" (p. 658).
q_0790.trap: (D) overreaches in the opposite direction from (B), and the qualifier is what this item turns on — a briefly hospitalized child should not be labeled detached, even though the chapter warns that the faster a child reaches this appearance, "the more likely it is that the child will be regarded as the ideal patient."

q_0791.topic: the three stages of separation anxiety
q_0791.stem: A 20-month-old's protest intensifies each time the nurse approaches the bedside. What should the nurse do?
options: Remain present and provide support through a quiet tone of voice, eye contact, and touch that communicates empathy
Stay away from the bedside, since the approach of a stranger clearly worsens the child's distress
Ask the parents to remain outside the room until the child's protest subsides
Document that the child is not yet ready for nursing interaction and reattempt in several hours
q_0791.rationale: The chapter directs that protest and despair are normal and that the nurse provides support "via their physical presence, using a quiet tone of voice, maintaining eye contact, and using touch in a way that establishes rapport and communicates empathy" (p. 665).
q_0791.trap: (B) is named by the chapter as a misreading: "Because the protests increase when a stranger approaches the child, they may interpret that reaction as meaning they should stay away" (p. 658); (C) inverts the primary goal, which is preventing separation, particularly in children under 5.

q_0792.topic: the three stages of separation anxiety
q_0792.stem: A nurse is documenting the behaviors of a separated toddler and must distinguish the despair stage from the other two. Which behaviors belong to despair? Select all that apply.
options: Is inactive and withdraws from others
Lacks interest in the environment and is uncommunicative
Regresses to earlier behavior such as thumb sucking, bedwetting, or use of a bottle
Is depressed and sad
Physically attacks strangers by kicking, biting, or hitting
q_0792.rationale: Box 21.1 lists for despair: "Is inactive; Withdraws from others; Is depressed, sad; Lacks interest in environment; Is uncommunicative; Regresses to earlier behavior" (p. 658).
q_0792.trap: (E) belongs to protest, specifically the toddler additions to that stage, and it is the option that separates a reader who has memorized the stages from one who has only memorized the list; the clinical stakes are in the course column, where despair carries the warning that the child's "physical condition may deteriorate from refusal to eat, drink, or move."

q_0793.stem: A 4-year-old admitted two days ago is refusing to eat, has trouble falling asleep, cries quietly, and repeatedly asks when her parents will come. The nurse considers whether this is separation anxiety. What is accurate?
options: It is separation anxiety; in preschoolers the protest behaviors are more subtle and passive than in toddlers
It is not separation anxiety, since preschoolers tolerate brief separations and develop substitute trust in other adults
It is not separation anxiety, since the behaviors are passive rather than the protest behaviors that define it
It is separation anxiety only if the child also displays overt aggression toward staff
q_0793.rationale: The chapter states that in preschoolers "the protest behaviors are more subtle and passive": "refusing to eat, experiencing difficulty in sleeping, crying quietly for their parents, continually asking when the parents will visit, or withdrawing from others," and adds that "Nurses need to be sensitive to these less obvious signs" (p. 660).
q_0793.trap: (B) uses a true sentence from the same paragraph — preschoolers are "more secure interpersonally than toddlers" — to reach the wrong conclusion, since illness renders them less able to cope; (C) applies the toddler's loud template and misses the age-specific presentation entirely.

q_0794.stem: A 9-year-old admitted for a femur fracture becomes irritable with his parents and withdraws from the staff. He tells the nurse he is fine and does not need anything. What does the chapter suggest is happening?
options: School-age children may need and desire parental guidance or support but be unable or unwilling to ask for it, fearing they will appear weak or childish
The behavior indicates the child has entered the despair stage of separation anxiety
The behavior indicates that school-age children are largely unaffected by hospitalization
The behavior is best addressed by increasing the child's independence and reducing adult involvement
q_0794.rationale: The chapter states that school-age children "may need and desire parental guidance or support from adults but may be unable or unwilling to ask for it," fearing they "will appear weak, childish, or dependent," and that negative feelings may surface as "irritability and aggression toward parents, withdrawal from hospital personnel" (p. 660).
q_0794.trap: (D) takes the child's stated self-sufficiency at face value and withdraws the support the chapter says he wants but cannot request; cultural expectations to "be brave and strong" push toward stoicism, which is why the stated request is not the reliable signal here.

q_0795.stem: A 15-year-old scheduled for a two-week admission is most likely to identify which loss as the severest emotional threat?
options: Loss of peer-group contact, with its loss of group status, group control, and group acceptance
Separation from her parents, which peaks in adolescence as autonomy develops
Loss of privacy during physical examinations and procedures
Falling behind in schoolwork and being unable to compete with classmates
q_0795.rationale: The chapter states that for adolescents "Loss of peer-group contact may pose a severe emotional threat" because of "loss of group status, inability to exert group control or leadership, and loss of group acceptance," and notes that although the group expresses concern, "they continue their group activities, quickly filling the gap of the absent member" (p. 660).
q_0795.trap: (D) is the school-age concern — worrying "that they will not be able to compete or fit in with their classmates" — and it is the closest distractor, since both involve peers; the discriminator is that the school-age worry is about keeping up while the adolescent's is about group membership itself.

q_0796.stem: A hospitalized 5-year-old has a dressing changed. Which fear is most consistent with the chapter's account of this age?
options: Fear of bodily injury, which may be addressed by applying a small bandage and leaving dressings in place
Fear of the resulting scar, which is the dominant body-image concern at this age
Fear of the operation itself and the stitches, more than of the pain
Fear of falling behind in kindergarten during the admission
q_0796.rationale: The chapter states that "Beyond early infancy, all children fear bodily injury," that young children's body boundaries are poorly defined so "applying a small Band-Aid usually reassures them," and that "Prematurely removing a dressing may cause these children considerable concern" (p. 667).
q_0796.trap: (B) is the adolescent concern — adolescents "may express concern about the actual procedure but be much more anxious over the resulting scar" — and (C) is the school-age concern; all three options are real chapter content attached to the wrong age, which is how the chapter's own review item is built.

q_0797.stem: A 2-year-old admitted for pneumonia is having temper tantrums, refusing meals, and has stopped using the toilet. His father asks whether hospitalization has set him back permanently. What should the nurse explain?
options: These behaviors are the toddler's response to separation, which is the greatest stress of hospitalization in early childhood, and if separation is avoided young children have a tremendous capacity to withstand other stress
These behaviors indicate the child has entered the detachment stage and needs psychiatric consultation
These behaviors are unrelated to hospitalization and reflect normal toddler negativism
These behaviors predict lasting developmental regression and should be addressed with a behavior plan
q_0797.rationale: The chapter states that separation anxiety "is the greatest stress imposed by hospitalization during early childhood" and that "If separation is avoided, young children have a tremendous capacity to withstand any other stress," listing tantrums, refusal of usual mealtime and toileting routines, and regression among toddler behaviors (p. 659).
q_0797.trap: (C) dismisses the behaviors as ordinary toddlerhood, and the chapter does note that such behaviors "may also be expressions of anger, a physiologic response to stress, or symptoms of illness" — so the alternatives are real, but the answer is not to stop looking at separation; (D) reads a temporary reaction as a lasting one.

q_0798.topic: preparing the child and family for hospitalization
q_0798.stem: The parents of a 6-year-old scheduled for elective surgery in three weeks ask when to tell her. What should the nurse advise?
options: About 1 week in advance, so she can assimilate the information and ask questions
On the morning of surgery, so she has no time to become anxious
Immediately, so she has the maximum time to prepare
One to two days in advance, which is the standard for all preschool and school-age children
q_0798.rationale: The chapter recommends preparing "Children 4 to 7 years old" about 1 week in advance "so that they can assimilate the information and ask questions," with a longer lead time for older children (p. 662).
q_0798.trap: (D) applies the young-child interval — "1 or 2 days before admission is sufficient" for young children, because they "may begin to wonder about what they observed" — to a 6-year-old; the two lead times are the pair distractors most often swap, and the governing principle throughout is that "a fear of the unknown exceeds fear of the known."

q_0799.topic: preparing the child and family for hospitalization
q_0799.stem: A 3-year-old is admitted emergently and there was no opportunity for preparation. What should the nurse do?
options: Orient the child and family to hospital routines, establish expectations, and allow for questions
Defer all orientation until the child is stable, to avoid adding to the stress of the admission
Provide the standard 1-week preparation content in condensed form during the admission
Direct orientation to the parents only, since the child is too young to benefit
q_0799.rationale: The chapter directs that when sudden illness makes preparation impossible, the nurse should still "orient the child and family to hospital routines, establish expectations, and allow for questions" (p. 662), and states that all children benefit from an introduction to the environment and routine of the unit.
q_0799.trap: (D) reasons from the child's age to exclude her, but the chapter's emergency guidance is the opposite — unless the situation is life threatening, "children need to participate in their care to maintain a sense of control" (p. 674).

q_0800.topic: preparing the child and family for hospitalization
q_0800.stem: A nurse is completing the nursing admission history on a 4-year-old. What is the main purpose of this history?
options: To assess the child's usual health habits at home so a more normal environment can be provided in the hospital
To obtain a complete medication history so safe orders can be written
To predict how the hospital stay is likely to proceed and guide roommate selection
To document baseline physical findings against which improvement can be measured
q_0800.rationale: The chapter states that "One of the main purposes of the history is to assess the child's usual health habits at home to promote a more normal environment in the hospital" (p. 662), and notes that the self-perception and role-relationship patterns "offer insight into the child's potential reaction to hospitalization, especially in terms of separation."
q_0800.trap: (B) is the option most people miss, because asking about medications sounds unarguably correct; the admission history in this chapter is a psychosocial instrument, and medication and physical data belong to the physical assessment, which the chapter routes to another chapter entirely.

q_0801.topic: preparing the child and family for hospitalization
q_0801.stem: During the admission history, a mother mentions that she gives her son an herbal preparation daily. He is scheduled for surgery tomorrow. What should the nurse do?
options: Document the herbal product in the preoperative assessment, because of possible anesthesia or surgical complications
Advise the mother to discontinue all herbal products permanently
Note it in the psychosocial history but exclude it from the preoperative record, since it is not a prescribed medication
Reassure the mother that herbal products do not interact with anesthesia
q_0801.rationale: The chapter states that "It is important that the use of any herbal or complementary therapy be noted in a preoperative assessment because of possible anesthesia or surgical complications related to herbal products" (p. 664).
q_0801.trap: (C) treats complementary therapy as outside the medical record, which is exactly the omission the instruction exists to prevent; (B) overcorrects into a directive the chapter does not give, since it treats complementary practices as something to assess and record rather than to forbid.

q_0802.topic: preparing the child and family for hospitalization
q_0802.stem: A nurse is preparing a room for a 14-year-old being admitted this afternoon. Which consideration does the chapter identify as minimum for room assignment?
options: Age, sex, and nature of the illness, with age grouping especially important for adolescents
Acuity level and projected nursing hours per shift
Insurance status and anticipated length of stay
Proximity to the nurses' station, regardless of the patient's age
q_0802.rationale: The chapter states that "The minimum considerations for room assignment are age, sex, and nature of the illness," expands this in Box 21.7 to developmental age, seriousness of diagnosis, communicability of illness, and projected length of stay, and notes that age grouping "is especially important for adolescents," who are often placed on their own unit or in a separate section (p. 664).
q_0802.trap: (D) is a real safety consideration in practice and is not what this chapter names; note also the preadmission instruction to "Prepare roommate(s) for the arrival of a new patient," which is the step most often forgotten.

q_0803.topic: minimizing separation and loss of control
q_0803.stem: A 3-year-old's mother must leave for several hours. Which nursing action best supports the child during her absence?
options: Encourage the mother to leave a favorite blanket or toy, and apply an identification band to it
Remove reminders of home so the child is not repeatedly reminded of the separation
Advise the mother to slip out while the child is distracted to avoid a scene
Keep the child occupied with new toys purchased from the gift shop
q_0803.rationale: The chapter directs parents to "leave favorite articles from home with the child, such as a blanket or a toy," explains the child's reasoning — "if the parents left this, the parents will surely return" — and adds that an identification band on the toy prevents loss and "provides a symbol that the toy is experiencing the same needs as the child" (p. 665).
q_0803.trap: (C) is the deception the chapter names as part of a "destructive cycle of misunderstanding and unmet needs"; (D) reverses the chapter's advice that familiar things beat new ones, since "it is often better to wait" on new toys because small children "need the comfort and reassurance of familiar things."

q_0804.topic: minimizing separation and loss of control
q_0804.stem: An 11-month-old must have a lengthy physical examination. What is the best means of minimizing the need for restraint?
options: Preserve parent-child contact, performing nearly the entire examination in the parent's lap
Use soft wrist restraints from the outset so the examination can proceed without interruption
Perform the examination while the infant sleeps to avoid resistance entirely
Have two staff members hold the infant so the parent is not distressed by participating
q_0804.rationale: The chapter states that "For young children, particularly infants and toddlers, preserving parent-child contact is the best means of decreasing the need for restraint," and that nearly the entire physical examination "can be done in a parent's lap" (p. 666).
q_0804.trap: (D) removes the parent for the parent's sake, which is not the chapter's approach; for painful procedures specifically, "the nurse should assess the parents' preferences for assisting, observing, or waiting outside the room" rather than deciding for them.

q_0805.topic: minimizing separation and loss of control
q_0805.stem: A hospitalized 9-year-old complains that he never knows what is going to happen next. Which intervention best addresses this?
options: Develop a written daily schedule with the child and parent, post it in the room, and make a clock available
Explain the unit's standing routine to the child at the start of each shift
Reduce the number of scheduled activities so the day is simpler to follow
Draw pictures of daily activities beside clock faces showing when each will occur
q_0805.rationale: A written daily schedule is "most suitable for non–critically ill school-age and adolescent children who have mastered the concept of time," is planned jointly by nurse, parent, and child, is posted in the room, and is accompanied by "a clock or watch available for the child's use" (p. 666).
q_0805.trap: (D) is the correct technique for a *younger* child — the chapter's Nursing Alert has the child draw or select pictures with a clock face beside each, so that "When the two match, the child knows it is time for a favorite activity"; the two interventions are matched to different ages and are the likeliest swap here.

q_0806.topic: minimizing separation and loss of control
q_0806.stem: A hospitalized 13-year-old resists every aspect of her care and complains that nothing is up to her. Which approach best addresses the dominant stressor for her age?
options: Allow her to wear street clothes, make choices about food and bedtime, and participate in planning her care
Increase parental presence at the bedside, since separation is the major stressor of hospitalization
Explain that hospital routines cannot be individualized and that cooperation will shorten the stay
Assign the same nurse each shift and limit the number of staff entering the room
q_0806.rationale: The chapter states that "The dependent role of the hospitalized patient imposes tremendous feelings of loss for older children," and lists "jointly planning care, time structuring, wearing street clothes, making choices in food selections and bedtime, continuing school activities, and rooming with an appropriate-age child" as interventions (p. 666).
q_0806.trap: (B) applies the intervention for the wrong age — separation is the dominant stressor for young children, while loss of control dominates for older ones, and matching the intervention to the age's dominant stressor is the organizing rule of this whole chapter.

q_0807.topic: minimizing separation and loss of control
q_0807.stem: The parents of a hospitalized 6-year-old ask whether they should stop disciplining him while he is ill. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue discipline, because it provides security and predictability, and removing all limits makes children fear something catastrophic will happen
Suspend discipline during the admission and resume it once the child is fully recovered
Transfer discipline to the nursing staff so the parents can remain a source of comfort
Continue discipline only for behaviors that pose a safety risk on the unit
q_0807.rationale: The chapter states that discipline "should be continued to provide a measure of security and predictability," that when ill children know their parents expect certain standards "they feel certain that they will recover," and that "Conversely, when all limits are removed, they fear that something catastrophic will happen" (p. 672).
q_0807.trap: (B) is the compassionate reflex and the one parents most often take, and it produces the outcome the chapter warns about; it also sets up the posthospital problem, since parents who suspend limits then read the child's reactions as evidence of being spoiled.

q_0808.topic: play and expressive activities in the hospital
q_0808.stem: A nurse uses puppets and replicas of hospital equipment to help a 5-year-old work through his fear of an upcoming procedure. How should this be classified?
options: Therapeutic play, a nondirective modality that nurses use to help children deal with concerns and fears
Play therapy, a psychologic technique for children with emotional disturbance
Diversional activity, since the purpose is to occupy the child before the procedure
Dramatic play therapy, a hybrid requiring certification in child life
q_0808.rationale: The chapter defines therapeutic play as "an effective, nondirective modality for helping children deal with their concerns and fears, and at the same time, it often helps the nurse gain insights into children's needs and feelings," and says it "should not be confused with play therapy, a psychologic technique reserved for use by trained and qualified therapists as an interpretative method with emotionally disturbed children" (p. 669).
q_0808.trap: (B) is the confusable pair and the one the chapter names explicitly; the discriminators are who does it and for whom — nurses with any child for therapeutic play, trained therapists with emotionally disturbed children for play therapy.

q_0809.topic: play and expressive activities in the hospital
q_0809.stem: A hospitalized 6-year-old is angry and has been hitting the bed rail. Which activity does the chapter identify as best suited to this?
options: Expressive activity such as a pounding board, clay, or beanbags, which permits the safe release of anger and hostility
Diversional activity such as a movie or a board game, chosen for his age and interests
A quiet activity, to avoid reinforcing the aggressive behavior
Deferral of all play until the anger has resolved
q_0809.rationale: The chapter describes expressive activities as "one of the best opportunities for encouraging emotional expression, including the safe release of anger and hostility," naming tension release through large-muscle activity, "pounding and throwing games," beanbags, a pounding board, clay, and play dough (p. 668).
q_0809.trap: (B) is the other real category and it does something different — diversional activities are recreation, selected on the basis of "age, interests, and limitations"; (C) treats the anger as misbehavior to be extinguished rather than an emotion needing an outlet.

q_0810.topic: play and expressive activities in the hospital
q_0810.stem: A nurse offers a hospitalized child a choice of two activities, and the child declines both. What has the nurse accomplished?
options: The nurse has offered the child a choice, perhaps one of very few real choices the child has had that day
Nothing, since the activity was refused and no therapeutic goal was met
The nurse has identified that the child is too ill for developmentally appropriate activity
The nurse has confirmed that the activities selected were above the child's developmental level
q_0810.rationale: The chapter states that "In the hospital environment, most decisions are made for the child; play and other expressive activities offer the child much-needed opportunities to make choices for themselves. Even if a child chooses not to participate in a particular activity, the nurse has offered the child a choice, perhaps one of only a few real choices the child has had that day" (p. 668).
q_0810.trap: (B) measures the intervention by participation, which is precisely what this passage rejects; note also that hospitalized children have lower energy than healthy peers, so the chapter advises selecting activities "simpler than would normally be chosen for the child's specific developmental level."

q_0811.topic: play and expressive activities in the hospital
q_0811.stem: A 4-year-old on a sodium-restricted diet asks to play with modeling dough, and another child on the unit has a wheat allergy. What should the nurse know?
options: Modeling dough is contraindicated for the child on salt restriction because salt is one of its major constituents, and flour-based dough is contraindicated for the child with wheat allergy
Modeling dough is safe for both, since it is not ingested
Only the wheat-allergic child is at risk, since dietary sodium restriction applies to food alone
Both children should be offered modeling dough with supervision to ensure it is not eaten
q_0811.rationale: The chapter states that "a child who is allergic to wheat should not be given modeling dough made with flour" and that "A child on a restricted salt intake should not play with modeling dough because salt is one of its major constituents" (p. 669).
q_0811.trap: (C) is the more tempting half-right answer, because a skin-contact salt exposure sounds harmless; the chapter treats both as contraindications, and this is a place where a medical limit constrains play rather than the other way round — although the chapter also notes that "a procedure can be postponed briefly to allow the child to complete a special activity."

q_0812.topic: play and expressive activities in the hospital
q_0812.stem: A 5-year-old will not answer the nurse's questions about how he feels regarding his upcoming surgery. Which approach does the chapter identify as most likely to elicit what he is worried about?
options: Offer a puppet, since children see puppets as peers and will tell them feelings they hesitate to express to adults
Ask the parents to relay the child's concerns, since he is most open with them
Provide a detailed explanation of the surgery, since his silence indicates he does not understand
Defer the conversation until after surgery, when he can describe what he experienced
q_0812.rationale: The chapter states that in dramatic play "Most children see [puppets] as peers and readily communicate with them. Children will tell the puppet feelings that they hesitate to express to adults" (p. 669), and adds that a drawing before surgery "may reveal unvoiced concerns about mutilation, body changes, and loss of self-control."
q_0812.trap: (B) routes around the child rather than to him; (C) assumes silence means a knowledge gap when the chapter treats it as a disclosure problem, and the same section notes that imagined reasons for illness, "particularly of a sexual nature," are exactly what children will not say aloud but will reveal through drawing or doll play.

q_0813.topic: supporting parents and siblings during hospitalization
q_0813.stem: The mother of a hospitalized infant admits to the nurse that she feels angry and guilty and is ashamed of both feelings. What is the nurse's best response?
options: Emphasize that each of those feelings is a normal, expected, and healthy response to stress
Reassure her that most parents do not experience such feelings and that they will pass quickly
Refer her to the hospital chaplain, since guilt is a spiritual rather than a nursing concern
Redirect the conversation to the infant's progress to relieve her distress
q_0813.rationale: The chapter notes that parents "resist admitting to such feelings because they expect others to disapprove of behavior that is less than perfect," and directs the nurse to emphasize "that each is a normal, expected, and healthy response to stress" (p. 672).
q_0813.trap: (B) normalizes by denying how common the feelings are, which contradicts the chapter and leaves the shame intact; (C) hands off a conversation the chapter assigns to the nurse, though it notes that parents with deep religious beliefs may appreciate clergy and "may not have sufficient energy to initiate the contact" themselves.

q_0814.topic: supporting parents and siblings during hospitalization
q_0814.stem: The 7-year-old sibling of a hospitalized child tells his parents he does not want to hear anything about his brother's illness. How should the nurse advise the parents?
options: Respect the sibling who avoids information as a means of coping
Provide the full explanation anyway, since avoidance is denial that must be worked through
Provide information only to the older siblings, who can process it
Wait until the hospitalized child is discharged before explaining anything
q_0814.rationale: The chapter directs the nurse to offer information to young as well as older siblings but to "respect the sibling who avoids information as a means of coping" (p. 672).
q_0814.trap: (B) reframes a coping style as pathology; (C) and (D) both withhold from a group the chapter says must not be skipped, since "Children in every age group deserve an explanation of the sibling's illness or hospitalization" — the aim being to minimize a sibling's fear of getting sick too or of having caused the illness.

q_0815.topic: supporting parents and siblings during hospitalization
q_0815.stem: A father tells the nurse that his wife is exhausted after five days of staying continuously at their daughter's bedside but feels she cannot leave. What should the nurse do?
options: Encourage brief absences, arrange sleeping quarters on the unit outside the child's room, and plan alternating visits with another family member
Reassure them that continuous parental presence is required for family-centered care
Suggest the mother assume more of the direct care, since involvement reduces parental anxiety
Ask the mother to go home for the remainder of the admission so she can recover
q_0815.rationale: The chapter names "neglect of the parent's need for sleep, nutrition, and relaxation" as a potential problem of continuous involvement and directs the nurse to encourage brief absences, arrange sleeping quarters, and plan alternating visits (p. 672); it adds that "24-hour responsibility may be too much for some parents."
q_0815.trap: (C) inverts the chapter's finding, since parents "more involved in direct care may feel more anxiety than those less involved"; (B) turns an offer into a requirement, when the chapter's point is that "Not all parents feel equally comfortable assuming responsibility for their child's care."

q_0816.topic: supporting parents and siblings during hospitalization
q_0816.stem: The parents of a 3-year-old being discharged tomorrow ask what to expect at home. What should the nurse prepare them for?
options: A period of initial aloofness toward them, usually lasting minutes, followed by clinging, demands for attention, and possible regression in newly learned skills
Immediate return to baseline behavior, since the admission was brief
Emotional coldness followed by intense demanding dependence and anger directed at them
Gradual improvement in behavior over several weeks with no intervening regression
q_0816.rationale: Box 21.2 describes young children's posthospital behaviors as "initial aloofness toward parents; this may last from a few minutes (most common) to a few days," frequently followed by dependency behaviors including clinging and demands for attention, plus "Regression in newly learned skills (e.g., self-toileting)" (p. 661).
q_0816.trap: (C) is the *older* child's pattern — "Emotional coldness followed by intense, demanding dependence on parents; Anger toward parents; Jealousy toward others"; preparing parents matters because parents who do not expect these reactions "may misinterpret them as evidence of the child's being spoiled and demand perfect behavior at a time when the child is still reacting to the stress."

q_0817.topic: supporting parents and siblings during hospitalization
q_0817.stem: A nurse is identifying children at higher risk for adverse effects of hospitalization. Which factors does the chapter list? Select all that apply.
options: Age between 6 months and 5 years
Male gender
A difficult temperament
Multiple and continuing stresses such as frequent hospitalizations
Being an only child with no siblings at home
q_0817.rationale: Box 21.3 lists "'Difficult' temperament; Lack of fit between child and parent; Age (especially between 6 months old and 5 years old); Male gender; Below-average intelligence; Multiple and continuing stresses (e.g., frequent hospitalizations)" (p. 661).
q_0817.trap: (E) is the plausible non-member; note that this age band, 6 months to 5 years, is a different number from the 6-to-30-month peak for separation anxiety itself, and the two are easily conflated because they overlap.

q_0818.topic: preparing for discharge and home care
q_0818.stem: A nurse on the pediatric unit is admitting a child with a new tracheostomy who will require complex home care. When should discharge planning begin?
options: During the admission assessment
When the child is medically stable enough to tolerate teaching
Forty-eight hours before the anticipated discharge date
When the discharge order is written
q_0818.rationale: The chapter states that "The preparation for hospital discharge and home care begins during the admission assessment," with short- and long-term goals established to meet the child's physical and psychosocial needs (p. 672).
q_0818.trap: (B) sounds clinically prudent and delays the assessment of the home and family that the whole plan depends on; the chapter also directs that "a care coordinator or manager should be included early in the discharge process."

q_0819.topic: preparing for discharge and home care
q_0819.stem: A nurse is teaching a mother to perform her son's dressing change before discharge. Which approach reflects the chapter's teaching plan?
options: Divide the skill into discrete steps, teach each step until it is learned, and request return demonstration before introducing new skills
Demonstrate the complete procedure twice, then have the mother perform the entire sequence at the end of the teaching
Provide detailed written instructions and have the mother practice at home, with a follow-up call to verify
Teach the skill on the day of discharge so it is fresh in the mother's memory
q_0819.rationale: The discharge teaching plan "incorporates levels of learning, such as observing, participating with assistance, and finally acting without help or guidance. The skill is divided into discrete steps, and each step is taught to the family member until it is learned. Return demonstration of the skill is requested before new skills are introduced" (p. 672).
q_0819.trap: (B) defers verification to the end, when the chapter checks each skill before moving on; (C) sends the family home to practice unsupervised, whereas the chapter's provision is a supervised "transition or trial period," especially valuable "when the family lives far from the hospital."

q_0820.topic: preparing for discharge and home care
q_0820.stem: A family is being discharged after their daughter's outpatient tonsillectomy. Which action is required before they leave?
options: Ensure all prescriptions are filled and given to the family, and provide detailed written instructions with telephone numbers for assistance
Provide verbal instructions and confirm the family can obtain prescriptions at their own pharmacy the next day
Schedule the family to return the following morning for written instructions and medications
Give written instructions only if the family requests them, to avoid overwhelming them at discharge
q_0820.rationale: The ambulatory discharge instructions direct the nurse to "Request that all prescriptions be filled and given to the family before discharge," and the home-care section states that "All families should receive detailed written instructions about home care, with telephone numbers for assistance, before they leave the hospital" (pp. 672, 674).
q_0820.trap: (B) is keyed in the chapter's own review item as a statement indicating a need for more teaching, and it is the most reasonable-sounding wrong answer in the section — going to a familiar pharmacy for counseling is sensible, and tomorrow is too late.

q_0821.topic: preparing for discharge and home care
q_0821.stem: A nurse is completing discharge teaching after a 5-year-old's outpatient surgery. Which instructions belong in that teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Explain how much nausea, vomiting, and fever are expected and exactly what to do beyond that range
Determine whether one person will have sole responsibility for the child's safety and comfort during transport
Give any prescribed pain medication before the family leaves the facility
Explain that the family will be contacted for follow-up, and that they should call sooner with any concerns
Instruct the family to withhold all fluids for 24 hours to prevent postoperative vomiting
q_0821.rationale: The fifteen-item discharge box directs the nurse to discuss nausea and vomiting and fever with explicit thresholds and actions, to determine whether a person other than the driver will be responsible for the child during transport, to give prescribed medication before leaving, and to explain the follow-up contact while inviting earlier calls (p. 674).
q_0821.trap: (E) is the non-member and it inverts the chapter's actual guidance, which is to give specific examples of clear fluids and to send a cup with a cap and straw for drinking in the car — with the single exception of oral facial surgery, where a straw may be contraindicated.

q_0822.topic: preparing for discharge and home care
q_0822.stem: A child is discharged from the ambulatory surgery unit at noon. When does the chapter's follow-up telephone system contact the family?
options: Within 48 to 72 hours after discharge
Within 24 hours after discharge
At the time of the first postoperative office visit
Only if the family has not called the unit within a week
q_0822.rationale: The chapter states that "A follow-up telephone call system allows for nurses to check on the child's progress within 48 to 72 hours after discharge," and adds that the call "provides an opportunity for the nurse to review discharge information and answer additional questions" (pp. 673–674).
q_0822.trap: (D) makes follow-up contingent on the family initiating it, which reverses the whole point of the system; the family is separately told they should not hesitate to call before the scheduled contact, so both directions of communication are open.

q_0823.stem: A 7-year-old arrives in the emergency department with a forearm fracture. The department is busy and the nurse considers proceeding quickly without explanation. What does the chapter advise?
options: Unless the emergency is life threatening, allow the child to participate, because the extra few minutes may save many more minutes of resistance during later procedures
Proceed without explanation, since speed is the priority in the emergency department
Explain everything only to the parents, since the child is too distressed to absorb information
Postpone all explanation until the child is admitted to the unit
q_0823.rationale: The chapter states that "Unless an emergency is life threatening, children need to participate in their care to maintain a sense of control," and that "the extra few minutes needed to allow children to participate may save many more minutes of useless resistance and uncooperativeness during subsequent procedures" (p. 674).
q_0823.trap: (B) is the time pressure the chapter names and then argues against on its own terms — participation is presented as the faster route overall, not merely the kinder one; other measures named are ensuring privacy, preserving parent-child contact, and personally remaining calm.

q_0824.stem: A child underwent an emergency procedure with no opportunity for preparation. What is the most useful approach afterward?
options: Listen to the explanations the child offers, using drawing, doll play, or storytelling, and then build on what the child already understands
Provide the complete procedural explanation that could not be given beforehand
Avoid revisiting the event, since discussing it may retraumatize the child
Ask the parents to explain the procedure once the child is calm
q_0824.rationale: The chapter states that counseling after the fact has therapeutic value and that the direction reverses: "instead of supplying information, the nurse listens to the explanations offered by the child," using "drawing, doll play, or storytelling," and then bases additional information on what the child already understands (p. 674).
q_0824.trap: (B) is the intuitive catch-up and it is backward for this situation; the reason matters, since children are "vulnerable to misinterpreting causes for stress" and the misconception has to be found before it can be corrected.

q_0825.stem: The parents of a child admitted unexpectedly to the intensive care unit appear overwhelmed. What is the most effective approach to their stress?
options: Ask them what they find stressful and implement interventions specific to what they name, repeating the assessment periodically
Provide the unit's standard family information packet and orientation to intensive care
Limit visiting hours until the child is stable so the parents can rest
Reassure them that parents of unexpectedly admitted children adjust within a few days
q_0825.rationale: The chapter names as the most effective coping strategy to "simply ask them what is stressful and implement interventions specific to their stress," repeating the assessment "periodically to account for changes in perceptions over time," and notes that "Parents experience significantly more stress when the admission is unexpected rather than expected" (p. 675).
q_0825.trap: (B) substitutes a generic list for the individualized assessment the chapter specifically recommends over it; (C) reduces the parental presence that the same section directs the nurse to encourage.

q_0826.stem: A new nurse asks how children in the intensive care unit manage to sleep. Which measures are consistent with the chapter's guidance? Select all that apply.
options: Cluster care so that treatments requiring equipment are performed at one time
Turn alarms as low as safely possible and keep equipment noise to a minimum
Schedule a time when the child is left undisturbed, and orient the child to day and time with a clock or calendar in view
Turn off bedside equipment that is not in use, such as suction and oxygen
Silence alarms during the night so the child can have uninterrupted sleep
q_0826.rationale: The chapter directs the nurse to "Perform treatments requiring equipment at one time," to "Turn alarms as low as safely possible," to keep equipment noise to a minimum, to "Schedule a time when child is left undisturbed," to "Orient child to day and time; have clocks or calendars in easy view," and to "Turn off bedside equipment that is not in use" (p. 674).
q_0826.trap: (E) fails on safety rather than on comfort, and the distinction is exact — the chapter permits lowering an alarm as far as is safe, never silencing it; note also that the uninterrupted sleep cycles the chapter gives are 60 minutes for infants and 90 minutes for older children, which distractors reverse.

q_0827.stem: A 4-year-old in the intensive care unit is not sleeping and startles at every sound. Besides noise, which environmental stressors does the chapter identify in this setting?
options: Constant lights that disturb day and night rhythms, unfamiliar smells, and the sense of urgency among staff
Frequent visitors and excessive parental presence at the bedside
The absence of age-appropriate roommates and the lack of a playroom
Unfamiliar food and the absence of family meal routines
q_0827.rationale: Box 21.11 lists among environmental stressors "Unfamiliar surroundings (e.g., crowding); Unfamiliar sounds; Unfamiliar people; Unfamiliar and unpleasant smells (e.g., alcohol, adhesive remover, body odors); Constant lights (disturb day/night rhythms); Activity related to other patients; Sense of urgency among staff" (p. 675).
q_0827.trap: (B) names parental presence as a stressor, which inverts the chapter's instruction to encourage parents to stay; the physical stressors are listed separately and include pain and discomfort, immobility, sleep deprivation, inability to eat or drink, and changes in elimination habits.

q_0828.topic: informed consent and assent in pediatric care
q_0828.stem: A nurse is reviewing what makes consent for a child's procedure valid. Which conditions does the chapter require? Select all that apply.
options: The person must be capable of giving consent, being over the age of majority and competent
The person must receive the information needed to make an intelligent decision
The person must act voluntarily, without force, fraud, deceit, duress, or coercion
The person must sign the consent form in the presence of the performing physician
q_0828.rationale: The chapter numbers exactly three conditions: capacity, adequate information, and voluntariness, defining the third as acting "voluntarily when exercising freedom of choice without force, fraud, deceit, duress, or other forms of constraint or coercion" (p. 678).
q_0828.trap: (D) confuses the evidence with the act, and the chapter separates them — "A signed consent form is the legal document that signifies that the process of informed consent has occurred" (p. 679); the condition most often dropped from recall is voluntariness, because it reads as too obvious to state.

q_0829.topic: informed consent and assent in pediatric care
q_0829.stem: A 9-year-old scheduled for a bone marrow aspiration says he does not want it done. His mother has signed the consent. What is accurate about his role in the decision?
options: His assent should be sought, but assent is an ethical requirement rather than a legal one
His refusal is legally binding and the procedure cannot proceed
Assent is not sought until adolescence, so his objection has no formal standing
His silence during the explanation would have constituted assent if he had not spoken
q_0829.rationale: The chapter states that assent applies to children "greater than 7 years with appropriate age, maturity, and psychologic state" (p. 678) and that "Assent is not a legal requirement but an ethical one to protect the rights of children" (p. 679).
q_0829.trap: (D) is the misreading the chapter forecloses in one sentence — "If the child or adolescent merely fails to object, this does not equate assent" (p. 678); (C) pushes the age cue to adolescence when the chapter's threshold is greater than 7 years.

q_0830.topic: informed consent and assent in pediatric care
q_0830.stem: A surgeon has explained a procedure to a child's parents and left the unit. The mother tells the nurse she is not sure what the alternatives were. What should the nurse do?
options: Notify the surgeon, since explaining the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives is the physician's legal responsibility
Explain the alternatives, since reinforcing the explanation is within the nurse's role
Witness the signature and document that the mother had questions
Ask the mother to sign and arrange for the surgeon to answer questions postoperatively
q_0830.rationale: The chapter assigns the roles explicitly: "It is the physician's legal responsibility to explain the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives," while the nurse "witnesses the patient's, parent's, or legal guardian's signature on the consent form and may reinforce what the patient has been told" (p. 679).
q_0830.trap: (B) stretches "reinforce what the patient has been told" into supplying information that was never given, which is the boundary this item tests; (C) and (D) both proceed to a signature while a condition of valid consent — adequate information — is unmet.

q_0831.topic: informed consent and assent in pediatric care
q_0831.stem: A 16-year-old arrives at the clinic alone. Which circumstance would make her an emancipated minor under the chapter's account?
options: She is married
She is 16, which in a few states meets the mature minor threshold
She has a part-time job and contributes to household expenses
She has a signed note from her parents authorizing treatment
q_0831.rationale: The chapter names the emancipating circumstances as "pregnancy, marriage, high school graduation, independent living, or military service" (p. 679).
q_0831.trap: (B) is the confusable pair — the mature minor exception is recognized in a few states "for children 14 years and older" and may require legal action, while emancipation follows from a named circumstance and carries no age; (D) describes consent by proxy, which is a different mechanism entirely.

q_0832.stem: A nurse is choosing words to explain an upcoming test to a 4-year-old. Which substitution is consistent with the chapter's guidance?
options: Say "medicine to help the place in your body show up on a picture" instead of "dye"
Say "we will fix your heart" instead of naming the surgery
Say "the cuff will squeeze your arm tightly" instead of "check your pressure"
Say "we will put you to sleep" to describe anesthesia gently
q_0832.rationale: Table 22.1 lists "dye" among the words to avoid, with that exact substitution (p. 680); the table's organizing logic is that each avoided word carries a second, frightening meaning.
q_0832.trap: (B) uses a word that is on the avoid list — "fix" implies the child is broken, and it is the entry most often misread as acceptable because it sounds gentle; (D) is also on the list, because it is what happens to a pet, and the substitution is "different kind of sleep so you won't feel anything"; (C) replaces the suggested "hug your arm" with a threat.

q_0833.stem: A nurse plans to demonstrate an upcoming procedure on a doll for a 2-year-old. Which doll should be used?
options: A doll from the unit's supply, because the child may believe her own favorite doll is really feeling the procedure
The child's own favorite doll, because familiarity makes the demonstration more meaningful
No doll, because toddlers cannot generalize from a demonstration
A doll chosen by the parents from home, since it will be more comforting
q_0833.rationale: The toddler preparation guidance directs the nurse to "Use play; demonstrate on doll but avoid child's favorite doll because child may think doll is really" feeling the procedure (p. 680), which is animism applied to the comfort object.
q_0833.trap: (B) and (D) both reach for the familiar object, which is right for almost every other comfort intervention in this chapter and wrong here; note the toddler's session should also be about 5 to 10 minutes and given shortly or immediately before the procedure, not a day ahead.

q_0834.stem: A nurse has drawn blood from a 4-year-old and the bleeding has stopped. Why does the chapter direct applying an adhesive bandage over the puncture site?
options: Because the preschooler fears that the body's contents will leak out through the opening
Because it prevents contamination of the site with skin flora
Because it marks the site for the next shift
Because bandages are a form of positive reinforcement after a procedure
q_0834.rationale: "Apply an adhesive bandage over puncture site" appears under the preschooler's "Fears of Bodily Harm, Intrusion, and Castration" (p. 680); the related instruction in the same block is to "Emphasize that no other body part will be involved."
q_0834.trap: (B) is a true statement about bandages that does not answer a developmental stem, which is what makes it the strongest distractor; note also the chapter's competing caution that adhesive bandages are an aspiration hazard in young children (p. 706), so the resolution is age and supervision rather than one rule for all.

q_0835.stem: A 10-month-old cries and struggles as soon as the nurse carrying a syringe enters the room, before anything has been done. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Older infants may associate objects, places, or persons with prior painful experiences and resist at the sight of them
This is stranger anxiety, which is unrelated to any previous procedure
Infants do not retain memories of past experiences, so the reaction must be to the nurse's manner
This indicates the infant is in pain from an unrecognized source
