q_0835.rationale: The chapter makes "Memory for Past Experiences" a developmental characteristic of infancy and builds four interventions on it, beginning "Realize that older infants may associate objects, places, or persons with prior painful experiences and will cry and resist at the sight of them" (p. 680).
q_0835.trap: (C) is the claim the chapter's own review item keys as wrong, and it is widely believed; the interventions that follow from the correct reading are to keep frightening objects out of view and to perform painful procedures in a separate room rather than in the crib.

q_0836.stem: A 5-month-old is scheduled for elective surgery at 10:00. Her mother asks how late she may breastfeed and whether formula would be different. What should the nurse tell her?
options: Breast milk requires a 4-hour fast and formula requires 6 hours, because nonhuman milk empties from the stomach like a solid
Both require a 4-hour fast, since both are liquids
Both require a 6-hour fast, since both are milk
Breast milk may be given up to 2 hours before, since it is treated as a clear liquid
q_0836.rationale: Table 22.2 gives clear liquids greater than 2 hours, breast milk 4 hours, and infant formula, nonhuman milk, and a light meal 6 hours, with the footnote explaining that "Because nonhuman milk is similar to solids in gastric emptying time, the amount ingested must be considered" (p. 686).
q_0836.trap: (B) and (C) collapse the two intervals, which is the most common error; note also that the fasting periods "apply to all ages" and are not scaled for a neonate, and that fasting too long is itself a harm — discomfort, headache, dehydration, hypoglycemia, and delayed discharge.

q_0837.stem: The parents of a child scheduled for surgery mention that an uncle had a dangerous reaction to anesthesia, but say their son had his tonsils out last year with no problem. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: He may still be susceptible to malignant hyperthermia, because a previous uneventful anesthetic does not exclude it
The uneventful prior surgery effectively rules out susceptibility
The family history is relevant only if the affected relative was a parent or sibling
Susceptibility is determined by preoperative laboratory screening rather than history
q_0837.rationale: The chapter states that a family or previous history of sudden high fever with surgery increases risk and adds directly that "Children who have successfully undergone prior surgery without adverse effects may still be considered susceptible" (p. 687).
q_0837.trap: (B) is the single most inviting wrong answer in this section, because a clean prior anesthetic feels like the strongest possible reassurance; the disorder is described as "a potentially fatal pharmacogenetic disorder of muscle metabolism" triggered by inhaled anesthetics and succinylcholine.

q_0838.stem: During surgery, end-tidal carbon dioxide begins climbing and the child develops tachycardia and muscle rigidity. Which action comes first?
options: Immediate discontinuation of the triggering agent
Application of ice packs to the groin, axillae, and neck
Administration of intravenous dantrolene sodium
Transfer to the intensive care unit
q_0838.rationale: The chapter orders treatment as discontinuation of the triggering agent, hyperventilation with 100% oxygen, intravenous dantrolene sodium, cooling measures if hyperthermic, and then intensive care for at least 36 hours (p. 687).
q_0838.trap: (C) names the definitive drug and is still not first, which is what this item turns on; (B) leads with cooling, which is step 4 and only if the child is actually hyperthermic — note that the symptom list leads with rising carbon dioxide, so temperature is the later finding despite the name of the disorder.

q_0839.stem: A nurse is preparing three children for surgery: a 6-month-old, a 3-year-old, and a 16-year-old. Which fears does the chapter attach to each?
options: Stranger anxiety in the infant, separation anxiety in the preschooler, and fear of injury or death in the adolescent
Separation anxiety in the infant, fear of injury in the preschooler, and stranger anxiety in the adolescent
Fear of death in all three, differing only in how it is expressed
Fear of the mask at induction in all three, which is the chapter's single named stress point
q_0839.rationale: The chapter states that children are at higher anesthetic and recovery risk "because of higher anxiety in the preoperative period associated with stranger anxiety (infants), separation anxiety (toddlers and preschoolers), and fear of injury or death (adolescents)" (p. 686).
q_0839.trap: (D) names a real stress point and makes it the only one, when the chapter lists six — admission, blood tests, preoperative medication, transport to the operating room, the mask at induction, and the postanesthesia care unit; note also that underpants or pajama bottoms are worn into the operating room and removed after induction.

q_0840.topic: fever versus hyperthermia and their management
q_0840.stem: A nurse is explaining why the same intervention does not work for every elevated temperature. What distinguishes fever from hyperthermia?
options: Fever raises the hypothalamic set point, so antipyretics work; in hyperthermia the set point is normal, so only cooling works
Fever is infectious and hyperthermia is not, which is why only fever responds to antipyretics
Fever exceeds 38 degrees Celsius and hyperthermia exceeds 40 degrees Celsius
Fever is regulated and self-limiting, so neither antipyretics nor cooling are indicated
q_0840.rationale: The chapter defines fever as "An elevation in set point such that body temperature is regulated at a higher level" and hyperthermia as "Body temperature exceeding the set point," and states that "Because the set point is normal in hyperthermia but increased in fever, different approaches must be used" (pp. 693–694).
q_0840.trap: (C) turns a mechanism into a number, and (B) uses etiology where the chapter uses physiology; the practical consequence is stated plainly — "antipyretics are of no value in hyperthermia because the set point is already normal."

q_0841.topic: fever versus hyperthermia and their management
q_0841.stem: A 3-year-old has a fever of 39.2 degrees Celsius and received acetaminophen 15 minutes ago. Her father is applying a cool wet washcloth and she has begun shivering. What should the nurse do?
options: Stop the cooling measure, and explain that environmental measures are applied about 1 hour after the antipyretic so the set point has come down
Continue the cooling measure, since shivering indicates the temperature is falling
Add a tepid sponge bath, which is the most effective measure for a febrile child
Remove all clothing and lower the room temperature until the shivering stops
q_0841.rationale: The chapter says traditional cooling measures "are effective if used approximately 1 hour after an antipyretic is given so the set point is lowered," and that shivering "is the body's way of maintaining the elevated set point by producing heat," greatly increasing metabolic requirements (p. 693).
q_0841.trap: (C) is the single most reliable distractor in the chapter, because tepid sponging for fever is what most people were taught — the chapter calls it ineffective for febrile children and adds the parenthesis that "these measures are effective for hyperthermia"; the metabolic cost of shivering is three to five times baseline.

q_0842.topic: fever versus hyperthermia and their management
q_0842.stem: The mother of a 2-year-old with a viral illness asks how often she may give acetaminophen and whether aspirin would work better. What should the nurse teach?
options: Acetaminophen may be given every 4 hours but no more than five times in 24 hours because of hepatotoxicity, and aspirin is not given to children because of its association with Reye syndrome
Acetaminophen may be given every 4 hours around the clock, and aspirin is an acceptable alternative if acetaminophen is unavailable
Ibuprofen should replace both, since it is approved from birth
Antipyretics should be given on a schedule until the temperature normalizes, whatever the child's comfort
q_0842.rationale: The chapter names acetaminophen the preferred drug with that interval and ceiling, states that aspirin "should not be given to children because of its association in children with influenza virus or chickenpox and Reye syndrome," and approves ibuprofen from 6 months (p. 693).
q_0842.trap: (B) is six doses, which exceeds the ceiling the hepatotoxicity warning sets; (D) inverts the chapter's endpoint, which is that "The child's level of discomfort is the best indication for continued treatment" and that the temperature "should not be repeatedly measured."

q_0843.topic: fever versus hyperthermia and their management
q_0843.stem: A 2-year-old had a 3-minute generalized seizure with a fever. The parents ask whether he has brain damage and whether scheduled acetaminophen will prevent another one. What should the nurse tell them?
options: A simple febrile seizure lasting less than 10 minutes does not cause brain damage, and evidence does not support antipyretics or anticonvulsants to prevent a second one
Brain damage is unlikely, and scheduled antipyretics are the standard preventive measure
A single febrile seizure predicts epilepsy, so anticonvulsant prophylaxis should be started
Recurrence is rare, occurring in fewer than 5% of children
q_0843.rationale: The chapter states that "Simple febrile seizures lasting less than 10 minutes do not cause brain damage or other debilitating effects" and that evidence does not support "antipyretic drugs or anticonvulsants to prevent a second febrile seizure" (p. 694).
q_0843.trap: (B) is the intervention most families expect and most clinicians once gave; (D) misstates the figure, since about 30% to 50% of children have subsequent febrile seizures — the 2% to 5% figure is the incidence of febrile seizures at all, in children 6 months to 5 years.

q_0844.topic: hospital safety, falls, and infection control precautions
q_0844.stem: A nurse is assigning precautions for newly admitted children. Which conditions require Airborne Precautions? Select all that apply.
options: Measles
Varicella, including disseminated zoster
Tuberculosis
Invasive Neisseria meningitidis disease
Respiratory syncytial virus in an infant
q_0844.rationale: Box 22.2 places measles, varicella including disseminated zoster, and tuberculosis under Airborne Precautions, which are for "serious illnesses transmitted by airborne droplet nuclei" (p. 696).
q_0844.trap: (D) is Droplet and (E) is Contact, and varicella is the member most often misassigned — chickenpox lesions are also a contact hazard, which is why the box notes that precautions "may be combined for diseases that have multiple routes of transmission"; the same organism can also split by site, as pharyngeal diphtheria is Droplet while cutaneous diphtheria is Contact.

q_0845.topic: hospital safety, falls, and infection control precautions
q_0845.stem: A child is placed on Droplet Precautions. What does the nurse need to know about the room?
options: Special air handling and ventilation are not required, because droplets do not remain suspended in the air
A negative-pressure room is required, as with any transmission-based precaution
Droplet Precautions replace Standard Precautions for the duration of the illness
Droplets travel about 20 feet, so visitors must remain outside the room
q_0845.rationale: The chapter states that large-particle droplets travel "usually 3 feet or less but up to 10 feet" and that "Because droplets do not remain suspended in the air, special air handling and ventilation are not required to prevent droplet transmission" (p. 696).
q_0845.trap: (C) is the more dangerous error and the chapter forecloses it directly — Transmission-Based Precautions "are to be used in addition to Standard Precautions"; (B) applies the airborne requirement, which exists precisely because those particles do stay suspended.

q_0846.topic: hospital safety, falls, and infection control precautions
q_0846.stem: A nurse is completing fall precautions for a hospitalized 6-year-old who walked independently at home. Which action is correct?
options: Assist the child with ambulation anyway, and keep dim lights on while she sleeps
Allow independent ambulation to the bathroom, since she walked well before admission
Turn all lights off at night to support normal sleep rhythms
Keep the door closed at night so hallway noise does not wake her
q_0846.rationale: The chapter directs the nurse to "Assist the child with ambulation even though he or she may have ambulated well before hospitalization," to "Keep lights on at all times, including dim lights while sleeping," and to "Keep the patient's door open unless isolation status prohibits" (p. 696).
q_0846.trap: (B) reasons from the child's baseline rather than from her current state, when postoperative status, sedation, and new lines all appear on the risk list; note the chapter also names the family daybed as a fall hazard, and instructs that patients who have been lying down "need to get up slowly, sitting on the side of the bed before standing."

q_0847.topic: hospital safety, falls, and infection control precautions
q_0847.stem: A nurse is about to change an infant's wet diaper with ordinary stool. Which action is consistent with the chapter's guidance?
options: Change the diaper without gloves, since the plastic lining is a sufficient barrier, and perform hand hygiene afterward
Wear gloves for every diaper change without exception
Wear gloves, and skip hand hygiene afterward since the hands stayed covered
Wear a gown and gloves, since all diaper changes involve body substances
q_0847.rationale: The chapter says that for loose or explosive stools the nurse should "wear gloves and possibly gowns" but that "Otherwise, the plastic lining of disposable diapers provides a sufficient barrier between the hands and body substances" (p. 696), while requiring hand hygiene after glove removal because "gloves fail to provide complete protection."
q_0847.trap: (C) is the substitution the chapter rules out, noting that "The absence of visible leaks does not indicate that gloves are intact"; (B) and (D) are the over-cautious answers, and the discriminating cue the chapter gives is the character of the stool. Note also its Nursing Alert that the stethoscope is itself a vector.

q_0848.stem: A nurse is auditing the unit for restraint use. Which of the following are NOT considered restraints under the chapter's definition? Select all that apply.
options: An armboard securing a peripheral intravenous line, not tied to the bed
Hand mitts that are not tied down and not paired with a wrist restraint
Crib side rails and a crib dome on an infant's bed
A mummy wrap used only for the duration of a throat examination
Tight tucking of sheets to prevent a child from moving in bed
q_0848.rationale: The chapter excludes an armboard "unless it is tied down to the bed or immobilizes the entire limb," hand mitts "unless tied down to the bed or used in conjunction with a wrist restraint," developmentally age-appropriate safety devices including crib side rails and crib domes, and a mummy wrap "When used only for the duration of the test or procedure" (pp. 698–699).
q_0848.trap: (E) is on the chapter's own list of restraints, alongside limb, elbow, and vest restraints, and it is the one that does not look like a device; each of the four correct options carries a condition that flips it, which is why this list is worth learning as conditions rather than as items.

q_0849.stem: A 7-year-old requires a behavioral restraint for violent behavior. How often must the order be renewed?
options: Every 1 hour
Every 2 hours
Every 4 hours
Every 15 minutes
q_0849.rationale: The chapter states that unless state law is more restrictive, behavioral restraints "must be reordered every 15 minutes for a personal restraint, every 1 hour for children under 9 years of age, and every 2 hours for children 9 to 17 years old; orders for adults 18 and older are required every 4 hours" (p. 698).
q_0849.trap: (D) is the interval for a personal restraint, meaning a physical hold, rather than for a mechanical one; the chapter's own review item shifts these intervals up one step and is keyed wrong, and note separately that an in-person evaluation is required within 1 hour and at least every 24 hours.

q_0850.stem: A nurse is applying wrist restraints to a child. Which technique is correct?
options: Secure the ties to the stationary bed frame, leave one finger breadth between the skin and the device, and use knots that allow quick release
Secure the ties to the side rails so the restraint moves with the rail
Leave two finger breadths of slack and use a secure knot that will not loosen
Place limb restraints above the level of the intravenous site so the line is protected
q_0850.rationale: The chapter directs that "Restraints with ties must be secured to the stationary bed or crib frame, not the side rails," and describes "leaving one finger breadth between skin and the device and tying knots that allow for quick release" (p. 699).
q_0850.trap: (B) is the error with the clearest mechanism — lowering the rail then drags the limb; (C) is the adult teaching for some devices and defeats emergency release; (D) reverses the instruction to place limb restraints "distal to the IV."

q_0851.stem: A restraint order for a child expires in 40 minutes, and the child is now calm, oriented, and cooperative. What should the nurse do?
options: Discontinue the restraint now, because release occurs as soon as it is safe even if the order timeframe has not expired
Maintain the restraint until the order expires, then reassess
Maintain the restraint and obtain a new order for the remaining time
Loosen the restraint but leave it applied until the provider evaluates the child
q_0851.rationale: The chapter states that "Discontinuation of restraints should occur as soon as it is safe, even if the order timeframe has not expired" (p. 698), and separately that the nurse "is responsible for selecting the least restrictive type of restraint" and must document alternatives considered first.
q_0851.trap: (B) treats the order as a duration rather than a ceiling, which is the most common misreading; the alternatives the chapter names — bringing the child to the nurses' station, diversional activities such as music, and parental participation — are what should have been tried and documented before the restraint went on.

q_0852.stem: A nurse is performing a heelstick on a 3-day-old. Which technique prevents necrotizing osteochondritis of the calcaneus?
options: Puncture no deeper than 2 mm, at the outer aspect of the heel, using an automatic lancet device
Puncture no deeper than 1 mm, at the inner aspect of the heel
Puncture at the center of the heel pad, where the tissue is thickest
Use a surgical blade for a controlled incision depth
q_0852.rationale: The chapter states that "To avoid osteochondritis, the puncture should be no deeper than 2 mm and should be made at the outer aspect of the heel," and that an automatic device "delivers a more precise puncture depth and is less painful than using a manual lancet" (p. 706).
q_0852.trap: (B) is the chapter's own review-item distractor, wrong on both numbers; (D) is an absolute contraindication — "A surgical blade of any kind is contraindicated" — and the long-term consequence of repeated trauma to the walking surface is fibrosis and scarring that interferes with locomotion.

q_0853.stem: A nurse is preparing to draw blood from a school-age child and wants to minimize pain. Which measures does the chapter endorse? Select all that apply.
options: Apply EMLA cream if more than 60 minutes are available, or LMX cream if only 30 minutes are available
Use the smallest-gauge needle that permits free flow of blood
Keep all equipment out of sight until it is used
Limit attempts to two operators with two attempts each before escalating
Have the child steady the finger firmly against the bedside table during a fingerstick
q_0853.rationale: The Atraumatic Care guidelines specify the EMLA and LMX application times, the smallest-gauge needle, keeping equipment out of sight, and a two-try-only policy meaning two operators with two attempts each, after which alternative access should be considered (p. 706).
q_0853.trap: (E) reverses an instruction in the same box — press the lancet device lightly against the skin and "avoid steadying the finger against a hard surface"; note also that the whole finger is massaged to maintain flow and the tip is never squeezed, because squeezing hemolyzes the sample and dilutes it with tissue fluid.

q_0854.stem: A nurse plans to apply EMLA cream before a newborn's heelstick. What should the nurse know?
options: EMLA has been found to be no more effective than placebo for heelsticks, while breastfeeding during the procedure has been more effective than sucrose in some studies
EMLA is the most effective option for heelsticks and should be applied 30 minutes beforehand
EMLA is contraindicated in preterm infants at any dose
Sucrose is more effective than breastfeeding and should be given 30 minutes before the stick
q_0854.rationale: The chapter states that EMLA, "Although safe for use in preterm infants when applied correctly, has been found to be no more effective than placebo in preventing pain during heelsticks," and that "Breastfeeding during a neonatal heelstick is effective in reducing pain and has been found to be more effective than sucrose in some studies" (p. 706).
q_0854.trap: (D) inverts the comparison and the timing, since sucrose is given as 2 ml to the tongue 2 minutes before the procedure; kangaroo care is the other endorsed measure and begins 10 to 15 minutes before the stick rather than afterward as comfort.

q_0855.stem: After an antecubital venipuncture on a 7-year-old, what should the nurse have the child do?
options: Hold pressure with the arm extended, because flexing the elbow increases bruising
Flex the elbow firmly to compress the site
Raise the arm above the head for 2 minutes
Apply a cold compress immediately to prevent hematoma
q_0855.rationale: The chapter directs applying pressure with the arm extended after an antecubital draw, since flexing increases bruising, and adds that if a hematoma does develop, "applying warm compresses to the ecchymotic area increases circulation, helps remove extravasated blood, and decreases pain" (p. 706).
q_0855.trap: (B) is standard adult practice and is what most learners will do by reflex; (D) reverses the temperature, since the chapter names warm compresses rather than cold for an established bruise. Note also the volume ceiling of 3 ml/kg in 24 hours, and less if the child is ill.

q_0856.stem: A parent asks how to measure 3 ml of an antibiotic suspension at home. What should the nurse recommend?
options: A calibrated oral syringe, which is the most accurate device for small amounts
A household teaspoon, which families find easiest to use consistently
A dropper, emptied into a medicine cup for a more exact reading
A molded plastic medicine cup, which is calibrated for pediatric doses
q_0856.rationale: The chapter states that "The most accurate means for measuring small amounts of medication is the plastic disposable calibrated oral syringe," and the American Academy of Pediatrics position that "Syringes are the preferred device for dosing accuracy," with liquid medications "dosed only in milliliters and never in teaspoons or other nonmetric units" (p. 709).
q_0856.trap: (C) compounds two errors the chapter names separately — the dropper "varies to a greater extent than the teaspoon or measuring cup," and "Emptying dropper contents into a medicine cup invites additional error" because liquid clings to the sides; (D) fails because families in one study "could not measure a 5-ml dose within 0.5 ml."

q_0857.stem: A toddler refuses a bitter liquid medication. Which approach does the chapter recommend?
options: Mix it with about 5 ml of a sweet-tasting substance such as jam or applesauce, avoiding essential food items
Mix it into the child's full bottle of formula so the whole dose is taken
Mix it into the child's usual milk, which masks bitterness best
Add it to a full serving of the child's favorite food so the taste is diluted
q_0857.rationale: The Atraumatic Care guidance is to "Mix the drug with a small amount (about 5 ml) of a sweet-tasting substance, such as flavored syrups, jam, fruit purees, sherbet, or applesauce; avoid essential food items because the child may later refuse to eat them" (p. 709).
q_0857.trap: (B) and (C) both use dairy, which the same box rules out "due to risk of interfering with absorption," and (B) additionally risks an incomplete dose if the bottle is not finished; (D) violates the small-amount rule and the essential-food rule at once.

q_0858.stem: A nurse is teaching a new graduate to give intramuscular injections to children. Which principles should be included? Select all that apply.
options: Immunizations at the ventrogluteal site have been found to have fewer local and systemic reactions
Placing the child supine on a parent's lap makes distraction and prevention of unexpected movement easier for the ventrogluteal site
The deltoid produces less pain and fewer side effects from the injectate than the vastus lateralis
Aspiration before an intramuscular vaccine is always required
Usually 2 ml is the maximum volume for a single site in small children and older infants
q_0858.rationale: The chapter states each of the three keyed points directly, and reports that aspiration "is no longer recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, World Health Organization, American Academy of Pediatrics, or Immunization Action Coalition" (pp. 711–712).
q_0858.trap: (D) fails on the word always — aspiration may still be indicated for medications such as penicillin into larger muscle groups, so the absolute is what makes it wrong; (E) doubles the narrative limit, which is "Usually 1 ml is the maximum volume that should be administered in a single IM site to small children and older infants."

q_0859.stem: A nurse must give an intramuscular injection to a 2-month-old. What is the maximum volume for a single site?
options: 0.5 ml, because the muscles of small infants may not tolerate more
1 ml, which is the pediatric maximum at any age
2 ml, as given in the site table for the vastus lateralis
There is no volume limit provided the muscle is large enough
q_0859.rationale: The chapter states that "The muscles of small infants may not tolerate more than 0.5 ml," while 1 ml is the usual maximum "to small children and older infants" (p. 711).
q_0859.trap: (C) quotes Table 22.5's "0.5 ml [infant] to 2.0 ml [child]" range and applies its upper figure to an infant; the two figures are one page apart and both are the chapter's, but a stem naming an infant takes the narrative limit. The governing principle is that "the larger the amount of solution, the larger the muscle at the injection site must be."

q_0860.stem: A nurse is selecting an intramuscular site for a 9-month-old receiving an immunization. Which site is correct?
options: The vastus lateralis, which is the site recommended for infants by the major immunization authorities
The deltoid, which produces the least pain and fewest local reactions
The dorsogluteal, which has the largest muscle mass
Any of the three, since the site table lists no age restrictions
q_0860.rationale: The chapter states that "The IM immunization site recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, World Health Organization, and American Academy of Pediatrics for infants is the anterolateral thigh or vastus lateralis" (p. 711).
q_0860.trap: (B) states a true advantage of the deltoid and ignores its age floor — it "can be used for small volumes of fluid in children as young as 18 months of age"; (C) names a site the chapter rules out under 10 years and does not include in its site table at all, except as the comparison the ventrogluteal beats on subcutaneous thickness.

q_0861.stem: A vesicant medication has leaked into the tissue around a child's intravenous catheter. How is this classified, and what distinguishes it?
options: Extravasation, because the agent is a vesicant; infiltration is the same event with a nonvesicant solution
Infiltration, because the volume is small; extravasation refers to larger leaks
Phlebitis, because any leakage inflames the vessel wall
Extravasation, because it is defined by the degree of tissue swelling rather than the drug
q_0861.rationale: The chapter separates the two by the agent: infiltration is a nonvesicant solution or medication into the tissue, while extravasation involves a vesicant, and "A vesicant or sclerosing agent causes varying degrees of cellular damage when even minute amounts escape into surrounding tissue" (p. 722).
q_0861.trap: (B) and (D) both define extravasation by size or severity, which is the intuitive and wrong reading — even minute amounts of a vesicant cause damage, which is exactly why the drug rather than the volume names the event.

q_0862.stem: A nurse observes blanching, edema, and streaking along the vein at a child's intravenous site during an infusion. What is the first action?
options: Stop the infusion
Notify the provider
Elevate the extremity
Apply the ordered antidote
q_0862.rationale: The chapter's Nursing Alert gives the sequence: "immediately stop the infusion, elevate the extremity, notify the provider, and initiate the ordered treatment as soon as possible" (p. 722).
q_0862.trap: (B) is the action nurses reach for under pressure, and it keeps the vesicant flowing while the call is placed; (C) and (D) are both real steps in the wrong position. The signs the alert lists are erythema, pain, edema, blanching, streaking along the vein, and a darkened area at the insertion site.

q_0863.stem: A nurse obtains a good blood return from a 4-month-old's peripheral catheter and concludes the line is patent. What should the nurse know?
options: A good blood return does not always indicate an intact line in small infants, and dependent areas such as the palm, the underside of the extremity, and behind the ears must be inspected
A good blood return reliably confirms patency at any age
Absence of a blood return always indicates infiltration
Infiltration is easier to detect in infants than in adults because their tissues are thinner
q_0863.rationale: The chapter states that "A good blood return, or lack thereof, is not always an indicator of infiltration in small infants" and directs that "Dependent areas, such as the palm and undersides of the extremity or the occiput and behind the ears, should be examined because infiltrations in these areas may not be readily visible" (p. 722).
q_0863.trap: (D) inverts the chapter's explanation, which is that "The increased amount of subcutaneous fat and the amount of tape used to secure the catheter often obscure the early signs of infiltration"; note also the instruction never to place the identification band on the same extremity as the intravenous site, because it can act as a tourniquet.

q_0864.stem: A nurse notes erythema at a child's intravenous insertion site. The child denies pain. How should this be interpreted?
options: Erythema is the initial sign of phlebitis, and pain may or may not be present
Without pain, the finding is not phlebitis and the line may be left in place
The finding indicates catheter-related bloodstream infection until proven otherwise
Phlebitis is diagnosed only when a palpable cord is present along the vein
q_0864.rationale: The chapter states that "The initial sign of phlebitis is erythema (redness) at the insertion site" and adds the caution that "Pain may or may not be present" (p. 722).
q_0864.trap: (B) waits for a sign that may never come; (C) overcalls it, since the chapter describes phlebitis as "largely a mechanical rather than infectious process" while still naming a bacterial type alongside mechanical and chemical causes.

q_0865.topic: eye, ear, and nose medication administration
q_0865.stem: A nurse is instilling ear drops in a 2-year-old. How should the auditory canal be straightened?
options: Gently pull the pinna downward and straight back
Gently pull the pinna upward and back
Pull the pinna straight out from the head
No manipulation is needed before instillation in young children
q_0865.rationale: The chapter directs that "For children younger than 3 years of age, the external auditory canal is straightened by gently pulling the pinna downward and straight back," while "The pinna is pulled upward and back in children older than 3 years of age" (p. 724).
q_0865.trap: (B) is the adult and older-child technique and is the reflex answer, and it does not straighten a young child's canal; the cutoff is 3 years, not 4 and not 5. After instillation the child lies on the unaffected side so the treated ear stays up.

q_0866.topic: eye, ear, and nose medication administration
q_0866.stem: A child is ordered both eye drops and eye ointment. What is the correct sequence?
options: Give the drops first, wait 3 minutes, then apply the ointment
Apply the ointment first so it holds the drops in place
Give them simultaneously to reduce the number of interventions
Give the drops first and apply the ointment immediately afterward
q_0866.rationale: The chapter's Drug Alert states, "If both eye ointment and drops are ordered, give drops first, wait 3 minutes, and then apply the ointment to allow each drug to work" (p. 724).
q_0866.trap: (B) blocks the drops from reaching the conjunctiva, and (D) drops the interval that lets each drug act. Note also that both preparations go into the conjunctival sac formed by pulling the lower lid down, never directly onto the eyeball, and ointment is applied inner canthus outward.

q_0867.topic: eye, ear, and nose medication administration
q_0867.stem: After instilling eye drops in a 5-year-old, the nurse wants to keep the child from tasting the medication. What should the nurse do?
options: Apply finger pressure to the lacrimal punctum at the inner aspect of the eyelid for 1 minute
Have the child rinse her mouth with water immediately
Wipe the eye from the outer canthus inward
Have the child keep the eye open until the drop is absorbed
q_0867.rationale: The chapter's Nursing Tip directs the nurse to "Apply finger pressure to the lacrimal punctum at the inner aspect of the eyelid for 1 minute to prevent drainage of medication to the nasopharynx" and the tasting of the drug (p. 723).
q_0867.trap: (C) reverses the wiping direction, which runs inner canthus outward to prevent contaminating the other eye; (D) reverses the instruction to "Gently close the eyelids to prevent expression of the medication." The parallel tip for ear drops is to warm refrigerated medication to room temperature, which prevents vertigo.

q_0868.topic: eye, ear, and nose medication administration
q_0868.stem: A nurse is giving nose drops to a 3-year-old who complains of a choking feeling. Which positioning prevents this?
options: Position the child with the head hyperextended over the edge of the bed or a pillow, and keep that position for 1 minute afterward
Sit the child upright with the chin tucked so the drops run forward
Place the child prone with the head turned to the side
Position the child supine with the head flat and neutral
q_0868.rationale: The chapter directs that "Unpleasant sensations associated with medicated nose drops are minimized when care is taken to position the child with the head extended well over the edge of the bed or pillow," and that after instillation "the child should remain in position for 1 minute to allow the drops to come in contact with the nasal surfaces" (pp. 723–724).
q_0868.trap: (B) and (D) both send the drops down the throat, producing precisely the strangling sensation the position exists to prevent; the same tip lists hyperextension as the route-specific measure for the nose, just as punctum pressure is for the eye and warming is for the ear.

q_0869.topic: enteral tube feeding and placement verification
q_0869.stem: A nurse must verify nasogastric tube placement before each feeding. Which methods does the chapter support? Select all that apply.
options: Testing the pH of the aspirate, where a value of 5 or less supports gastric placement
Visual inspection of the aspirate color
Carbon dioxide monitoring to determine whether the tube is in the respiratory tract
Measuring the external tube length against the measurement recorded at insertion
Gastric auscultation used by itself
q_0869.rationale: The chapter states that a pH of 5 or less supports gastric location, that aspirate colors are specific to the intended location though less accurate than pH, that carbon dioxide monitoring reliably detects respiratory placement, and that the external length should be measured at insertion and rechecked before each feeding (pp. 726, 728).
q_0869.trap: (E) is the method that cannot stand alone — "Auscultation as a verification tool is reliable only 60% to 80% of the time and should not be used without additional methods" — and the chapter notes it "is still widely used by nurses," which is why it is the distractor here rather than an outright absurdity.

q_0870.topic: enteral tube feeding and placement verification
q_0870.stem: A nurse aspirates fluid from a child's feeding tube and obtains a pH of 7. What does this indicate?
options: A pH greater than 5 does not reliably predict correct distal tip location and may indicate respiratory or esophageal placement or acid-suppressing medication
The tube is definitively in the respiratory tract and must be removed at once
The tube is correctly placed, since gastric pH is normally neutral in children
The result is uninterpretable and radiography is the only remaining option
q_0870.rationale: The chapter states that "A pH greater than 5 does not reliably predict correct distal tip location" and that "This may indicate respiratory or esophageal placement or the presence of medications to suppress acid secretion" (p. 726).
q_0870.trap: (B) overreads a nonspecific result, and (D) reaches for radiography when the chapter's own conclusion is that combining verification methods raises accuracy to 97% to 99%, close to radiography's 99%, and does so without repeated radiation exposure.

q_0871.topic: enteral tube feeding and placement verification
q_0871.stem: A nurse is giving a gavage feeding to a 6-week-old infant. Which technique is correct?
options: Give a gentle push with the plunger to start the flow, then remove the plunger and let the formula flow in by gravity
Use steady pressure on the plunger throughout to control the rate precisely
Infuse the feeding over 5 minutes to reduce the time the infant is disturbed
Warm the formula in the microwave to body temperature before the feeding
q_0871.rationale: The chapter directs the nurse to "Pour formula into the barrel of the syringe attached to the feeding tube. To start the flow, give a gentle push with the plunger but then remove the plunger and allow the fluid to flow into the stomach by gravity," with rate regulated by adjusting the height of the syringe (p. 728).
q_0871.trap: (D) is flatly forbidden — "Warm the formula to room temperature. Do not microwave!"; (C) compresses a feeding the chapter allows 15 to 30 minutes for, and the rate ceiling is 5 ml every 5 to 10 minutes in premature and very small infants and 10 ml per minute in older infants and children, to prevent nausea and regurgitation.

q_0872.topic: enteral tube feeding and placement verification
q_0872.stem: A gavage feeding has just been completed for a 3-month-old. How should the nurse position the infant?
options: With the head elevated 30 to 45 degrees or on the right side for 30 to 60 minutes
Flat and supine for 30 minutes to reduce the risk of falls
Prone with the head turned to the side for 1 hour
Upright and held for 5 minutes, then flat in the crib
q_0872.rationale: The chapter directs the nurse to "Position the child with the head elevated 30 to 45 degrees or on the right side for 30 to 60 minutes in the same manner as after any infant feeding to minimize the possibility of regurgitation and aspiration" (p. 728).
q_0872.trap: (B) and (C) both place the infant in positions the safe-sleep and aspiration rules argue against; note also that the tube is stabilized by taping to the cheek rather than to the nose or forehead, because of possible damage to the nostril.

q_0873.topic: fluid physiology and maintenance requirements in children
q_0873.stem: A nursing student asks why infants become dehydrated so much faster than adults. Which explanation reflects the chapter's physiology?
options: A far larger share of the infant's total body water sits in the extracellular compartment, which is the compartment lost first
Infants have less total body water than adults, so a given loss represents a larger fraction
The infant's intracellular compartment is disproportionately large and empties rapidly
Infants concentrate urine more efficiently, which accelerates free water loss
q_0873.rationale: Total body water falls from roughly 78% of body weight at birth to about 60% by the end of the first year, and the fall is almost entirely extracellular — about 45% at birth to roughly 25% at 1 year and 17% in adults — while intracellular water stays comparatively flat (Fig. 23.2, read from the artwork).
q_0873.trap: (B) inverts the proportion, since infants have *more* total body water than adults, not less; (D) reverses renal function, since immature kidneys concentrate urine *less* efficiently, which is a separate reason infants tolerate fluid loss poorly.

q_0874.topic: fluid physiology and maintenance requirements in children
q_0874.stem: A 15-kg child requires maintenance intravenous fluid. What is the daily volume?
q_0874.rationale: The chapter's maintenance formula is 100 ml/kg for the first 10 kg, then 1000 ml plus 50 ml/kg for each kilogram from 11 to 20 kg, then 1500 ml plus 20 ml/kg above 20 kg (Table 23.1, p. 737) — so 1000 ml for the first 10 kg plus 50 ml for each of the next 5 kg gives 1250 ml.
q_0874.trap: (C) stops at the first band and forgets the increment; (B) jumps to the 20-kg baseline, which applies only above 20 kg. The bands are cumulative, and that is where the arithmetic goes wrong.

q_0875.topic: fluid physiology and maintenance requirements in children
q_0875.stem: A child has a fever of 39 degrees Celsius. How does this affect fluid requirements?
options: Requirements increase by about 12% for each degree Celsius above normal
Requirements are unchanged, since fever does not alter insensible loss
Requirements decrease, because antidiuretic hormone rises with fever
Requirements increase by about 50% regardless of how high the fever is
q_0875.rationale: The chapter gives an added fluid requirement of 12% per 1 degree Celsius of fever, and separately gives the rise in insensible water loss as 7 ml/kg per 24 hours for each degree Fahrenheit above 99 (p. 736).
q_0875.trap: (C) invents a mechanism in the wrong direction; (D) replaces a graded adjustment with a flat one, which fails for a child whose fever is mild.

q_0876.topic: fluid physiology and maintenance requirements in children
q_0876.stem: A nurse is weighing a hospitalized infant with suspected fluid loss. Why does the chapter emphasize weight?
options: Weight is the most important determinant of the percentage of total body fluid lost in infants and young children
Weight correlates directly with serum sodium and replaces electrolyte measurement
Weight is the only sign that appears before a fluid deficit reaches 10%
Weight predicts the type of dehydration as well as its degree
q_0876.rationale: The chapter states that "Weight is the most important determinant of the percent of total body fluid loss in infants and younger children," while adding the practical difficulty that "often the preillness weight is unknown" (p. 743).
q_0876.trap: (C) understates the sensitivity of clinical assessment, since "Objective signs of dehydration are present at a fluid deficit of less than 5%"; (D) conflates degree with type, and type is determined by serum sodium rather than by weight.

q_0877.stem: An infant with gastroenteritis has a serum sodium of 142 mEq/L and has lost water and electrolytes in roughly balanced proportions. Which type of dehydration is this, and what is its chief danger?
options: Isotonic, and shock is the greatest threat to life
Hypotonic, and neurologic injury is the greatest threat
Hypertonic, and seizures are the greatest threat
Isotonic, and hypernatremic seizures are the greatest threat
q_0877.rationale: Isotonic dehydration keeps plasma sodium between 130 and 150 mEq/L with deficits "in approximately balanced proportions," is "the primary form of dehydration occurring in children," and the chapter states that "Shock is the greatest threat to life in isotonic dehydration" (pp. 742–743).
q_0877.trap: (D) keys the right type with the wrong danger, borrowing the hypertonic complication; the chapter's own review question offers oliguria, shock, arrhythmia, and hypotension for this, and hypotension is a *component* of shock and a late one, which is why it arrives too late in the sequence to be the answer.

q_0878.stem: A toddler has a serum sodium of 158 mEq/L after a week of high-protein nasogastric feedings. How should the nurse interpret the physical findings?
options: The physical signs understate the fluid lost, because the extracellular compartment stays proportionately larger
The physical signs overstate the fluid lost, because water has shifted out of the cells
The physical signs accurately reflect the deficit, as in any dehydration
Skin turgor will be the most reliable indicator of the true deficit
q_0878.rationale: In hypertonic dehydration water shifts from the intracellular to the extracellular compartment, so the extracellular volume is relatively maintained and signs are "less severe for the same fluid lost"; the chapter calls this type "the most dangerous" and requiring "much more specific fluid therapy" (pp. 742–743).
q_0878.trap: (B) is the mirror error and describes hypotonic dehydration, where signs are "more severe with smaller losses"; (D) picks the one sign Table 23.3 footnotes as less prominent in hypernatremia, so a child with unremarkable turgor and a sodium over 150 is worse off than he looks.

q_0879.stem: A nurse is assessing a 10-month-old for dehydration. Which findings indicate severe dehydration? Select all that apply.
options: Capillary refill greater than 4 seconds with tenting of the skin
Absent tears with sunken eyes
Hyperirritability progressing to lethargy
Deep and rapid respirations
Blood pressure normal with an orthostatic change under 10 mm Hg
q_0879.rationale: Table 23.3 assigns very delayed capillary refill greater than 4 seconds with tenting, absent tears with sunken eyes, hyperirritable-to-lethargic behavior, and hyperpnea to the severe column (p. 743).
q_0879.trap: (E) belongs to the mild column, and the orthostatic change is the giveaway — a change greater than 10 mm Hg marks moderate dehydration, while severe runs from orthostatic to frank shock. Note the capillary refill gradient across the whole table: under 2 seconds mild, 2 to 4 seconds moderate, over 4 seconds severe.

q_0880.stem: An infant has lost 7% of body weight with an acute illness. How should the nurse classify this?
options: Moderate dehydration, since the infant band runs 5% to 10%
Severe dehydration, since any loss over 6% is severe
Mild dehydration, since the infant band for mild extends to 10%
Moderate dehydration, since the band is the same at every age
q_0880.rationale: The chapter gives percentage-of-body-weight bands that differ by age: infants are mild under 5%, moderate 5% to 10%, and severe over 10%, while older children are mild under 3%, moderate 3% to 6%, and severe over 6% (p. 743).
q_0880.trap: (B) applies the older-child threshold to an infant, which is the swap this pair invites; the cue is that if the stem says infant, the numbers are roughly double. Note separately that the chapter calls acute loss expressed as 50 ml/kg mild and 100 ml/kg severe "a more accurate means."

q_0881.stem: A nurse is assessing a child for possible dehydration and wants the findings with the best predictive value. Which three does the chapter name?
options: Abnormal capillary refill, abnormal skin turgor, and abnormal respiratory pattern
Sunken fontanel, absent tears, and dry mucous membranes
Tachycardia, hypotension, and oliguria
Weight loss, urine specific gravity, and serum osmolality
q_0881.rationale: The chapter states twice that "the clinical signs of abnormal capillary refill, abnormal skin turgor, and abnormal respiratory pattern are the most useful in predicting dehydration of 5% or more in children" (pp. 743–744).
q_0881.trap: (C) leads with hypotension, which is a late finding throughout this chapter; (D) names a laboratory panel the same Research Focus box declines to endorse, since current evidence "did not support the routine use of ultrasound or urinalysis to determine dehydration severity."

q_0882.stem: A 3-year-old weighing 25 kg has a capillary refill of 4 seconds, is lethargic, and has voided once since yesterday. Which intravenous order should the nurse expect?
options: 500 ml of 0.9% sodium chloride over 20 minutes
500 ml of 5% dextrose in water over 20 minutes
500 ml of 0.45% sodium chloride over 20 minutes
250 ml of 5% dextrose in 0.45% sodium chloride over 60 minutes
q_0882.rationale: The initial phase uses an isotonic electrolyte solution — 0.9% sodium chloride or lactated Ringer, both close to the body's serum osmolality of 285 to 300 mOsm/kg — at 20 ml/kg as a bolus over 5 to 20 minutes (p. 745); 20 ml/kg of 25 kg is 500 ml.
q_0882.trap: (B), (C), and (D) are the three wrong versions the chapter's own review question offers — dextrose-containing and hypotonic solutions. The chapter states that dextrose "is contraindicated" in early rehydration, "but especially in diabetic ketoacidosis," and that isotonic fluids are safer than hypotonic in preventing severe hyponatremia.

q_0883.stem: A child in the subsequent phase of parenteral fluid therapy has a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L. What governs whether potassium is added to the fluid?
options: Potassium is withheld until kidney function is restored and assessed and circulation has improved
Potassium is added to the initial bolus, since the deficit is already documented
Potassium is withheld until the serum level falls below 3.0 mEq/L
Potassium is given only by rapid intravenous push to correct the level quickly
q_0883.rationale: The chapter states that in the subsequent phase "potassium is withheld until kidney function is restored and assessed and circulation has improved" (p. 745), and separately directs the nurse to "Assess for adequate renal output before administration" and to "administer potassium slowly" (p. 741).
q_0883.trap: (B) adds potassium to a bolus given to a child whose kidneys have not yet proven themselves, which is the classic error; (D) reverses the administration rule and would require continuous electrocardiographic monitoring even if it were correct.

q_0884.stem: A 9-month-old is brought in after a great-aunt gave him several bottles of plain water. He appears well hydrated but has had a generalized seizure and shows hypertonic reflexes. Which laboratory result does the nurse expect?
options: A serum sodium of 118 mEq/L
A serum glucose of 40 mg/dl
A serum pH of 7.20
A serum sodium of 158 mEq/L
q_0884.rationale: Children ingesting excessive electrolyte-free water "develop a concurrent decrease in serum sodium accompanied by central nervous system symptoms," and because water moves into the brain faster than sodium moves out, the child may show irritability, somnolence, vomiting, or generalized seizures while appearing well hydrated (p. 745).
q_0884.trap: (D) has the sodium moving in the wrong direction, and (B) and (C) are the metabolic distractors this scenario invites; the tell is that the child looks well hydrated, which separates water intoxication from dehydration with seizures. The chapter's named causes include incorrectly mixed formula, tap water enemas, and swimming lessons.

q_0885.stem: A mother of a 6-month-old asks what to offer when her baby seems thirsty between feedings. What should the nurse advise?
options: Offer no plain water routinely, and never dilute formula with extra water
Offer plain water freely between feedings, since it is calorie free
Offer diluted formula, which supplies both water and nutrition
Offer an oral rehydration solution as the routine between-feeding fluid
q_0885.rationale: The chapter's anticipatory guidance covers acceptable oral fluid intake in infants — "preferably no water" — cautions against diluting formula with extra water, and advises avoiding water enemas (pp. 746–747); incorrectly mixed formula is named as "one of the more common causes of water intoxication in infants."
q_0885.trap: (B) and (C) are both routes to the water intoxication the guidance exists to prevent; the underlying vulnerability is that an infant's thirst mechanism is not well developed, a decreased glomerular filtration rate cannot excrete a repeated water load, and antidiuretic hormone levels may not be maximally reduced.

q_0886.stem: A child receiving potassium-sparing diuretics has a potassium of 6.2 mEq/L. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Peaked T waves with a widened QRS complex
Bradycardia
Hyperreflexia
Flaccid muscle weakness and twitching
Notched or flattened T waves with a depressed ST segment
q_0886.rationale: Hyperkalemia produces a flat P wave, peaked T waves, a widened QRS, and an increased PR interval, together with muscle weakness, flaccid paralysis, twitching, hyperreflexia, bradycardia, and the risk of ventricular fibrillation (Table 23.2, pp. 739–742).
q_0886.trap: (E) is the hypokalemia electrocardiogram — notched or flattened T waves, a decreased ST segment, and premature ventricular contractions. The paired cue for the whole comparison is that hyporeflexia and tachycardia point to hypokalemia while hyperreflexia and bradycardia point to hyperkalemia.

q_0887.stem: A child develops tingling of the fingertips and carpal spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated. Which electrocardiographic change accompanies this imbalance?
options: A prolonged QT interval
A shortened QT interval
Peaked T waves
A flattened P wave
q_0887.rationale: The findings describe a positive Trousseau sign in hypocalcemia, whose manifestations include neuromuscular irritability, tingling of the nose, ears, fingertips and toes, tetany, laryngospasm, positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and a prolonged QT interval (Table 23.2, pp. 739–742).
q_0887.trap: (B) is the hypercalcemia finding, and the QT direction is the cleanest discriminator between the two — hypocalcemia prolongs it, hypercalcemia shortens it; hypercalcemia otherwise presents with constipation, muscle hypotonicity, and kidney stones.

q_0888.stem: A 4-month-old exclusively fed whole cow's milk develops tetany. What does the chapter identify as the mechanism?
options: An inappropriate calcium-to-phosphorus ratio in whole milk for a newborn
Insufficient total calcium content in cow's milk
Lactose intolerance causing calcium malabsorption
Excess vitamin D in fortified whole milk
q_0888.rationale: The chapter names as a cause of hypocalcemia "Cow's milk—tetany of the newborn (inappropriate calcium/phosphorus ratio in whole milk for newborn)," and its management includes avoiding cow's milk in infants younger than 12 months (Table 23.2).
q_0888.trap: (B) misidentifies the problem as quantity rather than ratio, which is the distinction the chapter draws; the other cause it names in the same row is exchange transfusion with citrated blood.

q_0889.stem: A neonate who has been breastfeeding poorly is intensely thirsty, has dry sticky mucous membranes, and is lethargic at rest but hyperirritable when aroused. What does the nurse suspect?
options: Hypernatremia from insufficient breast milk intake
Hyponatremia from free water intake
Hypokalemia from poor intake
Water excess from overfeeding
q_0889.rationale: The chapter names "Insufficient breast milk intake in neonate (dehydration hypernatremia)" as a cause, with manifestations of intense thirst, dry sticky mucous membranes, flushed skin, hoarseness, oliguria, and "lethargy at rest with hyperirritability when aroused" (Table 23.2), managed by ensuring adequate intake and lactation assistance before discharge.
q_0889.trap: (B) reverses the sodium direction for a presentation that is nearly pathognomonic; the lethargy-with-hyperirritability-on-stimulation pattern recurs in the hypertonic dehydration column of Table 23.4 and is the single most distinctive behavioral cue in this chapter.

q_0890.topic: types of shock and compensated versus hypotensive shock
q_0890.stem: A child develops shock after a tension pneumothorax. Which type is this, and what defines the category?
options: Obstructive shock, defined by mechanical obstruction of blood flow to or from the heart
Cardiogenic shock, defined by primary pump failure
Distributive shock, defined by reduced peripheral vascular resistance
Hypovolemic shock, defined by a reduction in the size of the vascular compartment
q_0890.rationale: Box 23.3 defines obstructive shock as "Mechanical obstruction of blood flow to or from the heart," with tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, and left ventricular outflow tract obstruction as its causes (p. 748).
q_0890.trap: (B) is the closest miss because both present with labored breathing, crackles, and hypotension on Table 23.5; the discriminator is the word mechanical, and that phrase belongs to obstructive alone.

q_0891.topic: types of shock and compensated versus hypotensive shock
q_0891.stem: A nurse is reviewing shock categories with a student who lists hypovolemic, cardiogenic, neurogenic, anaphylactic, and septic as the five types. How should this be corrected?
options: Neurogenic, anaphylactic, and septic shock are all subtypes of distributive shock, which is the fourth category
Anaphylactic shock is a subtype of hypovolemic shock because of the capillary leak
Septic shock is a subtype of cardiogenic shock because cardiac output falls
The list is correct, since the chapter names five types
q_0891.rationale: The chapter names four types — hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, and obstructive — and lists neurogenic, anaphylactic, and septic as the three distributive subtypes (p. 748).
q_0891.trap: (B) and (C) each attach a subtype to the wrong parent using a real feature of it as the excuse, which is how this distractor set is built; note also that hypovolemic shock is the most common type in children.

q_0892.topic: types of shock and compensated versus hypotensive shock
q_0892.stem: A 4-year-old after a motor vehicle collision has a heart rate of 158, cool mottled hands and feet, narrowing pulse pressure, and a blood pressure of 96/68. What stage of shock does this describe?
options: Compensated shock, since blood pressure is still normal
Hypotensive shock, since the pulse pressure is narrowing
Irreversible shock, since perfusion to the extremities has failed
No shock, since the blood pressure is within normal limits
q_0892.rationale: In compensated shock "cardiac output and systemic arterial BP are usually normal or increased," with early signs of apprehension, irritability, normal blood pressure, narrowing pulse pressure, thirst, pallor, and diminished urinary output; the Nursing Alert names "Unexplained mild tachycardia and a decrease in perfusion of the hands and feet" as the differentiating features (p. 749).
q_0892.trap: (D) is the answer the chapter exists to prevent, and it states the correction three separate times — "Hypotension is a late and poor prognostic sign of shock, so signs of shock must be recognized and appropriate interventions implemented before hypotension is evident."

q_0893.topic: types of shock and compensated versus hypotensive shock
q_0893.stem: A child in shock has an established airway. Which measures belong in the emergency management? Select all that apply.
options: Administer 100% oxygen
Give an isotonic crystalloid bolus of 20 ml/kg over 5 to 20 minutes
Keep the child flat with the legs raised above the level of the heart
Keep the child warm and calm, and monitor and treat pain
Administer calcium routinely to support myocardial contractility
q_0893.rationale: The Emergency Treatment box directs establishing an airway with 100% oxygen, restoring vascular volume, inotrope and vasopressor support, keeping the child flat with legs raised above the heart, and keeping the child warm and calm while treating pain (p. 751).
q_0893.trap: (E) is explicitly ruled out — routine calcium in a pediatric cardiac arrest "is not recommended unless there is documented evidence of hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, hypermagnesemia, or calcium channel blocker overdose." Note that oxygen is named "the first drug to be administered" in shock, and dopamine is the preferred inotrope because it also improves renal perfusion.

q_0894.topic: types of shock and compensated versus hypotensive shock
q_0894.stem: A child in hypovolemic shock has received two fluid boluses. Which finding indicates the boluses are working?
options: A rise in blood pressure together with a fall in heart rate
A rise in blood pressure with an unchanged heart rate
A fall in heart rate with an unchanged blood pressure
An increase in capillary refill time from 2 to 3 seconds
q_0894.rationale: The chapter states that success is judged by "increase in BP and decrease in heart rate" after boluses of 20 ml/kg of isotonic crystalloid repeated as necessary (p. 751).
q_0894.trap: (D) reads a worsening number as improvement, since capillary refill lengthening from 2 to 3 seconds moves toward the moderate band; note that fresh-frozen plasma is used to correct coagulopathies rather than as volume replacement, and albumin is the usual colloid because it stays in the vascular space longer than crystalloid.

q_0895.stem: A child with a proven urinary tract infection meets two systemic inflammatory response criteria, one of which is an abnormal temperature. How should this be classified?
options: Sepsis, which is the systemic inflammatory response syndrome in the presence of suspected or proven infection
Severe sepsis, since organ dysfunction is implied by meeting the criteria
Septic shock, since infection plus systemic inflammatory response defines shock
Systemic inflammatory response syndrome alone, since infection does not change the classification
q_0895.rationale: Box 23.4 defines sepsis as "SIRS in the presence of or as a result of suspected or proven infection," severe sepsis as "Sepsis plus cardiovascular organ dysfunction or ARDS or two or more other organ dysfunctions," and septic shock as sepsis with organ dysfunction and hypotension (p. 752).
q_0895.trap: (D) ignores the step the infection adds, and the chapter says so directly: the response "can occur in response to both infectious and noninfectious (e.g., trauma, burns) causes. When caused by infection, it is called sepsis." Note that the syndrome requires at least two of four criteria, one of which must be an abnormal temperature or leukocyte count.

q_0896.stem: A child with sepsis is warm and flushed with chills and fever, a normal blood pressure, and normal urinary output. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: This is the early hyperdynamic stage, in which the patient has the best chance for survival
This is the most dangerous stage, because vasodilation indicates circulatory collapse
This is not shock, because blood pressure and urinary output are normal
This is the cold hypodynamic stage presenting atypically
q_0896.rationale: The chapter describes stage 1 as "hyperdynamic, warm, or hyperdynamic-compensated," with warm flushed skin from vasodilation and increased cardiac output, normal blood pressure and urine output, and normal mentation, adding that "The patient has the best chance for survival in this stage" (p. 752).
q_0896.trap: (C) is the trap the chapter answers twice — "Children with septic shock often maintain a normal BP until they are severely ill. Shock may occur long before hypotension in children"; the counterintuitive part is that warm and flushed is the *better* stage, which (B) exploits.

q_0897.stem: A child with sepsis becomes hypothermic with cold extremities, weak pulses, and anuria. What does this indicate?
options: The hypodynamic or cold stage, the most dangerous stage, with multiorgan failure common
Improvement, since the fever has resolved
The normodynamic stage, which typically lasts several days
An anaphylactic component superimposed on the sepsis
q_0897.rationale: Stage 3, the "hypodynamic, or cold" stage, presents with hypothermia, cold extremities, weak pulses, hypotension, oliguria or anuria, severe lethargy or coma, and common multiorgan failure; the chapter calls it "the most dangerous stage of shock" (p. 752).
q_0897.trap: (B) reads a falling temperature as recovery, which is the same error the burn chapter warns about when a low or normal temperature signals overwhelming sepsis; (C) misassigns the duration, since the intermediate normodynamic stage "lasts only a few hours."

q_0898.stem: A nurse is caring for a child at risk for septic shock. Which early signs should prompt action?
options: Fever, tachycardia, and tachypnea
Hypotension and oliguria
Cold extremities and weak peripheral pulses
Altered level of consciousness and anuria
q_0898.rationale: The Nursing Alert states that "nurses caring for children at risk for septic shock should be alert to early signs: fever, tachycardia, and tachypnea," adding that "Subtle alterations in tissue perfusion and unexplained tachypnea and tachycardia often are early warning signs" (p. 754).
q_0898.trap: (B), (C), and (D) are all real findings in septic shock and all arrive in the later stages, which is exactly what makes them attractive and wrong here; acting on them means acting after the stage with the best survival has passed.

q_0899.topic: anaphylactic and toxic shock syndrome recognition
q_0899.stem: A child develops anaphylaxis 30 seconds after an intravenous medication is started. Another child develops symptoms 90 minutes after an exposure. What does the chapter say about the difference?
options: The rapidity of the reaction is directly related to its intensity, so the sooner the onset the more severe the reaction
Delayed reactions are more severe, because more antigen has been absorbed
Onset time does not predict severity
A reaction beginning after 1 hour is not anaphylaxis
q_0899.rationale: The chapter states that symptoms usually begin "within seconds or minutes" of exposure and that "The rapidity of the reaction is directly related to its intensity—the sooner the onset, the more severe the reaction," while noting that onset "may be delayed for as long as 2 hours" (p. 754).
q_0899.trap: (D) would rule out a real and still-dangerous presentation; note the penicillin-specific windows the chapter gives, an immediate onset within 1 hour of administration or an accelerated onset 1 to 72 hours after.

q_0900.topic: anaphylactic and toxic shock syndrome recognition
q_0900.stem: A nurse is teaching about the most likely triggers of anaphylaxis. Which statement is accurate?
options: Food allergy is the most common cause outside the hospital, while medication and latex allergies are more common in the hospital
Food allergy is the most common cause in both settings
Insect stings are the most common cause outside the hospital
Latex allergy is the most common cause in both settings
q_0900.rationale: The chapter states that "Food allergy is the most common cause of anaphylaxis outside the hospital, whereas medication and latex allergies are more common in the hospital" (p. 754).
q_0900.trap: (B) and (D) each generalize one setting's answer to both, and the setting is what the item turns on; mechanistically the reaction releases histamine from mast cells, causing vasodilation and increased capillary permeability, which is why anaphylaxis is classified as a distributive shock.

q_0901.topic: anaphylactic and toxic shock syndrome recognition
q_0901.stem: An adolescent presents with sudden high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, profound hypotension, and a diffuse macular erythroderma. Which findings would support a probable diagnosis of toxic shock syndrome? Select all that apply.
options: A fever of 38.9 degrees Celsius or higher
Desquamation of the palms and soles 1 to 2 weeks after onset
Hypotension below the fifth percentile for age
Involvement of three or more organ systems
A positive blood culture for group A streptococcus
q_0901.rationale: Box 23.7 lists the criteria as fever of 38.9 degrees Celsius or higher, diffuse macular erythroderma, desquamation particularly of palms and soles 1 to 2 weeks after onset, hypotension, and involvement of three or more organ systems, with the diagnosis probable when four of five major criteria are met (p. 756).
q_0901.trap: (E) is excluded by the criteria themselves, which require that blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures be negative for organisms other than *Staphylococcus aureus*; the causative toxin is toxic shock syndrome toxin-1, and about half of cases occur in menstruating women and are usually associated with tampon use.

q_0902.topic: anaphylactic and toxic shock syndrome recognition
q_0902.stem: A nurse is teaching a group of adolescent girls about reducing the risk of toxic shock syndrome. Which instruction reflects the chapter?
options: Avoid superabsorbent tampons, and do not leave any tampon in place for more than 4 to 6 hours
Change tampons every 12 hours and use superabsorbent products overnight
Use tampons only overnight and sanitary napkins during the day
Tampon use carries no risk provided menses are regular
q_0902.rationale: The chapter advises that "Young girls are advised not to use superabsorbent tampons and not to leave any tampon in the body for more than 4 to 6 hours," and notes that avoiding tampons "offers the most certain preventive measure" (p. 756).
q_0902.trap: (B) doubles the dwell time and recommends the absorbency the chapter rules out; (C) inverts the alternating pattern the chapter suggests, which is to use napkins during the night, when at home during the day, and when flow is slight.

q_0903.topic: burn depth, extent, and severity classification
q_0903.stem: A child has a burn involving the epidermis and varying degrees of the dermis. The area is painful, moist, red, and blistered. How should the nurse classify this burn?
options: Partial-thickness, or second degree
Superficial, or first degree
Full-thickness, or third degree
Fourth degree
q_0903.rationale: Partial-thickness burns involve the epidermis plus varying degrees of dermis and are "Painful, moist, red, and blistered," with deep dermal burns appearing mottled pink, red, and white with blisters and edema (p. 758).
q_0903.trap: (B) is excluded by the blisters, since in a superficial burn "blisters do not form" and the injury is epidermal only, healing in 3 or 4 days without scarring; (C) would be dry and leathery with thrombosed vessels visible.

q_0904.topic: burn depth, extent, and severity classification
q_0904.stem: The parents of a child with extensive third-degree burns ask why their daughter needs so much pain medication when they were told full-thickness burns destroy the nerves. What should the nurse explain?
options: The burned areas lack sensation, but most such burns have partial-thickness areas at the periphery with intact nerve endings, and excised eschar and donor sites expose nerve fibers
Full-thickness burns are painless, so the medication is for anxiety rather than pain
The nerve endings regenerate within 24 hours, restoring full sensation
The pain originates entirely from the dressing changes rather than the wound
q_0904.rationale: The chapter states that full-thickness burns "lack sensation in the area of injury because of the destruction of nerve endings" and then immediately adds that most have partial-thickness areas at the periphery with intact nerve endings, that excised eschar and donor sites contain exposed nerve fibers, and that pain returns as fibers regenerate — concluding that "children often experience severe pain related to the size and depth of the burn" (p. 758).
q_0904.trap: (B) states the half-truth as the whole truth, and an option asserting that a child with third-degree burns needs no analgesia is wrong in this chapter.

q_0905.topic: burn depth, extent, and severity classification
q_0905.stem: A nurse is estimating burn extent in a 1-year-old. How does the pediatric rule of nines differ from the adult chart?
options: The head and neck are 18% and each lower extremity is 14%
The head and neck are 9% and each lower extremity is 18%, as in adults
The head and neck are 14% and each lower extremity is 18%
The trunk and arms are proportionately larger than in the adult
q_0905.rationale: The chapter gives the infant's head and neck as 18% of total body surface area and each lower extremity as 14%, with the trunk and arms roughly the same proportions as the adult; the modified rule deducts 1% from the head and adds 0.5% to each leg for each year of life after age 2 (p. 757).
q_0905.trap: (B) applies the adult chart unchanged, which underestimates the burn because it under-weights the head — the Lund-Browder chart makes the same point, giving half a head as 9.5% at birth and 3.5% in an adult while half a thigh runs the other way.

q_0906.topic: burn depth, extent, and severity classification
q_0906.stem: A 6-year-old has a 5% total body surface area partial-thickness burn of both hands. How should this be graded?
options: It is not a minor burn, because burns of the hands are excluded from the minor category regardless of extent
It is a minor burn, because it is under 10% of total body surface area
It is a major burn, because all partial-thickness burns of the hands require a burn center
It is a moderate burn, because the hands count double in the extent calculation
q_0906.rationale: Table 23.8's footnote states that minor burns "exclude any burn involving the face, hands, feet, perineum, or crossing joints; circumferential burns; electrical injuries; any injury complicated by inhalation injury or concomitant trauma; and children with psychosocial factors affecting the injury" (p. 758).
q_0906.trap: (B) applies the percentage band without reading the exclusions, which is the whole point of the footnote; the chapter separately flags hands, feet, and joints because scar formation there interferes with growth and development.

q_0907.topic: burn depth, extent, and severity classification
q_0907.stem: A 20-month-old and an 8-year-old sustain burns of similar magnitude. What does the chapter say about their relative risk?
options: Children younger than 2 years have a significantly higher mortality rate than older children with burns of similar magnitude
Mortality is similar at all ages when the burn magnitude is matched
The older child is at higher risk because of greater body surface area
Mortality differences appear only above 50% total body surface area
q_0907.rationale: The chapter states that "Children younger than 2 years of age have a significantly higher mortality rate than older children with burns of a similar magnitude" (p. 760), attributing it to minimal protein stores, an immature immune response, a greater proportion of body water intolerant of rapid shifts, and immature renal function; in children older than 3 years mortality is similar to that of adults.
q_0907.trap: (C) reasons from size in the wrong direction; note also that very young children sustain deeper injuries "because of the thin nature of infant skin," and that cellular death can continue at the wound site for up to 48 hours, so both depth and area can expand past the first estimate.

q_0908.topic: emergency burn management and fluid resuscitation
q_0908.stem: A child's clothing has caught fire. Which actions should the rescuer take at the scene? Select all that apply.
options: Place the child horizontal and roll in a blanket, taking care not to cover the head and face
Apply a single brief application of tepid water to large denuded areas
Trim around clothing that adheres to the burn rather than pulling it off
Remove jewelry from the burned area
Apply ice packs continuously to limit the depth of injury
q_0908.rationale: The chapter directs smothering the flames with the child horizontal while not covering the head and face because of inhaled toxic fumes, cooling large denuded areas with "a single application of tepid water," trimming around adherent clothing rather than pulling, and removing jewelry because of heat transfer and constriction from edema (p. 764).
q_0908.trap: (E) reverses a stated rule — "Continuous wet dressings or the application of ice promotes vasoconstriction because of cooling, resulting in impaired circulation to the burned area and increased tissue damage." Note that remaining vertical risks igniting the hair or inhaling flames, heat, or smoke.

q_0909.topic: emergency burn management and fluid resuscitation
q_0909.stem: A toddler has spilled a caustic powder onto her forearm. What should the nurse do first?
options: Brush the powder off the skin, then flush with water
Flush immediately with copious water to dilute the agent
Apply a neutralizing agent appropriate to the chemical
Cover the area with a dry dressing and transport without intervention
q_0909.rationale: The chapter directs that a chemical in powder form should be brushed off and not have water added, because water spreads the caustic agent, while liquid chemical burns are flushed with copious water during transport (p. 764).
q_0909.trap: (C) is contraindicated for both forms — "The use of neutralizing agents on the skin is contraindicated"; (B) is correct for a liquid and wrong for a powder, which is the distinction the item turns on.

q_0910.topic: emergency burn management and fluid resuscitation
q_0910.stem: A 10-year-old weighing 34 kg has extensive second- and third-degree burns and is receiving fluid resuscitation. Which finding indicates the resuscitation is adequate?
options: An hourly urine output of about 30 ml
An hourly urine output of about 30 ml/kg
A systolic blood pressure within normal limits for age
A central venous pressure above 12 mm Hg
q_0910.rationale: The chapter gives the target as "an hourly urinary output of 30 ml in older children and 0.5 to 1 ml/kg in children weighing less than 30 kg," restated later as 30 to 50 ml/hr in children over 30 kg (pp. 765, 770).
q_0910.trap: (C) is ruled out by the chapter's own Nursing Alert — "Blood pressure can remain normotensive even in a state of hypovolemia" — and the stated reliable indicators are capillary refill, alterations in sensorium, and urinary output. Note that the chapter's own review item prints its correct option as 30 ml/kg, which is a units error in the source; the text's figure is per hour, not per kilogram.

q_0911.topic: emergency burn management and fluid resuscitation
q_0911.stem: A child is 60 hours post-burn and urine output has risen sharply. The resident asks the nurse to increase intravenous fluids to match the output. How should the nurse respond?
options: Question the order, because diuresis at 48 to 72 hours reflects interstitial fluid returning to the vascular compartment and matching it can cause circulatory overload
