q_1152.rationale: Box 29.1 lists an unusual mass or swelling, unexplained paleness and loss of energy, easy bruising, persistent localized pain or limping, prolonged unexplained fever or illness, frequent headaches often with vomiting, sudden eye or vision changes, and unexplained rapid weight loss (p. 1078).
q_1152.trap: (E) lacks the qualifier every real entry carries — the chapter states that "Cancers in children are often difficult to recognize. Therefore being alert to the persistence of possible signs and symptoms is essential," and the operative word throughout the box is persistence.

q_1153.topic: cancer warning signs and diagnostic workup in children
q_1153.stem: A parent reports that her 5-year-old has a swollen lymph node. What additional findings would make this concerning for malignancy?
options: Fever for more than 1 week, recent weight loss, or an abnormal chest radiograph
Any palpable node larger than 1 cm
Tenderness of the node on palpation
A node that has been present for 3 days
q_1153.rationale: The chapter states that "enlarged, firm lymph nodes in a child with fever for more than 1 week, a recent history of weight loss, or an abnormal chest x-ray film may indicate a serious disease and should be evaluated further" (p. 1079).
q_1153.trap: (B) and (C) each treat a single node characteristic as sufficient, and a swollen node alone is not the cancer cue in this chapter — all three of the named qualifiers do the work, which is why they are stated together.

q_1154.topic: cancer warning signs and diagnostic workup in children
q_1154.stem: A parent brings in a photograph showing a white glow in her toddler's pupil instead of the normal red reflex. What should the nurse recognize?
options: Leukocoria, which can be a sign of retinoblastoma
A normal photographic artifact requiring no follow-up
Cataract, which is unrelated to malignancy
Strabismus, which is the most common presenting sign of eye tumors
q_1154.rationale: The chapter describes leukocoria or white eye reflex as a yellow or whitish glow in the pupil, as opposed to the normal red pupillary reflex, noted in photographs, and states it can be a sign of retinoblastoma (pp. 1079, 1102).
q_1154.trap: (D) names the second most common sign rather than the first — strabismus results from poor fixation of the visually impaired eye — and (B) dismisses a finding whose "fleeting nature... often results in a delayed diagnosis," which is precisely why a photograph matters.

q_1155.topic: cancer warning signs and diagnostic workup in children
q_1155.stem: A nurse is explaining childhood cancer to a parent who asks what she could have done to prevent it. What is accurate?
options: There are no generally recognized preventive measures for childhood cancer, because lifestyle risk factors drive adult rather than childhood cancer
Dietary changes in early childhood substantially reduce risk
Avoiding all environmental exposures prevents most childhood cancers
Childhood cancer is the leading cause of death in children ages 1 to 15
q_1155.rationale: The chapter states that lifestyle risk factors drive adult cancer rather than childhood cancer, and that there are no generally recognized preventive measures for childhood cancer (pp. 1072–1073).
q_1155.trap: (D) overstates a real statistic, since cancer is the leading cause of death *from disease* in children ages 1 to 15 rather than the leading cause of death overall; the distinction matters when counseling families, and so does the fact that nothing they did or failed to do caused this.

q_1156.stem: A nurse is preparing to handle chemotherapeutic agents. Which precautions does the chapter direct? Select all that apply.
options: Prepare the drugs in a ventilated preparation room
Wear gloves and protective clothing
Use face and eye protection and a respirator when indicated
Place sterile gauze at every connection point
Recap needles carefully before disposal
q_1156.rationale: The chapter's handling precautions name a ventilated preparation room, gloves and protective clothing, face and eye protection with a respirator when indicated, and sterile gauze at every connection point (p. 1076).
q_1156.trap: (E) reverses an explicit instruction — do not recap or break needles — and it is the kind of action that reads as careful while creating the exposure the whole list exists to prevent.

q_1157.stem: A nurse notes swelling and a lack of blood return at a peripheral intravenous site during a chemotherapy infusion. What should the nurse do first?
options: Stop the infusion immediately
Slow the infusion and apply a warm compress
Flush the line with saline to confirm patency
Notify the practitioner before changing anything
q_1157.rationale: The chapter directs stopping the chemotherapy infusion immediately at the first sign of infiltration (p. 1076).
q_1157.trap: (C) pushes more vesicant into the tissue while testing a line that has already failed; note that the action differs for a suspected hypersensitivity reaction, where the nurse discontinues the drug, flushes and maintains the line with saline, and monitors vital signs — infiltration means stop, hypersensitivity means stop and keep the line open.

q_1158.stem: A child is scheduled for chemotherapy known to cause nausea. When should antiemetics be given?
options: On a schedule, before chemotherapy and around the clock for at least 24 hours after
As needed, once nausea develops
Only if vomiting occurs more than three times
After the infusion is complete, to avoid drug interactions
q_1158.rationale: The chapter directs giving antiemetics on a schedule, before chemotherapy and around the clock for at least 24 hours after, rather than as needed, with the rationale of preventing anticipatory nausea (p. 1081).
q_1158.trap: (B) is standard practice for most symptoms and is specifically wrong here, because once anticipatory nausea is established it becomes conditioned and far harder to treat; note also that nausea and vomiting are usually not indications for stopping the chemotherapy itself.

q_1159.stem: A child receiving vincristine has not had a bowel movement in 4 days. What should the nurse recommend?
options: A stool softener, increased activity, and a laxative such as polyethylene glycol
Increased dietary fiber as the primary intervention
A rectal suppository for prompt relief
Fluid restriction to firm the stool
q_1159.rationale: The chapter states that "Increased fiber may not be effective because the increased bulk tends to increase fecal distention and discomfort without producing the necessary mechanical stimulation," directing stool softeners, activity, and laxatives such as polyethylene glycol instead (p. 1082).
q_1159.trap: (C) is contraindicated, since rectal temperatures and suppositories are avoided in the child with cancer — an instruction that appears three separate times in this chapter; (B) is the intuitive constipation answer and the one the chapter specifically rules out for this cause.

q_1160.stem: A child beginning induction for acute lymphoblastic leukemia develops flank pain, muscle cramps, and tetany. Which laboratory pattern should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Hyperuricemia
Hyperphosphatemia
Hyperkalemia
Hypocalcemia
Hypercalcemia
q_1160.rationale: The chapter defines tumor lysis syndrome by "hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hyperkalemia," resulting from rapid release of intracellular contents during lysis of malignant cells, typically during the initial treatment period (p. 1078).
q_1160.trap: (E) uses the pattern against the reader — three of the four values go up and calcium is the outlier that goes down, so an option offering the calcium in the same direction as the rest is the designed error.

q_1161.stem: A child with tumor lysis syndrome is at risk for acute renal failure. Which intervention addresses the mechanism?
options: Aggressive intravenous fluids with allopurinol or rasburicase to reduce uric acid
Fluid restriction to reduce renal workload
Potassium supplementation to correct the electrolyte shift
Calcium restriction to prevent stone formation
q_1161.rationale: The chapter states that "The crystallization of uric acid that can occur with hyperuricemia can lead to acute renal failure," and directs frequent serum chemistries and urine pH, strict intake and output, aggressive intravenous fluids, and allopurinol, noting that hyperuricemia "is now effectively treated with recombinant urate oxidase, or rasburicase," which converts uric acid to the more soluble allantoin (p. 1078).
q_1161.trap: (C) would worsen an already elevated potassium, and (B) removes the very intervention that clears the uric acid load; risk factors for this syndrome are a high white cell count at diagnosis, large tumor burden, chemosensitivity, and a high proliferative rate.

q_1162.stem: A child newly diagnosed with leukemia has a white blood cell count of 130,000/mm3 with respiratory distress and confusion. What is this, and what is the mechanism?
options: Hyperleukocytosis, in which capillary obstruction and microinfarction produce organ dysfunction
Tumor lysis syndrome, in which electrolyte shifts produce neurologic change
Superior vena cava syndrome, in which a mediastinal mass obstructs venous return
Disseminated intravascular coagulation, in which microthrombi consume clotting factors
q_1162.rationale: The chapter defines hyperleukocytosis as "a peripheral white blood cell count greater than 100,000/mm3, [which] can lead to capillary obstruction, microinfarction, and organ dysfunction," with respiratory distress, cyanosis, and neurologic changes (p. 1078).
q_1162.trap: (B) is the other early-treatment emergency in the same patient and is a metabolic rather than a rheologic problem; the distinguishing feature here is the cell count itself, and management is rapid cytoreduction with hydration, urinary alkalinization, and allopurinol.

q_1163.stem: A child with Hodgkin lymphoma develops cyanosis of the face and neck, facial and upper extremity edema, and distended neck and chest veins. What is the priority?
options: Airway protection and alleviation of respiratory distress
Immediate lumbar puncture to assess for central nervous system involvement
Elevation of the lower extremities to improve venous return
Fluid bolus to improve perfusion
q_1163.rationale: The chapter describes superior vena cava syndrome from space-occupying chest lesions, "especially from Hodgkin disease and NHL," presenting with cyanosis of the face, neck, and upper chest, facial and upper extremity edema, and distended neck and chest veins, managed by "Airway protection and alleviation of respiratory distress" (p. 1078).
q_1163.trap: (D) treats the distention as hypovolemia when the problem is obstructed return; note that the second leading cause of this syndrome is thrombotic complications of implantable intravenous devices, so a child with a port belongs on this differential too.

q_1164.topic: infection and bleeding risk in the child with cancer
q_1164.stem: A child receiving chemotherapy has a white blood cell count of 1000/mm3, with 7% neutrophils and 7% bands. What is the absolute neutrophil count, and what does it mean?
options: 140/mm3, which places the child at high risk for overwhelming infection
1400/mm3, which is mildly reduced but not high risk
70/mm3, since only segmented neutrophils are counted
140/mm3, which is within normal limits during chemotherapy
q_1164.rationale: The chapter's guideline directs determining the total percentage of neutrophils including polys or segs and bands, then multiplying the white cell count by that percentage — so 7% plus 7% is 14%, and 0.14 times 1000 is 140/mm3; the at-risk child is the one with fever and a count below 500/mm3 (p. 1079).
q_1164.trap: (C) drops the bands, which the calculation explicitly includes; (D) normalizes a value more than threefold below the risk threshold. Note the clinical trap in the same paragraph — the usual signs of inflammation may be absent, but "fever will occur," so fever is the reliable sign precisely when redness and pus are not.

q_1165.topic: infection and bleeding risk in the child with cancer
q_1165.stem: A child with an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm3 is being cared for at home. Which instructions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid crowded areas such as shopping centers
Report fever promptly, since it may be the only sign of infection
Siblings may receive live measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines
Use acetaminophen rather than aspirin for fever or pain
Isolate the child from any sibling who has recently received a live vaccine
q_1165.rationale: The chapter advises cautious isolation from crowded areas when the count falls below 500/mm3, notes that fever occurs even when other signs do not, states that siblings and family members "can receive live MMR and varicella vaccine without risk to the child who is immunosuppressed," and substitutes acetaminophen for aspirin (pp. 1079–1080, 1084).
q_1165.trap: (E) over-applies the live-vaccine rule — the restriction is on the patient receiving them, not on the household, and isolating the child from a recently vaccinated sibling imposes a separation the chapter does not require.

q_1166.topic: infection and bleeding risk in the child with cancer
q_1166.stem: A child receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 18,000/mm3. Which finding should the nurse expect, and which action is appropriate?
options: Spontaneous gum or nose bleeding may occur, and pressure is applied at the site without disturbing clot formation
Spontaneous bleeding is not expected until the count falls below 5000/mm3
Prophylactic platelet transfusion should be given regardless of bleeding
Rectal temperatures should be taken to avoid oral mucosal trauma
q_1166.rationale: The chapter states that severe spontaneous internal hemorrhage "usually does not occur until the platelet count is 20,000/mm3 or less," that spontaneous gum or nose bleeding appears below that level, and that for the most common bleeds — epistaxis and gingival bleeding — "applying pressure at the site without disturbing clot formation is the general rule" (pp. 1079–1080).
q_1166.trap: (D) reverses a rule stated three times in this chapter, since the rectal area is prone to ulceration and rectal temperatures and suppositories are avoided; (C) over-treats, since platelet transfusions "are generally reserved for active bleeding episodes that do not respond to local treatment."

q_1167.topic: infection and bleeding risk in the child with cancer
q_1167.stem: A child with cancer has a platelet count of 85,000/mm3 and wants to ride his bicycle. What should the nurse advise?
options: Avoid activities that might cause injury or bleeding while the count is below 100,000/mm3
Bicycle riding is safe at any platelet count above 20,000/mm3
All activity should be restricted until the count exceeds 150,000/mm3
Activity restriction applies only to contact sports at any count
q_1167.rationale: The chapter directs that children with low platelet counts, usually below 100,000/mm3, "should avoid activities that might cause injury or bleeding, such as riding bicycles or skateboards, skating, climbing trees or playground equipment, and contact sports," and that once the count rises "these restrictions are not necessary" (p. 1080).
q_1167.trap: (B) applies the spontaneous-bleeding threshold to an activity decision, and the chapter deliberately keeps four platelet numbers apart for four different decisions — 20,000 for spontaneous bleeding, 100,000 for activity, 40,000 with granulocytes of 500 for toothbrushing, and transfusion reserved for refractory active bleeding.

q_1168.topic: infection and bleeding risk in the child with cancer
q_1168.stem: A child with cancer develops stomatitis. Which oral care measure does the chapter recommend?
options: A soft sponge toothbrush, avoiding lemon glycerin swabs and hydrogen peroxide
Viscous lidocaine for a young child before meals
Hydrogen peroxide rinses to debride the ulcerations
Lemon glycerin swabs to stimulate salivation
q_1168.rationale: The chapter directs a soft sponge toothbrush for stomatitis and states that lemon glycerin swabs and hydrogen peroxide are avoided for their drying effect and, for lemon, its acidity on eroded tissue (p. 1082).
q_1168.trap: (B) names an agent the chapter rules out in young children, because viscous lidocaine "may depress the gag reflex and increase aspiration risk" and has been associated with seizures; toothettes are the fallback when counts fall below the 500 and 40,000 thresholds.

q_1169.stem: A 4-year-old newly diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia presents with pallor, recurrent infections, and petechiae. What accounts for all three?
options: Bone marrow infiltration producing anemia, infection from neutropenia, and bleeding from decreased platelet production
Direct organ infiltration by leukemic cells in the skin and lungs
A paraneoplastic autoimmune process
Side effects of induction chemotherapy, which has not yet begun
q_1169.rationale: The chapter names three main consequences of bone marrow infiltration: "(1) anemia from decreased erythrocytes, (2) infection from neutropenia, and (3) bleeding from decreased platelet production" (p. 1086).
q_1169.trap: (D) attributes the presentation to treatment that has not started, which is a common misreading when the findings resemble chemotherapy toxicity; sorting each presenting sign into one of the three categories is what makes this material tractable.

q_1170.stem: A child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is entering the phase that begins immediately after diagnosis. What defines it?
options: Induction, lasting 4 to 5 weeks, using corticosteroids, vincristine, and L-asparaginase, aiming for less than 5% blasts in the marrow
Maintenance, lasting 2 to 3 years, using daily mercaptopurine and weekly methotrexate
Consolidation, using cyclophosphamide, cytarabine, and mercaptopurine
Delayed intensification, repeating the induction drugs at higher doses
q_1170.rationale: The chapter states that induction begins almost immediately after diagnosis and "lasts for 4 to 5 weeks," that "The principal drugs are the corticosteroids (dexamethasone or prednisone), vincristine, and L-asparaginase," and that complete remission is "the presence of less than 5% blast cells in the bone marrow and no detectable leukemia in extramedullary sites" (pp. 1086–1087).
q_1170.trap: (B) names the final phase, which runs 2 to 3 years; note that the period immediately after remission is critical, because myelosuppression leaves "the body defenseless against invading organisms... and susceptible to spontaneous hemorrhage."

q_1171.stem: Why does every child with acute lymphoblastic leukemia receive central nervous system prophylaxis?
options: Leukemic cells in the central nervous system are protected by the blood-brain barrier from systemic chemotherapy
All children have detectable central nervous system disease at diagnosis
Cranial radiation is required in every case
The central nervous system is the most common site of the primary tumor
q_1171.rationale: The chapter states that because leukemic cells in the central nervous system are protected by the blood-brain barrier, "all children receive CNS prophylactic therapy," delivered as intrathecal chemotherapy plus central nervous system–directed systemic chemotherapy, with cranial radiation reserved for those at highest risk of relapse (pp. 1086–1087).
q_1171.trap: (C) generalizes a treatment the chapter restricts to the highest-risk group; note that the central nervous system and the testes are the two named "sanctuaries" for leukemic cells requiring specific therapy.

q_1172.stem: A family asks why adherence matters so much during maintenance therapy. What should the nurse explain?
options: Anything less than 95% adherence increases the risk of relapse
Missing occasional doses has no measurable effect on outcome
Adherence matters only during induction
Doses may be doubled to make up for missed ones
q_1172.rationale: The chapter states that "A critical challenge during maintenance therapy is medication adherence because it has been shown that anything less than 95% adherence increases the risk of relapse," with treatment continuing for 2 to 3 years (p. 1087).
q_1172.trap: (D) proposes a correction that would risk toxicity without restoring the missed exposure; the 95% figure is unusually specific and is the reason adherence is monitored rather than assumed.

q_1173.stem: A nurse is comparing acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukemia. Which statement is accurate?
options: There is no established clinical staging system for acute myeloid leukemia, which is considered disseminated at diagnosis, and its treatment is more intense and shorter
Acute myeloid leukemia uses the same induction-through-maintenance sequence as lymphoblastic disease
Acute myeloid leukemia has a higher 5-year survival than lymphoblastic disease
Central nervous system irradiation is routine in acute myeloid leukemia
q_1173.rationale: The chapter states that "There is no established clinical staging system for AML; it is considered disseminated at diagnosis," that "Treatment for AML is generally more intense and of shorter duration than treatment for ALL," with maintenance not used in most regimens, and that "CNS irradiation is not usually used in AML treatment" (p. 1087).
q_1173.trap: (C) reverses the prognosis, since almost 80% of children with lymphoblastic disease live 5 years or longer while myeloid disease carries 68% 5-year survival under 15 years; note also the two distinctive myeloid skin findings, leukemia cutis in blue or purple and blue-green chloromas around the eyes.

q_1174.stem: A lymph node biopsy in an adolescent shows Reed-Sternberg cells. What does this establish?
options: Hodgkin lymphoma, since these cells are absent in the other lymphomas
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, since these cells are characteristic of it
Either lymphoma, since the cells appear in both
Leukemia with nodal involvement
q_1174.rationale: The chapter states that "The presence of Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells is considered diagnostic of Hodgkin disease because it is absent in the other lymphomas" (p. 1089).
q_1174.trap: (B) reverses the finding, and the consequence is more than nomenclature — the staging system used for Hodgkin lymphoma "is not used for NHL," so the diagnosis determines how the disease is staged as well as what it is called.

q_1175.stem: A nurse is comparing the epidemiology of the childhood lymphomas. Which statement is accurate?
options: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common in children overall, while Hodgkin disease shows a striking increase in ages 15 to 19
Hodgkin disease is more common in children than non-Hodgkin lymphoma at every age
Both peak in the preschool years
Hodgkin disease is most common before 5 years of age
q_1175.rationale: The chapter states that "In children NHL is more common than Hodgkin disease," and that "Hodgkin disease is extremely rare before 5 years of age, [with] a striking increase in children ages 15 to 19" (pp. 1088–1089).
q_1175.trap: (D) inverts the age distribution exactly — the rarity before 5 and the adolescent spike are what make age itself a useful discriminator when a lymphoma is suspected.

q_1176.stem: An adolescent with a mediastinal lymphoma develops facial swelling and dyspnea that worsen when lying flat. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Superior vena cava syndrome, requiring airway protection
Tumor lysis syndrome, requiring rasburicase
Spinal cord compression, requiring magnetic resonance imaging
Disseminated intravascular coagulation, requiring heparin
q_1176.rationale: The chapter names space-occupying chest lesions "especially from Hodgkin disease and NHL" as the cause of superior vena cava syndrome, presenting with cyanosis and edema of the face, neck, and upper chest with distended veins, and directs airway protection (p. 1078).
q_1176.trap: (C) is the other structural emergency in this chapter, but its initial manifestation is back pain rather than facial swelling, and magnetic resonance imaging is its gold standard; the positional worsening here points to venous obstruction.

q_1177.stem: A child with a lymphoma develops back pain, extremity weakness, and loss of bladder control. What is the priority action?
options: Obtain magnetic resonance imaging, which is the gold standard for diagnosing spinal cord compression
Begin physical therapy for the weakness
Obtain a lumbar puncture to assess for malignant cells
Schedule a bone scan for the following week
q_1177.rationale: The chapter names back pain as "a common initial manifestation" of spinal cord compression, with sensation change, extremity weakness, loss of bowel and bladder function, and respiratory insufficiency, and states that "MRI is the gold standard for diagnosis," with high-dose steroids and emergent radiation or laminectomy if indicated (p. 1078).
q_1177.trap: (D) treats an emergency as routine follow-up, and the neurologic deficits here are time-critical; note that a lumbar puncture is also avoided in the presence of increased intracranial pressure elsewhere in this chapter.

q_1178.stem: A 6-year-old has headaches worst on awakening and vomiting unrelated to feeding, with ataxia and nystagmus. Which tumor location does this suggest?
options: Infratentorial, which accounts for about 60% of pediatric brain tumors
Supratentorial, which typically presents with seizures
Spinal, which presents with back pain
The location cannot be inferred from symptoms
q_1178.rationale: The chapter states that "the most common symptoms of infratentorial brain tumors are headache, especially on awakening, and vomiting that is not related to feeding," with cerebellar involvement producing nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria, and dysmetria, and that about 60% of pediatric tumors are infratentorial (p. 1092).
q_1178.trap: (B) names the supratentorial picture, which "more commonly include seizures, personality or behavioral changes, visual disturbances, and hemiparesis"; the location matters because it determines the postoperative positioning order.

q_1179.stem: A child has just returned from resection of an infratentorial brain tumor. How should the nurse position the child?
options: Flat, on either side, but not on the operative side
With the head elevated above the level of the heart
In Trendelenburg position to promote venous return
Prone with the head turned to the operative side
q_1179.rationale: The chapter gives site-specific positioning: infratentorial goes flat, on either side, not on the operative side; supratentorial goes with the head elevated above the heart (p. 1095).
q_1179.trap: (B) is correct for the other site and is the swap this pair exists to catch; (C) is contraindicated after both types, and the chapter directs notifying the practitioner before lowering the head even for impending shock.

q_1180.stem: A nurse notes colorless drainage on the dressing of a child who had a craniotomy yesterday. What should the nurse do?
options: Report it immediately, since colorless drainage is cerebrospinal fluid
Reinforce the dressing and reassess at the end of the shift
Remove the dressing to inspect the wound
Document it as expected serous drainage
q_1180.rationale: The chapter directs that colorless drainage on a craniotomy dressing is cerebrospinal fluid and is reported immediately, along with sluggish, dilated, or unequal pupils (p. 1094).
q_1180.trap: (C) violates a separate instruction — reinforce a soiled craniotomy dressing rather than removing it — so an option that combines the wrong urgency with the wrong technique is doubly wrong; (D) normalizes the one drainage characteristic that signals a dural leak.

q_1181.stem: A nurse is assessing a child with a brain tumor for signs of increased intracranial pressure. Which vital sign pattern is expected?
options: Decreased pulse and respirations, increased blood pressure, and decreased pulse pressure
Increased pulse and respirations, decreased blood pressure, and widened pulse pressure
Increased pulse with unchanged blood pressure
Decreased blood pressure with widened pulse pressure
q_1181.rationale: Table 29.4 lists decreased pulse and respiration, increased blood pressure, decreased pulse pressure, and hypothermia or hyperthermia among the vital sign findings, directing that pulse and respirations be monitored for 1 full minute with the pulse pressure recorded (p. 1092).
q_1181.trap: (B) is the shock pattern, which runs the opposite way on every value; the vomiting in this setting is also distinctive — progressively projectile, worse in the morning, and relieved by moving about and changing position.

q_1182.stem: A child with a suspected brain tumor and signs of increased intracranial pressure is scheduled for diagnostic testing. Which test does the chapter identify as the gold standard, and which is avoided?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging is the gold standard, and lumbar puncture is avoided because of the danger of brainstem herniation
Computed tomography is the gold standard, and magnetic resonance imaging is avoided
Lumbar puncture is the gold standard, and imaging is avoided
Electroencephalography is the gold standard, and imaging is avoided
q_1182.rationale: The chapter states that "The gold standard diagnostic procedure is MRI," with computed tomography used in urgent cases when magnetic resonance imaging is unavailable, and that "In the presence of increased ICP, LP is avoided due to the danger of possible brainstem" herniation (p. 1092).
q_1182.trap: (C) proposes the one procedure the chapter specifically warns against in this setting, and the reason is mechanical rather than diagnostic — removing fluid below an obstructed compartment invites herniation.

q_1183.stem: A 2-year-old has a firm, nontender, irregular abdominal mass that crosses the midline. Which tumor does this suggest?
options: Neuroblastoma
Wilms tumor
Rhabdomyosarcoma
Hepatoblastoma
q_1183.rationale: The chapter states that with abdominal tumors "the most common presenting sign is a firm, nontender, irregular mass in the abdomen that crosses the midline (in contrast to Wilms tumor, which is usually confined to one side)" (p. 1096).
q_1183.trap: (B) is the confusable partner, and midline crossing is the single discriminator the chapter gives explicitly; the median age also differs, about 19 months for neuroblastoma and 44 months for unilateral Wilms tumor.

q_1184.stem: A child is being evaluated for suspected neuroblastoma. Which laboratory study does the chapter name?
options: Urinary catecholamine metabolites, vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid
Serum alpha-fetoprotein
Urinary protein and creatinine ratio
Serum renin
q_1184.rationale: The chapter states that because neuroblastomas excrete epinephrine and norepinephrine, "urinary excretion of catecholamine metabolites (vanillylmandelic acid [VMA] and homovanillic acid [HVA]) is measured before therapy," and these markers monitor response and detect relapse (p. 1096).
q_1184.trap: (D) belongs to Wilms tumor, where hypertension arises from excess renin secretion; each tumor has its own biochemical signature, which is another way the two abdominal masses separate.

q_1185.stem: A 3-year-old is admitted with a suspected Wilms tumor. Which nursing action is essential?
options: Do not palpate the abdomen, and post a sign on the bed
Palpate the abdomen once each shift to track the mass size
Measure abdominal girth every 2 hours with deep palpation
Encourage the child to lie prone to reduce pressure on the mass
q_1185.rationale: The chapter states that "the most important" preoperative concern is "not to palpate the tumor unless absolutely necessary because manipulation of the mass may cause dissemination of cancer cells to adjacent and distant sites," and a Nursing Alert directs posting a sign on the bed reading "Do not palpate abdomen" (p. 1100).
q_1185.trap: (B) and (C) are both ordinary nursing assessments that are specifically harmful here, which is what makes this the chapter's clearest single nursing action; careful bathing and handling also matter in preventing trauma to the tumor site.

q_1186.stem: A child with a Wilms tumor has a blood pressure of 132/86 mm Hg. What explains this?
options: Excess renin secretion by the tumor
Pain from abdominal distention
Fluid overload from preoperative hydration
Catecholamine secretion by the tumor
q_1186.rationale: The chapter states that "Hypertension, probably caused by secretion of excess amounts of renin by the tumor, occurs occasionally," and directs monitoring blood pressure preoperatively for this reason (pp. 1099–1100).
q_1186.trap: (D) names the neuroblastoma mechanism; note that the mass in Wilms tumor is "firm, nontender, confined to one side, and deep within the flank," and unlike the liver "it does not move with respiration," while hematuria occurs in fewer than one-fourth of children.

q_1187.stem: A child is recovering from nephrectomy for Wilms tumor. Which assessment is a priority because of a specific treatment complication?
options: Gastrointestinal activity, because vincristine-induced adynamic ileus can cause intestinal obstruction
Neurologic status, because of the risk of intracranial hemorrhage
Respiratory rate, because of the risk of pulmonary edema
Urine output only, since the remaining kidney is the sole concern
q_1187.rationale: The chapter directs monitoring gastrointestinal activity — bowel movements, bowel sounds, distention, and vomiting — because of the risk of intestinal obstruction from vincristine-induced adynamic ileus, radiation-induced edema, and postsurgical adhesions, along with frequent blood pressure evaluation and observation for infection (p. 1100).
q_1187.trap: (D) narrows the assessment to the obvious organ and misses the drug effect, which is what makes this complication easy to overlook; the recovery period is otherwise described as usually rapid.

q_1188.stem: An adolescent has localized pain in the distal femur that is relieved by holding the leg flexed. A radiograph shows a lesion in the metaphysis. Which tumor is most likely?
options: Osteosarcoma
Ewing sarcoma
Rhabdomyosarcoma
Osteomyelitis
q_1188.rationale: The chapter identifies osteosarcoma as "the most common bone tumor in adolescents and young adults," arising from bone-forming mesenchyme in the metaphyseal region, most often the distal femur, and notes that bone tumor pain "is often relieved by a flexed position, which relaxes the muscles overlying the stretched periosteum" (p. 1097).
q_1188.trap: (B) arises "in the marrow spaces of the bone rather than from osseous tissue," in the shaft rather than the metaphysis; note the shared trap that this pain is often attributed to trauma or dismissed as growing pains.

q_1189.stem: A child with a bone tumor has fever and systemic symptoms in addition to localized pain. Which tumor does this favor, and how does treatment differ?
options: Ewing sarcoma, which more often has systemic symptoms and is treated with radiation
Osteosarcoma, which more often has systemic symptoms and is treated with radiation
Ewing sarcoma, which is treated surgically without radiation
Osteosarcoma, which is treated with radiation rather than surgery
q_1189.rationale: The chapter states that "Systemic symptoms (such as fever) and other clinical symptoms (such as spinal cord compression and respiratory distress) are more frequent in patients with Ewing sarcoma," which is treated with radiation, unlike osteosarcoma (pp. 1097–1099).
q_1189.trap: (D) assigns radiation to the wrong tumor, which matters because the treatment difference is one of the two clean discriminators between them; the other is the site of origin, marrow space against osseous tissue.

q_1190.stem: A 2-year-old's parents notice a whitish glow in one pupil in photographs, and the child has developed strabismus. What is the likely diagnosis and its usual prognosis?
options: Retinoblastoma, with an overall 10-year survival near 90%
Congenital cataract, which does not affect survival
Retinoblastoma, with an overall survival below 50%
Optic glioma, which presents with proptosis
q_1190.rationale: The chapter names leukocoria as the first sign of retinoblastoma and strabismus as "The next most common sign... resulting from poor fixation of the visually impaired eye," and states that "The overall 10-year survival rate is nearly 90% for unilateral and bilateral tumors" (pp. 1102–1103).
q_1190.trap: (C) understates a prognosis that is among the best in this chapter; note that blindness is usually a late sign, and that retinoblastoma, like neuroblastoma, may spontaneously regress.

q_1191.stem: Parents of a child with retinoblastoma ask whether their other children are at risk. What should the nurse know about the hereditary pattern?
options: About 25% are bilateral and hereditary and 15% are unilateral and hereditary, with a germline RB1 mutation present in the hereditary form
All cases are hereditary and all siblings will be affected
No cases are hereditary, so siblings carry no increased risk
Only bilateral cases can be hereditary, so unilateral disease carries no family risk
q_1191.rationale: The chapter states that "60% are unilateral and nonhereditary (also called sporadic), 25% are bilateral and hereditary, and 15% are unilateral and hereditary," with a germline RB1 mutation in the hereditary form, and that children with hereditary disease tend to be diagnosed at a younger age (p. 1102).
q_1191.trap: (D) is the intuitive assumption that bilaterality equals heritability, and the 15% unilateral-hereditary group is exactly what it misses; blood and tumor samples can be tested for the mutation, which is how that group is identified.

q_1192.stem: A 7-year-old with a brain tumor is being monitored for raised intracranial pressure. Which findings are late signs? Select all that apply.
options: Bradycardia
Extension or flexion posturing
Cheyne-Stokes respirations
Alterations in pupil size and reactivity
Forceful vomiting
q_1192.rationale: Box 30.1 places bradycardia, decreased motor response to command, decreased sensory response to painful stimuli, alterations in pupil size and reactivity, extension or flexion posturing, Cheyne-Stokes respirations, papilledema, decreased consciousness, and coma in the late column (p. 1111).
q_1192.trap: (E) is an early sign in children, along with headache, nausea, diplopia, seizures, drowsiness, and declining school performance; the whole structure of this box is an early-versus-late sort, and a four-option item usually offers three from one column and one from the other.

q_1193.stem: A child who had a shunt revision this morning has nausea, a headache, irritability, and a heart rate that has fallen from 96 to 62 over the last hour. Which finding is the priority?
options: The decrease in heart rate
The nausea and refusal to eat
The headache
The irritability and sleepiness
q_1193.rationale: Bradycardia appears on the late-signs list of Box 30.1, so it signals decompensation rather than early pressure (p. 1111); the other three are real signs of shunt obstruction but sit on the early list (p. 1163).
q_1193.trap: (B), (C), and (D) are all genuinely abnormal and all genuinely common, which is what makes them attractive — a priority question asks for the most ominous finding rather than the most frequent one, and this is how the chapter's own review question is constructed.

q_1194.stem: A nurse is assessing a child with a head injury and wants the earliest indicator of neurologic change. What should the nurse monitor?
options: Level of consciousness, since alterations in consciousness appear earlier than vital sign or focal changes
Blood pressure, since a widening pulse pressure is the first warning in children
Pupillary response, since papilledema appears within the first hours
Deep tendon reflexes, which change before consciousness does
q_1194.rationale: The chapter states that "Assessment of level of consciousness (LOC) remains the earliest indicator of improvement or deterioration in neurologic status," and that "alterations in consciousness appear earlier than alterations of vital signs or focal neurologic signs" (pp. 1112, 1130).
q_1194.trap: (B) applies the adult Cushing picture, which the chapter says "rarely occur[s] in children or are very late signs"; (C) misplaces papilledema, which "takes 24 to 48 hours to develop" and so "will not be evident early in the course of unconsciousness."

q_1195.stem: A nurse is positioning a child with increased intracranial pressure. Which measures are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Elevate the head of the bed 15 to 30 degrees
Maintain the head in midline to facilitate venous drainage
Use vibration rather than percussion if airway clearance is needed
Hyperventilate with 100% oxygen before suctioning if it is unavoidable
Turn the child side to side every 2 hours
q_1195.rationale: The Nursing Alert directs elevating the head 15 to 30 degrees with the head midline "to facilitate venous drainage and avoid jugular compression"; the chapter adds that vibration "does not increase ICP" and "should be tried first," and that unavoidable suctioning "should be used judiciously and preceded by hyperventilation with 100% oxygen" (pp. 1120–1121).
q_1195.trap: (E) is contraindicated in this specific situation — "Turning side to side is contraindicated because of the risk of jugular compression" — even though 2-hourly repositioning is correct for skin and lungs in nearly every other context, which is what makes it the designed error.

q_1196.stem: A child with increased intracranial pressure from head trauma is prescribed a corticosteroid. What should the nurse recognize?
options: Corticosteroids are not recommended for cerebral edema secondary to head trauma
Corticosteroids are first-line for all causes of cerebral edema
Corticosteroids are contraindicated in cerebral edema of any cause
Corticosteroids should be given only after mannitol has failed
q_1196.rationale: The chapter states that "Administration of adrenocorticosteroids is not recommended for cerebral edema secondary to head trauma," while they remain useful for edema from inflammatory causes (p. 1120).
q_1196.trap: (B) generalizes a true statement about inflammatory edema to a cause where the evidence does not support it, and (C) overcorrects in the other direction — the distinction is the cause of the edema, not the drug.

q_1197.topic: consciousness assessment and the unconscious child
q_1197.stem: A child has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7. What does this indicate, and what does it trigger?
options: Coma, which triggers intracranial pressure monitoring
Mild impairment requiring hourly reassessment only
Normal function, since 7 is within the normal range
Brain death, since a score below 8 is incompatible with recovery
q_1197.rationale: The chapter gives 15 as normal, 8 or below as defining coma and triggering intracranial pressure monitoring, 5 or below as predicting poor outcome, and 3 as deep coma or death (p. 1113).
q_1197.trap: (D) confuses a coma threshold with a death threshold, which are five points apart on this scale; note that for subdural hematoma a different number governs — a score of 12 or less, or a drop of 2 or more points, means calling the neurosurgeon.

q_1198.topic: consciousness assessment and the unconscious child
q_1198.stem: An unconscious child is admitted after a fall. What is the first priority of care?
options: Establishing an adequate airway, within a circulation-airway-breathing sequence
Obtaining a computed tomography scan before any intervention
Administering mannitol to reduce pressure
Inserting a nasogastric tube to prevent vomiting
q_1198.rationale: The chapter directs emergency measures "toward ensuring circulation, airway, and breathing (CAB)" and states that "Respiratory effectiveness is the primary concern in the care of the unconscious child, and establishment of an adequate airway is always the first priority" (p. 1119).
q_1198.trap: (B) delays airway management for imaging, and the reason it matters is stated plainly — "Cerebral hypoxia at normal body temperature that lasts longer than 4 minutes often causes irreversible brain damage." Note also that in a head injury the airway is opened with a jaw thrust rather than a chin lift.

q_1199.topic: consciousness assessment and the unconscious child
q_1199.stem: An unconscious child has a urine output of 15 ml/hr, a urine specific gravity of 1.030, and a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L. What does this suggest?
options: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone, which is treated with fluid restriction
Diabetes insipidus, which is treated with fluid replacement
Acute kidney injury, which is treated with diuretics
Dehydration, which is treated with a fluid bolus
q_1199.rationale: Table 30.2 contrasts the two syndromes on urine output, specific gravity, and serum sodium, with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone producing low output, concentrated urine, and low sodium (p. 1121).
q_1199.trap: (D) is the trap the chapter names explicitly — the low urine output "might be erroneously interpreted as a sign of dehydration," which reverses the treatment from fluid restriction to fluid replacement and worsens the hyponatremia.

q_1200.topic: consciousness assessment and the unconscious child
q_1200.stem: A child with a head injury has an oral temperature of 40.2 degrees Celsius. What does the chapter direct?
options: Vigorous cooling is needed to prevent brain damage above 40 degrees Celsius, with antipyretics for fever and cooling devices for hyperthermia
No intervention, since fever is protective after brain injury
Cooling devices for fever and antipyretics for hyperthermia
Tepid sponging as the first measure at any temperature
q_1200.rationale: The chapter states that vigorous cooling is "needed to prevent brain damage if the rectal temperature exceeds 104°F (40°C)," and that "Antipyretics are the method of choice for fever reduction; cooling devices are used for hyperthermia" (pp. 1119, 1121).
q_1200.trap: (C) reverses the two methods, which is the swap this pair exists to catch — the set point determines which works, exactly as in the fever chapter earlier in the book.

q_1201.stem: A 6-year-old struck his head, was briefly dazed but never lost consciousness, and is confused with no memory of the event. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: A concussion, whose hallmarks are confusion and amnesia rather than loss of consciousness
Not a concussion, since consciousness was never lost
A cerebral contusion, since amnesia indicates structural injury
A normal response to a minor blow requiring no evaluation
q_1201.rationale: The chapter defines concussion as "an alteration in mental status with or without loss of consciousness," and names the belief that loss of consciousness is the hallmark "a common misconception" — the hallmarks being confusion and amnesia (p. 1124).
q_1201.trap: (B) is the misconception stated as a rule; (C) overreaches, though the chapter cautions that a contusion's "signs and symptoms may be clinically indistinguishable from those of concussion," so the two cannot always be separated clinically.

q_1202.stem: A 4-year-old struck his head, was briefly unconscious, then talked normally for 40 minutes before deteriorating rapidly. Which injury does this suggest?
options: Epidural hematoma
Subdural hematoma
Diffuse axonal injury
Cerebral contusion
q_1202.rationale: Table 30.3 characterizes epidural hematoma as usually occurring over 2 years of age, arterial or venous, usually unilateral, lenticular on computed tomography, with skull fracture in 70% of cases, and the lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration is its classic story (p. 1126).
q_1202.trap: (B) is the confusable partner and runs the other way on every feature — usually under 1 year, almost always venous, 75% bilateral, crescentic on computed tomography, with seizures in 75% and retinal hemorrhages very frequent.

q_1203.stem: A 5-month-old has bilateral subdural collections and retinal hemorrhages. What should the nurse consider?
options: Inflicted injury, since bilateral collections and retinal hemorrhages point to a subdural hematoma from shaking
An epidural hematoma from an accidental fall
A normal variant of infant imaging
Bacterial meningitis with subdural effusion
q_1203.rationale: Table 30.3 lists subdural hematoma as usually under 1 year, 75% bilateral, with retinal hemorrhages "Very frequent," and the fact bank notes that a stem mentioning retinal hemorrhages, bilateral collections, or an infant who was shaken points to a subdural collection (p. 1126).
q_1203.trap: (D) names a real cause of subdural effusion — the meningitis section states that "Subdural effusions often occur" — but it does not explain retinal hemorrhages, which is the finding that shifts the differential toward inflicted trauma.

q_1204.stem: A child struck in the occiput has injury to the frontal and temporal regions. What explains this?
options: Contrecoup injury, where the brain collides with surfaces opposite the point of impact
Coup injury, where bruising occurs at the point of impact
Diffuse axonal injury, which is always bilateral
A skull fracture propagating across the vault
q_1204.rationale: The chapter describes "bruising at the point of impact (coup) or at a distance as the brain collides with the unyielding surfaces opposite or far removed from the point of impact (contrecoup)," and gives this exact worked example — "a blow to the occipital region can cause severe injury to the frontal and temporal areas of the brain" (p. 1124).
q_1204.trap: (B) names the injury at the site of the blow, which is the other half of the pair; the terms are distinguished by location relative to the impact rather than by severity.

q_1205.stem: A child is being discharged after a mild head injury. Which situation would make the nurse recommend hospitalization for observation instead?
options: A language or communication barrier that may hinder the family's learning
A single episode of vomiting at the scene
A brief headache that has resolved
A parent who asks multiple questions about warning signs
q_1205.rationale: The chapter states that "language or other communication barriers or even emotional trauma, may hinder learning and make it difficult for families to feel confident caring for their child at home," which is a reason to hospitalize for observation (p. 1129); this is the basis of the chapter's own review question about phone triage.
q_1205.trap: (D) reverses the meaning of an engaged parent, who is better prepared rather than less; the discharge criteria turn on whether the family can reliably observe and act, not on the severity of the initial symptoms alone.

q_1206.stem: A nurse is assessing a 9-month-old for possible bacterial meningitis. Which findings fit this age group? Select all that apply.
options: Fever with poor feeding and vomiting
Marked irritability
Frequent seizures, often accompanied by a high-pitched cry
Bulging fontanel
Positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, which are reliable at this age
q_1206.rationale: Box 30.6 gives the 3-month-to-2-year picture as fever, poor feeding, vomiting, marked irritability, frequent seizures often with a high-pitched cry, bulging fontanel, and possible nuchal rigidity (p. 1135).
q_1206.trap: (E) reverses an explicit statement — for this age group "Brudzinski and Kernig signs not helpful in diagnosis," since they are "Difficult to elicit and evaluate in this age-group"; in neonates the neck is usually supple, so a 6-month-old with a supple neck has not ruled out meningitis.

q_1207.stem: Cerebrospinal fluid from a child shows an elevated white cell count with neutrophils, elevated protein, and decreased glucose. What does this indicate?
options: Bacterial meningitis, since decreased glucose is the fastest single discriminator
Viral meningitis, since the white cell count is elevated
Normal cerebrospinal fluid for a febrile child
Tuberculous meningitis specifically
q_1207.rationale: Table 30.4 contrasts bacterial fluid — elevated white cells with neutrophils, elevated protein, decreased glucose, positive Gram stain, turbid, elevated opening pressure — against viral fluid, which shows slightly elevated white cells with lymphocytes, normal or slightly increased protein, and normal glucose (p. 1138).
q_1207.trap: (B) uses the raised cell count, which both share, rather than the values that separate them; glucose is the value the fact bank singles out as the fastest cut, because bacteria consume it and viruses do not.

q_1208.stem: A child is admitted with suspected bacterial meningitis and antibiotics have just been started. What should the nurse tell the family about isolation?
options: Respiratory isolation remains in place for at least 24 hours after antibiotics are started
No isolation is needed now that antibiotics have been started
Enteric precautions are needed for 48 hours
Isolation continues until cerebrospinal fluid cultures are negative
q_1208.rationale: The chapter directs respiratory isolation for at least 24 hours after antibiotics are started for suspected bacterial meningitis (p. 1137), and this is the keyed answer to the chapter's own review question.
q_1208.trap: (B) treats the antibiotic as ending the requirement when it actually starts the clock, and (C) is wrong on route — the precautions are respiratory rather than enteric. Note that meningococcal meningitis "is the only type readily transmitted by droplet infection from nasopharyngeal secretions," though the isolation rule applies to suspected bacterial meningitis generally.

q_1209.stem: What is the major nursing priority when a child is admitted with suspected bacterial meningitis?
options: Administer antibiotics as soon as they are ordered, with isolation started at the same time
Obtain a full neurologic examination before any medication
Await culture results before beginning antibiotics
Position the child with the head of the bed flat and a pillow under the head
q_1209.rationale: The chapter states that "A major priority of nursing care of a child suspected of having meningitis is to administer antibiotics as soon as they are ordered," with isolation instituted at the same time (p. 1137).
q_1209.trap: (C) delays treatment for a result that takes far longer than the window in which antibiotics change outcome; (D) reverses the comfort positioning, since most children "are more comfortable without a pillow under their head but with the head of the bed slightly elevated."

q_1210.stem: A child recovering from bacterial meningitis is being discharged. Which follow-up does the chapter specifically direct?
options: Auditory evaluation shortly after discharge, since deafness is the most common permanent sequela
Repeat lumbar puncture at 1 month
Ophthalmologic evaluation at 6 months
No specific follow-up is needed once the child is afebrile
q_1210.rationale: The chapter states that damage to the eighth cranial nerve "is usually followed by permanent deafness, the most common permanent neurologic sequela of bacterial meningitis," and that "Hearing loss is common. The patient should undergo auditory evaluation shortly after discharge" (pp. 1136–1137).
q_1210.trap: (D) discharges a child without the one test the chapter names by name; note that a petechial or purpuric rash in an ill child may mean meningococcemia and "must receive immediate medical attention," which is a separate teaching point for families.

q_1211.topic: submersion injury, encephalitis, and reye syndrome
q_1211.stem: A child is pulled from a pool after an estimated 3 minutes, with sinus rhythm, reactive pupils, and responsiveness at the scene. What does the chapter say about prognosis and disposition?
options: These features predict a good outcome, but the child is still admitted for 24 hours of observation
The child may be discharged from the scene if fully alert
The prognosis cannot be estimated from scene findings
The cold water will have been neuroprotective, improving the outlook further
q_1211.rationale: The chapter states that submersion under 5 minutes with sinus rhythm, reactive pupils, and responsiveness at the scene predicts a good outcome, while over 10 minutes with no response to advanced life support within 25 minutes predicts the worst, and it directs 24-hour admission for observation (pp. 1131–1133).
q_1211.trap: (D) states a belief the chapter explicitly retracts — cold water "had previously been thought to be somewhat neuroprotective, but it is not"; the diving reflex is real but does not make the outcome good.

q_1212.topic: submersion injury, encephalitis, and reye syndrome
q_1212.stem: A nurse is planning care for a child admitted with encephalitis. What isolation is required?
options: None, though good hand washing technique is always used
Respiratory isolation for 24 hours after antimicrobials begin
Contact precautions for the duration of the illness
Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room
q_1212.rationale: The chapter states for encephalitis that "Isolation of the child is not necessary; however, always use good hand washing technique" (p. 1140).
q_1212.trap: (B) applies the meningitis rule to a different disease, and the pair is worth holding together — meningitis gets respiratory isolation, encephalitis does not, and the discriminator is the disease rather than the severity of the presentation.

q_1213.topic: submersion injury, encephalitis, and reye syndrome
q_1213.stem: A child recovering from varicella develops persistent vomiting and progressive neurologic deterioration, and Reye syndrome is suspected. Which exposure should the nurse ask about?
options: Aspirin or other salicylate use during the viral illness
Acetaminophen use during the viral illness
Ibuprofen use during the viral illness
Antibiotic use during the viral illness
q_1213.rationale: The chapter links Reye syndrome to salicylate use during a viral illness, which is the reason aspirin is withheld from children with influenza or chickenpox throughout this book (p. 1141).
q_1213.trap: (B) and (C) name the substitutes rather than the culprit; the same association drives the instruction elsewhere to hold aspirin in a child with Kawasaki disease who is exposed to chickenpox or influenza.

q_1214.topic: submersion injury, encephalitis, and reye syndrome
q_1214.stem: A nurse is reviewing the mechanisms of cerebral edema after brain injury. Which statement is accurate?
options: Cytotoxic edema results from direct cell injury with intracellular swelling and often irreversible damage, while vasogenic edema results from increased capillary permeability without primary nerve cell injury
Cytotoxic edema results from capillary leak and is reversible
Vasogenic edema results from direct cell injury and is irreversible
The two are the same process described at different stages
q_1214.rationale: The chapter defines cytotoxic edema as "a result of direct cell injury… caused by intracellular swelling," where "In many cases the brain cells are irreversibly damaged," and vasogenic edema as "due to increased permeability of capillary endothelial cells," where "the nerve cells are not primarily injured" (p. 1127).
q_1214.trap: (B) and (C) swap the two mechanisms, and the practical consequence is prognostic — whether the cells themselves have been injured determines whether resolving the edema restores function.

q_1215.stem: A 7-year-old has had one unprovoked generalized tonic-clonic seizure. The parents ask whether this means epilepsy and whether daily medication is needed. What should the nurse explain?
options: A single seizure is not classified as epilepsy and is generally not treated with long-term antiepileptic drugs
Any seizure establishes epilepsy and requires lifelong medication
Epilepsy is diagnosed after any two seizures regardless of interval
Medication is started after the first seizure in every case to prevent recurrence
q_1215.rationale: The chapter states that "A single seizure is not classified as epilepsy and is generally not treated with long-term antiepileptic drugs," with epilepsy requiring two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or one plus a 60% recurrence probability (p. 1142).
q_1215.trap: (C) drops the interval requirement, which is part of the definition; the distinction matters because it determines whether a child is committed to years of daily medication after a single event.

q_1216.stem: A teacher reports that a 6-year-old has brief staring episodes several times a day. How can an absence seizure be distinguished from daydreaming?
options: A child who is daydreaming responds to touch, while a child having an absence seizure cannot
Daydreaming episodes are shorter than absence seizures
Absence seizures are followed by postictal sleepiness and daydreaming is not
Absence seizures are accompanied by incontinence
q_1216.rationale: The chapter states that "Children who are daydreaming will respond to touch, whereas those who are having an absence seizure cannot," adding that absence seizures have "no postictal sleepiness," are "not accompanied by incontinence," and produce amnesia for the episode (p. 1146).
q_1216.trap: (C) and (D) each name a feature the chapter assigns to absence seizures in the negative — their absence is what makes the episodes easy to miss, and the interruptibility test is what a teacher or parent can actually perform.

q_1217.stem: A child started on an antiepileptic drug 10 days ago develops a rash. What should the nurse advise?
options: Stop the drug, and have the child evaluated within 24 hours or sooner if edema or respiratory problems develop
Continue the drug and give an antihistamine
Hold the drug and call the office in the morning
Halve the dose and continue while monitoring the rash
q_1217.rationale: The chapter states that "The drug should be stopped with any signs of a rash," with evaluation "within 24 hours or sooner if the child develops edema or respiratory problems" (p. 1149).
q_1217.trap: (B) and (D) both continue exposure to a drug that may be producing a hypersensitivity reaction; (C) gets the first half right and adds a delay the instruction does not permit.

q_1218.stem: A child's electroencephalogram is normal, and the parents conclude that the seizures have resolved. How should the nurse respond?
options: A normal recording does not rule out seizures, because it lasts about 1 hour and may show normal activity between events
A normal recording confirms that the seizures have resolved
A normal recording means the original diagnosis was incorrect
A normal recording means medication can be stopped immediately
q_1218.rationale: The chapter states that the recording "lasts approximately 1 hour, and therefore may show normal interictal activity," so a normal study does not exclude a seizure disorder (p. 1148).
q_1218.trap: (D) would act on the misreading in the most consequential way, and the chapter separately notes that "The most common cause of status epilepticus in children taking antiepileptic medications is missed medication."

q_1219.stem: A parent asks whether a child with well-controlled epilepsy may play sports. What should the nurse advise?
options: Sports are encouraged with a helmet for head protection, with water activities the standing exception requiring supervision
All sports should be avoided because of injury risk
Only non-contact sports are permitted, and swimming is unrestricted
Sports are permitted only after 2 years seizure free
q_1219.rationale: The chapter states that "Children with epilepsy are not at increased risk for injury with the exception of head injury," so the answer is helmets rather than restriction, and that "Only children with frequent seizures must avoid these activities"; water is the standing exception, requiring eyes-on supervision when swimming and an adult within arm's reach in natural water (pp. 1152–1155).
q_1219.trap: (C) gets the restriction backward by freeing the one activity that needs supervision; showers are preferred to baths, and the bathroom door is not locked.

q_1220.topic: seizure first aid and status epilepticus
q_1220.stem: A child begins a tonic-clonic seizure in the classroom. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Time the seizure episode
Ease the child to the floor and place something soft under the head
Turn the child to the side if vomiting occurs
Clear the area of hard objects
Place a padded tongue blade between the teeth
q_1220.rationale: The Emergency Treatment box directs remaining calm, timing the episode, easing the child down, placing a pillow or folded blanket under the head, loosening restrictive clothing, removing eyeglasses, clearing hazards, allowing the seizure to end without interference, and turning the child to one side if vomiting occurs (p. 1154).
q_1220.trap: (E) is one of three things the chapter forbids — do not restrain, do not put anything in the mouth, and do not give food or liquids — and a Nursing Alert repeats it: "do not place a solid object between the child's teeth." This is the single most common wrong option in seizure items.

q_1221.topic: seizure first aid and status epilepticus
q_1221.stem: Why is a child placed on the side during and after a tonic-clonic seizure?
options: The swallowing reflex is lost and salivation increases, so side-lying facilitates drainage and helps maintain a patent airway
Side-lying shortens the duration of the seizure
Side-lying prevents the tonic phase from progressing to the clonic phase
Side-lying reduces intracranial pressure during the event
q_1221.rationale: The chapter states that during and sometimes after a tonic-clonic seizure "the swallowing reflex is lost, salivation increases," and the tongue is hypotonic, so "the child is at risk for aspiration and airway occlusion. Placing the child on the side facilitates drainage and helps maintain a patent airway" (pp. 1152, 1154).
q_1221.trap: (B) and (C) assign the position a therapeutic effect on the seizure itself, and the chapter is explicit that "It is impossible to physically stop a seizure once it has begun, and no attempt should be made to do so."

q_1222.topic: seizure first aid and status epilepticus
q_1222.stem: A child has been seizing continuously for 8 minutes. How is this classified, and when should treatment begin?
options: Impending status epilepticus, with treatment beginning within 5 minutes
Status epilepticus, defined as any seizure over 5 minutes
A simple prolonged seizure, with treatment after 30 minutes
Not yet requiring treatment until 30 minutes have elapsed
q_1222.rationale: The chapter defines status epilepticus as "a continuous seizure that lasts more than 30 minutes or a series of seizures from which the child does not regain a premorbid level of consciousness," and impending status epilepticus as "a continuous seizure or series of seizures lasting between 5 and 30 minutes with the designation that treatment should begin within 5 minutes" (p. 1150).
q_1222.trap: (D) waits for the full 30-minute definition before acting, which is exactly what the impending category exists to prevent; the chapter calls status epilepticus "a medical emergency that requires immediate intervention to prevent possible brain injury or death."

q_1223.topic: seizure first aid and status epilepticus
q_1223.stem: A child in status epilepticus has intravenous access. Which drug does the chapter name as first line?
options: Intravenous diazepam or lorazepam
Intravenous phenytoin
Oral levetiracetam
Intravenous phenobarbital
q_1223.rationale: The chapter states that with intravenous access, "IV diazepam or lorazepam (Ativan) is the first-line drug of choice," with phenytoin or fosphenytoin followed by phenobarbital as the next line if a benzodiazepine is ineffective (p. 1150).
q_1223.trap: (B) and (D) are the second-line agents presented as first, and the chapter adds the principle that decides several stems: "It appears that the exact medication chosen is less important than choosing the one that can be administered fastest" — which is why buccal or intranasal midazolam and rectal diazepam are used when there is no line.

q_1224.stem: A 20-month-old had a 2-minute generalized seizure with a temperature of 39.4 degrees Celsius and has no history of afebrile seizures. Which criteria define a febrile seizure?
options: No history of afebrile seizures, a temperature of at least 38 degrees Celsius, and an age between 6 and 60 months
Any seizure occurring with a fever at any age
A seizure lasting more than 15 minutes with fever
A seizure with fever in a child with a family history of epilepsy
q_1224.rationale: The chapter's three-part definition states that "children who have a febrile seizure cannot have a history of afebrile seizures, must have a temperature of at least 38°C (100.4°F), and must be between the age of 6 and 60 months" (p. 1157).
q_1224.trap: (B) drops both the age band and the prior-seizure exclusion, which are what make this a distinct entity; febrile seizures are "the most common type of seizure, affecting 2% to 4% of children."

q_1225.stem: The parents of a child who had a simple febrile seizure ask how to prevent another one. What should the nurse explain?
options: Antipyretics relieve fever-associated discomfort but appear to be ineffective in preventing seizures
Scheduled acetaminophen during every illness will prevent recurrence
Daily antiepileptic medication is recommended after a first febrile seizure
Tepid sponging at the first sign of fever prevents recurrence
q_1225.rationale: The chapter states that "Antipyretic therapy during febrile illness offers symptomatic relief for fever-associated symptoms but appears to be ineffective in preventing seizures," restating that "Attempts to lower the temperature will not prevent a seizure," and that "There is no benefit of antiepileptic prophylaxis in these children" (p. 1157).
q_1225.trap: (D) names a measure the chapter rejects on three separate grounds — tepid sponging is ineffective at lowering temperature significantly, the shivering increases metabolic output, and the cooling causes discomfort.

q_1226.stem: A child has a febrile seizure that is still ongoing after 5 minutes. What should parents be instructed to do?
options: Call for emergency assistance, and do not place a child who is actively seizing in the car
Drive the child to the emergency department immediately
Wait another 10 minutes before seeking help
Give a dose of antipyretic and observe at home
q_1226.rationale: The Nursing Alert states that "If a febrile seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, parents should seek medical attention immediately. Instruct parents to call for emergency assistance (911) and not to place the child who is actively having a seizure in the car" (p. 1157).
q_1226.trap: (B) is the instinct of most parents and creates the exact hazard the alert names; for prolonged recurrent febrile seizures over 5 minutes the chapter endorses acute treatment with rectal diazepam, buccal lorazepam, or intranasal midazolam. Reassurance is evidence-based here, since studies show no difference in intelligence, memory, behavior, or academic performance afterward.

q_1227.stem: A child has hydrocephalus caused by obstruction to the flow of cerebrospinal fluid through the ventricular system. How is this classified?
options: Noncommunicating, which is the same as obstructive
Communicating, since the ventricles remain connected
Communicating, since absorption is impaired
Neither, since obstruction is a separate category
q_1227.rationale: The chapter defines communicating hydrocephalus as "impaired absorption of CSF fluid within the subarachnoid space" and noncommunicating as "obstruction to the flow of CSF through the ventricular system" (p. 1159).
q_1227.trap: (C) attaches the absorption mechanism to the wrong term, and the naming is counterintuitive enough to be worth holding as a pair — noncommunicating equals obstructive.

q_1228.stem: A child has just returned from ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. How should the nurse position the child?
options: Flat, on the unoperated side, to avoid complications from too-rapid reduction of intracranial fluid
With the head of the bed elevated 30 degrees to reduce intracranial pressure
On the operated side to promote drainage
In Trendelenburg position to maintain cerebral perfusion
q_1228.rationale: The chapter directs positioning "carefully on the unoperated side to prevent pressure on the shunt valve," with the child remaining flat "to help avert complications resulting from too-rapid reduction of intracranial fluid" (p. 1164).
q_1228.trap: (B) applies the increased-pressure rule to a situation where the risk has reversed — before shunting the danger is too much pressure, and immediately after it is lowering the pressure too fast; this contradiction between the two rules is deliberate and is the point of the item.

q_1229.stem: A nurse is caring for a child after shunt placement. Which assessments are indicated? Select all that apply.
options: Pupil dilation, since pressure compresses or stretches the oculomotor nerve on the same side
Abdominal distention and constipation, since cerebrospinal fluid may cause peritonitis or ileus
Temperature, poor feeding, vomiting, and decreased responsiveness as signs of infection
Testing any suspected incisional drainage for glucose
Vigorous range of motion to prevent contractures
q_1229.rationale: The chapter directs neurologic assessment including pupil dilation and blood pressure, observation for abdominal distention and constipation "because CSF may cause peritonitis or a postoperative ileus as a complication of distal catheter placement," monitoring for infection signs, and inspecting the incision and testing suspected drainage for glucose "an indication of CSF" (p. 1164).
q_1229.trap: (E) is not among the postoperative directives and runs against the general instruction elsewhere that range of motion in a child with raised pressure is performed "gently but should not be performed vigorously."

q_1230.stem: A school-age child with a shunt has nausea, refusal to eat, headache, and increasing sleepiness. What should the nurse suspect?
options: Shunt obstruction, since these are early signs of increased intracranial pressure in an older child
Gastroenteritis, since the symptoms are gastrointestinal
Normal postoperative recovery
Shunt infection, which presents only with these findings
q_1230.rationale: The chapter lists nausea and refusal to eat, headache, and irritability with sleepiness among the signs of shunt obstruction (p. 1163), and states that in older children "the most valuable indicators of increasing ICP are an alteration in the child's level of consciousness, complaint of headache, and changes in interaction with the environment" (p. 1164).
q_1230.trap: (B) is the natural first reading of vomiting and anorexia in a child, and it is why shunt malfunction is missed; note the earlier priority point that if bradycardia is also present, that late sign outranks all of these.

q_1231.stem: The parents of a child with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt ask about sports. What should the nurse advise?
options: Contact sports such as football, rugby, boxing, and wrestling are prohibited, while swimming, soccer, and track are acceptable and encouraged
All sports are prohibited because of the risk of shunt damage
All sports are permitted without restriction
Only swimming is prohibited, because of infection risk
q_1231.rationale: The chapter states that "Contact sports such as football, rugby, boxing, and wrestling are usually prohibited if a person has a VP shunt; other sports such as swimming, soccer, and track are acceptable and even encouraged for the child's physical and emotional health," with helmets required for skating, skiing, biking, and skateboarding (p. 1164).
q_1231.trap: (B) removes activity the chapter actively encourages for physical and emotional health, and (D) restricts the wrong sport; note that most children who require shunting "must depend on the shunt for the remainder of their life," so the guidance is about living with it rather than avoiding activity.

q_1232.topic: growth failure evaluation and growth hormone therapy
q_1232.subtopic: distinguishing the causes of short stature
q_1232.stem: A 7-year-old boy is referred for short stature. He grew normally through his first year and has since followed a curve below the 3rd percentile. He is chubby, his body proportions are normal for his age, and he looks younger than 7. Intelligence testing is normal. Which feature most helps the nurse distinguish growth hormone deficiency from failure to thrive?
options: His well-nourished, even chubby, appearance
His height below the 3rd percentile
His normal intelligence testing
His normal skeletal proportions
q_1232.rationale: "Height may be stunted more than weight because, with good nutrition, these children can become overweight or even obese," and the chapter names the consequence outright: "Their well-nourished appearance is an important diagnostic clue to differentiation from other disorders such as failure to thrive" (p. 1173).
q_1232.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because it is the finding that brought the child in, but a height below the 3rd percentile is where every short-stature workup starts and separates nothing; (D) is equally true of a malnourished child, since "Skeletal proportions are normal for the age" in GH deficiency but proportion is not what undernutrition disturbs first.

q_1233.topic: growth failure evaluation and growth hormone therapy
q_1233.subtopic: distinguishing the causes of short stature
q_1233.stem: Two 9-year-old girls are evaluated for short stature. One has a markedly delayed bone age; the other's bone age matches her chronologic age. How should the nurse interpret the two films?
options: The girl whose bone age is not delayed has the more concerning finding
The girl with the profoundly delayed bone age has a confirmed endocrine diagnosis
Neither film adds anything, because bone age is not part of a growth workup
The delayed bone age means that girl's short stature is now irreversible
q_1233.rationale: "a bone age that is not delayed in a short child is of much greater concern and may, in fact, be of some diagnostic value under certain circumstances" (p. 1175). Most conditions that slow linear growth also retard skeletal maturation, so a delayed film is the expected and nonspecific result.
q_1233.trap: (B) is the intuitive inversion, because an abnormal test feels more diagnostic than a normal one, and Box 31.5 forecloses it: "Observation of even a profoundly delayed bone age is never diagnostic or even indicative of a specific diagnosis" (p. 1175). (D) reverses the meaning entirely, since delay indicates the short stature is to some extent still recoverable "because linear growth will continue until epiphyseal fusion is complete."

q_1234.topic: growth failure evaluation and growth hormone therapy
q_1234.stem: A 10-year-old is beginning recombinant growth hormone. Which combination of instruction and expectation should the nurse give the family?
options: Give the injection at bedtime, and expect the fastest growth in the first year with the child still remaining shorter than peers
Give the injection at bedtime, and expect the child to reach an average adult height for the family
Give the injection with breakfast, and expect growth to accelerate further with each year of treatment
Give the injection at bedtime, and expect therapy to continue to age 18 regardless of bone age
q_1234.rationale: The Drug Alert states that "GH is most effective when it is administered at bedtime," because physiologic release normally follows "during the first 45 to 90 minutes after the onset of sleep" (p. 1176).
