"Maximum growth velocity occurs in the first year of treatment," after which "growth rates decline" (pp. 1175–1176), and the honest ceiling is that "individuals who receive treatment remain shorter than their peers" (p. 1176).
q_1234.trap: (B) gets the timing right and the promise wrong, which is the harder error to catch, because a family hearing the drug's name expects a normal adult height and the nurse who confirms it has set up the disappointment the chapter warns about; (C) inverts the growth-velocity curve, which is steepest at the start.

q_1235.topic: growth failure evaluation and growth hormone therapy
q_1235.stem: An adolescent girl has been on growth hormone for 5 years. Her growth rate is now under 1 inch per year and her bone age is 14.5 years. Her 15-year-old brother, also on growth hormone, has a bone age of 14 years. Which statement is correct?
options: The girl meets a criterion to stop therapy that her brother does not yet meet
Both of them now meet the criteria to stop therapy
Neither meets the criteria, because bone age is not used in this decision
The brother meets the criterion, since boys finish growing earlier than girls
q_1235.rationale: "Growth rates of less than 1 inch per year and a bone age of more than 14 years in girls and more than 16 years in boys are often used as criteria to stop GH therapy" (p. 1176). Her bone age is past 14; his is well short of 16. The decision itself is shared: "The child, family, and health care team make the decision jointly to stop GH therapy."
q_1235.trap: (D) is the reflex error because girls are taught to mature earlier, so a reader who remembers the direction without the numbers attaches the earlier stopping point to the wrong child; (B) applies one threshold to both sexes, which is the same swap in a different shape.

q_1236.stem: Two patients have growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas: an 8-year-old and a 30-year-old. The child is growing rapidly in height with proportional weight gain and an enlarging head circumference. The adult has a broadening jaw, enlarged hands, and separating teeth, with no change in height. What accounts for the difference?
options: The epiphyses are still open in the child and have closed in the adult
The child's tumor secretes a larger quantity of growth hormone
The adult's tumor is also secreting thyroid-stimulating hormone
The adult has had the tumor for a longer period
q_1236.rationale: "Excess GH before closure of the epiphyseal shafts results in proportional overgrowth of the long bones," while "If oversecretion of GH occurs after epiphyseal closure, growth is in the transverse direction, producing a condition known as acromegaly" (p. 1176). Gigantism also produces "Proportional enlargement of head circumference."
q_1236.trap: (D) pulls hardest because acromegaly genuinely is diagnosed late — patients are identified "as much as 10 years after their symptoms first appear" (p. 1177) — so the duration in the option is a true fact recruited to explain the wrong thing. The single variable is whether the growth plates are open.

q_1237.stem: An adolescent diagnosed with acromegaly after epiphyseal closure asks whether treatment will bring his height back down. Which response is accurate?
options: Treatment will not reduce your height, but it will prevent further excess growth
Treatment will gradually return your height toward your predicted adult height
Your height can be reduced, but only with transsphenoidal resection of the tumor
Height is never affected in acromegaly, so there is nothing to reduce
q_1237.rationale: "Although medical treatment of acromegaly will not reduce a patient's height, it will prevent further excess growth" (p. 1177).
q_1237.trap: (C) is the plausible-but-adjacent version, and it is the most convincing wrong answer because it names the right operation: "Transsphenoid surgery (TSS) is the most common surgical treatment for pituitary adenoma" (p. 1177). Naming a real procedure makes a false promise sound informed.

q_1238.stem: A 7-year-old girl and a 7-year-old boy are each being evaluated for central precocious puberty. Which statement should guide the nurse's expectations for the two workups?
options: The boy is far more likely to have a CNS lesion, but both children still require a brain MRI
The girl is far more likely to have a CNS lesion, so only she requires a brain MRI
Neither child needs imaging if the rest of the physical examination is normal
The boy is far more likely to have a CNS lesion, so imaging is reserved for boys
q_1238.rationale: "CPP occurs more frequently in girls and is usually idiopathic, with 95% demonstrating no causative factor," whereas "A CNS insult or structural abnormality occurs in more than 75% of boys with CPP" (p. 1178). The imaging rule is nevertheless universal: "In every case, an MRI of the brain should be performed to assess for hypothalamic brain tumor."
q_1238.trap: (D) is more tempting than (B)'s outright inversion, because it gets the epidemiology exactly right and then draws the wrong conclusion from it. Probability shapes the level of suspicion, not the imaging rule, and the phrase the chapter uses is "In every case."

q_1239.stem: The mother of an 8-year-old girl with central precocious puberty asks how to manage her daughter's development. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Dress and activities should match her chronologic age rather than her physical development
Her sexual interest and mental age are those of an 8-year-old
She may be fertile, even at this age
Estrogen-containing birth control pills should be started now as a precaution
The hardest period is usually the school years before adolescence
q_1239.rationale: "Dress and activities for the physically precocious child should be appropriate to the chronologic age"; "Sexual interest is not usually advanced beyond the child's chronologic age, and parents need to understand that the child's mental age is congruent with the chronologic age"; "the nurse should emphasize to parents that the child may be fertile"; and "The most difficult time for the child is usually the school years before adolescence. After puberty, physical differences from peers are no longer present" (p. 1178).
q_1239.trap: (D) is the one wrong option, and it is wrong for a physiologic reason rather than a moral one: "hormonal forms of birth control, such as estrogen pills, prematurely initiate epiphyseal closure, resulting in stunted linear growth" (p. 1178). The chapter also states that "Usually no form of contraception is necessary unless the child is sexually active," so the option fails twice.

q_1240.topic: diabetes insipidus and siadh in children
q_1240.stem: A 5-month-old is brought in for persistent irritability and crying. The mother reports the baby quiets when given a bottle of plain water but keeps fussing after formula feedings. The infant has lost weight and soaks through an unusual number of diapers. Which condition does this picture suggest?
options: Diabetes insipidus
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Congenital hypothyroidism
q_1240.rationale: "In the infant the initial symptom is irritability that is relieved with feedings of water but not milk" (p. 1178), and the chapter repeats the clue under nursing care management: "persistent irritability and crying in an infant that is relieved only by bottle-feedings of water" (p. 1179). The infant is also "prone to severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, hyperthermia, azotemia, and potential circulatory collapse."
q_1240.trap: (C) pulls because polyuria, thirst, and weight loss belong to both diseases, and the water-not-milk detail is the only thing in the stem that separates them. Teaching families that "DI is a different condition from DM" is itself a stated nursing action (p. 1179), which is a fair signal that the confusion is expected.

q_1241.topic: diabetes insipidus and siadh in children
q_1241.stem: A school-age child is undergoing a water deprivation test. Which finding requires the nurse to terminate the fluid restriction?
options: Weight loss of 4% of body weight
Urine that remains dilute despite the restriction
The child complaining of intense thirst
A urine output that exceeds the measured intake
q_1241.rationale: "A weight loss between 3% and 5% indicates significant dehydration and requires termination of the fluid restriction" (p. 1179). The test requires "strict monitoring of fluid intake and urinary output, measurement of urine concentration (specific gravity or osmolality), and frequent weight checks."
q_1241.trap: (B) and (D) are the abnormal results the test exists to produce, since in DI "fluid restriction has little or no effect on urine formation but causes weight loss from dehydration" (p. 1178) — they are findings to record, not reasons to stop. Thirst is expected throughout, and the Nursing Alert warns that small children need close observation "to prevent them from drinking, even from toilet bowls, flower vases, or other unlikely sources of fluid" (p. 1179).

q_1242.topic: diabetes insipidus and siadh in children
q_1242.stem: A child with polyuria and polydipsia is given a test dose of aqueous vasopressin, and the urine osmolality does not change. What does this result indicate?
options: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, in which the renal tubules do not respond to the hormone
Central diabetes insipidus, in which too little antidiuretic hormone is produced
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
Compulsive water drinking from a psychogenic cause
q_1242.rationale: "Unresponsiveness to exogenous vasopressin usually indicates nephrogenic DI" (p. 1179), a form described as "a rare hereditary disorder affecting primarily males and caused by unresponsiveness of the renal tubules to the hormone" (p. 1178). The mirror result confirms the other form: "a rise in urine osmolality after vasopressin administration indicates central DI."
q_1242.trap: (B) is the mirror error and names the commoner disease, so the reflex is to answer with the diagnosis rather than with the test result; the test exists precisely because hormone replacement works in one form and is useless in the other. (D) is a genuine differential the chapter raises, but it is settled by psychologic consultation, not by the vasopressin response.

q_1243.topic: diabetes insipidus and siadh in children
q_1243.stem: A parent of a child taking twice-daily DDAVP calls to report that the child urinates more than usual in the early evening, before the bedtime dose. What should the nurse explain?
options: Some breakthrough urination in the evening is deliberate, guarding against overmedication
The dose is too low and should be increased tonight
The child most likely missed the morning dose
The medication should be changed to the parenteral route
q_1243.rationale: Breakthrough "urination is allowed during the evening hours as a precaution against overmedication" (p. 1179). The twice-daily schedule is timed at bedtime "to allow the child to sleep through the night and in the morning to allow fewer interruptions in the school day."
q_1243.trap: (B) is the intuitive answer, because the symptom the drug was given to control has reappeared, and it is the one that causes harm: "The signs of overmedication are similar to manifestations associated with the syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH)" (p. 1179). Over-treated diabetes insipidus becomes the opposite disorder.

q_1244.topic: diabetes insipidus and siadh in children
q_1244.stem: Two days after a craniotomy, a child develops a serum sodium of 121 mEq/L, rising urine osmolality, weight gain, nausea, and irritability. Which is the immediate management of choice?
options: Fluid restriction
Intranasal DDAVP
Free water boluses through the nasogastric tube
A rapid infusion of hypertonic saline
q_1244.rationale: "Fluid restriction is the immediate management of choice" in SIADH (p. 1179). "Excess ADH causes free water to be reabsorbed from the kidneys. As increased free water circulates, serum osmolality goes down, and urine osmolality inappropriately increases," and the danger is cerebral: "When hyponatremia occurs acutely, swelling of the brain occurs."
q_1244.trap: (B) is the mirror error, since DDAVP is the diabetes insipidus treatment (p. 1179) and giving more antidiuretic hormone here deepens the retention; (D) names a real therapy but skips a step, because "Severe SIADH may require hypertonic saline infusion that is only given in the hospital setting under close supervision" — it follows fluid restriction rather than replacing it.

q_1245.topic: pediatric hypothyroidism goiter and hashimoto disease
q_1245.stem: The parents of an 11-year-old newly diagnosed with acquired hypothyroidism ask whether their daughter will have lasting intellectual problems. Which response is accurate?
options: Intellectual disability is not associated with hypothyroidism acquired at this age, because brain growth is nearly complete by 2 to 3 years
Intellectual disability is likely unless replacement begins within about two weeks
The intellectual outcome depends entirely on how high the TSH is at diagnosis
About half of children with any form of hypothyroidism have intellectual disability
q_1245.rationale: "Because brain growth is nearly complete by 2 to 3 years of age, intellectual disability and neurologic sequelae are not associated with juvenile hypothyroidism" (p. 1180). Box 31.7 supplies the reason: thyroid hormone "Affects central nervous system development and cerebration during first 2 to 3 years," a window that has already closed for this child.
q_1245.trap: (B) moves the consequence of the congenital form onto an acquired case, which is the stage swap this pair is built on: "If left untreated, congenital hypothyroidism causes mental retardation" (p. 1180), and that is why newborn screening exists.

q_1246.topic: pediatric hypothyroidism goiter and hashimoto disease
q_1246.stem: A child with severe acquired hypothyroidism is started on L-thyroxine, and the dose is to be increased in steps over 4 to 8 weeks. A parent asks why the full dose is not simply given now. Which explanation is correct?
options: Gradual increases avoid producing symptoms of hyperthyroidism
The thyroid gland needs time to begin producing its own hormone again
A full dose would suppress the pituitary permanently
The drug must be titrated to the child's weight, which takes several weeks to establish
q_1246.rationale: "In children with severe symptoms, the restoration thyroid function is achieved more gradually with administration of increasing amounts of L-thyroxine over a period of 4 to 8 weeks. This is done to avoid symptoms of hyperthyroidism" (p. 1180).
q_1246.trap: (B) sounds physiologic and describes the wrong organ's recovery — that is the rationale for tapering exogenous steroids so the pituitary can resume secreting ACTH (p. 1188), not for ramping thyroid replacement. (D) invents a titration reason the chapter does not give.

q_1247.topic: pediatric hypothyroidism goiter and hashimoto disease
q_1247.stem: A 13-year-old is found on routine examination to have a symmetric, firm, nontender enlargement of the thyroid gland. What can the nurse conclude from the enlargement alone?
options: Nothing about thyroid function, since a goiter occurs with deficient, excessive, or normal hormone secretion
That the child is hypothyroid
That the child is hyperthyroid
That the gland is malignant until proven otherwise
q_1247.rationale: "A goiter is an enlargement or hypertrophy of the thyroid gland. It may occur with deficient (hypothyroid), excessive (hyperthyroid), or normal (euthyroid) TH secretion" (p. 1181). In chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis specifically, "Most children are euthyroid, but some display symptoms of hypothyroidism. Others have signs suggestive of hyperthyroidism."
q_1247.trap: (B) is the reflex pick because goiter is most often taught beside iodine deficiency; (D) takes only half of the nodule rule, which has two halves that must be kept together: "Nodules are rarely caused by a cancerous tumor but always require evaluation" (p. 1181).

q_1248.topic: pediatric hypothyroidism goiter and hashimoto disease
q_1248.stem: A 14-year-old is diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis (Hashimoto disease). Which conditions does the chapter name as clustering in the families of these children? Select all that apply.
options: Graves disease
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Addison disease
Pernicious anemia
Cystic fibrosis
q_1248.rationale: "In families this disease is closely related to other thyroid disorders (e.g., Graves disease, idiopathic hypothyroidism, idiopathic myxedema) and autoimmune disorders (e.g., pernicious anemia, Addison disease, type 1 DM, and hypoparathyroidism)" (p. 1181). The mechanism is shared: "Thyroid cell damage and death are autoimmune mediated by T cells and cytokines."
q_1248.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it is chosen on the wrong principle. Cystic fibrosis does run in families, so a reader selecting on heritability takes it; the thread holding this list together is autoimmunity, not inheritance.

q_1249.topic: graves disease and thyroidectomy care in adolescents
q_1249.stem: A 13-year-old started methimazole for Graves disease six weeks ago and calls the clinic with a sore throat and a temperature of 38.9°C. What is the nurse's correct response?
options: Have the child examined now, because sore throat and fever accompany agranulocytosis
Advise acetaminophen and fluids, and call back if there is no improvement in three days
Reassure the family that this is an expected effect of the drug in the first months
Instruct the family to double the next dose, because fever raises thyroid hormone demand
q_1249.rationale: "The most serious side effect of ATDs is agranulocytosis (severe leukopenia), which generally occurs within the initial weeks or months of therapy. It is usually accompanied by a sore throat and fever" (p. 1182). The Drug Alert repeats it: because these symptoms "accompany the grave complication of leukopenia, these children should be examined if such symptoms occur" (p. 1183). Treatment is "immediate discontinuation of the drug and the administration of antibiotics and glucocorticoids until symptoms resolve."
q_1249.trap: (B) is the advice a sore throat earns in any other child, which is exactly why the alert is printed twice in two pages; (C) inverts the meaning of the timing, since the first weeks to months are when the risk is highest, not when the symptom is harmless.

q_1250.topic: graves disease and thyroidectomy care in adolescents
q_1250.stem: An adolescent scheduled for subtotal thyroidectomy has been taking oral iodine for several weeks preoperatively and admits she stopped because of the taste. Which risk should the nurse address first?
options: Thyroid crisis, which sudden discontinuation can precipitate
Delayed wound healing after the operation
Hypocalcemia before the surgery
Loss of the preparation's antibacterial effect
q_1250.rationale: "Compliance with iodine therapy is essential to avoid the danger of thyroid crisis after sudden discontinuation" (p. 1183). Thyroid storm "may be precipitated by acute infection, surgical emergency, or discontinuation of antithyroid therapy," and presents as "acute onset of severe irritability and restlessness, vomiting, diarrhea, hyperthermia, hypertension, severe tachycardia, and prostration," with "rapid progression to delirium, coma, and death" (p. 1182).
q_1250.trap: (C) names the right complication at the wrong moment, since hypoparathyroidism follows removal of the gland rather than preceding it (p. 1183). The palatability problem has its own answer and it is not stopping the drug: mix the preparation "with a strong-tasting fruit juice, such as grape or punch flavors," and give it "through a straw."

q_1251.topic: graves disease and thyroidectomy care in adolescents
q_1251.stem: A child returns from a subtotal thyroidectomy. How should the nurse position the neck, and why?
options: Slightly flexed, to avoid strain on the sutures
Hyperextended, to keep the airway open
Rotated to one side, to encourage drainage
In whatever position the child prefers, since position does not affect the suture line
q_1251.rationale: "Postoperative care involves positioning with the neck slightly flexed to avoid strain on the sutures and observation for bleeding and complications," and "The children learn to support the neck in this position when they sit up" (p. 1183).
q_1251.trap: (B) is the mirror error and it is drawn from a real instruction elsewhere in the same chapter: in a newborn born with a goiter, "Hyperextension of the neck often facilitates breathing" (p. 1181). Same organ, opposite position, and what changes the answer is whether there is a suture line to protect or an airway to open.

q_1252.topic: graves disease and thyroidectomy care in adolescents
q_1252.stem: On the first day after thyroidectomy, a 15-year-old who was cheerful before surgery is now anxious and tearful and says she feels low. Vital signs are stable and the dressing is dry. What should the nurse suspect?
options: Early hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism
A normal emotional reaction to having had surgery
Damage to the laryngeal nerve
Thyroid storm
q_1252.rationale: The Nursing Alert states that "The earliest indication of hypoparathyroidism may be anxiety and mental depression, followed by paresthesia and evidence of heightened neuromuscular excitability" — Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign, and tetany (p. 1183). "The nurse should observe for signs of hypoparathyroidism, which causes hypocalcemia, in the immediate postoperative period."
q_1252.trap: (B) is the humane reading and the dangerous one, because the mood change here arrives before the classic calcium signs and is easy to accept at face value; (C) would announce itself as "severe stridor or hoarseness" (p. 1183) rather than as a change in affect.

q_1253.topic: parathyroid disorders and calcium balance in children
q_1253.subtopic: reading the calcium and phosphorus pair
q_1253.stem: A child's laboratory results show a decreased serum calcium with an increased serum phosphorus. Which group of findings should the nurse expect?
options: Muscle cramps, tingling of the hands and feet, and a positive Trousseau sign
Muscle weakness, constipation, and confusion
Polyuria, renal colic, and hypertension
Spontaneous fractures and vague bone pain
q_1253.rationale: "The diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism is made on the basis of clinical manifestations associated with decreased serum calcium and increased serum phosphorus" (p. 1184). "Muscle cramps are an early symptom, progressing to numbness, stiffness, and tingling in the hands and feet. A positive Chvostek or Trousseau sign or laryngeal spasms may be present" (p. 1183).
q_1253.trap: (B), (C), and (D) are all genuine findings of the opposite disorder — Box 31.9 lists weakness and fatigability, constipation, confusion and delusions, polyuria and polydipsia, renal colic, hypertension, and spontaneous fractures under hyperparathyroidism (p. 1184). Low calcium excites the neuromuscular system; high calcium sedates it.

q_1254.topic: parathyroid disorders and calcium balance in children
q_1254.subtopic: reading the calcium and phosphorus pair
q_1254.stem: A child with chronic renal failure develops secondary hyperparathyroidism. Which treatment should the nurse expect?
options: Oral calcium salts, high-dose vitamin D, and a low-phosphorus diet
Measures to lower the serum calcium, since hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcemia
Immediate parathyroidectomy
Fluid restriction with a high-phosphorus diet
q_1254.rationale: Because the underlying renal disorder is irreversible, "treatment is aimed at raising serum calcium levels to inhibit the stimulatory effect of low levels on the parathyroid. This includes oral administration of calcium salts, high doses of vitamin D to enhance calcium absorption, a low-phosphorus diet, and administration of a phosphorus-mobilizing aluminum hydroxide to reduce phosphate absorption" (p. 1184).
q_1254.trap: (B) is the reflex inversion and the most harmful option, because the name of the disease points at hypercalcemia while the secondary form is being driven by a low calcium the treatment must raise; (C) belongs to the primary form, where "The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is adenoma of the gland."

q_1255.topic: parathyroid disorders and calcium balance in children
q_1255.subtopic: reading the calcium and phosphorus pair
q_1255.stem: A child is returning from a parathyroidectomy. Which items and precautions should the nurse have in place? Select all that apply.
options: Injectable calcium gluconate at the bedside
Seizure precautions
Observation for stridor, hoarseness, and a feeling of tightness in the throat
A tracheostomy set near the bed
Withholding all calcium-containing foods
q_1255.rationale: "Because hypocalcemia is a potential complication, observing for signs of tetany, instituting seizure precautions, and having calcium gluconate available for emergency use are part of the nursing care" (p. 1185). The hypoparathyroidism section supplies the rest: watch for "signs of laryngospasm such as stridor, hoarseness, and a feeling of tightness in the throat," and "A tracheostomy set and injectable calcium gluconate should be located near the bedside for emergency use" (p. 1184).
q_1255.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it inverts the postoperative problem. Removing overactive parathyroid tissue drops the serum calcium, so what follows surgery is the risk of tetany, not of hypercalcemia — the same reversal that makes hypoparathyroidism a watched complication after thyroidectomy (p. 1183).

q_1256.topic: adrenocortical insufficiency and cushing syndrome in children
q_1256.stem: A toddler with meningococcemia develops hypotension, cold clammy skin, and spreading purpura despite adequate antibiotic therapy, and adrenal crisis is suspected. What is the correct first action?
options: Institute cortisol replacement immediately, since improvement with cortisol confirms the diagnosis
Draw plasma cortisol and ACTH levels and wait for the results before giving any steroid
Give a bolus of dextrose-free normal saline and reassess in one hour
Obtain an adrenal ultrasound to look for hemorrhage into the gland
q_1256.rationale: "There is no rapid, definitive test for confirmation of acute adrenocortical insufficiency," and cortisol and ACTH levels are "too time consuming to be practical for initial diagnosis" (p. 1186). "Because there is no real danger in administering a cortisol preparation for a short period, it is important to institute treatment immediately. Improvement with cortisol therapy confirms the diagnosis."
q_1256.trap: (B) is the option that sounds rigorous and is the one the chapter rules out; the same permission is restated for families as "there is no physical harm in treating for suspected adrenal insufficiency that is not present, but the consequence of not treating acute adrenal insufficiency can be fatal" (p. 1191). (C) gets the fluid right and the composition wrong, because "Normal saline containing 5% glucose is given parenterally to replace lost fluid, electrolytes, and glucose" — cortisol deficiency causes hypoglycemia, so the resuscitation fluid treats two problems at once.

q_1257.topic: adrenocortical insufficiency and cushing syndrome in children
q_1257.stem: A school-age child with Addison disease develops a fever and an ear infection. What should the nurse teach the parents about the hydrocortisone dose?
options: Triple the dose, to meet the body's increased need for glucocorticoids
Keep the dose unchanged, since this is a minor illness
Halve the dose, because fever already raises endogenous cortisol
Hold the dose until the fever resolves
q_1257.rationale: "During stressful situations (e.g., fever, infection, emotional upset, or surgery), the dosage must be tripled to accommodate the body's increased need for glucocorticoids," and "Failure to meet this requirement will precipitate an acute crisis" (p. 1187).
q_1257.trap: (B) is the quietest wrong answer and the commonest one, because nothing in the stem looks like an emergency yet and an ear infection is an ordinary childhood event. The chapter sets the threshold lower than it feels by naming emotional upset in the same list as surgery, and (C) inverts the physiology entirely: the failing adrenal is what cannot raise cortisol under stress.

q_1258.topic: adrenocortical insufficiency and cushing syndrome in children
q_1258.stem: A parent calls to say their child with chronic adrenocortical insufficiency has vomited the morning hydrocortisone dose twice and is now sleepy. What should the nurse advise?
options: Treat this as an emergency, giving the prefilled hydrocortisone injection if trained and seeking care immediately
Wait two hours and retry the oral dose with crackers
Skip today's dose and resume the schedule tomorrow
Give a double oral dose with an antacid to reduce gastric irritation
q_1258.rationale: "Sudden termination of the drug because of inadequate supplies or inability to ingest the oral form because of vomiting places the child in danger of an acute adrenal crisis" (pp. 1187–1188). "Ideally, families will have a prefilled syringe of hydrocortisone and have training to administer this drug during a crisis," and "Any evidence of acute insufficiency is reported to the practitioner immediately" (p. 1188).
q_1258.trap: (D) is built from a true fact used in the wrong situation: cortisone does cause "gastric irritation, which is minimized by ingestion with food or the use of an antacid" (p. 1188), but a route that is already failing cannot be rescued by what is mixed into it. (C) treats a missed dose as recoverable, which is true of almost every other drug a child takes.

q_1259.topic: adrenocortical insufficiency and cushing syndrome in children
q_1259.stem: A child on prolonged high-dose corticosteroid therapy is being assessed. Which set of findings is expected?
options: Hypertension, hypokalemia, alkalosis, and hyperglycemia
Hypotension, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia
Hypertension, hyperkalemia, acidosis, and hypoglycemia
Hypotension, hypokalemia, alkalosis, and hyperglycemia
q_1259.rationale: Table 31.1 pairs each sign with its cause: hypertension and arteriosclerosis arise from "Increased salt and water retention (hypervolemia)," hypokalemia and alkalosis from "Increased excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions," and glycosuria from "Increased gluconeogenesis by liver and decreased rate of glucose utilization by cells" (p. 1188).
q_1259.trap: (B) is the complete mirror image and names the adrenal-insufficiency signature of hyponatremia with hyperkalemia and hypoglycemia (pp. 1172, 1186). Both pictures come from the same axis, so a reader who remembers "a steroid problem" without the direction will take it. (C) and (D) each swap a single value, which is how a half-remembered pair fails in practice.

q_1260.topic: adrenocortical insufficiency and cushing syndrome in children
q_1260.stem: A child whose cushingoid appearance developed during long-term prednisone therapy is having the drug discontinued. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: The dose is tapered gradually rather than stopped
Abrupt withdrawal can precipitate acute adrenal insufficiency
While the steroid continues, it is given early in the morning
The cushingoid appearance is reversible once the steroids are discontinued
The dose should be moved to the evening so it does not interfere with the school day
q_1260.rationale: "This condition is reversible after the steroids are gradually discontinued," and "Abrupt withdrawal will precipitate acute adrenal insufficiency" (p. 1188). Tapering allows "the anterior pituitary an opportunity to secrete increasing amounts of ACTH to stimulate the adrenals to produce cortisol." On timing: "Giving the drug early in the day maintains the normal diurnal pattern of cortisol secretion" (p. 1189).
q_1260.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it comes with the friendliest rationale, which is what makes it selectable: "If given during the evening, it is more likely to produce symptoms because endogenous cortisol levels are already low, and the additional supply exerts more pronounced effects" (p. 1189). Convenience is not the variable being managed; the diurnal rhythm is.

q_1261.stem: A newborn girl has ambiguous genitalia and congenital adrenal hyperplasia is suspected. Which diagnostic studies should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Newborn screening measurement of 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Serum 17-ketosteroid levels
Pelvic ultrasonography
Serum electrolytes
Serum calcium and phosphorus studies
q_1261.rationale: "Newborn screening is currently done in all 50 states by measurement of the cortisol precursor 17-hydroxyprogesterone"; "Definitive diagnosis is confirmed by evidence of increased 17-ketosteroid levels in most types of CAH"; ultrasonography "readily identifies the absence or presence of female reproductive organs or male testes in a newborn or child with ambiguous genitalia"; and "In complete 21-hydroxylase deficiency, blood electrolytes demonstrate loss of sodium and chloride and elevation of potassium" (p. 1190).
q_1261.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it belongs to a different gland: "Blood studies to identify elevated calcium and decreased phosphorus levels are routinely performed" is the hyperparathyroidism workup (p. 1184). Every option here is a real sentence from this chapter, which is what makes the misplaced one hard to see.

q_1262.stem: A 5-year-old boy has pubic hair, an enlarged penis, acne, and a deepening voice, but his testes remain small. Which explanation fits these findings?
options: The androgen is adrenal rather than gonadal in origin, as in congenital adrenal hyperplasia
He has central precocious puberty, with early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
He has premature pubarche, an incomplete variant with no other signs of puberty
He has a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma
q_1262.rationale: "in contrast to precocious puberty, breasts do not develop in girls, and they remain amenorrheic and infertile. In boys, the testes remain small, and spermatogenesis does not occur" (p. 1190), because the androgen driving virilization comes from the adrenal cortex.
q_1262.trap: (B) is the reflex answer and the testes are what defeat it: in central precocious puberty the axis drives the gonads, producing "early maturation and development of the gonads, with secretion of sex hormones, development of secondary sexual characteristics, and sometimes production of mature sperm and ova" (p. 1177). (C) fails on the stem's own breadth, since premature pubarche is "early development of sexual hair" appearing "without other signs of puberty" (p. 1178) and this child has several.

q_1263.stem: A child with episodic hypertension, headache, tachycardia, weight loss, and diaphoresis is being evaluated for pheochromocytoma. Which action must the nurse avoid?
options: Palpating the abdominal mass
Monitoring blood glucose and urine acetone daily
Keeping the environment restful and free of emotional stress
Encouraging the parents to room in and participate in care
q_1263.rationale: The Nursing Alert is explicit: "Do not palpate the mass. Preoperative palpation of the mass releases catecholamines, which can stimulate severe hypertension and tachyarrhythmias" (p. 1191).
q_1263.trap: The prohibited action hides inside a list of correct ones, because (B), (C), and (D) are all stated interventions — "Note daily blood glucose levels, urine acetone, and any signs of hyperglycemia and report immediately," an environment "made conducive to rest and free of emotional stress," and parents "encouraged to room-in with their child and to participate in care" (p. 1191). Abdominal palpation is routine assessment everywhere else, which is why it has to be ruled out by name.

q_1264.topic: type 1 diabetes insulin therapy and glucose monitoring
q_1264.stem: A 9-year-old is admitted after two weeks of weight loss despite constant hunger, bed-wetting after years of dryness, and unrelenting thirst. Which statement about the likely type of diabetes is correct?
options: This abrupt presentation with the three Ps and weight loss describes type 1, in which insulin deficiency is absolute
This describes type 2, in which insulin deficiency is absolute
This describes type 2, because type 2 accounts for 85% to 90% of the diabetic population
Presentation cannot suggest the type; only islet cell antibodies can
q_1264.rationale: Table 31.2 gives type 1 an abrupt onset with "Three Ps common, polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia" in an underweight child, against type 2's gradual onset in an overweight one whose presenting symptoms "May be related to long-term complications" (p. 1192). Type 1 destruction of the insulin-producing cells "usually leads to absolute insulin deficiency," while type 2 combines resistance with "relative (rather than absolute) insulin deficiency."
q_1264.trap: (C) quotes the table accurately and applies it to the wrong population. The 85% to 90% figure describes the entire diabetic population, while the narrative on the same page says that "In children younger than 10 years old, most diabetes cases are type 1." A stem about a child wants type 1; a stem about diabetes generally wants type 2.

q_1265.topic: type 1 diabetes insulin therapy and glucose monitoring
q_1265.stem: A parent is drawing 6 units of regular insulin and 14 units of NPH into one syringe. Which sequence is correct?
options: Air into the NPH vial, air into the regular vial, withdraw the regular insulin, then withdraw the NPH
Air into the regular vial, air into the NPH vial, withdraw the NPH, then withdraw the regular insulin
Withdraw the NPH first, so the cloudy insulin is not contaminated by the clear
Draw the two insulins into separate syringes, since they cannot be mixed
q_1265.rationale: The four steps as printed: "(1) inject the measured amount of air (equivalent to the dosage) into the long-acting insulin; (2) inject the measured amount of air into the rapid-acting (clear) insulin without removing the needle; (3) withdraw the clear insulin; and (4) insert the needle (already containing the clear insulin) into the long-acting (cloudy) insulin and then withdraw the desired amount" (p. 1203). The Nursing Alert gives the reason: withdrawing the clear insulin first "avoids contaminating the short-acting insulin with the longer-acting insulin."
q_1265.trap: (C) is the mirror error and it protects the wrong vial. Note that the air sequence runs opposite to the insulin sequence, so a family who has memorized only "clear before cloudy" can still reverse the air steps, and that is exactly the item (B) is built from.

q_1266.topic: type 1 diabetes insulin therapy and glucose monitoring
q_1266.stem: An adolescent is playing in a tennis tournament this afternoon and asks where to inject her morning insulin. Which guidance is correct?
options: Choose a site other than the exercising extremity, because exercise enhances absorption from exercised muscles
Use the arm she serves with, so the insulin is available faster during play
Use the abdomen, because abdominal absorption is the slowest of the sites
Site does not matter as long as she rotates within one area
q_1266.rationale: "absorption is also altered by vigorous exercise, which enhances absorption from exercised muscles. Therefore it is recommended that a site be chosen other than the exercising extremity (e.g., avoiding legs and arms when playing in a tennis tournament)" (p. 1203).
q_1266.trap: (C) reverses Table 31.6, which gives the abdomen a very fast rate with a very short duration and the buttock a very slow rate with a very long duration (p. 1203); (D) discards the reason rotation exists, which is that "insulin absorption is slowed by fat pads that develop in overused injection areas" (p. 1202).

q_1267.topic: type 1 diabetes insulin therapy and glucose monitoring
q_1267.stem: An 8-year-old's home log shows glucose values almost entirely within range, but the hemoglobin A1C is 10.5%. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: The A1C reflects the average glucose of the previous 2 to 3 months and detects nonadherence, so the log and the A1C disagree
The A1C is unreliable in children under 10 and should be repeated
The log is the accurate record, since the A1C reflects only the past week
An A1C of 10.5% is good control for a school-age child
q_1267.rationale: Glucose attaches irreversibly to hemoglobin for the red cell's roughly 120-day life, so the value "reflects the average blood glucose levels over the previous 2 to 3 months," and the test is used for "detecting incorrect testing, monitoring the effectiveness of changes in treatment, defining patients' goals, and detecting nonadherence" (p. 1196).
q_1267.trap: (D) fails against the chapter's own grading, where "levels of 10% or higher" are poor control and the school-age target is under 8% (p. 1196); (C) shortens the window to the interval a family can actually influence in the days before a clinic visit, which is precisely the wish the test is designed to defeat.

q_1268.topic: type 1 diabetes insulin therapy and glucose monitoring
q_1268.stem: A nurse is reviewing glucose goals for a 4-year-old and for a 16-year-old with type 1 diabetes. Which statement is correct?
options: The preschooler is allowed to run higher, because of high risk and vulnerability to hypoglycemia
The preschooler should be held to the tighter target, to protect the developing brain from hyperglycemia
Both should be held to a premeal range of 90 to 130 mg/dl
Targets are set by duration of diabetes rather than by age
q_1268.rationale: Table 31.3 gives children under 6 a premeal range of 100 to 180 mg/dl, a bedtime range of 110 to 200 mg/dl, and an A1C at or below 8.5%, with the stated rationale "High risk and vulnerability to hypoglycemia." Adolescents over 12 are held to 90 to 130 mg/dl before meals and an A1C under 7.5% (p. 1196).
q_1268.trap: (B) is the intuitive inversion, since tighter control sounds more protective for the youngest patient, and it misreads the rationale column: the danger being guarded against in a small child is the low, not the high. (C) applies the adolescent row to a preschooler, which is the same swap with the numbers attached.

q_1269.topic: hypoglycemia hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis in children
q_1269.stem: A nurse is teaching parents to recognize hypoglycemia in their child. Which findings should they be taught to attribute to a low blood glucose? Select all that apply.
options: An onset over minutes rather than days
Pallor and sweating
Shakiness, hunger, and headache
Tremors, progressing late to dilated pupils and seizure
Deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations
q_1269.rationale: Table 31.5 gives hypoglycemia a rapid onset in minutes, pallor with sweating, a shaky feeling with hunger, headache and dizziness, tremors, and the late signs "Hyperreflexia, dilated pupils, seizure" with shock and coma (p. 1197). The adrenergic wave — "tachycardia, tremors, sweating, irritability, aggression, and hunger" — arrives before the neuroglycopenic one.
q_1269.trap: (E) is the one wrong option and it belongs to the opposite state: hyperglycemia produces "Deep, rapid (Kussmaul)" respirations while hypoglycemia leaves them shallow or normal (p. 1197). Because both states open with a change in behavior, the chapter's own instruction is not to reason it out but to test: "the simplest way to differentiate between the two is to test the blood glucose level."

q_1270.topic: hypoglycemia hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis in children
q_1270.stem: A school-age child's fasting glucose has been high every morning. The evening intermediate-acting insulin has been increased twice with no improvement. A 2 AM glucose is drawn and is 48 mg/dl. What does this indicate, and how is it treated?
options: The Somogyi effect, treated by decreasing the nocturnal insulin dose
Insulin waning, treated by increasing the nocturnal insulin dose further
The dawn phenomenon, for which no change is required
Missed doses, which should be addressed by questioning the family about adherence
q_1270.rationale: "The Somogyi effect may occur at any time but often entails an elevated blood glucose level at bedtime and a drop at 2 AM, with a rebound rise following," produced by "counterregulatory hormones (epinephrine, GH, and corticosteroids), which are stimulated by hypoglycemia." The treatment is "decreasing the nocturnal insulin dose to prevent the 2 AM hypoglycemia" (p. 1198).
q_1270.trap: (B) is the mirror error and it makes the child worse with every increase. Insulin waning is "a progressive rise in blood glucose levels from bedtime to morning" with no low at any point, and it is the one "treated by increasing the nocturnal insulin dose" (p. 1198). All three causes of morning hyperglycemia look identical at breakfast, and only the middle-of-the-night value separates them.

q_1271.topic: hypoglycemia hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis in children
q_1271.stem: A 6-year-old with type 1 diabetes is found unresponsive at school with jerking movements of the arms. The school nurse has a glucometer, orange juice, and a glucagon emergency kit at hand. What should be done?
options: Administer glucagon and position the child on the side
Give 4 ounces of orange juice and recheck the glucose in 15 minutes
Check the blood glucose and wait for the result before taking any action
Give nothing and call for transport, since the cause is not established
q_1271.rationale: The Emergency Treatment box directs that a severe reaction with unresponsiveness, unconsciousness, or seizures be treated by administering "glucagon as prescribed," followed by a planned meal or snack when the child can eat (p. 1204). The Nursing Alert adds that "Vomiting may occur after administration of glucagon; therefore precautions against aspiration must be taken (e.g., placing the child on the side) because the child often becomes unconscious" (p. 1198).
q_1271.trap: (B) is the correct treatment for the mild and moderate levels of that same box, and giving it here risks aspiration in a child who cannot protect an airway; only the severity changes the route, not the substance. (C) delays treatment for a test, against the chapter's stated default: "When in doubt, it is best to assume hypoglycemia and treat" (p. 1198).

q_1272.topic: hypoglycemia hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis in children
q_1272.stem: A father calls about his 5-year-old with type 1 diabetes, who has a cold, is eating very little, and has ketones in the urine. Which response is best?
options: Encourage calorie-free fluids, continue the insulin, and check glucose and ketones every 3 hours
Hold the insulin until the child is eating normally again
Give an extra dose of insulin now and call back tomorrow
Bring the child to the emergency department immediately
q_1272.rationale: "The goals during an illness are to restore euglycemia, treat urinary ketones, and maintain hydration"; "Monitor blood glucose levels and urinary ketones every 3 hours"; and the priority is stated plainly: "Although insulin and diet are important tools in sick-day care, fluids are the most important intervention. Fluids must be encouraged to prevent dehydration and to flush out ketones" (p. 1198).
q_1272.trap: (B) follows a sensible-sounding rule about matching insulin to food intake and is flatly contradicted: "Insulin should never be omitted during an illness, although dosage requirements may increase, decrease, or remain unchanged" (p. 1198). (D) is premature against the chapter's own thresholds for calling, which are vomiting more than once, glucose remaining above 240 mg/dl, or ketones that stay high, none of which the stem establishes.

q_1273.topic: hypoglycemia hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis in children
q_1273.stem: A 10-year-old is admitted in diabetic ketoacidosis. The serum potassium is 4.8 mEq/L, the child has not yet voided, and a 0.9% saline bolus is infusing. What is correct about potassium replacement?
options: Potassium waits until the level is known to be normal or low, voiding is observed, and insulin has been given, and it is never given as a rapid bolus
Potassium should be given now as an IV bolus, since total body potassium is depleted
Potassium is unnecessary, because the serum level is normal
Potassium is added only once the level falls below 3.0 mEq/L
q_1273.rationale: The Nursing Alert states that "Potassium must never be given until the serum potassium level is known to be normal or low and urinary voiding is observed," and "Never give potassium as a rapid IV bolus, or cardiac arrest may result" (p. 1198). Replacement begins once renal function is established, meaning the child is "voiding at least 25 ml/hr," and insulin has been given.
q_1273.trap: (C) is the trap the chapter builds deliberately two pages earlier: "The total body potassium is then decreased even though the serum potassium level may be elevated as a result of the decreased fluid volume in which it circulates" (p. 1193), so a reassuring value does not mean there is no deficit. (B) has the physiology right and the route lethal.

q_1274.topic: hypoglycemia hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis in children
q_1274.stem: A child in diabetic ketoacidosis is estimated to be 10% dehydrated. Which approach to replacing the fluid deficit is current?
options: Replace the deficit evenly over 36 to 48 hours, to reduce the risk of cerebral edema
Replace 50% of the deficit over the first 8 to 12 hours and the remainder over the next 16 to 24 hours
Replace the entire deficit within the first 4 hours, to restore perfusion quickly
Withhold fluids until the insulin infusion has brought the glucose below 300 mg/dl
q_1274.rationale: "Current trends suggest more cautious fluid management to reduce the risk of cerebral edema. Therefore the fluid deficit should be replaced evenly over a period of 36 to 48 hours" (p. 1198). The initial hydrating solution is 0.9% saline, and insulin follows the rehydration bolus "because serum glucose levels fall rapidly after volume expansion" (pp. 1198–1199).
q_1274.trap: (B) is the schedule the chapter prints and then supersedes — "Traditionally, deficits have been replaced at a rate of 50% over the first 8 to 12 hours" (p. 1198) — so it is the option that is correct in an older text and wrong here, which makes it the most defensible-looking distractor. (D) reverses the order of fluids and insulin.

q_1275.topic: wound healing phases and factors that delay it
q_1275.stem: A nurse is teaching a student about wound healing. In what order do the four phases occur?
options: Inflammation, fibroplasia, contraction, maturation
Fibroplasia, inflammation, contraction, maturation
Inflammation, contraction, fibroplasia, maturation
Contraction, inflammation, fibroplasia, maturation
q_1275.rationale: The chapter names them once, in order: "The nonspecific repair mechanism of wound healing with scar formation involves the processes of inflammation, fibroplasia, scar contraction, and scar maturation" (p. 1210). Inflammation is "The initial response at the site of injury"; fibroplasia "continues 5 days to 4 weeks"; contraction "helps bring wound edges closer together"; and with maturation "the scar becomes pale, does not tan when exposed to sunlight, will not sweat or produce hair, and may itch" (p. 1211).
q_1275.trap: (C) is the likeliest error, because contraction sounds like something the clot does early, when in fact it is "Fibroblast movement" during and after fibroplasia that draws the edges together (p. 1211). (B) puts repair before the vascular and cellular response that prepares the tissue for it.

q_1276.topic: wound healing phases and factors that delay it
q_1276.stem: A child's wound is 10 days old, and shiny granulation tissue is visible as the nurse changes the dressing. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: The wound is in the fibroplasia phase, and granulation tissue bleeds profusely if disturbed
The wound is in the inflammatory phase and is at its weakest point
The wound is fully matured and needs no special handling
Granulation tissue indicates infection and should be reported
q_1276.rationale: "Fibroplasia (granulation or proliferation), the second phase of healing, continues 5 days to 4 weeks," and the warning attached to it is specific: "The wound is fragile at this time, and granulation tissue bleeds profusely if disturbed" (p. 1211).
q_1276.trap: (B) names a real fragility statement belonging to a different phase — the wound "is weakest" during "the first 3 to 5 days after injury" (pp. 1210–1211) — and a 10-day-old wound is past it. Two fragility warnings, two phases, and the one that answers a dressing-change question is the second. (D) reads healthy repair as pathology.

q_1277.topic: wound healing phases and factors that delay it
q_1277.subtopic: what helps and what delays healing
q_1277.stem: Which factors delay wound healing? Select all that apply.
options: Cleansing the wound with hydrogen peroxide
A dry wound environment
Vitamin C deficiency
Systemic corticosteroid therapy
A moisture-retentive occlusive dressing
q_1277.rationale: Table 32.1 pairs each factor with its mechanism: hydrogen peroxide is "Toxic to fibroblasts; can cause subcutaneous gas formation (mimics gas-forming infection)"; a dry wound environment "Allows epithelial cells to dry out and die; impairs migration of epithelial cells across wound surface"; vitamin C deficiency "Inhibits formation of collagen fibers and capillary development"; and corticosteroids "Inhibit fibroblast proliferation" and "Depress formation of granulation tissue" (p. 1211).
q_1277.trap: (E) is the one wrong option, and it is the intervention the whole chapter argues for: "An acute full-thickness wound kept in a moist environment usually reepithelializes in 12 to 15 days, whereas the same wound kept open to the air heals in approximately 25 to 30 days" (p. 1211).

q_1278.topic: wound healing phases and factors that delay it
q_1278.subtopic: what helps and what delays healing
q_1278.stem: A parent says she is keeping her child's abrasion uncovered so a good scab can form. What should the nurse explain?
options: A moist, covered wound resurfaces in roughly half the time of one left open to air
A dry scab is the best protection a wound can have against infection
The scab should be lifted daily so the wound underneath can be inspected
Covering the wound traps bacteria and causes infection
q_1278.rationale: "Emphasis has shifted from interventions directed at maintaining a dry environment that promotes eschar formation to those that promote a moist, crust-free environment that enhances the migration of epithelial cells across the wound and facilitates resurfacing," with 12 to 15 days moist against 25 to 30 days open to air. Eschar "interferes with healing by preventing wound contraction" (p. 1211).
q_1278.trap: (C) adds a second error to the first, since scabs "are allowed to slough off without assistance; picking or early removal may cause scarring and secondary infection" (p. 1215). (D) states the belief the moist-wound evidence overturned — moist wound healing in fact "decreases pain and inflammation" and creates the conditions for autolytic debridement (p. 1212).

q_1279.topic: wound healing phases and factors that delay it
q_1279.subtopic: what helps and what delays healing
q_1279.stem: A contaminated laceration is deliberately left open and then sutured several days later, once granulation tissue is present. How should the nurse describe this?
options: Healing by tertiary intention, in which closure is intentionally delayed
Healing by secondary intention, because the wound edges could not be approximated
Wound dehiscence, a complication of the original repair
Healing by primary intention, because the wound was sutured in the end
q_1279.rationale: Tertiary intention "takes place when suturing is delayed after injury or the wound later breaks down and is sutured or resutured when granulation is present," and the chapter gives the reason: "Frequently, suturing of a contaminated wound is deliberately delayed to afford better removal of infection before closing" (p. 1211).
q_1279.trap: (C) reads a planned decision as a failure, which is the error this category invites — delayed closure is a choice. (B) describes wounds "in which the edges cannot be approximated, such as an avulsion or a third-degree burn"; here they could be approximated, and were not, on purpose.

q_1280.topic: wound care dressings and topical therapy in children
q_1280.stem: Parents ask what to use to clean their child's minor wound at home. What should the nurse advise?
options: Normal saline, because nothing should go into a wound that you would not put in the eye
Hydrogen peroxide, to bubble debris out of the wound
Povidone-iodine, to prevent infection
Rubbing alcohol, to disinfect the surface
q_1280.rationale: The Nursing Alert is written as a rule of thumb: "Do not put anything in a wound that you would not put in the eye. The safest solution is normal saline" (p. 1214). Parents are cautioned "to avoid povidone-iodine, alcohol, and hydrogen peroxide because these products are toxic to wounds."
q_1280.trap: (B) and (C) are the two products a family most likely already owns, and both sit in Table 32.1's delay-healing list — hydrogen peroxide is "Toxic to fibroblasts" and povidone-iodine "Toxic to white and red blood cells and fibroblasts" (p. 1211). Povidone-iodine carries an added pediatric caution, since it "may be absorbed through the skin in neonates and young children."

q_1281.topic: wound care dressings and topical therapy in children
q_1281.stem: A parent calls, alarmed that the gel under her child's hydrocolloid dressing looks like yellow pus and smells faintly fruity. The surrounding skin looks normal and the child is afebrile. What should the nurse say?
options: This is normal leakage under this type of dressing
Remove the dressing at once and bring the child in for a wound culture
Start the leftover antibiotic ointment from the child's last infection
Clean the wound with hydrogen peroxide before reapplying the dressing
q_1281.rationale: Nursing Alert: "Advise parents that the yellow gel forming under hydrocolloid dressings may look like pus and has a distinct odor (somewhat fruity) but is normal leakage" (p. 1215). The signs that would matter are different ones — increased erythema beyond the wound margin, edema, purulent exudate, odor, pain extending beyond the margin, and increased temperature (p. 1214) — and none is present.
q_1281.trap: (B) is the reasonable-sounding overreaction this alert exists to prevent; the two alerts sit one page apart and are built to be confused. (D) compounds it, since hydrogen peroxide is among the products parents are told to keep out of a wound (p. 1214).

q_1282.topic: wound care dressings and topical therapy in children
q_1282.stem: Which findings should the nurse teach parents to report as signs of wound infection? Select all that apply.
options: Redness extending beyond the wound margin
Purulent exudate
Pain extending beyond the wound margin
Increased temperature
Shiny pink granulation tissue in the wound bed
q_1282.rationale: The Nursing Alert lists the signs as "Increased erythema, especially beyond wound margin," edema, purulent exudate, odor, "Pain at the site or extending beyond the wound margin," and "Increased temperature" (p. 1214).
q_1282.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it describes healing rather than infection: granulation tissue is the highly vascular, "shiny connective tissue" of the second phase of repair (p. 1211). Note that two of the four correct options are defined by extension past the margin — redness and pain confined to the wound itself are the expected inflammatory response.

q_1283.topic: wound care dressings and topical therapy in children
q_1283.stem: A preschooler is discharged with two topical preparations that must be applied in a specific order. Which nursing action best supports correct use at home?
options: Mark the containers 1 and 2, and give written instructions along with a demonstration
Tell the parents to apply whichever preparation the child tolerates better first
Instruct the parents to apply a thick layer of each so fewer applications are needed
Give verbal instructions only, to avoid overwhelming the family with paperwork
q_1283.rationale: The Nursing Alert is the most concrete teaching instruction in the chapter: "Provide written instructions and demonstrate to parents the correct amount of topical medication to apply (e.g., size of a pea; thin film to cover). If more than one preparation is to be applied, mark the containers 1 and 2 to help parents remember the correct order for application to the skin" (p. 1214).
q_1283.trap: (C) is the assumption most families make unprompted, and it is wrong twice over: "one thick application of topical medication is not equivalent to several thin applications" (p. 1235), and a child's skin is "more absorbent" (p. 1213), so the excess is absorbed rather than wasted. The same alert says that "more medication or increased frequency of applications is not better."

q_1284.topic: bacterial and viral skin infections in children
q_1284.stem: A 3-year-old has moist erosions on the face covered with heavy, honey-colored crusts. Which teaching is most important?
options: Keep the child from touching the lesions, because impetigo spreads easily by self-inoculation
Isolate the child from all contact until every lesion has healed completely
Scrub the crusts off with a stiff cloth at each dressing change
Prepare the family for permanent scarring
q_1284.rationale: "Impetigo contagiosa and MRSA infection can easily spread by self-inoculation; therefore caution the child against touching the involved area" (p. 1216). Table 32.3 describes the lesion exactly — exudate that "dries to form heavy, honey-colored crusts" — and labels it "Autoinoculable and contagious."
q_1284.trap: (D) inverts the prognosis, since impetigo "Tends to heal without scarring unless secondary infection" (p. 1216). (B) overreaches: the child does need separate washcloths and towels and daily clothing changes washed in hot water, but full isolation is reserved for a viral exanthem or an easily spread vector such as lice (p. 1214).

q_1285.topic: bacterial and viral skin infections in children
q_1285.stem: An adolescent has several tender, inflamed lesions involving multiple adjacent hair follicles on the back of the neck and asks whether he should squeeze them. How should the nurse respond?
options: These lesions should never be squeezed, because squeezing risks worsening or spreading the infection
Squeezing will speed resolution as long as the hands are washed first
They can be opened at home with a sterile needle
They will resolve faster under a high-potency topical steroid
q_1285.rationale: The comments column for folliculitis, furuncle, and carbuncle states that "Lesions should never be squeezed" (p. 1216), and the nursing text gives the reasoning: squeezing "will not hasten the resolution of the infection and that there is a risk of making the lesion worse or spreading the infection. No attempt should be made to puncture the surface of the pustule with a needle or sharp instrument."
q_1285.trap: (C) is the half measure a family reaches for once told not to squeeze, and the same sentence refuses it. (D) reaches for the wrong drug class entirely: the management is cleanliness, "Local warm, moist compresses," topical or systemic antibiotics, and incision and drainage of severe lesions — and folliculitis is one of only two conditions in this chapter for which heat is indicated at all (pp. 1213, 1216).

q_1286.topic: bacterial and viral skin infections in children
q_1286.stem: A 9-year-old is diagnosed with herpes zoster following a dermatome on the trunk, and the parents ask what to expect. Which response is accurate?
options: Pain in children is usually minimal, and postherpetic pain does not occur in children
He should be warned to expect months of nerve pain after the rash clears
He poses no risk to others, since shingles is a reactivation rather than a new infection
The rash will cross the midline and become generalized within a few days
q_1286.rationale: The comments column states "Pain in children usually minimal" and "Postherpetic pain does not occur in children" (p. 1218). The virus "has affinity for posterior root ganglia, posterior horn of spinal cord, and skin," and lesions appear as "crops of vesicles usually confined to dermatome following along course of affected nerve."
q_1286.trap: (B) imports an adult complication into a pediatric case, and it is the warning most people have heard attached to shingles. (C) is right about the mechanism and wrong about the consequence: "Chickenpox may follow exposure; isolate affected child from other children in a hospital or school" (p. 1218), so a susceptible child exposed to these lesions can develop varicella.

q_1287.topic: bacterial and viral skin infections in children
q_1287.stem: A parent asks about treating the several warts on her otherwise healthy 7-year-old's fingers. Which response reflects the chapter's guidance?
options: Warts tend to disappear spontaneously, treatment is not uniformly successful, and most destructive techniques leave scars
Warts should be removed promptly, because untreated warts become malignant
Warts should be treated at once with liquid nitrogen to protect the rest of the family
Warts are not contagious, so no precautions are needed at all
q_1287.rationale: Table 32.4 opens the management column for verruca with "Not uniformly successful," and the comments read "Tend to disappear spontaneously," "Course unpredictable," and "Most destructive techniques tend to leave scars" (p. 1218).
q_1287.trap: (D) contradicts that same comments column, which calls warts "Autoinoculable"; the argument for restraint is that the treatment costs more than the disease, not that the disease cannot spread. (C) also misses the caution that "Repeated irritation will cause to enlarge."

q_1288.subtopic: ringworm of the scalp and body
q_1288.stem: A 6-year-old has scaly, circumscribed patches of hair loss on the scalp, and tinea capitis is diagnosed. The parent asks whether an antifungal cream will clear it. What should the nurse explain?
options: Scalp ringworm requires an oral antifungal such as griseofulvin or terbinafine
An over-the-counter antifungal cream applied twice daily is sufficient
A topical antifungal combined with a high-potency steroid is the usual treatment
No treatment is needed, since the hair loss resolves on its own
q_1288.rationale: "Oral antifungal agents are the only effective means for treating systemic fungal infections and tinea capitus" (p. 1214), and Table 32.5 gives management as "Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine," with oral ketoconazole for difficult cases and selenium sulfide shampoo twice weekly to decrease fungal shedding (p. 1218).
q_1288.trap: (C) sounds like it addresses both the fungus and the inflammation, and the chapter forbids it twice: combining a topical antifungal with a high-potency steroid "may lead to further infection" (p. 1218), and over-the-counter hydrocortisone "may further aggravate inflammation caused by fungus or bacteria" (p. 1213). A steroid on a fungal rash is wrong on two separate pages.

q_1289.subtopic: ringworm of the scalp and body
q_1289.stem: A child is starting griseofulvin for tinea capitis. Which instruction is most important?
options: Give the drug with high-fat foods, and continue the full course even after the scaling clears
Give the drug on an empty stomach for the best absorption
Stop the drug once the lesions are no longer visible
Expect the course to last about seven days
q_1289.rationale: Families are taught to give "the medication with high-fat foods for best absorption," and the adherence risk is named directly: "because subjective symptoms subside, children or parents may be tempted to decrease or discontinue the drug," even though "the therapy frequently continues for weeks or months" (p. 1218).
q_1289.trap: (B) applies the ordinary empty-stomach rule for oral antibiotics to a drug whose absorption depends on fat; (C) and (D) both underestimate a course measured in weeks to months, and (C) is the specific behavior the chapter predicts. For long courses, "periodic testing is required to monitor leukopenia and assess liver and renal function."

q_1290.subtopic: ringworm of the scalp and body
q_1290.stem: A child has a round, erythematous, scaling patch on the forearm that is spreading outward with a clearing center. Which combination of actions is correct?
options: Scrape the advancing periphery for microscopic examination, and have the household pets examined
Scrape the clear center, where the organism is most concentrated
Keep the child home from school until the lesion has completely cleared
Apply the topical antifungal only to the visible ring, stopping when it disappears
q_1290.rationale: "Diagnosis is made from microscopic examination of scrapings taken from the advancing periphery of the lesion, which almost always produces a scale" (p. 1218), because the lesion "spreads peripherally and clears centrally." Tinea corporis is "Usually of animal origin from infected pets," so "all household pets should be examined for the disorder."
q_1290.trap: (C) is stricter than the source, which says "The child may return to school after the therapy is initiated" (p. 1218). (D) stops short in both space and time: the topical is "applied 2.5 cm (1 inch) beyond periphery of lesion," and "application continued 1-2 weeks after no sign of lesion."

q_1291.topic: contact dermatitis and poison ivy in children
q_1291.stem: A school-age child has a widespread, symmetric, itchy rash over most of the trunk and limbs, with no sharply demarcated borders. Which cause is most likely?
options: A generalized irritant such as bubble bath, laundry soap, body soap, or lotion
The nickel snap on the child's jeans
Mascara
Ultraviolet injury
q_1291.rationale: The chapter turns distribution into a diagnostic method: a generalized eruption is "more likely to be caused by bubble bath, laundry soap, body soap, or lotion," a rash around the eyes suggests mascara, a rash on skin covered by clothing but not by undergarments suggests wool, and a rash on uncovered skin suggests ultraviolet injury (p. 1222).
q_1291.trap: (B) names the offender families never guess, and it is a real one — "nickel found in jewelry and the snaps on sleepers and denim" (p. 1222) — but a point contact produces a localized reaction with "a sharp demarcation between inflamed and normal skin" (p. 1219). This rash has no such border, so the exposure was not a point contact.

q_1292.topic: contact dermatitis and poison ivy in children
q_1292.stem: What is the major goal of treatment in contact dermatitis?
options: Preventing further exposure of the skin to the offending substance
Applying a high-potency topical steroid until the rash clears
Starting a systemic antihistamine and an oral antibiotic
Covering the area so the rash cannot spread to other body sites
q_1292.rationale: "The major goal in treatment is to prevent further exposure of the skin to the offending substance," and "Provided there is no further irritation, the skin's normal recuperative powers will often produce healing without treatment" (pp. 1219, 1222).
q_1292.trap: (B) treats the visible problem while leaving the cause in place, which is why the rash returns, and it runs against the chapter's stated stance that practitioners "aim to avoid overtreatment, particularly in young children" (p. 1212). (D) assumes a dermatitis spreads from the rash itself, which is the misconception the poison ivy section exists to refute.

q_1293.topic: contact dermatitis and poison ivy in children
q_1293.stem: A child runs through poison ivy while camping. What should the nurse instruct the family to do first?
options: Flush the skin with cold running water, preferably within 15 minutes, without scrubbing
Wash the area vigorously with a harsh soap and a washcloth
Apply calamine lotion and wait to see whether a rash develops
Cover the area with an occlusive dressing so the oil cannot spread
q_1293.rationale: "When it is known that the child has made contact with the plant, the area is immediately flushed (preferably within 15 minutes) with cold running water to neutralize the urushiol not yet bonded to the skin. Once the oil has been removed from the skin, the allergen has been neutralized" (p. 1223). Clothing that touched the plant is removed with care and laundered in hot water and detergent.
q_1293.trap: (B) is the instinctive response, and the chapter names it a contraindication with a mechanism attached: harsh soap and scrubbing "removes protective skin oils and dilutes the urushiol, allowing it to spread" (p. 1223). The window matters because "The earlier the skin is cleansed, the greater the chance of removing the urushiol before it attaches to the skin."

q_1294.topic: contact dermatitis and poison ivy in children
q_1294.stem: A child with weeping poison ivy lesions has been kept home so classmates will not catch it, and the parents are covering the blisters to stop the rash from spreading. How should the nurse respond?
options: The rash cannot be spread to another child, and it does not spread from blister serum or from scratching
The rash is contagious until every lesion has crusted over
Scratching spreads the rash to new sites, so the blisters must stay covered
The blister fluid contains urushiol and will spread the rash on the child's own skin
q_1294.rationale: "The rash that results from poison ivy cannot be spread to another child; only direct contact with the oil can cause the response," and "Although the lesions do not spread by contact with the blister serum or from scratching, they can become secondarily infected" (p. 1223). The lesions "dry and heal spontaneously, and itching stops by 10 to 14 days."
q_1294.trap: (C) and (D) are the two halves of the same near-universal belief, and the chapter denies both in one sentence while keeping the one real risk it leaves standing — scratching does not spread the rash, but it can infect it.

q_1295.topic: arthropod bites stings and tickborne disease in children
q_1295.stem: A child is stung by a bee and the stinger is visible in the skin. What is the first action?
options: Remove the stinger as quickly as possible
Apply a cool compress and observe for 10 minutes before touching the site
Cover the stinger with a baking soda paste to neutralize the venom
Give an oral antihistamine and then remove the stinger
q_1295.rationale: "As long as the stinger remains in the skin, the muscles push the stinger deeper, and the venom is pumped into the wound. The best approach is to remove the stinger as quickly as possible and to get away from the vicinity of other insects to prevent further injury" (p. 1225). The treatment column leads with "Carefully scrape off stinger or pull out stinger as quickly as possible" (p. 1224).
q_1295.trap: (C) and (D) are both genuine later steps — cleansing, cool compresses, a household paste of lemon juice, aspirin, or baking soda, then antihistamines — and each delays the one action that stops venom from continuing to be injected. The table does not prefer scraping to pulling; it prefers speed.

q_1296.topic: arthropod bites stings and tickborne disease in children
q_1296.stem: A camp nurse is teaching counselors about arachnids. Which ones require immediate medical attention? Select all that apply.
options: Scorpion
Black widow spider
Brown recluse spider
Tarantula
Chigger
q_1296.rationale: "Only scorpions and two spiders, the brown recluse and the black widow, inject venom deadly enough to require immediate attention. Children bitten by these arachnids must receive medical attention as soon as possible" (p. 1224).
q_1296.trap: (D) is the wrong option most often selected, because a tarantula is the most alarming of the five to look at, and the chapter names it specifically in order to exclude it: "Most arthropods in the United States, including tarantulas, are relatively harmless" (p. 1224). Chiggers cause "Erythematous papules" and intense itching and nothing worse.

q_1297.topic: arthropod bites stings and tickborne disease in children
q_1297.stem: A child is bitten by a spider bearing a fiddle-shaped mark on its head. Three days later the site shows a purple, star-shaped area. What should the nurse expect?
options: A necrotic ulcer over the next one to two weeks, managed with antibiotics and corticosteroids
Antivenin, which is the specific treatment for this spider's necrotoxin
Rapid dizziness, weakness, and abdominal pain from a neurotoxin
Complete resolution within 48 hours using cool compresses alone
q_1297.rationale: The brown recluse is "recognized by fiddle-shaped mark on head," and its venom "contains powerful necrotoxin." The course is "mild to severe pain in 2-8 hours; purple, star-shaped area in 3-4 days; necrotic ulceration in 7-14 days," treated with cool compresses, "antibiotics, corticosteroids," pain relief, and sometimes a skin graft; "Wounds heal with scar formation" (p. 1225).
q_1297.trap: (B) and (C) both belong to the black widow, which carries "a red or orange hourglass-shaped marking on underside," whose venom "has neurotoxic action," and for whom antivenin is the treatment (p. 1225). Neuro belongs to one spider and necrosis to the other, and the antivenin follows the neurotoxin.

q_1298.topic: arthropod bites stings and tickborne disease in children
q_1298.stem: A parent finds an attached tick on a child's scalp. What should the nurse instruct?
options: Grasp the tick with tweezers as close to the skin as possible and pull straight up with steady, even pressure
Cover the tick with petroleum jelly so that it backs out on its own
Twist the tick counterclockwise until it releases
Take the child to the emergency department, since only a clinician should remove a tick
q_1298.rationale: "Grasp tick with tweezers (forceps) as close as possible to point of attachment"; "Pull straight up with steady, even pressure"; and if bare hands must be used, "use a tissue to touch tick during removal; wash hands thoroughly with soap and water" (p. 1225). Afterward, "wash the bite area with an iodine scrub, rubbing alcohol, or plain soap and water" (p. 1229).
q_1298.trap: (B) is the best-known home method, and the chapter rejects it by name: "The application of nail polish or petroleum jelly is not recommended and does not appear to have an effect on tick withdrawal as has been hypothesized" (p. 1229). Speed is what matters, because a tick "Must attach and feed for 1-2 hours to transmit disease" (p. 1225).

q_1299.topic: arthropod bites stings and tickborne disease in children
q_1299.stem: A 9-year-old who camped two weeks ago has an expanding bull's-eye lesion on the thigh with fever and headache. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Oral doxycycline
Oral amoxicillin, since this is a school-age child
A Lyme serologic titer drawn at the time of the tick bite
Intravenous ceftriaxone for early localized disease
q_1299.rationale: "Children older than 8 years of age are treated with oral doxycycline," while "amoxicillin is recommended for children younger than 8 years of age" (p. 1229). The lesion described is erythema migrans, which develops "in 3 to 30 days" at the bite site as "a large circumferential ring with a raised, edematous doughnut-like border resulting in a bull's-eye appearance" (p. 1228).
