q_1299.trap: (B) is the right answer for a 7-year-old and wrong here by a single year, which is the entire point of the age rule. (D) borrows a late-disease drug, since "Neurologic, cardiac, and arthritic manifestations are managed with oral or intravenous antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, or penicillin G" (p. 1229). (C) fails on timing: serologic testing at the time of a recognized bite "is not recommended because antibodies are not detectable in most persons."

q_1300.topic: scabies and pediculosis capitis in children
q_1300.stem: A 4-year-old is diagnosed with scabies and her 6-year-old brother with head lice. Which statement about their treatments is correct?
options: Scabies is treated with permethrin 5% cream and head lice with permethrin 1% cream rinse
Both are treated with permethrin 1% cream rinse
Scabies is treated with permethrin 1% cream rinse and head lice with permethrin 5% cream
Both are treated with lindane, the drug of choice in young children
q_1300.rationale: For scabies, "The drug of choice in children and infants older than 2 months of age is permethrin 5% cream (Elimite)" (p. 1226). For head lice, "The drug of choice for infants and children is permethrin 1% cream rinse (Nix), which kills adult lice and nits" (p. 1227).
q_1300.trap: (C) is the swap this material sets up by using one drug at two strengths in two vehicles for two infestations, and it is the cleanest error available here. (D) names a drug the chapter refuses outright: "Lindane can be neurotoxic and is contraindicated by the American Academy of Pediatrics" (p. 1226).

q_1301.topic: scabies and pediculosis capitis in children
q_1301.stem: The parents of a child with scabies ask why the entire household needs treatment when no one else has a rash. What is the best explanation?
options: It takes 30 to 60 days for symptoms to appear, so close contacts may already be infested without knowing it
The mite survives in bedding for months, so everyone must be treated to clear the house
The medication prevents infestation in people who have not been exposed
Only those with visible burrows need treatment; the others can wait and see
q_1301.rationale: "Because of the length of time between infestation and physical symptoms (30 to 60 days), all persons who were in close contact with the affected child need treatment," which "may include boyfriends or girlfriends, babysitters, grandparents, and immediate family members." "The objective is to treat as thoroughly as possible the first time" (p. 1226).
q_1301.trap: (D) is the reasonable-sounding half measure that guarantees reinfestation, since the people who look clear today are the ones who will break out next month. (B) misplaces the mite, which burrows "into the stratum corneum of the epidermis (never into living tissue)" on a host to lay its eggs.

q_1302.topic: scabies and pediculosis capitis in children
q_1302.stem: A school nurse examining a child's scalp finds tiny whitish oval specks near the occiput that do not brush off, sitting about 4 mm from the scalp. How should this be interpreted?
options: Viable nits, since they adhere to the hair shaft and sit within 6 mm of the scalp
Dandruff, which is white and sits close to the scalp
Empty nit cases, since hatched nits remain near the scalp
Hair spray residue, which cannot be told from nits without a microscope
q_1302.rationale: "The nits, or eggs, appear as tiny whitish oval specks adhering to the hair shaft about 6 mm (0.25 inch) from the scalp," and "The adherent nature of the nits distinguishes them from dandruff, which falls off readily." "Empty nit cases, indicating hatched lice, are translucent rather than white and are located more than 6 mm from the scalp" (p. 1226). The female "lays her eggs at night at the junction of a hair shaft and close to the skin because the eggs need a warm environment."
q_1302.trap: (C) inverts both discriminators at once, since the hatched cases are the ones farther out and the translucent ones. (B) fails on the single bedside test that settles it, which is whether the specks come away.

q_1303.topic: scabies and pediculosis capitis in children
q_1303.stem: A parent finishes the permethrin 1% treatment for head lice and asks what comes next. Which instruction is correct?
options: Repeat the treatment in 7 to 10 days, because nits shed into the environment can hatch in that time
No repeat is needed, since permethrin kills adult lice and nits
Repeat the treatment daily for a week
Spray the house with insecticide to prevent reinfestation
q_1303.rationale: "Most experts advise a second treatment at 7 to 10 days to ensure a cure" (p. 1227), and the interval matches the life cycle: "nits are shed into the environment and are capable of hatching in 7 to 10 days; retreatment is required." Daily combing with a metal nit comb is a control measure after treatment.
q_1303.trap: (B) quotes the drug's own description accurately — permethrin "kills adult lice and nits" (p. 1227) — and still reaches the wrong conclusion, because "none of the pediculicides is 100% effective in killing all the eggs." (D) is refused by name: "Spraying with insecticide is not recommended because of the danger to children and animals."

q_1304.topic: scabies and pediculosis capitis in children
q_1304.stem: Which statements should the nurse include when teaching a family about head lice? Select all that apply.
options: Anyone can get head lice, regardless of age, socioeconomic level, or cleanliness
Lice do not jump or fly; they are transmitted on personal items
Lice are not carried or transmitted by pets
Wash bedding and clothing in water over 130 degrees Fahrenheit and dry on hot for at least 20 minutes
Coating the hair with mayonnaise or petroleum jelly will smother the lice
q_1304.rationale: "Nurses should emphasize that anyone can get pediculosis; it has no respect for age, gender, socioeconomic level, or cleanliness"; "Lice do not jump or fly, but they can be transmitted from one person to another on personal items"; and "Lice are not carried or transmitted by pets" (pp. 1226, 1227). The prevention box directs families to "Machine wash all washable clothing, towels, and bed linens in water greater than 130" degrees Fahrenheit "and dry them in a hot dryer for at least 20 minutes."
q_1304.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it names the remedies families have most often already tried: of petroleum jelly, oils, vinegar, butter, alcohol, and mayonnaise, "there is no evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of these remedies" (p. 1227).

q_1305.stem: Which interventions can the nurse safely recommend for a 10-month-old with diaper dermatitis? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a zinc oxide or petrolatum ointment to protect the skin
Change the diaper as soon as it becomes wet
Expose the skin to air to dry
Use a hair dryer on a low setting to dry the area
Switch the family to cloth diapers only
q_1305.rationale: The Family-Centered Care box directs the family to "Apply ointment, such as zinc oxide or petrolatum, to protect skin, especially if skin is very red or has moist, open areas," and to "Expose healthy or only slightly irritated skin to air, not heat, to dry completely" (p. 1233). "Changing the diaper as soon as it becomes wet eliminates a large part of the problem," because "The most significant factor amenable to intervention is the moist environment created in the diaper area" (p. 1232).
q_1305.trap: (D) is unsafe and is named: "The use of a hair dryer or heat lamp is not recommended because these devices can cause burns" (p. 1232). (E) moves the family the wrong way, since superabsorbent disposable diapers reduce diaper dermatitis by binding water, buffering pH, and keeping urine and feces from mixing (pp. 1232–1233), and inadequately rinsed cloth diapers are themselves listed as a source of soap and detergent irritation.

q_1306.stem: A 9-month-old has a beefy red rash involving the inguinal folds with scattered satellite lesions, unchanged after two weeks of barrier ointment. What does this suggest?
options: Candida albicans infection, which involves the folds and produces satellite lesions
Irritant diaper dermatitis, which is worst inside the skin folds
An allergic reaction to the barrier ointment
Contact dermatitis from the diaper wipes
q_1306.rationale: "Candida albicans infection produces perianal inflammation and a maculopapular rash with satellite lesions that may cross the inguinal fold," whereas an eruption on "the convex surfaces of buttocks, inner thighs, mons pubis, and scrotum" but "sparing the folds" is chemical irritation from urine and feces (p. 1232). Yeast "is seen in up to 90% of infants with chronic diaper dermatitis and should be considered in diaper rashes that are recalcitrant to treatment."
q_1306.trap: (B) attaches the right disease name to the wrong distribution, and distribution is the whole discriminator here: folds spared means irritant, folds involved with satellites means yeast. The two-week failure to respond is a second clue pointing the same way.

q_1307.stem: A parent asks whether cornstarch can be used in the diaper area, having heard that it feeds yeast. Which response is accurate?
options: Cornstarch does not promote fungal growth, and it is preferred over talc because of inhalation safety
Cornstarch does promote candidal growth and should be avoided
Talcum powder is the safer choice for infants
Powders of any kind are equally safe and may be shaken directly over the infant
q_1307.rationale: "A common misconception about using cornstarch on skin is that it promotes the growth of C. albicans. Neither cornstarch nor talcum powder promotes the growth of fungi under conditions normally found in the diaper area. On the basis of safety in terms of inhalation injury, cornstarch is the preferred product. Talcum powder should not be used" (p. 1233).
q_1307.trap: (D) drops the technique that is the entire inhalation precaution: "first shake it into your hand and then apply it to the diaper area" (p. 1233), never over the baby, and keep the container closed and out of reach. (C) reverses the safety comparison the chapter draws.

q_1308.topic: atopic dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis in children
q_1308.stem: A parent of a 4-month-old with atopic dermatitis says she has stopped bathing the baby because baths seem to dry the skin further. What should the nurse teach?
options: Bathing is appropriate, but an emollient must go on within 3 minutes afterward, while the skin is still damp
Baths should be limited to once a week for a child with eczema
Bubble bath should be added to soften the water
The skin should be allowed to air dry completely before any product is applied
q_1308.rationale: "A tepid bath with a mild soap (Dove or Neutrogena), no soap, or an emulsifying oil followed immediately by application of an emollient (within 3 minutes) assists in trapping moisture and preventing its loss," and the caution is exact: "excessive bathing without emollient application only dries out the skin" (p. 1234). The Nursing Alert repeats it: the emollient goes on "immediately after bathing (while the skin is still slightly moist) to prevent drying" (p. 1235).
q_1308.trap: (D) is the intuitive error and it is precisely what makes a bath harmful in this disease, because the water evaporates before anything traps it. (C) names an irritant the chapter tells families to avoid in three separate places (pp. 1212, 1222, 1234).

q_1309.topic: atopic dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis in children
q_1309.stem: A nurse compares a 5-month-old and a 5-year-old, both with atopic dermatitis. Which distribution should the nurse expect?
options: Face, scalp, neck, and extensor surfaces in the infant; flexural areas, wrists, and ankles in the older child
Flexural areas in the infant; extensor surfaces in the older child
The same distribution in both, since age does not change the pattern
Palms and soles in both, which is the hallmark of atopic dermatitis
q_1309.rationale: Box 32.3 gives the infantile form as "Generalized, especially face, scalp, neck, and extensor surfaces of extremities" and the childhood form as "Flexural areas (antecubital and popliteal fossae, neck), wrists, ankles, and feet" (p. 1233).
q_1309.trap: (B) is the mirror error and the cleanest level swap in this section, since the two surfaces are exact opposites and the only variable separating them is the child's age. The appearance shifts with the distribution: erythema, vesicles, weeping, and crusting in infancy, and lichenification with dry, hyperpigmented patches later.

q_1310.topic: atopic dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis in children
q_1310.stem: Which measures are appropriate in managing a school-age child's atopic dermatitis? Select all that apply.
options: A mildly sedating antihistamine at night, because pruritus increases at night
Keeping fingernails cut short, clean, and filed frequently
Laundering clothes in a mild detergent and running a second wash cycle with no detergent
Reporting honey-colored crusts or pustules with surrounding erythema
Applying one thick layer of the topical medication rather than several thin ones
q_1310.rationale: "Because pruritus increases at night, a mildly sedating antihistamine may be needed," while nonsedating agents "may be preferred for daytime pruritus relief" (p. 1234). "Fingernails and toenails are cut short, kept clean, and filed frequently to prevent sharp edges" (p. 1234). "Putting the clothes through a second complete wash cycle without using detergent reduces the amount of residue remaining in the fabric" (p. 1235). And lesions are examined for infection, "usually honey-colored crusts or pustules with surrounding erythema. Any signs of infection are reported to the practitioner" (p. 1235).
q_1310.trap: (E) is the wrong option and the source names it as the misconception to correct: "one thick application of topical medication is not equivalent to several thin applications and that excessive use of an agent (particularly steroids) can be hazardous" (p. 1235).

q_1311.topic: atopic dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis in children
q_1311.stem: A mother brings her 6-week-old with thick, adherent, yellowish, oily scales on the scalp. She rinses the hair but avoids shampooing because she is afraid of hurting the soft spot. Which response is best?
options: Explain that the fontanel does not puncture or tear with mild pressure, and demonstrate shampooing
Reassure her that avoiding the scalp is appropriate until the fontanel closes
Tell her a medicated antiseborrheic shampoo is required
Advise her to comb the dry crusts off before shampooing
q_1311.rationale: "Cradle cap may be prevented with adequate scalp hygiene. Frequently, parents omit shampooing the infant's hair for fear of damaging the soft spots, or fontanels. The nurse should discuss how to shampoo the infant's hair and emphasize that the fontanel is similar to skin anywhere else on the body, it does not puncture or tear with mild pressure," and education "may need to include a demonstration" (p. 1235).
q_1311.trap: (C) overtreats a condition the chapter handles simply: "Shampooing should be done daily with a mild soap or commercial baby shampoo; medicated shampoos are not necessary" (p. 1235). (D) reverses the technique, since the shampoo is "allowed to remain on the scalp until the crusts soften" and only then does a fine-tooth comb or soft facial brush lift them.

q_1312.stem: A 15-year-old with acne says he has started scrubbing his face four times a day with an abrasive antibacterial soap, having read that acne is caused by dirt. How should the nurse respond?
options: Surface dirt does not cause acne, and vigorous scrubbing with antibacterial soap damages the skin
Scrubbing is correct, but twice a day is enough
Antibacterial soap is the most effective first-line acne treatment
He should add an abrasive cleanser for better exfoliation
q_1312.rationale: "Dirt or oil on the surface of the skin does not cause acne" (p. 1236). "Gentle cleansing with a mild cleanser once or twice daily is usually sufficient. Antibacterial soaps are ineffective and may be drying when used in combination with topical acne medications," and adolescents need education about what damages the skin, "such as too vigorous scrubbing" (pp. 1236–1237).
q_1312.trap: (B) corrects the frequency while endorsing the method, leaving the damaging part in place — the problem is the scrubbing and the product, not the count. (C) elevates an ineffective product over benzoyl peroxide, which "is effective against both inflammatory and noninflammatory acne and is an effective first-line agent."

q_1313.stem: An adolescent starting tretinoin asks when to apply it. Which instruction is correct?
options: Apply it at night, and use a sunscreen of at least SPF 15 during the day
Apply it in the morning, when oil production is greatest
Apply it immediately after washing the face, to aid absorption
Apply it at night, and skip sunscreen, which clogs the pores
q_1313.rationale: "The avoidance of the sun and the daily use of sunscreen must be emphasized because sun exposure can result in severe sunburn. Adolescents should be advised to apply the medication at night and to use a sunscreen with a sun protection factor (SPF) of at least 15 in the daytime" (p. 1236).
q_1313.trap: (C) takes a real detail from the same paragraph and reverses it: "The medication should not be applied for at least 20 to 30 minutes after washing to decrease the burning sensation" (p. 1236). (D) keeps the correct timing and drops the half that prevents the injury. Whatever the regimen, "improvement may not be apparent for at least 6 weeks."

q_1314.stem: A 17-year-old girl is starting isotretinoin for severe cystic acne. Which statement by the adolescent indicates that teaching has been effective?
options: I have to use effective contraception during treatment and for a month after I finish
I can stop my contraception as soon as I take the last dose
The main thing to watch for is bleaching of my clothes
My skin should clear within about a week
q_1314.rationale: "The most significant side effects of this drug are the teratogenic effects. Isotretinoin is absolutely contraindicated in pregnant women," and "Sexually active young women must use an effective contraceptive method during treatment and for 1 month after treatment" (p. 1237). Treatment runs 20 weeks, and the adolescent is also monitored "for depression, depressive symptoms, and suicidal ideation" and for elevated cholesterol and triglyceride levels.
q_1314.trap: (B) drops the trailing month, which is the detail most often lost because it sounds administrative rather than teratogenic. (C) belongs to a different drug — benzoyl peroxide bleaches "sheets, bedclothes, and towels," and "The adolescent can be reassured that skin bleaching will not occur" (p. 1236) — and (D) contradicts the timeline shared by every acne drug in the chapter.

q_1315.subtopic: airway and resuscitation at the scene
q_1315.stem: A school nurse finds a 10-year-old unresponsive at the base of a climbing structure after a fall. How should the airway be opened?
options: With a modified jaw thrust, without head tilt or chin lift
With a head tilt–chin lift, the standard maneuver for any child
With a head tilt–chin lift, followed by a jaw thrust if it fails
Not at all until emergency medical services arrive
q_1315.rationale: "When spinal trauma is a possibility, open the airway using the modified jaw thrust maneuver, which is accomplished by grasping the angles of the victim's lower jaw and lifting with both hands, one on each side, and displacing the mandible upward and outward (without head tilt or chin lift)" (p. 1241). The box restates it: in a child "with head, trunk, or multisystem trauma, modified jaw thrust is preferred method."
q_1315.trap: (B) is the correct maneuver only once trauma has been excluded, and it cannot be excluded here: "Spinal cord injury is always suspected in a patient with head, trunk, or multisystem trauma," and only in a fully equipped trauma center "can spinal cord injury be ruled out or diagnosed. Therefore the patient is treated as if injury were present" (p. 1241). (D) leaves the airway closed while waiting.

q_1316.subtopic: airway and resuscitation at the scene
q_1316.stem: A bystander finds an unresponsive, pulseless 6-year-old after an unwitnessed collapse. What is the correct sequence?
options: Perform 2 minutes of CPR, then activate emergency medical services and call for a defibrillator
Activate emergency medical services first, then begin CPR
Activate emergency medical services and wait for the defibrillator before starting compressions
Give two rescue breaths, then activate emergency medical services
q_1316.rationale: "Activate the EMS system if child appears to be pubertal or older or if witnessed sudden collapse. If child has not reached puberty, perform 2 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) (as per assessment); then activate EMS and call for an automatic external defibrillator (AED)" (p. 1241). Compressions run "at a rate of at least 100 compressions per minute," and interruptions are kept under 10 seconds.
q_1316.trap: (B) is the correct sequence for a pubertal child or a witnessed sudden collapse, and this child is neither, which is the entire point of the age split. (C) delays the only intervention maintaining perfusion.

q_1317.stem: A teenager has a deep thigh laceration with arterial bleeding and a piece of metal protruding from the wound. Direct pressure, elevation, and arterial pressure-point compression have failed, and a tourniquet is applied. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The tourniquet is a last resort, used only after the other measures fail
Once applied, the tourniquet is not loosened
The protruding object is left in place
Keeping the tourniquet in place gives a better chance of survival, even if it costs the limb
The tourniquet should be briefly released every 15 minutes to perfuse the limb
q_1317.rationale: The hemorrhage sequence is direct pressure, elevation, arterial pressure point, then "Apply tourniquet only as a last resort. Once a tourniquet is applied, it should not be loosened" (p. 1241), and "Do not remove objects protruding from child's body." The reasoning is systemic rather than local: "If the tourniquet is loosened or removed, the toxins can be released into the circulation in high concentrations and may induce a systemic, deadly tourniquet shock. With the tourniquet in place, the patient has a better chance of survival, even though it may mean the loss of a limb" (p. 1242).
q_1317.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it is the intuitive one, since periodic release sounds like limb-sparing care. It is the exact action the chapter forbids, and the harm it names is to the whole patient, not to the leg.

q_1318.topic: physiologic and psychologic effects of immobilization
q_1318.subtopic: what immobility does to each system
q_1318.stem: A 9-year-old is immobilized for several weeks after significant trauma. Which effects should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Orthostatic intolerance
Deep vein thrombosis
Pneumonia from pooled secretions
Renal calculi
Diarrhea
Constipation and fecal impaction
q_1318.rationale: "Immobility has three major cardiovascular consequences: orthostatic intolerance, increased workload of the heart, and thrombus formation" (p. 1243). Respirations become "slower and more shallow" and "A weak and ineffectual cough reflex contributes to stasis of secretions," with atelectasis and pneumonia as the complications (p. 1244). "The urinary system is designed to function in an upright posture," and settled particulate matter "may serve as nuclei for calculi formation or as foci for infection." "Slowing of stool in the colon causes the feces to become hard (fecal impaction)."
q_1318.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it inverts the gastrointestinal effect, since immobility slows the gut rather than speeding it. This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 1, where diarrhea and a sense of euphoria are the two excluded options — the documented psychologic response is anxiety, depression, and regression, not elation.

q_1319.topic: physiologic and psychologic effects of immobilization
q_1319.subtopic: what immobility does to each system
q_1319.stem: A child has been on bed rest for 5 days after a spinal injury, with no range-of-motion exercises. Which statement is accurate?
options: Inactive muscle loses strength at about 3% per day, and contractures develop unless range of motion is reestablished within 3 to 7 days
Muscle strength is preserved for the first 2 weeks of bed rest
Contractures take at least 6 weeks of immobility to develop
Contractures affect the extensor muscles first, because they are the stronger group
q_1319.rationale: "Inactive muscle loses strength at the rate of 3% per day," and "unless range of motion is reestablished within 3 to 7 days, contractures will develop." The frequent sites are "hip flexion, knee flexion, plantar flexion of the feet, and shoulder stiffness" (p. 1243).
q_1319.trap: (D) reverses the muscle balance that produces the deformity, since "body flexor muscles are stronger than extensor muscles" (p. 1243) — which is why every site the chapter lists is a flexion contracture. (B) and (C) both grant the child time the physiology does not give.

q_1320.topic: physiologic and psychologic effects of immobilization
q_1320.subtopic: what immobility does to each system
q_1320.stem: A nurse turns an immobilized child and finds a red area over the sacrum that is still red 40 minutes later. What does this indicate?
options: A pressure area is developing, and treatment should begin now
Normal reactive hyperemia, which requires no action
An early sign of deep vein thrombosis
A contact reaction to the bed linen, requiring only a linen change
q_1320.rationale: Normal reactive hyperemia "should disappear within 5 to 15 minutes," and "Prolonged redness (>30 minutes) indicates that a pressure area is developing and treatment should begin" (p. 1245). The visible change understates the damage: "The skin changes observed may represent the top of a cone-shaped area with widespread tissue destruction, beneath which tissue rapidly ulcerates and creates a large pressure ulcer that sometimes extends to the bone."
q_1320.trap: (B) is correct for redness that fades within 15 minutes, and the 30-minute mark is the entire discriminator. The other areas to check by name are the occiput, trochanter, and heel.

q_1321.topic: physiologic and psychologic effects of immobilization
q_1321.stem: A hospitalized school-age child in traction has become tearful, has begun bed-wetting again, and wants to be fed. What is the most useful nursing response?
options: Accept the regression as expected, and involve the child in planning the daily routine and choosing clothes
Tell the child that behaving like a baby will not help him get better
Restrict visitors so the child can rest and settle
Take over all of the child's care to reduce his frustration
q_1321.rationale: "Children seek attention by reverting to earlier developmental behaviors, such as wanting to be fed, bed-wetting, and baby talk" (p. 1246), and the chapter names the intervention: "One of the most useful interventions to help children cope with immobility is participation in their own care. Self-care to the maximum extent possible is usually well received by children. They can help plan their daily routine, select their diet (when possible), and choose the clothes they are to wear" (p. 1247).
q_1321.trap: (D) is kindly meant and removes the one thing that helps, because immobilization has already taken the child's normal outlet: "Children respond to anxiety with increased activity. Removal of this power deprives them of necessary input and a natural outlet for their feelings and fantasies" (p. 1246). (B) shames a normal response and adds to the guilt the chapter says to correct with "It just happened—it was an accident."

q_1322.topic: cast care and neurovascular assessment in children
q_1322.stem: A 12-year-old whose long-leg fiberglass cast was applied this morning reports pain rated 10 out of 10 at 2 AM. The pillows have been pushed off the bed, the toes are edematous, and a finger will not slip under the cast edge. What is the priority action?
options: Notify the surgeon of the findings immediately
Give the ordered opioid, elevate the limb on pillows, and reassess in an hour
Reassess in 2 to 3 hours to see whether the pain settles
Withhold analgesia so the pain can be evaluated accurately
q_1322.rationale: This is compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, edema, and a cast acting as a tourniquet. "Permanent muscle and tissue damage can occur within a few hours" (p. 1252), and the Nursing Alert directs the nurse to "Immediately report any observations that include the five Ps of ischemia: pain, especially with passive range of motion; pallor; pulselessness (an ominous and late sign); paresthesia; and paralysis."
q_1322.trap: (B) contains two real interventions and still fails, because it does not report and because "Elevation of the affected extremity is not recommended and may further decrease blood flow to the area" once compartment syndrome is suspected (p. 1265). Elevation is right for a freshly casted limb and wrong here, which is the pairing this item is built on. (C) spends time the tissue does not have.

q_1323.topic: cast care and neurovascular assessment in children
q_1323.stem: A child with a forearm fracture reports burning pain and numbness in the fingers. The radial pulse is palpable and capillary refill is brisk. What should the nurse conclude?
options: Compartment syndrome is still possible, and sensory deficit is the most reliable finding
Circulation is intact, so compartment syndrome is ruled out
Numbness is expected after any fracture and needs no action
The finding is reassuring, because pulselessness is an early sign of compartment syndrome
q_1323.rationale: "A palpable peripheral pulse and brisk capillary refill may be present despite increasing compartmental pressure," and "Sensory deficit in the affected limb is reported to be the most reliable physical finding of compartment syndrome" (p. 1265). Manifestations "may occur as early as 30 minutes after the ischemia develops."
q_1323.trap: (D) inverts the timing and is the most dangerous option, since pulselessness is named as "an ominous and late sign" (p. 1252). (B) draws a reassuring conclusion from the one finding that cannot support it. The clock is short: ischemia lasting as little as 6 hours can cause contracture, and "A great deal of muscle damage occurs after 12 to 24 hours."

q_1324.topic: cast care and neurovascular assessment in children
q_1324.stem: A toddler is in a plaster hip spica cast. Which instructions should the nurse give? Select all that apply.
options: Leave the cast uncovered so it dries from the inside out
Handle a wet cast with the palms of the hands
Turn the child at least every 2 hours so the cast dries evenly
Use a heated fan or hair dryer to speed the drying
Report the cast if it becomes too loose
q_1324.rationale: "The cast must remain uncovered to allow it to dry from the inside out. A wet plaster cast should be supported by a pillow covered with plastic and handled by the palms of the hands to avoid indenting the cast and creating pressure areas. Turning the child in a plaster cast at least every 2 hours will help dry a body cast evenly" (p. 1252). Parents are also told to seek care "if the cast becomes too loose because a loose cast no longer serves its purpose."
q_1324.trap: (D) is the wrong option and it fails twice over: "Heated fans or dryers are not used because they cause the cast to dry on the outside and remain wet beneath. They may also cause burns from heat conduction by the cast to the underlying tissue" (p. 1252).

q_1325.topic: cast care and neurovascular assessment in children
q_1325.stem: A cast is being applied to a 5-year-old's forearm. Which statement about the procedure is accurate?
options: Both plaster and synthetic materials generate heat as they set, and warmer water increases the burn risk
Only plaster generates heat; synthetic material stays cool
Warm water should be used, because it makes application more comfortable
The cast saw used at removal will cut skin on contact, so the child should be warned
q_1325.rationale: "Both types of casting material produce heat from a chemical reaction activated by water immediately after application" (p. 1250), and Table 33.2 states that "the more rapid the drying time, the greater the likelihood of burning; therefore it is recommended to use tepid or cool water to slow drying time and decrease chemical heat produced; the warmer the water, the faster the material dries or hardens" (p. 1251).
q_1325.trap: (D) is the reverse of what a preschooler should be told, and the explanation that defuses the fear is specific: because a cast saw "works by vibration," it "cuts only the hard surface of the cast" and "will not cut when placed lightly on the skin" (p. 1252). Children describe the feeling as tickly. This matters at this age because toddlers and preschoolers "do not have easily defined body boundaries."

q_1326.topic: traction and mobilization devices in children
q_1326.stem: A child in skeletal traction needs to be repositioned higher in the bed. What should the nurse do?
options: Reposition the child without lifting or releasing the traction weights
Lift the weights briefly while a second nurse moves the child
Remove the weights, reposition, and then reapply them
Leave the child as is, since a child in skeletal traction is never repositioned
q_1326.rationale: Nursing Alert: "Skeletal traction is never released by the nurse (except under direct supervision by the provider). This precaution includes not lifting the weights that are applying traction (e.g., for moving the child in bed or repositioning)" (p. 1255). The reason is in the physics: "The continuous maintenance of traction is important during this phase because releasing the traction allows the muscle to contract normally and again cause malpositioning of the bone ends" (p. 1254).
q_1326.trap: (B) and (C) both look like reasonable ways to make a routine nursing task easier, and both undo the muscle fatigue traction exists to produce. (D) overcorrects into immobility, which brings its own set of complications.

q_1327.topic: traction and mobilization devices in children
q_1327.stem: A child is in Russell traction with a padded sling under the knee. Which nursing observation is most specific to this device?
options: Confirming that hip flexion remains at the prescribed angle, and watching for footdrop
Confirming that the legs remain fully extended
Confirming that the halo pin sites are clean and dry
Confirming that the weights rest on the floor between treatments
q_1327.rationale: Russell traction "uses skin traction on the lower leg and a padded sling under the knee," and "Hip flexion must remain at the prescribed angle to prevent fracture malalignment." The nurse also watches that "damage to the peroneal nerve under the knee does not cause footdrop" (p. 1254).
q_1327.trap: (B) describes Buck extension, "a type of skin traction applied with the legs in an extended position" (p. 1254) — the two skin tractions differ precisely in whether the hip and knee are flexed. (D) would release the traction altogether; countertraction is adjusted by elevating the foot of the bed, not by resting the weights.

q_1328.topic: traction and mobilization devices in children
q_1328.stem: A child arrives in the emergency department after a traumatic finger amputation, and the severed part has been brought in. How should it be handled?
options: Rinse gently with normal saline, wrap loosely in sterile gauze, place in a watertight bag, and chill the bag in ice water without packing it in ice
Place the part directly on ice to keep it as cold as possible
Immerse the part in normal saline in an open container at room temperature
Scrub the part clean and wrap it tightly in dry gauze
q_1328.rationale: The Nursing Alert gives the sequence: "1. Rinse limb gently with normal saline. 2. Loosely wrap limb in sterile gauze. 3. Place wrapped limb in a watertight bag. 4. Chill bag, without freezing, in ice water. Do not pack in ice because this may harm tissue. 5. Label with child's name, date, and time, and transport with the child to the hospital" (p. 1256).
q_1328.trap: (B) is the instinctive version and the alert excludes it by name, because direct contact with ice damages the very tissue the surgeon needs. (D) reverses both handling instructions at once, since rinsing is gentle and wrapping is loose.

q_1329.topic: pediatric fractures bone healing and bone fragility
q_1329.stem: A 3-year-old fell from a slide and is walking with a limp, refusing to bear full weight on one leg. A parent says nothing can be broken because she is walking. How should the nurse respond?
options: Walking does not rule out a fracture, and a small child who refuses to walk or crawl should be strongly suspected of having one
Walking on a leg does rule out a fracture in a child this age
Radiographs in young children are highly reliable, so a negative film will settle it
Pain would be severe and constant if a fracture were present
q_1329.rationale: Nursing Alert: "A fracture should be strongly suspected in a small child who refuses to walk or crawl. However, the fact that a child walks on a suspected fractured extremity does not rule out a fracture" (p. 1264). The anatomy explains it: "the fracture is remarkably stable because of the usually intact periosteum. The child may even be able to use an affected arm or walk on a fractured leg" (p. 1263).
q_1329.trap: (C) overstates the imaging, since much of a young child's skeleton "is composed of radiolucent growth cartilage that does not appear on radiographs," and films "are sometimes less reliable than gross deformity and point tenderness in predicting extremity fractures" (p. 1263).

q_1330.topic: pediatric fractures bone healing and bone fragility
q_1330.stem: A 2-year-old and a 15-year-old each sustain a femoral shaft fracture. What should the nurse expect?
options: The toddler will heal considerably faster, because healing time is inversely related to age
Both will heal in about the same time, since bone healing is age independent
The adolescent will heal faster, because of greater bone mass
Neither will heal without internal fixation, since nonunion is common in children
q_1330.rationale: "Healing is more rapid in children, and the rapidity is inversely related to the child's age. The younger the child, the more rapid the healing process. Nonunion of bone fragments is uncommon" (p. 1260). Femoral shaft healing times are given by age as 2 to 3 weeks in the neonatal period, 4 weeks in early childhood, 6 to 8 weeks in later childhood, and 8 to 12 weeks in adolescence (p. 1263).
q_1330.trap: (D) inverts the pediatric advantage, since nonunion is specifically called uncommon. Remodeling runs the same direction: "The younger the child and the closer the proximity of the fracture to the growth plate, the greater the degree of remodeling that is able to take place" (p. 1263).

q_1331.topic: pediatric fractures bone healing and bone fragility
q_1331.stem: An adolescent's ankle is forcibly inverted during a game. Which statement explains why the injury pattern in a growing child differs from an adult's?
options: Ligaments are stronger than bone in a growing child, and the growth plate is the weakest part, so injury occurs at the physis
Ligaments are weaker than bone at every age, so a ligament tear is the expected injury
The growth plate is the strongest part of a child's bone and protects the joint from injury
Children's bones are more brittle than adults', so a complete fracture is expected
q_1331.rationale: "Ligaments are stronger than bone, and the physis (growth plate) is the weakest part of the bone. The more typical site of injury is at the growth plate" (p. 1269). Before physeal closure, joint injuries are "more likely to cause separation of the epiphysis from the metaphysis (growth plate injury) than dislocation" (p. 1268).
q_1331.trap: (D) reverses the mechanical property that defines pediatric fractures: "The pliable bones of the growing child are more porous than those of the adult, which allows them to bend, buckle, and break in a 'greenstick' manner" (p. 1260). (C) contradicts the sentence that opens the Salter-Harris classification, which names the physis as the weakest point of long bones and therefore "a frequent site of injury during childhood trauma."

q_1332.topic: pediatric fractures bone healing and bone fragility
q_1332.stem: An infant with osteogenesis imperfecta is admitted. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Lift gently by the buttocks or support with pillows for diaper changes, never by the ankles
Obtain blood pressures with a manual cuff
Handle and hold the infant with compassion rather than avoiding contact
Screen a child with current or healing fractures for osteogenesis imperfecta before concluding abuse
Anticipate intellectual disability along with the skeletal findings
q_1332.rationale: "Even changing a diaper may cause a fracture in severely affected infants. These children should never be held by the ankles when being diapered but should be gently lifted by the buttocks or supported with pillows." "It is recommended that blood pressure be obtained with a manual cuff to prevent fractures." And the counterweight is stated explicitly: "nurses should not be afraid to touch or handle the infant or child with OI. Such children need compassionate handling and care as much as any other patient" (p. 1287). On the differential: "Children with current fractures or healing fractures should be screened for OI; the assumption that abuse or neglect is the cause of fractures in children must be carefully evaluated by a multidisciplinary team."
q_1332.trap: (E) is the wrong option and the chapter says the opposite plainly: these children, "although smaller in stature than same-age children, have normal intelligence and should receive adequate information and instructions regarding their care" (p. 1287).

q_1333.topic: sports injury heat illness and the young athlete
q_1333.stem: An adolescent felt a pop in the knee, had immediate pain that quickly subsided, has little swelling, and says the joint feels loose. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: A severe (grade III) sprain, because laxity rather than pain indicates severity
A mild (grade I) sprain, because pain and swelling are minimal
A muscle strain, because laxity is a common strain finding
A contusion, because the pain settled quickly
q_1333.rationale: A grade III sprain involves "total loss of ligamentous continuity … Pain is immediate but subsides because none of the pain fibers is being stretched. Swelling may be minimal because hemorrhage extravasates outside of the area into soft tissues" (p. 1269). "The presence of joint laxity is the most valid indicator of the severity of a sprain," and the athlete "complains that the joint 'feels loose' or as if 'something is coming apart' … Pain is seldom the principal subjective symptom."
q_1333.trap: (B) is the intuitive reading and it is exactly backward, since less pain and less swelling is worse here rather than better. (C) misapplies laxity, because strains are graded the same way "except that the degree of laxity does not apply," and complaints of laxity are rare even in a severe strain.

q_1334.topic: sports injury heat illness and the young athlete
q_1334.stem: A child sustains an ankle injury during a soccer game. Which immediate measures are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Apply ice with a layer of cloth between the pack and the skin
Compress and elevate the ankle several inches above the level of the heart
Avoid any liniment or heat-producing preparation before the ankle is examined
Keep each ice application intermittent, never exceeding 30 minutes at a time
Apply a heating pad first, to relax the muscle before evaluation
q_1334.rationale: "Soft tissue injuries should be iced immediately," with "A single layer of the wrap or cloth … placed over the injured area to protect the skin under the ice pack." "Ice therapy should be intermittent, and ice should never be applied for more than 30 minutes at a time to prevent tissue damage." "The point of injury must be kept several inches above the level of the heart for therapy to be effective." And parents are cautioned "against using any form of liniment or other heat-producing preparation before examination" (p. 1269).
q_1334.trap: (E) is the wrong option, and the reason is concrete: "If the injury requires casting or splinting, the heat generated in the enclosed space can produce extreme discomfort and may even cause tissue damage" (p. 1269). Note that the chapter carries two ice limits — 20 minutes in the fracture Emergency Treatment box (p. 1264) and 30 minutes here — and the emergency figure is the more conservative of the two.

q_1335.topic: sports injury heat illness and the young athlete
q_1335.stem: A 14-year-old cross-country runner is diagnosed with a tibial stress fracture and told to rest. What does that mean here?
options: Reduced activity with alternative exercise such as pool running, cycling, or swimming, not bed rest or casting
Complete bed rest until the pain resolves
Immobilization in a long-leg cast for 6 weeks
Continuing the same training, since stress fractures heal with use
q_1335.rationale: "Rest is the primary therapy, usually interpreted as reduced activity and the use of alternative exercise—not bed rest or immobilization with casting." "It is important to keep the child or adolescent mobile, and training can be continued," with pool running named as the worked example because it "uses the same movements as running but without the weight bearing" (p. 1270).
q_1335.trap: (D) is the version the athlete will prefer, and the chapter forbids it by name: athletes "should seek assistance when an injury is suspected and not 'work through' injuries caused by overuse—for example, shin splints, stress fractures, tendinitis, and apophysitis" (p. 1267). Note too that early films are often unhelpful, since "callus formation is not yet evident."

q_1336.topic: sports injury heat illness and the young athlete
q_1336.subtopic: heat illness and sudden cardiac events
q_1336.stem: A 13-year-old collapses during football practice. The skin is hot and dry, the core temperature is 105°F, and the athlete is confused. What is the correct management?
options: Move to a cool environment, remove clothing, apply cool water and fans, cool to 102°F, and transport emergently without giving an antipyretic
Move to a cool environment, provide rest and oral fluids; external cooling is not necessary
Give acetaminophen to bring the temperature down, then reassess
Give salt tablets with oral fluids, since this is sodium depletion
q_1336.rationale: Heatstroke "represents a failure of normal thermoregulatory mechanisms," with rapid onset, a temperature "typically higher than 104°F (40°C)," disorientation, and sweating that "may not be present." Treatment is "relocation to a cool environment, removal of clothing, application of cool water (wet towels or immersion), and use of fans," and "The child should be emergently transported to the nearest hospital." Cooling continues "until core temperature reaches 102°F (38.9°C) to prevent overcooling. Antipyretics are not used because they are metabolized by the liver, which is already not functioning properly" (p. 1271).
q_1336.trap: (B) is the treatment for heat exhaustion, where the sensorium is clear and "External cooling methods are not necessary" (p. 1271); the altered mentation and the temperature are what move this case into a different syndrome. (C) reaches for the one drug class the chapter excludes, and (D) treats heat cramps, whose mechanism is sodium depletion with normal mentation and usually normal vital signs.

q_1337.topic: sports injury heat illness and the young athlete
q_1337.subtopic: heat illness and sudden cardiac events
q_1337.stem: An adolescent athlete asks the school nurse how to prepare for a hot afternoon tournament. Which advice is correct?
options: Drink 5 to 8 ounces of water every 15 to 20 minutes, without waiting for thirst
Use thirst as the guide, since it reliably signals early fluid deficit
Take salt tablets beforehand to replace what will be lost in sweat
Use an energy drink, which improves endurance in adolescent athletes
q_1337.rationale: "Water is recommended as the best drink for most athletes, and current recommendations are to take 5 to 8 oz of water every 15 to 20 minutes" (p. 1271), and "Although thirst is experienced early in dehydration, it is unreliable as an indicator of fluid deficit." "Fluids should never be restricted during activity."
q_1337.trap: (C) is refused by name: "The use of salt tablets or table salt is unnecessary and may actually be harmful," and "it is more important to replace water than sodium and chloride" (pp. 1271–1272). (D) is also refused: "Energy drinks are not recommended in children and adolescents participating in sports activities, and there is no evidence of an increase in performance."

q_1338.topic: sports injury heat illness and the young athlete
q_1338.subtopic: heat illness and sudden cardiac events
q_1338.stem: After a 14-year-old athlete's sudden death, a school board asks the nurse whether an automatic external defibrillator would help. Which statement is accurate?
options: An automatic external defibrillator can be effective in resuscitating a child or adolescent with a shockable rhythm
Automatic external defibrillators should be used only by trained health care personnel
Automatic external defibrillators are not designed for use in children
A school program would benefit adult staff but not student athletes
q_1338.rationale: "Appropriate use of an automatic external defibrillator (AED) by civilian bystanders or health care workers may save the life of an athlete," and a school-based program "provides a high survival rate for student athletes and nonathletes" (p. 1274). The trauma box directs bystanders to turn on the defibrillator and follow its directions for children (p. 1241). The most frequent medical cause of sudden death during sport is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
q_1338.trap: (B) and (C) are the two beliefs that keep a defibrillator locked in an office, and the source defeats both in a single sentence by naming civilian bystanders and by giving the survival figure for student athletes specifically. This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 4.

q_1339.topic: scoliosis and spinal deformities in adolescents
q_1339.stem: A 12-year-old girl who is still growing has a 30-degree idiopathic thoracic curve. What management should the nurse expect?
options: Bracing, with the goal of slowing progression rather than curing the curve
Observation only, since curves under 45 degrees never progress
Spinal fusion, since any curve over 25 degrees is surgical
Exercise and chiropractic treatment in place of a brace
q_1339.rationale: "For moderate curves (25 to 45 degrees) in the growing child and adolescent, bracing may be the treatment of choice" (p. 1276), while "Surgical intervention may be required for correction of severe curves or those measuring 45 degrees or more" (p. 1277). The honest framing belongs in the teaching: "Historically bracing has not been shown to be curative; the goal is to slow the progression of the curvature to allow skeletal growth and maturity."
q_1339.trap: (D) offers the substitutions families ask about, and the evidence does not support them: evidence for exercise and chiropractic treatment is "very limited," transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation "has proved to be an ineffective treatment," and "Exercises are of benefit when used in conjunction with bracing" rather than instead of it (p. 1277). (B) collapses three separate degree bands into one.

q_1340.topic: scoliosis and spinal deformities in adolescents
q_1340.stem: During scoliosis screening a 12-year-old is found to have a left thoracic curve, back pain, and a hairy patch over the sacrum. What do these findings suggest?
options: A possible intraspinal abnormality, for which an MRI is usually obtained
Typical adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, managed by observation
A postural variation requiring no follow-up
A compensated curve, since the head will align with the gluteal cleft
q_1340.rationale: "The presence of pain, sacral dimpling or hairy patches, cutaneous vascular changes, absent or abnormal reflexes, bowel or bladder incontinence, or left thoracic curve may indicate an intraspinal abnormality such as syringomyelia, diastematomyelia, or tethered cord syndrome. An MRI scan is usually obtained for evaluation" (p. 1276).
q_1340.trap: (B) is what these findings look like at a glance, and each of the three in the stem sits on the list that excludes it. (D) confuses a red flag with an ordinary finding: "Often a primary curve and a compensatory curve will place the head in alignment with the gluteal cleft. With an uncompensated curve, however, the head and hips are not aligned." Screening itself is scheduled by sex — girls at 10 and 12 years, boys once at 13 or 14.

q_1341.topic: scoliosis and spinal deformities in adolescents
q_1341.stem: An adolescent 3 days after posterior spinal fusion develops epigastric pain, belching, nausea, and copious vomiting that worsens when supine. What should the nurse suspect and do?
options: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome; reposition to left lateral decubitus or prone and notify the provider
Expected postoperative ileus; increase the opioid dose for comfort
Wound infection; obtain a culture of the incision
Delayed neurologic injury; test lower extremity strength only
q_1341.rationale: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome "may occur several days after spinal surgery; this involves duodenal compression by the aorta and superior mesenteric artery and may result in acute partial or complete duodenal obstruction. Clinical manifestations include epigastric pain, belching, nausea, and copious vomiting; symptoms are aggravated in the supine position and often relieved with the patient in a left lateral decubitus or prone position" (p. 1278).
q_1341.trap: (B) names a complication that is also on this chapter's postoperative list, and it misses the positional pattern that identifies this one. (D) points at a genuine risk, since "delayed paralysis may develop that requires surgical intervention," but nothing in the stem is neurologic and neurologic checks here are continuous rather than a reaction to vomiting. Every position change is a log roll, to protect the fusion and instrumentation.

q_1342.topic: congenital hip and foot deformities in infants
q_1342.stem: A 4-month-old is being examined for possible developmental dysplasia of the hip. Which finding is the most sensitive at this age?
options: Limited hip abduction
A positive Ortolani sign
A positive Barlow sign
An audible clunk during hip examination
q_1342.rationale: "The Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers are most reliable from birth to 4 weeks of age. Adduction contractures develop at about 6 to 10 weeks of age, and the Ortolani sign disappears. After this time, the most sensitive test is limited hip abduction" (p. 1280). Other findings at this age include the Galeazzi sign and asymmetric thigh and gluteal folds.
q_1342.trap: (B) and (C) are the two maneuvers every student learns first, and both have already expired by 4 months — a stage swap the chapter sets up in one sentence. (D) is dismissed outright: "The audible clunk is not pathologic," arising from breaking surface tension, knee rotation, or snapping gluteal tendons.

q_1343.topic: congenital hip and foot deformities in infants
q_1343.stem: Parents of a 2-day-old newly diagnosed with developmental dysplasia of the hip are being taught about the Pavlik harness. Which instructions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Check two to three times a day for red areas under the straps and at skin folds
Do not adjust the harness
Always place the diaper under the straps
Avoid lotions and powders under the straps
Remove the harness whenever the infant seems uncomfortable
q_1343.rationale: The skin care instructions are printed verbatim: "Check frequently (at least two to three times per day) for red areas under the straps and at skin folds"; "Gently massage healthy skin under the straps once a day to stimulate circulation"; "In general, avoid lotions and powders because they can cake and irritate the skin"; "Always place the diaper under the straps." And "Parents should be instructed not to adjust the harness" (p. 1281).
q_1343.trap: (E) is the wrong option, because the harness is "worn continuously until the hip is stable on both clinical and ultrasound examination, usually within 6 to 12 weeks," and whether it may be removed at all "is determined individually on the basis of the provider's recommendations" (p. 1281). Interruptions cost more than they appear to: treatment begun before 2 months of age "achieves the highest rate of success."

q_1344.topic: congenital hip and foot deformities in infants
q_1344.stem: An 11-month-old is diagnosed with developmental dysplasia of the hip. What treatment should the nurse expect?
options: Closed reduction with a spica cast for approximately 12 weeks
A Pavlik harness worn continuously for 6 to 12 weeks
Observation, since the hip will stabilize once the child walks
Open reduction with pelvic osteotomy, which is standard at this age
q_1344.rationale: "In the child 6 to 24 months of age, the Pavlik harness has a low success rate. Therefore surgical treatment with a closed reduction is recommended, and the child is placed in a spica cast for approximately 12 weeks"; an open reduction follows only if the hip is not reducible (p. 1281).
q_1344.trap: (B) is the newborn treatment, which is exactly why this chapter's own review item on hip dysplasia turns on the child's age. (C) ignores the governing principle: "The longer treatment is delayed, the more severe the deformity, the more difficult the treatment, and the less favorable the prognosis."

q_1345.topic: congenital hip and foot deformities in infants
q_1345.stem: A newborn's forefoot is adducted with a kidney-shaped lateral border, but the heel and ankle are neutral and ankle range of motion is normal. The parents ask about corrective shoes. What should the nurse explain?
options: This is metatarsus adductus, which usually corrects on its own by about age 4; bracing and corrective shoes have not been shown to be effective
This is clubfoot, and serial casting will begin within the first month of life
Corrective shoes will realign the forefoot within a few months
Surgery is usually required during the first year
q_1345.rationale: Metatarsus adductus is "the most common congenital foot deformity," and the source names the confusion itself: "Unlike a clubfoot, with which it is often confused, the angulation occurs at the tarsometatarsal joint, while the heel and ankle remain in a neutral position. Ankle range of motion is normal" (p. 1283). "The majority of cases spontaneously correct with no treatment over the first 4 years of life. Interventions such as stretching and bracing or corrective shoes have not been shown to be effective."
q_1345.trap: (B) applies the Ponseti protocol to the wrong deformity, since clubfoot adds "forefoot adduction, cavus, hindfoot varus, and ankle equinus" and this newborn's ankle is normal. Both deformities carry the same additional instruction: "A thorough hip examination should be performed" because of the associated risk of hip dysplasia.

q_1346.topic: hip disorders and orthopedic infections in older children
q_1346.stem: A 6-year-old boy has an intermittent limp and complains of knee pain, but the knee examination is entirely normal. What should the nurse suspect?
options: A hip disorder such as Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, which commonly refers pain to the knee
A knee sprain that will resolve with rest
Growing pains, which characteristically localize to the knee
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis of the knee
q_1346.rationale: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is "a self-limiting disorder in which there is avascular necrosis of the femoral head," and "most cases occur as an isolated event in boys between 4 and 8 years of age." Onset "is usually insidious, and the history may reveal only intermittent appearance of a limp on the affected side," while "The pain may be experienced in the hip, along the entire thigh, or in the vicinity of the knee joint" (p. 1282). Initial therapy is "rest or activity restrictions and limited weight bearing."
q_1346.trap: (D) would give a warm, swollen joint with morning stiffness, and this knee is normal on examination. Knee pain with a normal knee is the cross-cut that sends the examiner to the hip, and it applies to slipped capital femoral epiphysis too, where pain may be felt in "hip, groin, thigh, or knee" (p. 1283).

q_1347.topic: hip disorders and orthopedic infections in older children
q_1347.stem: A 13-year-old boy with obesity has hip pain, holds the affected leg flexed, abducted, and externally rotated, and cannot bear weight. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is diagnosed. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Immediate non–weight bearing, with surgery generally within 24 hours of the onset of acute symptoms
A trial of rest and NSAIDs with weight bearing as tolerated
Abduction bracing for containment of the femoral head
Discharge home with follow-up in 2 weeks
q_1347.rationale: "Once the diagnosis is established, the child should be non–weight bearing to prevent further slippage. SCFE is an emergency and requires early diagnosis and treatment," and "Most surgeons prefer to take the child to surgery within 24 hours of the onset of acute symptoms and avoid further risk of avascular necrosis" (p. 1283). The child typically "lies stiff with the lower extremity flexed, abducted, and externally rotated because of the pain."
q_1347.trap: (C) borrows the containment strategy used for Legg-Calve-Perthes, where rest, activity restriction, and abduction bracing really are the initial management (p. 1282). The two hip disorders look similar in the hallway and differ entirely in urgency. Note also that obesity is a strong association rather than a requirement: "SCFE can also occur in children who are not obese."

q_1348.topic: hip disorders and orthopedic infections in older children
q_1348.stem: A 4-year-old has a fever and a knee that is swollen, warm, erythematous, and exquisitely painful, and resists any movement of it. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: Joint aspiration with Gram stain and culture, followed by surgical decompression and irrigation
Moist heat and range-of-motion exercises, as for arthritis
Radiographs to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention
Observation for 48 hours to see whether the swelling resolves
q_1348.rationale: In septic arthritis, "The affected joint is aspirated and the specimen evaluated by Gram stain, culture, and determination of leukocyte count," and "Surgical decompression of the joint along with irrigation and debridement is recommended" (p. 1286). The picture is "severe joint pain, swelling, warmth of overlying tissue, and occasionally erythema. The child is resistant to any joint movement," and "The most common causative organism is S. aureus."
q_1348.trap: (B) is the correct comfort measure for juvenile idiopathic arthritis and dangerously wrong here, and the chapter supplies the one-sentence discriminator: "Erythema is not typical, and a warm, painful red joint is always suspect for infection" (p. 1288). (C) waits on a study that cannot help yet, since "Early radiographic findings are limited to soft tissue swelling."

q_1349.topic: hip disorders and orthopedic infections in older children
q_1349.stem: A 9-year-old with suspected osteomyelitis has a radiograph showing only soft tissue swelling. What should the nurse understand about the workup and treatment?
options: Radiographic changes beyond soft tissue swelling appear only after 2 to 3 weeks, so cultures are obtained and intravenous antibiotics begun without waiting for the film to change
The unremarkable radiograph rules out osteomyelitis
A bone scan will confirm or exclude the diagnosis
Antibiotics should be withheld until the organism is definitively identified
q_1349.rationale: "Radiographic signs, except for soft tissue swelling, are evident only after 2 to 3 weeks" (p. 1285). "Organism identification and antibiotic susceptibility testing are essential for effective therapy," so cultures of aspirated subperiosteal pus, blood, joint fluid, and infected skin are taken first, and "After culture specimens are obtained, empiric therapy is started with IV antibiotics covering the most likely organisms," continued "for at least 4 weeks." Surgical aspiration and drainage "should be performed as soon as possible."
q_1349.trap: (C) overreads a study the chapter qualifies: a bone scan "is useful in locating multiple sites; however, it is not a diagnostic test" (p. 1285). (D) gets the sequence half right and stops in the wrong place — cultures precede antibiotics, but antibiotics do not wait for the result.

q_1350.topic: juvenile idiopathic arthritis and lupus in children
q_1350.stem: A 4-year-old with oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis and a positive antinuclear antibody is due for follow-up. Which examination is essential, and why?
options: Regular slit-lamp examination, because chronic anterior uveitis is usually asymptomatic and can cause permanent vision loss
Annual visual acuity screening, which will detect uveitis early
Fundoscopic examination for cotton wool spots
No eye examination unless the child reports eye pain or redness
q_1350.rationale: "Slit-lamp ophthalmologic examinations at regular intervals are required to diagnose chronic anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) … however, most cases are asymptomatic. Consequently, routine slit-lamp examinations are critical. The children at greatest risk for development of uveitis have pauciarticular disease and a positive antinuclear antibody" (p. 1289). Uveitis "may cause permanent vision loss if undiagnosed and not aggressively treated."
q_1350.trap: (D) follows ordinary clinical logic and misses the point entirely, because this complication announces itself only after the damage is done. (C) borrows the ophthalmologic findings of lupus — "Cotton wool spots, papilledema, retinopathy" (p. 1292) — which belong to the other rheumatic disease in this chapter.

q_1351.topic: juvenile idiopathic arthritis and lupus in children
q_1351.stem: Which teaching points are correct for a school-age child with juvenile idiopathic arthritis? Select all that apply.
options: Attend school even on days when the joints hurt
Use moist heat, most practically a bath, for pain and stiffness
Continue regular play, exercise programs, and sports unless there is a specific risk of injury
Discourage daytime naps, because inactivity provokes stiffness
Apply ice to painful joints as the standard comfort measure
q_1351.rationale: "School-aged children should attend school, even on days when there is joint pain. Staying home will not improve arthritis" (p. 1291). "Application of heat has been beneficial to children with arthritis. Moist heat is best for relieving pain and stiffness, and the most efficient and practical method is via the bathtub" (p. 1291). "Unless there is a specific risk of injury related to arthritis, the child should not be restricted from regular play, dance, exercise programs, and even individual and team sports" (p. 1290), and "Daytime naps are discouraged, especially because inactivity provokes stiffness."
q_1351.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it is correct for a different problem in the same chapter, since ice belongs to acute soft tissue injury under RICE (p. 1269) while chronic arthritis calls for heat. Reaching for the familiar sports-injury measure is the error this pairing is designed to catch.

q_1352.topic: juvenile idiopathic arthritis and lupus in children
q_1352.stem: An adolescent with juvenile idiopathic arthritis is starting weekly low-dose methotrexate. Which instruction set is correct?
options: Take a daily folic acid supplement, take the dose at bedtime to reduce nausea, avoid alcohol, and expect regular liver enzyme and blood count monitoring
Take the dose daily, and expect no laboratory monitoring
Continue the drug through any illness, including varicella
Add over-the-counter ibuprofen for episodes of fever
q_1352.rationale: "A daily folic acid supplement can help reduce the occurrence of oral ulcers. Taking methotrexate at bedtime may help reduce nausea." "Alcohol consumption … increases the risk of hepatotoxicity," and "Laboratory monitoring of liver enzyme levels and blood counts is crucial" (p. 1289). "Weekly low-dose methotrexate therapy is usually the first DMARD used."
q_1352.trap: (C) contradicts a specific instruction: "During some illnesses, especially varicella, methotrexate should be discontinued because it can suppress the immune response" (p. 1289). (D) adds the drug class the teaching excludes, since patients are told to "avoid additional over-the-counter NSAIDs and to take acetaminophen for episodes of fever."

q_1353.topic: juvenile idiopathic arthritis and lupus in children
q_1353.stem: An adolescent with systemic lupus erythematosus feels well and asks why she needs urine testing at every visit. What is the best explanation?
options: Lupus nephritis is usually asymptomatic, so urine and renal function monitoring is how it is detected
The urine test tracks the progression of the malar rash
Urine testing is required only while she is on corticosteroids
She may stop the testing once she has been symptom free for a year
q_1353.rationale: "Lupus nephritis is usually asymptomatic; consequently, monitoring of urine and renal function is required to detect disease. Kidney biopsy is required for lupus nephritis classification" (pp. 1292–1293). The same silent-complication logic runs through this disease, which is why the nurse should also "Assess school performance and emotional stability at each visit as possible indicators of central nervous system involvement" (p. 1293).
q_1353.trap: (D) ties monitoring to symptoms in a disease whose most serious organ involvement produces none, which is exactly the reasoning the surveillance schedule exists to displace. (C) attaches the monitoring to a drug rather than to the disease.

q_1354.topic: juvenile idiopathic arthritis and lupus in children
q_1354.stem: A 16-year-old is being evaluated for lupus-like symptoms. Which history question is most important for the nurse to ask?
options: Whether she is taking minocycline for acne
Whether she has recently changed her diet
Whether she uses a sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher
Whether she has had a recent tetanus booster
q_1354.rationale: "Some commonly used drugs such as minocycline, procainamide, hydralazine, and chlorpromazine can cause lupus-like symptoms. Minocycline, a common acne treatment, may not be considered important by the teenager and omitted from the history," and the distinction matters because "Drug-induced lupus resolves with time after the triggering medication has been discontinued" (p. 1293).
q_1354.trap: (C) names a real and heavily emphasized teaching point — sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or more, hats, protective clothing, and the "slip, slop, slap" rule (p. 1294) — but it belongs to management after a diagnosis rather than to the differential. What the history has to surface here is a drug the teenager does not think of as medicine.

q_1355.topic: upper and lower motor neuron lesions in children
q_1355.subtopic: reading the lesion from the examination
q_1355.stem: A child is assessed after a traumatic spinal cord injury, once the flaccid phase has resolved. Which findings are expected?
options: Spastic paralysis below the lesion, exaggerated tendon reflexes, a Babinski reflex, and no muscle wasting
Flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, and marked atrophy
Flaccid paralysis with hyperreflexia
Normal reflexes with preserved strength
q_1355.rationale: Box 34.9 gives the upper motor neuron syndrome as "Spastic paralysis in muscle groups below lesion (intact reflex arcs below lesion)," "Hyperreflexia with tendon reflexes exaggerated, Babinski reflex present," "No wasting of muscle mass because of increased muscle tone," and "Flexion contractures and spasms of muscle groups below lesion level common" (p. 1329).
q_1355.trap: (B) is the lower motor neuron picture, and the chapter assigns each to its population in one sentence: "Most SCIs involve upper motor neurons; children born with spinal cord defects have primarily lower motor neuron deficits" (p. 1329). A myelomeningocele stem should read flaccid and a traumatic injury stem spastic. (C) mixes one finding from each column, which is how a half-remembered pair fails.

q_1356.topic: upper and lower motor neuron lesions in children
q_1356.subtopic: reading the lesion from the examination
q_1356.stem: A child is being worked up for progressive weakness, and the serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. What does this suggest?
options: A muscle disease such as muscular dystrophy, because creatine kinase is not elevated in neurogenic disease
An anterior horn cell disease such as spinal muscular atrophy
A peripheral nerve disorder such as Guillain-Barre syndrome
Nothing, since creatine kinase rises with any cause of weakness
q_1356.rationale: Creatine kinase "is released in large amounts in some muscular diseases, such as MD. CK is not elevated in neurogenic disease" (p. 1299). In Duchenne muscular dystrophy the level is dramatic and early: "Serum CK levels are extremely high in the first 2 years of life, before the onset of clinical weakness" (p. 1341).
q_1356.trap: (B) and (C) are both real causes of weakness in this chapter and both are neurogenic, so the enzyme is precisely what sorts them from a myopathy. The chapter's own framework is anatomic: the most useful classification "defines the site of origin of the pathologic lesion: the anterior horn cells of the spinal cord, the peripheral nerves, the neuromuscular junction, and the muscles" (p. 1298).

q_1357.topic: upper and lower motor neuron lesions in children
q_1357.subtopic: reading the lesion from the examination
q_1357.stem: A nurse is reviewing how different disorders block neuromuscular transmission. Which pairing is correct?
options: Botulism blocks the release of acetylcholine, while myasthenia gravis blocks the receptor sites
Botulism blocks the receptor sites, while myasthenia gravis blocks acetylcholine release
Both act by inhibiting cholinesterase
Neither acts at the neuromuscular junction
q_1357.rationale: Transmission happens in three steps — release, diffusion to receptor sites, and removal by cholinesterase — and "Interference at any of these three steps will block transmission of nerve impulses and prevent muscular contraction" (p. 1299). "toxins that prevent the release of acetylcholine are those that produce the paralysis of botulism and tick paralysis," while action at receptor sites "is also blocked by the drug curare" and by the antibodies of myasthenia gravis. Botulism toxin "exerts its effect by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction" (p. 1325).
q_1357.trap: (B) swaps the two, and the swap matters clinically because the treatments diverge completely: botulism is treated by neutralizing the toxin with immune globulin, while myasthenia gravis is treated with cholinesterase inhibitors that leave more acetylcholine at the receptor. (C) describes the step blocked by organophosphate insecticide poisoning.

q_1358.topic: cerebral palsy classification and risk factors
q_1358.stem: A nursing student asks what the single most important risk factor for cerebral palsy is. Which answer is correct?
options: Preterm birth of extremely and very low birth weight infants
Birth asphyxia
Chorioamnionitis
Intraventricular hemorrhage
q_1358.rationale: "Although CP occurs in term births, preterm birth of ELBW and VLBW infants continues to be the single most important risk factor for CP" (p. 1301). The chapter also revises the older teaching: "Although the prevalent traditional hypothesis has been that CP results from perinatal problems, especially birth asphyxia, it is now believed that CP results more often from existing prenatal brain abnormalities."
q_1358.trap: (B) is the retired hypothesis and the one most people were taught first. (C) and (D) are real risk factors, which is what makes them selectable, but chorioamnionitis carries the caveat that "not all term infants exposed to chorioamnionitis develop CP," and intraventricular hemorrhage is named as a risk in low-birth-weight infants specifically, which makes it a consequence of the same prematurity the correct answer names. This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 3.

q_1359.topic: cerebral palsy classification and risk factors
q_1359.stem: A 3-month-old at risk for cerebral palsy is generally hypotonic, and a parent asks whether this rules out the spastic type. What should the nurse explain?
options: Early neurologic manifestations are usually generalized hypotonia, which may last weeks to as long as a year before spasticity appears
Hypotonia rules out spastic cerebral palsy, which is hypertonic from birth
Hypotonia at this age is always a normal finding
The diagnosis can be confirmed now on the basis of tone alone
q_1359.rationale: "Early neurologic manifestations are usually generalized hypotonia or decreased tone that lasts for a few weeks or may extend for months or even as long as a year" (p. 1301). The diagnosis takes time: "motor impairment associated with voluntary control is usually not apparent until after 2 to 4 months of age at the earliest. More often the diagnosis cannot be confirmed until the age of 1 or 2 years" (p. 1304).
q_1359.trap: (B) is the stage swap this section is built on, because spastic cerebral palsy does not start out spastic. (D) overstates what tone can settle, and the chapter cuts the other way as well: "some children who show signs consistent with CP before 2 years do not demonstrate such signs after 2 years."

q_1360.topic: cerebral palsy classification and risk factors
q_1360.stem: Which findings in an infant should raise concern for cerebral palsy? Select all that apply.
options: Preferential use of one hand at about 6 months of age
Persistence of primitive infantile reflexes
An obligatory tonic neck response
Rigidity and extension of the whole body when pulled to a sitting position
Absence of hand dominance at 4 years of age
q_1360.rationale: "An early sign is preferential unilateral hand use that may be apparent at approximately 6 months of age. Hand dominance does not normally develop until the preschool years" (p. 1301). "Persistence of primitive reflexes is one of the earliest clues to CP" (p. 1303), and Box 34.3 lists an "Obligatory tonic neck reflex at any age." "When pulled to a sitting position, the child may extend the entire body and be rigid and unbending at the hip and knee joints. This is an early sign of spasticity" (p. 1302).
q_1360.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it inverts the hand-preference rule: what concerns the examiner is dominance appearing too early, not too late, because dominance normally does not emerge until the preschool years.

q_1361.topic: cerebral palsy classification and risk factors
