q_1361.stem: A school nurse hears a teacher say that a student with spastic cerebral palsy and dysarthria must be cognitively impaired. How should the nurse respond?
options: Children with cerebral palsy have a wide range of intelligence, and 50% to 60% are within normal limits; speech difficulty is often misread as cognitive impairment
The teacher is correct, since cerebral palsy always involves cognitive impairment
Only children with athetoid cerebral palsy have normal intelligence
Intelligence cannot be assessed in a child whose speech is unclear
q_1361.rationale: "Intellectual impairment is a concern, although children with CP have a wide range of intelligence, and 50% to 60% are within normal limits," and "Speech difficulties are often interpreted as a sign of cognitive impairment" (p. 1303). The chapter adds that "Many persons with CP who have severely limiting physical involvement actually have the least intellectual impairment," and that improved communication devices "have revealed that some people with quadriplegic spastic CP have normal intelligence."
q_1361.trap: (C) takes a true comparative statement — "As a group, children with athetosis and ataxia are intellectually superior to those with other types of CP" — and converts it into an exclusion the same paragraph refutes. (D) restates the assumption that created the problem.

q_1362.topic: cerebral palsy therapy and family care
q_1362.stem: A nurse is teaching a parent to feed a toddler with cerebral palsy who has difficulty sucking and swallowing. Which position should be used?
options: A more flexed sitting position, with the arms brought forward
Semireclining, so gravity assists the flow
Fully supine with the neck extended
Prone across the parent's lap
q_1362.rationale: "Children should be fed in the normal eating position. When they have difficulty sucking and swallowing, it is tempting to hold them in a semireclining posture to make use of gravity flow. However, this method does not promote active swallowing, and the neck hyperextension may even interfere with swallowing. A more flexed sitting position, with the arms brought forward to decrease the tendency toward back and neck extension, is more natural during bottle- or spoon-feeding and encourages active swallowing" (p. 1307).
q_1362.trap: (B) is named in the source as the tempting option and refused in the same sentence, and (C) deepens the same problem, since the neck hyperextension is what interferes with the swallow. The stakes are concrete: coughing and choking while eating "may predispose the child with CP to aspiration, which may not be readily apparent" (p. 1303).

q_1363.topic: cerebral palsy therapy and family care
q_1363.stem: A child with an intrathecal baclofen pump is admitted with high fever, rebound spasticity, itching, and rapid deterioration, and sepsis is suspected. What else should the nurse consider?
options: Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal, which can mimic sepsis and is treated by reestablishing the dose
An expected adverse effect of baclofen that will resolve on its own
Botulinum toxin overdose from a recent injection
A seizure disorder unrelated to the pump
q_1363.rationale: "Abrupt withdrawal of intrathecal baclofen, especially at high doses, may result in adverse effects such as rebound spasticity, pruritus, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, multiorgan failure, and death; in some cases intrathecal baclofen withdrawal may mimic sepsis." Treatment "centers on reestablishing the medication dosage, with improvements observed within 1 to 2 hours" (p. 1306).
q_1363.trap: (B) treats a potentially fatal withdrawal as a nuisance effect. (C) reaches for the other spasticity drug in the chapter, whose adverse effects are far milder — "pain at the injection site and a temporary weakness" — and whose action peaks at 2 weeks rather than producing an acute crisis (p. 1305).

q_1364.topic: cerebral palsy therapy and family care
q_1364.stem: A school-age child with spastic cerebral palsy is falling below the 5th percentile for weight. Which statement should guide the nurse's plan?
options: Children with spasticity expend more energy and often require more energy intake than same-age peers
Caloric intake should be restricted, since children with cerebral palsy gain weight easily
Growth below the 5th percentile is expected in this population and needs no intervention
Feeding difficulty is the only possible cause, so a gastrostomy should be placed
q_1364.rationale: "Children with spasticity expend more energy and often require more energy intake than same-age counterparts to maintain adequate growth," and "children with CP are at risk for failure to thrive, and the nurse must ensure an adequate caloric intake," with high-calorie supplements sometimes needed after 1 year of age (p. 1309). The balance is named too: monitor growth on a standardized growth chart while "avoiding overfeeding and obesity."
q_1364.trap: (C) is close to a real observation — "Growth is affected in children with spastic tetraplegia, and many children remain below the 5th percentile for age and sex" (p. 1308) — and turns an expected difficulty into a reason not to act, which is the plausible-but-adjacent move. (B) reverses the risk for this subgroup entirely. More frequent rest periods belong in the plan as well, because the effort of daily activities is itself the drain.

q_1365.topic: cerebral palsy therapy and family care
q_1365.stem: A child with cerebral palsy is admitted for orthopedic surgery, and the mother says she is exhausted and asks whether she must stay overnight. What is the best response?
options: Respect her preference, since a hospitalization may be the first chance for a parent to defer care and the respite may be crucial
Insist that she room in, since parental presence always improves outcomes
Explain that the nursing staff cannot manage her child's care without her
Suggest she stay but sleep in the waiting area
q_1365.rationale: Rooming-in has real benefits, "but it is equally important to remember that a hospitalization may be the first time a parent can defer care to a nurse and not be the primary caregiver. This respite may be crucial to the parent's well-being. Respect the parent's preference in this regard" (p. 1310).
q_1365.trap: (B) states a principle that is true often enough to become a reflex, and this chapter names the exception explicitly, because the family of a child with cerebral palsy has been delivering continuous care at home for years. (C) is untrue and produces guilt on top of exhaustion.

q_1366.topic: neural tube defects and myelomeningocele care
q_1366.stem: A woman whose first child was born with a myelomeningocele asks about folic acid before her next pregnancy. What should the nurse advise?
options: 4 mg daily under a practitioner's supervision, beginning at least 1 month before conception and through the first trimester, and not from a multivitamin alone
0.4 mg daily, the same as for all women of childbearing age
4 mg daily, taken as extra multivitamin tablets
No supplement, since folic acid is already added to cereal grain products
q_1366.rationale: All women of childbearing age take "a multivitamin with 0.4 mg folic acid daily," while a woman with a previously affected pregnancy takes 4 mg daily "under a practitioner's supervision, beginning at least 1 month before they plan a pregnancy and through the first trimester because the neural tube closes about 1 month after conception" (p. 1311). And "Supplementation of 4 mg of folate should not be given solely in multivitamin preparations because of the risk for overdose of other vitamins" (p. 1317).
q_1366.trap: (B) applies the general-population dose to a woman whose recurrence risk is 3% to 4% (p. 1313), and the tenfold difference between the two numbers is the entire point of the pair. (C) has the right dose in the wrong vehicle, which is exactly what the overdose caution exists to prevent.

q_1367.topic: neural tube defects and myelomeningocele care
q_1367.stem: A newborn has a saclike protrusion over the lumbar spine. Which finding would distinguish a myelomeningocele from a meningocele?
options: A neurologic deficit below the lesion
The presence of a visible sac
A location in the lumbosacral region
An elevated maternal alpha-fetoprotein level
q_1367.rationale: A meningocele "encases meninges and spinal fluid but no neural elements," while a myelomeningocele "contains meninges, spinal fluid, and nerves," and the chapter states the consequence directly: "Neurologic deficit is not associated with meningocele but occurs in varying, often serious, degrees in myelomeningocele" (pp. 1312–1313).
q_1367.trap: (B) and (C) belong to both, since each is a form of spina bifida cystica, "a visible defect with an external saclike protrusion," and the lumbar or lumbosacral area is the commonest site for either. What separates them is what is inside the sac and therefore what works below it.

q_1368.topic: neural tube defects and myelomeningocele care
q_1368.stem: A newborn with an unrepaired myelomeningocele is admitted. Which nursing actions are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Cover the sac with a sterile, moist, nonadherent dressing using normal saline
Change the dressing every 2 to 4 hours and inspect the sac for leaks and irritation
Keep the infant prone
Avoid rectal temperatures
Apply a diaper over the defect to contain stool
q_1368.rationale: "Before surgical closure, the myelomeningocele is kept from drying by the application of a sterile, moist, nonadherent dressing. The moistening solution is usually sterile normal saline. Dressings are changed frequently (every 2 to 4 hours), and the sac is closely inspected for leaks, abrasions, irritation, and signs of infection." "Before surgery the infant remains in the prone position to minimize tension on the sac and the risk of trauma" (p. 1318). The safety rule is separate: "Avoid taking rectal temperatures in affected infants. Because bowel sphincter function is frequently affected, the thermometer can cause irritation and rectal prolapse" (p. 1313).
q_1368.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it is the instinct of anyone caring for a newborn passing stool continuously: "Diapering the infant may be contraindicated until the defect has been repaired and healing is well advanced" (p. 1318). Note that the continual passage of stool is itself "often misinterpreted as diarrhea."

q_1369.topic: neural tube defects and myelomeningocele care
q_1369.stem: A neonate born 6 hours ago has a myelomeningocele that is leaking cerebrospinal fluid. When should surgical closure occur?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 24 to 72 hours, the usual window
After about a week, to allow the infant to stabilize
After hydrocephalus has been ruled out
q_1369.rationale: "Most authorities believe that early closure, within the first 24 to 72 hours, offers the most favorable outcome. Surgical closure within the first 24 hours is recommended if the sac is leaking CSF" (p. 1314), and earlier still is preferred: "Early closure, preferably in the first 12 to 18 hours, not only prevents local infection and trauma to the exposed tissues but also avoids stretching other nerve roots."
q_1369.trap: (B) is the general rule, and this infant meets the stated exception to it. (D) inverts the sequence, since hydrocephalus commonly declares itself only "after the primary closure of the opening on the back" (p. 1313). Delay also costs the kidneys: "Increased incidence of febrile UTIs, vesicoureteral reflux, and hydronephrosis have been shown when closure is delayed past 72 hours" (p. 1314).

q_1370.topic: neural tube defects and myelomeningocele care
q_1370.stem: An infant has had surgical repair of a myelomeningocele. Which complication should the nurse most anticipate?
options: Hydrocephalus
Chiari II malformation
Latex allergy
Tethered cord syndrome
q_1370.rationale: "approximately 80% to 85% of children with SB develop hydrocephalus," and "Although present at birth, hydrocephalus may not be apparent until shortly thereafter, or after the primary closure of the opening on the back" (p. 1313). Postoperative care therefore includes measuring head circumference daily and examining the fontanels "for signs of tension or bulging" (p. 1318).
q_1370.trap: (B) is a real association in about 80% of these infants, but it is a coexisting malformation rather than a postoperative complication and is treated "only when the child is symptomatic" (p. 1315). (C) develops over years of repeated exposure rather than in the first postoperative week (p. 1319), and (D) is "more common during periods of rapid growth" (p. 1315). All three are true of this population, and none is what the nurse watches for now. This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 1.

q_1371.topic: neurogenic bladder bowel and latex allergy in spina bifida
q_1371.stem: A 4-year-old with spina bifida is at risk for urinary system distress. What management should the nurse expect?
options: Clean intermittent catheterization, typically combined with an antispasmodic medication
An indwelling catheter for continuous drainage
DDAVP, to reduce urine output
The Mitrofanoff procedure as the first-line approach
q_1371.rationale: For a child with evidence of, or at risk for, urinary system distress, management is "clean intermittent catheterization (CIC), typically in combination with an antispasmodic medication such as oxybutynin or propantheline" (p. 1316). "CIC is not intended to prevent spontaneous voiding. Instead, it ensures routine, regular bladder evacuation, further preventing deleterious elevation of intravesical pressures."
q_1371.trap: (D) is a real option and a surgical one, reserved for "When the child cannot attain continence by conservative measures" (p. 1316), so it answers a different question than the one asked. (C) belongs to diabetes insipidus rather than to a neurogenic bladder, and (B) is not the described management and carries its own infection risk. This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 4.

q_1372.topic: neurogenic bladder bowel and latex allergy in spina bifida
q_1372.stem: Two children with myelomeningocele are compared: one leaks urine almost constantly, the other stays dry between catheterizations. Which statement is accurate?
options: The child with more severe leakage is less predisposed to serious urinary tract infections, because the detrusor leak point pressure is lower
The drier child has the safer bladder
Leakage has no relationship to upper urinary tract risk
Both carry identical risk, determined only by the level of the lesion
q_1372.rationale: "When the magnitude of the pressure required to drive urine across the abnormal sphincter is greater than 40 cm H2O (the detrusor leak point pressure) and the compliance of the bladder wall is low, the risk of urinary system distress is high" (p. 1315). "When the detrusor leak point pressure is lower than 40 cm H2O, urinary leakage is more severe, although the risk of urinary system distress is lessened. Thus the child with more severe urinary incontinence is less predisposed than the 'drier' child to serious urinary tract infections" (p. 1316).
q_1372.trap: (B) is what continence intuitively suggests, and the chapter states the reverse in so many words. The pressure the bladder generates, not the dryness of the diaper, is what threatens the kidneys.

q_1373.topic: neurogenic bladder bowel and latex allergy in spina bifida
q_1373.stem: A 7-year-old with myelomeningocele is starting a bowel program. Which recommendation is correct?
options: Diet modification, regular toilet habits, and a fiber supplement of the child's age in years plus 5 grams per day
A clear liquid diet until continence is achieved
Daily enemas as the first-line measure
No intervention, since fecal continence is not attainable in spina bifida
q_1373.rationale: "Some degree of fecal continence can be achieved in most children with myelomeningocele with diet modification, regular toilet habits, and prevention of constipation and impaction. It is frequently a lengthy process." "Dietary fiber supplements (recommended age of child in years + 5 g/day), laxatives, suppositories, or enemas aid in producing regular evacuation" (p. 1317).
q_1373.trap: (D) writes off an outcome the chapter says is usually attainable, and continence here is not cosmetic: incontinence leads "to significant, and sometimes devastating, problems with growth and developmental tasks, including establishing independence and social and intimate relationships." (C) moves an adjunct to the front of the plan.

q_1374.topic: neurogenic bladder bowel and latex allergy in spina bifida
q_1374.stem: A nurse is taking a preoperative history. Which approach to latex allergy is correct?
options: Ask every patient about latex sensitivity as a routine part of the preoperative history
Ask only patients with spina bifida or urogenital anomalies
Rely on skin prick testing rather than on the history
Ask only if the parent raises the concern
q_1374.rationale: "The identification of those sensitive to latex is best accomplished through careful screening of all patients. During the health interview with the parent or child, ask all patients, not only those at risk, about sensitivity to latex. Be certain this is a routine part of all preoperative and preprocedural histories" (p. 1319).
q_1374.trap: (B) narrows the screen to the population in which the association was first described. (C) leans on a test the chapter distrusts: skin prick and provocation testing "carry the risk for allergic reaction or anaphylaxis," and "none of these tests demonstrates complete diagnostic reliability, and they should not be the sole determinant." The interview also has to reach nonmedical items such as "water toys, pacifiers, and plastic storage bags," and the cross-reacting foods banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut (p. 1320).

q_1375.stem: A 6-year-old develops weakness that began in the legs about 10 days after a viral illness and is ascending, with depressed reflexes and flaccid paralysis. Which condition is this, and what is the treatment?
options: Guillain-Barre syndrome, treated primarily with intravenous immunoglobulin given within 2 weeks of onset
Botulism, treated with botulism immune globulin
Guillain-Barre syndrome, treated with corticosteroids alone
Myasthenia gravis, treated with a cholinesterase inhibitor
q_1375.rationale: Guillain-Barre syndrome is "an uncommon acute demyelinating polyneuropathy with a progressive, usually ascending flaccid paralysis," typically beginning "approximately 10 days after a nonspecific viral infection," with "Proximal muscle weakness progressing to paralysis usually occurs before distal weakness" and tendon reflexes "depressed or absent" (p. 1322). "IVIG is now recommended as the primary treatment of GBS when administered within 2 weeks of disease onset" (p. 1323).
q_1375.trap: (C) attaches a plausible antiinflammatory to a demyelinating disease, and the chapter refuses it: "Corticosteroids alone do not decrease the symptoms or shorten the duration of the disease" (p. 1323). (B) names the disease whose paralysis runs the other way, beginning with cranial nerve signs and descending.

q_1376.stem: An adolescent with Guillain-Barre syndrome is intubated and nearly completely paralyzed. Which nursing considerations are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Cognitive function remains intact, so procedures and treatments should be explained
Recovery of muscle strength progresses in the reverse order of onset
Resuscitation equipment is kept at the bedside during the acute phase
The head of the bed is elevated 30 degrees to help prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia
Continuous sedation should be maintained, since the child cannot perceive the environment
q_1376.rationale: "Although the child may have a generalized paralysis, cognitive function remains intact; therefore it is important for nursing care to involve communication with the child or adolescent regarding procedures and treatments that may be frightening, especially if mechanical ventilation is required" (p. 1323). "The recovery of muscle strength progresses in the reverse order of onset of paralysis, with lower extremity strength being the last to recover." The bedside list is "oxygen source, appropriate-size insufflation bag and mask, endotracheal intubation and suctioning equipment, tracheotomy tray, and vasopressor drugs," and pneumonia prevention includes "elevating the head of the bed 30 degrees."
q_1376.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it rests on the exact assumption the chapter corrects: a paralyzed child in this disease is awake and aware, which is why communication is listed as nursing care rather than as a kindness.

q_1377.stem: A child is admitted with generalized tetanus. Which set of nursing measures is correct?
options: Minimize sound, touch, and light; use standard precautions rather than isolation; and plan active immunization during recovery
Place the child in isolation, since tetanus is communicable
Keep the room brightly lit and the child stimulated, to assess mentation
Omit immunization after recovery, since the illness confers immunity
q_1377.rationale: "every effort should be made to control or eliminate stimulation from sound, light, and touch," because "The slightest noise, a gentle touch, or bright light triggers convulsive muscular contractions that last seconds to minutes" (pp. 1324–1325). "Standard precautions for the child with tetanus are recommended; isolation is not recommended," and "When the child recovers, active immunization should take place because contraction of the disease does not confer a permanent immunity" (p. 1325).
q_1377.trap: (D) is the assumption that holds for many infections and specifically does not hold here. (B) treats a toxin-mediated wound infection as a communicable disease. (C) trades a seizure trigger for information the nurse already has, since mentation is unaffected throughout: "the patient remains alert, and pain and distress are reflected in a rapid pulse, sweating, and an anxious expression."

q_1378.stem: A fully immunized 10-year-old whose last booster was 3 years ago has a deep puncture wound contaminated with soil. What should the nurse anticipate?
options: A tetanus toxoid booster as soon as possible after the injury
Tetanus immunoglobulin, because the wound is contaminated
No intervention, since the child is fully immunized
Both tetanus immunoglobulin and toxoid, at separate sites
q_1378.rationale: For a more serious wound — contaminated, puncture, crush, or burn — in an immunized child, the child is "given a tetanus toxoid booster prophylactically as soon as possible after injury." "Protective levels of antibody are maintained for at least 10 years. Therefore antitoxin is not indicated for the fully immunized child" (p. 1324).
q_1378.trap: (B) and (D) both give immunoglobulin, which belongs to the unprotected or inadequately immunized child with a tetanus-prone wound, where "Concurrent administration of both TIG and tetanus toxoid at separate sites is recommended." The child's immune status, not the dirt in the wound, decides which column applies, and (C) would be correct only for a clean, minor wound.

q_1379.stem: A 3-month-old presents with constipation, generalized weakness, a weak cry, poor feeding, and diminished reflexes, and infant botulism is suspected. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Botulism immune globulin intravenously is given without waiting for laboratory confirmation
Antibiotics are not part of management, and aminoglycosides may worsen the condition
Honey should not be given to infants younger than 12 months
Spinal muscular atrophy type 1 and sepsis are common initial misdiagnoses
Equine antitoxin is the treatment of choice in infants
q_1379.rationale: "Treatment consists of immediate administration of botulism immune globulin intravenously (BIG-IV) without delaying for laboratory diagnosis." "Antibiotic therapy is not part of the management because the botulinum toxin is an intracellular molecule and antibiotics would not be effective; aminoglycosides in particular should not be administered because they may potentiate the blocking effects of the neurotoxin" (p. 1326). The Nursing Alert directs that "honey not be given to infants younger than 12 months." And "SMA type 1 and metabolic disorders are often mistaken for infant botulism … Presenting clinical signs also often mimic those of sepsis in young infants" (p. 1325).
q_1379.trap: (E) is the wrong option, excluded by age: "Trivalent equine botulinum antitoxin and bivalent antitoxin, used in adults and older children, are not administered to infants" (p. 1326). Constipation as the presenting symptom, and an acute onset in a previously well infant, are what point away from spinal muscular atrophy.

q_1380.topic: myasthenia gravis and spinal muscular atrophy
q_1380.stem: A 12-year-old with juvenile myasthenia gravis taking neostigmine develops lacrimation, salivation, abdominal cramps, sweating, diarrhea, and bradycardia along with increased weakness. What should the nurse suspect?
options: Overmedication, since these are signs of parasympathetic stimulation
A myasthenic crisis from undermedication
An allergic reaction to neostigmine
An unrelated gastrointestinal infection
q_1380.rationale: "The child must be observed for signs of parasympathetic stimulation from overmedication. These signs include lacrimation, salivation, abdominal cramps, sweating, diarrhea, vomiting, bradycardia, and weakness of respiratory muscles" (p. 1326).
q_1380.trap: (B) is the hard call, because weakness belongs to both states and is the symptom that prompts a family to give more drug. The cholinergic findings are the tell. In untreated disease the pattern is different again: "The signs and symptoms are more pronounced in the late afternoon and evening. Rest can help relieve the symptoms, but exercise and stress worsen them."

q_1381.topic: myasthenia gravis and spinal muscular atrophy
q_1381.stem: A child with myasthenia gravis is scheduled for surgery and has a suspected respiratory infection. Which agents should be avoided?
options: Neuromuscular-blocking agents such as pancuronium or succinylcholine, and aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin
Acetaminophen and ibuprofen
Influenza vaccine
Cholinesterase inhibitors
q_1381.rationale: The Drug Alert states: "Avoid neuromuscular-blocking agents such as pancuronium or succinylcholine in patients with MG because they may induce paralysis that can last for weeks. Avoid aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin because they potentiate MG symptoms" (p. 1327).
q_1381.trap: (C) is the opposite of the recommendation, since "yearly influenza vaccination is recommended" precisely because "Respiratory viral infections are a common precipitating cause of a myasthenia crisis" (p. 1327). (D) names the treatment rather than a hazard.

q_1382.topic: myasthenia gravis and spinal muscular atrophy
q_1382.stem: An infant born to a mother with myasthenia gravis has generalized weakness, hypotonia, ptosis, and a weak cry. What should the nurse tell the parents?
options: Symptoms usually disappear within 2 to 3 weeks, and the infant is not at increased risk of myasthenia gravis later in life
The condition persists throughout life and is relatively resistant to drug therapy
The infant will require a thymectomy
The findings confirm a familial, non-immune form of the disease
q_1382.rationale: Neonatal transient myasthenia gravis results from "transplacentally acquired maternal acetylcholine receptor antibodies," occurs in "approximately 10% to 20% of infants born to mothers with MG," and "Symptoms usually disappear within 2 to 3 weeks"; these infants "are not at increased risk of MG later in life," and "There is no evidence of neurologic damage" (p. 1327).
q_1382.trap: (B) and (D) describe the congenital form, "a rare familial abnormality of neuromuscular transmission that is not immunologically mediated," which persists lifelong and occurs in infants whose mother "usually does not have the disease." The mother's diagnosis in the stem is the detail that sorts the two. (C) applies a treatment that "is not effective for familial and congenital forms of MG."

q_1383.topic: myasthenia gravis and spinal muscular atrophy
q_1383.stem: A 4-month-old has inactivity, a frog-leg posture, generalized weakness, absent deep tendon reflexes, a weak cry and cough, and diaphragmatic breathing, but is alert with normal sensation. What should the nurse understand?
options: Spinal muscular atrophy type 1 is autosomal recessive, intellect is normal, and restrictive lung disease is the most serious complication
Intellectual impairment is expected alongside the motor findings
The disorder is acquired and will resolve with supportive care
Deep tendon reflexes are typically brisk in this condition
q_1383.rationale: Spinal muscular atrophy type 1 is "characterized by progressive weakness and wasting of skeletal muscles caused by degeneration of anterior horn cells. It is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait" (p. 1320). The type 1 sign set includes the frog-leg position, "Absent deep tendon reflexes," "Diaphragmatic breathing with sternal retractions," "Weak cry and cough," "Alert facies," and "Normal sensation and intellect." "Restrictive lung disease is the most serious complication of SMA" (p. 1321).
q_1383.trap: (B) is the assumption an alert but profoundly weak infant invites, and the source names normal intellect explicitly, which is why "verbal, tactile, and auditory stimulation are important aspects of developmental care" (p. 1321). (D) inverts the reflex finding, which is what places the lesion at the anterior horn cell rather than above it.

q_1384.topic: spinal cord injury levels and acute management
q_1384.subtopic: at the scene and on arrival
q_1384.stem: An adolescent is thrown from a bicycle and a spinal cord injury is suspected. What is correct about the initial management?
options: Open the airway with a jaw thrust, and maintain spinal immobilization until injury has been ruled out by a thorough neurologic assessment
Open the airway with a head tilt–chin lift, and release immobilization once the child can move the fingers
Defer airway management until imaging is complete
Release immobilization once the initial neurologic examination is normal
q_1384.rationale: "The initial management of the child with a suspected SCI should begin with an assessment of the ABCs: airway, breathing, and circulation. The airway should be opened using the jaw-thrust technique to minimize damage to the cervical spine" (pp. 1331–1332). "In the emergency department, spinal immobilization should be maintained until a thorough neurologic assessment is completed and spinal cord injury is ruled out" (p. 1332).
q_1384.trap: (D) is the tempting option because a normal examination feels like an answer, and it is not one here: "25% to 50% of children with SCI will have a delay in the onset of neurologic abnormalities ranging from 30 minutes to 4 days" (p. 1330). (B) opens the airway with the maneuver that moves the cervical spine.

q_1385.topic: spinal cord injury levels and acute management
q_1385.subtopic: at the scene and on arrival
q_1385.stem: An adolescent sustains a complete spinal cord injury at C6. What should the nurse expect regarding ventilation?
options: The child is unlikely to be ventilator dependent, since the diaphragm is innervated at C5, but respiratory reserve is reduced
The child will require continuous mechanical ventilation
Respiratory function will be entirely normal
A tracheostomy will be required immediately
q_1385.rationale: Table 34.1 places the diaphragm at C5, and the narrative states the boundary twice: "The child with a high-level cervical injury (C3 and above) requires continuous ventilatory assistance," and "Children with lesions below the C4 level are seldom ventilator dependent, but pulmonary vital capacity is significantly reduced" (p. 1334). At C5 the table records "Abdominal respiration" with "Poor respiratory reserve" (p. 1327).
q_1385.trap: (C) overshoots in the other direction, because the same sentence that spares this child the ventilator also says vital capacity is significantly reduced. (B) applies the high-cervical rule to a level well below it.

q_1386.topic: spinal cord injury levels and acute management
q_1386.stem: A rehabilitation nurse is setting goals for two adolescents with complete injuries, one at C6 and one at C7. Which statement is accurate?
options: The C7 injury gains triceps function and can lift body weight, allowing almost complete independence within the limits of a wheelchair
Both will require an attendant for all transfers
The C6 injury will allow independent ambulation with braces
Neither will achieve functional use of the upper extremities
q_1386.rationale: At C7 the "Triceps and finger flexion and extensor muscle" are innervated, the child is "able to lift body weight," and the goal is "Almost complete independence within limitations of wheelchair," including rolling over in bed, sitting up in bed, and eating independently. At C6 there is wrist extension and good elbow flexion, and the child is "Able to assist in dressing and transfer" (p. 1327).
q_1386.trap: (C) borrows an ambulation goal from a far lower level, since it is T10 to L2 that achieves "Ambulation with bilateral long braces using four-point or swing-through crutch gait." (B) understates C7 and overstates the attendant requirement, which belongs at C5.

q_1387.topic: spinal cord injury levels and acute management
q_1387.stem: A child admitted with a new thoracic spinal cord injury has flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes below the lesion. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Spinal shock, in which flaccidity is later replaced by spinal reflex activity and increasing spasticity
A permanent lower motor neuron pattern that will not change
Autonomic dysreflexia
An incomplete injury, since reflexes are absent
q_1387.rationale: Spinal shock syndrome produces "flaccid paralysis below the level of the damage … caused by the sudden disruption of central and autonomic pathways," with "the absence of reflexes at or below the cord lesion, with flaccidity or limpness of the involved muscles, loss of sensation and motor function, and autonomic dysfunction" (p. 1330). "Most children with an SCI experience some spinal shock," and afterward "flaccid paralysis is replaced by spinal reflex activity and increasing spasticity" (p. 1331).
q_1387.trap: (C) names a complication that arrives later, once reflex activity returns, "especially when the lesions are above the midthoracic level" (p. 1331) — it cannot be present while the child is areflexic. (B) reads an acute, temporary phase as the final picture, which is the timing error this section is built on.

q_1388.topic: autonomic dysreflexia and long-term spinal cord injury care
q_1388.stem: A 14-year-old with a cervical spinal cord injury is on a standing table in physical therapy and becomes flushed and diaphoretic with a pounding headache. Blood pressure is rising and the heart rate is 50. What should the nurse do first?
options: Palpate the bladder for distention
Lower the child to a supine position and elevate the legs
Administer the ordered analgesic for the headache
End the therapy session and return the child to bed
q_1388.rationale: This is autonomic dysreflexia, whose signs are "a flushing face, sweating forehead, pupillary constriction, marked hypertension, headache, and bradycardia" (p. 1331). The stated sequence is that "vital signs, including blood pressure, are taken while the bladder is checked for distention (the usual precipitating cause). The bladder is drained slowly; if this does not relieve symptoms, any tight clothing is loosened, and the bowel is checked for the pressure of impacted feces" (p. 1335).
q_1388.trap: (B) treats this as orthostatic intolerance, which the chapter says to rule out quickly but which produces a drop in blood pressure and lightheadedness rather than a spike with headache and sweating (p. 1336). (C) relieves the symptom and abandons the search for the trigger, and "It can be a catastrophic event unless the irritation is relieved" (p. 1331). This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 2.

q_1389.topic: autonomic dysreflexia and long-term spinal cord injury care
q_1389.stem: Two children with spinal cord injury are assessed. One has hypertension with bradycardia; the other has hypotension with bradycardia and peripheral vasodilation. How should the nurse interpret these?
options: The first has autonomic dysreflexia and the second has neurogenic shock
Both have autonomic dysreflexia
The first has neurogenic shock and the second has autonomic dysreflexia
Bradycardia excludes both diagnoses
q_1389.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia produces "marked hypertension, headache" with bradycardia (p. 1331), while "Neurogenic shock consists of hypotension, bradycardia, and vasodilation. Inotropic medications may be required to maintain adequate perfusion" (p. 1334).
q_1389.trap: (C) is the mirror error, and bradycardia is what makes it available, since it appears in both pictures. The blood pressure is the only finding that separates them, and it sends the treatment in opposite directions.

q_1390.topic: autonomic dysreflexia and long-term spinal cord injury care
q_1390.stem: Which factors can precipitate autonomic dysreflexia in a child with a spinal cord injury? Select all that apply.
options: A full bladder
Fecal impaction
Tight clothing
A pressure ulcer
A meal high in sodium
q_1390.rationale: The trigger is "visceral distention or irritation, particularly of the bowel or bladder," and "The precipitating stimulus may be merely a full bladder or rectum" (p. 1331). The fuller list adds "bowel impaction and abdominal distention, pressure ulcers, tight clothing, burns, DVT, menses, trauma, fractures, pregnancy, labor, surgery or invasive procedures, any painful stimulus, and hyperthermia" (pp. 1335–1336).
q_1390.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it borrows a cardiovascular association that does not belong here. The unifying principle is a noxious or distending stimulus below the level of the lesion that the child cannot feel, which is exactly why the assessment starts at the bladder and moves to the bowel.

q_1391.topic: autonomic dysreflexia and long-term spinal cord injury care
q_1391.stem: An adolescent with a lumbar-level spinal cord injury asks why the team wants him upright in braces part of each day when a wheelchair is easier. What is the best response?
options: Being weight bearing at least part of the time minimizes the risk of osteoporosis and hypercalcemia
Braces will restore normal walking
Wheelchair use should be avoided entirely
Bracing requires less energy than wheelchair mobility
q_1391.rationale: "It is especially vital that children with lumbar levels of injury be taught to walk functionally so that they are weight bearing at least part of the time; this minimizes the risk of osteoporosis and hypercalcemia" (p. 1331).
q_1391.trap: (D) reverses the comparison the chapter gives: "The energy required in walking with crutches and braces is two to four times greater than that required for normal walking," while "Wheelchair mobility has the advantages of requiring no more energy than normal walking" (p. 1336). That is also why (C) fails — the wheelchair is the efficient option rather than a concession, and the standing time is prescribed for the bones, not for getting anywhere.

q_1392.topic: duchenne muscular dystrophy and juvenile dermatomyositis
q_1392.stem: Which statements accurately describe Duchenne muscular dystrophy? Select all that apply.
options: The absence of dystrophin leads to muscle fiber degeneration
Onset is usually between 3 and 5 years of age
Affected boys have a waddling gait and lordosis and fall frequently
Ambulation usually becomes impossible by about 12 years of age
Cognitive and intellectual impairment is rare
q_1392.rationale: "The absence of dystrophin leads to a number of problems in muscle, including muscle fiber degeneration" (p. 1339). Box 34.13 gives "Early onset, usually between 3 and 5 years of age" and "Loss of independent ambulation by 9–12 years of age," and the clinical course states that "affected boys have a waddling gait and lordosis, fall frequently" and "Ambulation usually becomes impossible by 12 years of age" (p. 1340).
q_1392.trap: (E) is the wrong option and it reverses a finding the chapter states plainly: "Mild to moderate mental impairment is commonly associated with MD. The mean intelligence quotient (IQ) is approximately 20 points below normal, and frank mental deficit is present in 20% to 30% of these children" (p. 1340). This is the chapter's own NCLEX question 5.

q_1393.topic: duchenne muscular dystrophy and juvenile dermatomyositis
q_1393.stem: The parents of a 7-year-old with Duchenne muscular dystrophy point out his large, firm calves and ask whether extra effort and exercise could halt the disease. How should the nurse respond?
options: The enlarged calves are fatty infiltration rather than strength, and effort cannot stop the progression, although staying as active as possible delays wheelchair dependence
The large calves show preserved muscle, so strengthening exercises can reverse the weakness
Rest is the priority, and activity should be limited
Nothing affects the timing of wheelchair dependence
q_1393.rationale: "Muscles, especially in the calves, thighs, and upper arms, become enlarged from fatty infiltration and feel unusually firm or woody on palpation" (p. 1340). The misconception is named in the source: "Many parents erroneously believe that by exerting sufficient effort, the child can overcome the weakness and prevent progression of the disease process" (p. 1342). And activity still matters: "In general, children who remain as active as possible are able to avoid wheelchair confinement for a longer time" (p. 1341).
q_1393.trap: (C) is the intuitive response to a wasting disease and it accelerates the problem, since physical therapy "should begin if bed rest extends beyond a few days" and the daily goal for a well child with moderate disability is "at least 3 hours of ambulation." (D) discards the one variable the family can still influence.

q_1394.topic: duchenne muscular dystrophy and juvenile dermatomyositis
q_1394.stem: A 7-year-old girl has proximal symmetric muscle weakness, a violet discoloration of the eyelids, and raised lesions over the knuckles and knees, with elevated muscle enzymes. Which nursing priorities apply?
options: Ensuring an adequate airway because of the risk of aspiration pneumonia, and teaching daily sunscreen use with adequate calcium and vitamin D
Withholding all physical therapy until the rash resolves
Avoiding sun exposure only during disease flares
Anticipating distal muscle weakness as the earliest finding
q_1394.rationale: Juvenile dermatomyositis presents with "bilateral symmetric proximal weakness; a characteristic heliotropic rash of the eyelids; Gottron papules on the knuckles, knees, and elbows," and elevated serum enzymes (p. 1338). "A common problem in JDM is aspiration pneumonia, and measures should be taken to ensure the child has an adequate airway at all times." "All children with JDM should use a sunscreen to protect against ultraviolet A and B rays. Vitamin D and adequate dietary intake of calcium are also recommended."
q_1394.trap: (B) withholds the therapy the chapter calls essential: "Physical therapy is essential to prevent contracture deformity and to rebuild muscle strength," and "Meticulous skin care is an important nursing consideration." (D) inverts the pattern, since "Distal muscle strength and reflex responses remain unaffected" while the proximal limb and trunk muscles are the ones that weaken.
